In the third incarnation, they became Dantavakra and Shishupal.

Since Lakshmiji wished to see the leela, she came as the Earth; when Hiranyaksha carried her off, the Sanakadik came in the form of Prahlad, and Bhagwan came in the forms of Varaha and Narsingh. In the second incarnation, when they came as Ravana and Kumbhakarna, the Sanakadik came as Vibhishan, Lakshmiji came in the form of Sita, and Bhagwan came in the form of Ram. In the third incarnation, when they came as Dantavakra and Shishupal, Lakshmiji came in the form of Rukmini; when Shishupal set about abducting Rukmini, Bhagwan came in the form of Krishna, and the Sanakadik came in the form of Bhishma. In this way Bhagwan showed his grace toward Lakshmi, and the fault of the Sanakadik...

...had been averted. But the devotees of God do not choose any of the four kinds of liberation (mukti), because liberation itself is as troublesome as punishment — it belongs to the created realm of Omkar, so that whoever attains any of these four liberations must, when the age of dissolution ends and God recreates the universe anew, come back once more into worldly existence. For this reason liberation has been likened to a dark well, because liberated souls remain bound within the very bondage of that liberation. Therefore it is said in Krishnadas's Parichari:

_Jaiso narak taisi e mukti, jiv abujh jaane nahi bhakti_ (Just as hell is full of suffering, so is this liberation of the Omkar realm; but a soul without such understanding does not know the way — that of loving devotion — to escape it.)

By worshipping God out of enmity, one may still receive liberation from Him, but it is of the terrible, extremely harsh kind called sayujya (absorption into His form). A sakhi tells how the Lord gave Shishupal this harsh liberation of dominion:

_So gali Shishupal dei, chakra kaayo tab shish, te ja samaano aapman, so jan Jivanke is_ (Shishupal hurled a hundred abuses at the Lord, yet [Krishna] kept count of them one by one and did not hold it against him as a disgrace; only when the hundred was complete did the discus take his head — and that very soul was merged into the Lord Himself. Such is the recompense the Lord gives Jivanji's people.)

When Shishupal had given Lord Krishna a hundred abuses, the Lord cut off his head with the Sudarshan discus, and merged the radiance of Shishupal's soul into that very form which is dear to Jivanji as his object of worship, granting him sayujya liberation.

There are four kinds of liberation, and their chief qualities are: (1) salokya — the devotion by which God places the soul in His own abode; (2) sarupya — the second, by which liberation makes the soul like unto God; (3) samipya, the third, by which He keeps the soul within His own sight, that is, near Himself; (4) sayujya, the fourth, in which He merges the soul into His own being. Of these four, sayujya liberation is by far the most terrible — He grants it only to His very greatest enemy. Whoever attains this liberation cannot come out of it for crores upon crores of ages. The Lord told the gatekeepers [Jaya and Vijaya] that they could attain liberation after seven births, but they refused it. Without taking human birth, one cannot attain devotion to Vasudev, that is, Vishnu-bhakti.

Those who do not practise devotion to Vishnu are reckoned as demon-like, and it is they who must undergo this harsh liberation. Brahmins who cling to the worship etc. of Shiva-devotion and other deities, engaging in such ritual observances — regarding the Brahmins among them who are wicked, Prabhudatt Brahmachari wrote, addressing the two wrathful Brahmins whom Chaitanya Mahaprabhu had subdued:

In the time of Mahaprabhu Gaurangdev too, two cruel, base-acting young Brahmins named Jagai and Madhai (Jagannath and Madhav) lived in Navadwip. _Rakshasah kalim ashritya jayate brahmayonishu_ (in the age of Kali, demons will be born on earth in the form of Brahmins). Direct proof of this scriptural statement is seen in the lives of these two brothers, Jagai and Madhai. (Haji no. 413, p.491.)

Even Liberation herself longs to attain liberation and become devotion; therefore it is said:

_Mukti kahat Gopaalso, meri mukti karaay, Vrajraj udi mastak chadhe, mukti mukt ho jaay_ (Liberation herself says to Lord Krishna: O Lord, grant me liberation too — let me come to Vrindavan. If even the dust of Vrindavan should rise and settle upon my head, then I, Liberation, shall myself become liberated and blessed — Liberation shall become Devotion.)

There is a sakhi stating that human birth is favourable for devotion to Vishnu:

_Mata hamare Janki, pita hamare Ram, jug jug maagu Jivna, charan kal vishram_ ||1|| (Jivandasji Maharaj says: my mother is Sita and my father is Ram; age after age, forever, I ask only to remain sheltered at Your lotus feet, in Your abode.)

_Mata pita hamare Jivna, sadhu sadguru Ram, aur kachhu maagu nahi, do charan kamal nijdham_ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: my mother and father are the saint and the true guru, and Ram — the saint and true guru are my mother, Ram is my father. Beyond this I ask nothing more; only place me at Your feet and grant me devotion to Your own name.)

_Pita hamara Ramji, mata satvanti naar, jug jug maagu Jivna, ghar manav avatar_ ||3|| (Jivandasji Maharaj says: my father is Ram and my mother is the chaste Sita. Age after age I ask only this — that You take human incarnation and grant me human birth, so that I may render You devotion.)

_Kabir mansa janam durlabh hai, dehi na varamvaar, tarvar je fal jhad pade, so bahorin laage daar_ ||4|| (Das Kabirji says: human birth is exceedingly rare to attain; the body is not given again and again. As a fruit that falls from a tree cannot attach itself to the branch once more,)

so if we waste this human birth in vain, it is exceedingly hard to obtain it again. Therefore, having taken this human birth, one should strive to attain devotion and make the birth fruitful. There is a sakhi comparing this to the tree and its fruit.

_Guru taruvar Govind jal, sevak fal samaan, taavdit laaga rahe, to nipaje niravaan_ ||1|| (The guru is like the tree, and the formless, unmanifest Lord is like the water; the disciple-devotee is like the fruit. If that fruit remains attached, by the stalk of devotion, to the tree that is the true guru — that is, if he keeps practising devotion — he will surely attain deliverance.)

Without accepting a guru, one who worships God directly cannot receive God's grace — just as a fruit draws nourishment such as water through the tree, but if that same fruit falls straight into the water, it can draw no nourishment from it. Only while attached to the tree does it receive nourishment; likewise, without a guru, Govind cannot be attained.

_Guru bemukh jo Hari bhaje, taaka kaaj na hoy, uncha chadhi nicha gire, paai taaka kaaj ja khoy_ (If one turns away from the guru and worships the Lord without him, his purpose is not accomplished; like one who climbs high and then falls low, whatever he had gained he loses along with his purpose.)

If one goes against the guru and worships God without a guru, his welfare is not accomplished — just as, after reaching a high state, if one falls into a low one, then whatever high standing had been gained becomes entirely useless.

_Aadha mata sadhka, jahan Parbrahmki aash, pura mata tahan Jivna, jahan sadguru shabda vishwas_ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: if a seeker practises worship by placing his trust directly on devotion to the Supreme Brahman alone, his practice is incomplete; but if he practises devotion with faith in the true guru's teaching, that devotion is whole and complete.)

_Aadha mata kon kaamka, jo paave Vaikunthko dhaam, taathe bhagati bhali Jivna, kabahu sant sangat vishram_ (What use is an incomplete practice, even if it brings only the attainment of the abode of Vaikuntha alone? Better than that — [Jivandasji Maharaj says] — is devotion obtained through the true guru, for then one may also, from time to time, find the joy of the company of saints.)

_Guru bin mala ferate, guru bin dharta dhyan, guru bin sab nishphal gaya, puchho Ved Puran_ (Whether one tells the rosary in devotion without having taken a guru, or meditates upon God without a guru, whatever one does without a guru goes to waste — you may seek the opinion of the Vedas and Puranas on this too, and they will give you the very same verdict.)

_Kabir bichhadanmein dukh hai, jaise fal aur daal, uhaanse bichhada so gir pada, so tarat hi pakde haal_ (Das Kabirji says: there is great suffering in separation, like the suffering between a fruit and its branch — once parted from the branch it falls to the ground, and death seizes it at once.)

_Fal tuti jalmein pada, Khoji na miri pyaas, guru taji Govind bhaje, taahi narak nivaas_ (Khojiji says: a fruit that breaks off and falls into water cannot draw nourishment from that water, and its thirst is not quenched; likewise, one who abandons the guru and worships Govind must dwell in hell.)

_Mathethi guru utre, shabda bemukh hoy, Khoji haal fanfedsi, raakha na sake hoy_ (Khojiji says: if the guru is cast off from over your head and you turn your face from his teaching, Death will search you out and seize you however it pleases, and no one will be able to save you.)

_Durlabh deho manushi, taame durlabh gurugyan, gyani durlabh bhakti hai, durlabh Hari rasapan_ (Gnaniji Maharaj says: human birth is rare to attain, and rarer still within it is the guru's teaching; devotion too is rare even for the wise to obtain, and rarest of all is to drink the nectar of the Lord's loving devotion.)

Speaking of the tree and the fruit, it is said in the Samagam that if a soul, on account of the fault of the fruit and the tree having become separated, takes birth again, it may still obtain devotion to Vishnu; but if it desires devotion out of enmity, how can it attain the highest abode? Such a one attains only the way of Death.

The Testimony of Narsinh Mehta Concerning Devotion to Vishnu

Narsinh Mehta's Witness Among the Vaishnavs of Maryada

Sanaka and the other sages are themselves a form of Kaal (Death); so, although devotion may arise through their company, they become enemies of that very devotion. Jivanji Maharaj has said, in the Das Ang:

_Ahan mite nahin Jivna, Sanakadikso saadh, Brahmaadi rach pach mue, ahan badi upaadh_ ||3|| (Jivandasji says: even in seekers as great as Sanaka and his brothers, the ego could not be erased; likewise Brahma and other gods, though such great beings, became engrossed in this very ego of "I am Brahman" and were destroyed by it. This ego, then, is indeed a most terrible calamity.)

It is said:

_Maina na mai na kahi, daam lage das vees, bakrine mai mai kahin, turat kataaya sheesh_ (The myna made the sound "I am not, I am not," and so its worth came to be only ten or twenty rupees; but the goat made the sound "I, I," and so its head had to be cut off at once.)

Ego is the greatest and hardest of all obstacles; even Sanaka and his brothers could not rid themselves of it. Though he preserved a five-year-old's body through mastery of the yogic power of levitation, his temperament was not truly innocent like a child's — he was in fact deeply learned, a man of knowledge; and "jnaanam bharah kriyaam vinaa" — knowledge without practice is a mere burden; the one who speaks but does not act, his words are useless. Narsinh Mehta's testimony is presented in this chapter to show this. The Lord has kept gatekeepers such as Jaya and Vijaya; Sanaka and his brothers won a victory over their bodies, but such gatekeepers are themselves the very manifestation of ego, and whoever wins a victory in that manner cannot help but develop ego. Therefore the company of those who breed such ego is useless. Narsinh Mehta's testimony tells us whose company one should keep to attain welfare — it must be the company of the Lord's devotee-saints alone, for only they can do us good. His hymn on this is presented here.

(Raag Prabhati Sindhudo)

_Tara dasna dasni nitya sangat vina, bhrashht thay Bhudhara man maru; dushtni sangate dushta drushte kari, shravan kirtan nav thay taru; jire vish paane pela durijan dauhela, vish paan karta tan tej hanse; tuj thaki vegalo teni sangat kare, janam kotitana sukrat harse; jire amritni upama sadhune nav ghate, Rahuni dushhtata nav gai jehene; Prahlade Naradni garbh sangat kari, vash kidha Vaikunthanath tehene; jire char muktitani jugat hai jugati, te mahe tahera nav re ratve; behu kar jodine Narsaiyo vinave, janamo janam tari bhaktiyache_ (O Bhudhar! Without constant company with the servants of Your servants, my mind grows corrupted and impure. From the company of the wicked, seeing with wicked eyes, my ear and my tongue can no longer perform Your hearing and singing of praise. Those base people partake of the poison [of sensual pleasure and intoxication], and by such indulgence their spiritual radiance is destroyed; whoever keeps company with such a person, one far removed from You, loses the merit earned across hundreds of millions of births. Even the comparison to nectar does not suit the saints — it is too small a praise for them — for even Rahu, who once drank nectar itself, never lost his base and wicked nature; yet Prahlad, who kept company with Narada while still in the womb, thereby brought the Lord of Vaikuntha under his sway. As for the various means of attaining the four kinds of liberation, Your devotees have no interest in them at all. With both hands joined, Narsaiyo humbly entreats You: birth after birth, I beg only for Your devotion.)

To say with the mouth "I am a servant of Your servants" is easy, but to embody it in conduct is difficult. Kabir says:

_Kabir das kahaavat sukh hai, mai daasanka daas, ab to sabthe ehi bhali, je paanv talki ghaas_ (Das Kabirji says: it is a pleasant thing merely to say with the mouth, "I am the servant of Your servants." But now, of everything, the best is this — to become like the grass trampled beneath the feet.)

Das Kabirji says: to say with the mouth that one is even a servant of Your servants is easy; but only when the true test of becoming a real devotee arrives — the suffering of being crushed underfoot like grass — does one understand how difficult it truly is.

_Kaheni nishri khaand hai, raheni latta loh, kaheni kahe ne raheni rahe, aisa virla kau_ (To speak with the mouth is sweet as pure sugar, but to live it out in conduct is as hard as heated iron; one who speaks as he lives and lives as he speaks — such a sincere person is rare indeed.)

In the Mahabharat, the words of Virat and Vidur concerning the disposition of a servant are found in the Pandav Gita, verse 21:

_Vasudevasya ye bhaktah shaantastadgatchetasah, tesham daasasya daasoham bhaveyam janmajanmani_ ||21|| (May I, birth after birth, become the servant of the servants of those devotees of Lord Vasudev who are peaceful, and whose minds and hearts are wholly absorbed in Him.)

In the Adi Puran it is said:

_Ye me bhaktajanah Partha, na te janah [bhaktah], madbhaktaanaam cha ye bhaktaste me bhaktaastama mataah_ (The Lord tells Arjun: O Partha! Those who are devoted to Me alone are not, in the fullest sense, [true] devotees. The very best devotees are those who are devoted to My own devotees.)

In the Vishnu Puran it is said:

_Archditva tu Govind tadiyaan archayatu yah, na sa bhagvato gneyah kevalam dambhikah smritah. (Tasmaan sarvaprayatnena vaishnavaan pujayet sada.)_ (One who worships the Lord but does not also worship the Lord's devotees, the Vaishnavs, should not be considered a true devotee — he is to be regarded only as a hypocrite. Therefore one should always strive, in every way, to worship the Vaishnavs [together with the Lord]; for God is deeply pleased above all by the worship offered to His devotees.)

Vritrasur prays to the Lord — Bhagavat, Skandh 6, Adhyay 11:

_Aham Hare tava paadaikamula daasaanudaaso bhavitaasmi bhuyah, manah smaretaasupateh gunaanste, grunaante, gruneeta vaakkarma karotu kaamah_ ||24|| (O Hari! A soul ought to have no desire of any kind, yet I do have one desire — that I may become, again and again, a servant of the servants of those who take shelter solely at Your lotus feet. May my mind ever remember Your virtues, O Lord of my life-breath; may my speech sing Your praises; and may my body render You service — grant me this grace.)

Speaking of the Vaishnavs of maryada in the age of Kali, it is said in the Samagam, verse 51:

_Naasti Vishnoh param saadhyam, naasti Vishnoh param padam, naasti Vishnoh param dhyaanam, naasti muktistva-avaishnave_ ||51|| (There is no goal higher than Vishnu; there is no higher station than Vishnu; there is no higher object of meditation than Vishnu; and the Vaishnavs seek no liberation apart from this.)

Thus the Vaishnavs have no need to worship any deity apart from Vishnu — so why should they worship other gods? Since Vishnu grants no higher station to seek, why should they strive after any other? If they come to regard Vasudev and other gods as one and the same, they will be reckoned non-devotees and will not attain the fruit of liberation and deliverance. In the following verse it is likewise said:

_Naasti Vishnoh param sthaanam, naasti Vishnoh param tapah, naasti Vishnoh param gnaanam naasti, Vishnoh param dhanam_ ||52|| (There is no place higher than Vishnu; there is no austerity higher than Vishnu; there is no knowledge higher than Vishnu; there is no wealth higher than Vishnu.)

The Vaishnavs have already obtained the station that is Vasudev Himself, so why should they go to any other place? They already possess the austerity that is devotion to Vasudev, so what use would any other austerity be to them? They already possess the knowledge that is Vasudev, so why should they put into practice any other, ritual-based knowledge? If they were to act according to such ritual knowledge, they would be called non-Vaishnavs. In support of the devotion to Vishnu stated in verses 51 and 52 of the Samagam, those who earlier copied the Samagam have taken note of verses 26 and 29 of the Bhagavat, Skandh 1, Adhyay 2:

_Mumukshavo ghorroopaan hitva bhootapateenath, Naaraayanakalauh shaanta bhajanti hyanasuchavah_ ||26|| (Those who wish to cross this ocean of worldly existence, though they harbour ill will toward none, do not worship Bhairav and other deities of terrible form belonging to tamas and rajas; instead they worship Lord Narayan and His incarnations of sattva.)

_Vasudevaparam gnaanam Vasudevaparam tapah, Vasudevaparo dharmo Vasudevapara gatih_ ||29|| (The essential aim and fulfilment of every kind of knowledge, austerity, and spiritual path lies solely in yoking human beings to Lord Shri Krishna.)

_Brahma Vishnu Mahesh-aadyaa yasyaamsha lokasaadhakaah, tam Aadidevam Shri Ramam vishuddham paramam bhajet_ (Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesh, who assist the world, are themselves but portions of that very Ram; it is He, the primordial and purest Lord, Shri Ram, whom the seeker of liberation should worship.)

In the Padma Puran too a similar shloka occurs:

_Ramaanna-kti paro devo Ramaannaasti param vratam, nahi Ramaat paro yogo nahi Ramaat param makhah_ (There is no deity greater than Ram; there is no vow greater than Ram; there is no path of yoga greater than Ram; and there is no sacrifice greater than Ram.)

_Vaishnavaah paramo dharmo vaishnavaah paramam tapah, vaishnavaah paramo-aaraadhyo vaishnavaah paramam guruh_ (To be a Vaishnav is itself the highest religion; being a Vaishnav is the highest object of worship; and a Vaishnav is himself the highest guru.)

For a devotee of Vishnu, no mantra, scripture or sacrificial rite is at all necessary — this is shown in verse 53:

_Kim tasya bahubhir mantraih shastraiva bahuvistaraih, vajapeya sahasraischa bhaktau rijyo Janardanah_ ||53|| (For every devotee, what use are many mantras? What use are vast scriptures? And what use are even a thousand Vajapeya sacrifices? Vishnu can be attained by devotees alone.)

Numerous scriptures, Puranas or studies are of no need at all to the Vaishnavs, or indeed to anyone. If one lets go of devotion to Vasudev and takes up instead whatever scriptural rites, Puranic observances or forms of worship, none of it is of any use. In the age of Kali, it is Vasudev Himself who serves His Vaishnavs; that is why He is called by the names Govindji and Janardan.

The Vajapeya sacrifice — in this sacrifice, grain and ghee are meant to be consumed. In earlier times it was performed on occasions of celebrating a victory; later it came to be performed for the coronation of kings or for religious consecration. Formerly, Brahmins and Kshatriyas performed it in order to gain prosperity. Wheat and liquor are used in this sacrifice, and seventeen of each required item are used. As gifts, seventeen elephants or seventeen horses, seventeen nishka (gold coins or a gold necklace), seventeen maidservants, one thousand seven hundred cows, and seventeen chariots must be given; the prince would shoot seventeen arrows. It is said that Brahma produced this sacrifice from his upward-facing mouth. It is a shrauta sacrifice which, according to the Shatapath Brahman, only a Brahmin or Kshatriya may perform; this sacrifice is held superior to the Rajasuya. A necessary part of it is a chariot race in which the performer of the sacrifice must be the victor. In Hillebrandt's view this resembles the Olympic games, though it appears to have developed out of chariot racing; Oldenberg's view seems more fitting — that for Brahmins this sacrifice was a preliminary rite before assuming the priesthood, and for kings, a preliminary rite before coronation. (Najar no. 1, p.133.)

The Muktishastra, p.47, states that the Veda does not prescribe violence. There is a sacrifice called Vajapeya in which twenty-seven animals are killed, and in the Ashvamedh two hundred sixty animals are killed, and their flesh is eaten by all — the Brahmins, the performer of the sacrifice, and the rest of the people.

In verse 53, the word Janardan has been used for God, thereby describing God as the one who serves His Vaishnavs; emphasis has been placed on this word.

Janardan — one who stirs up and agitates the wicked, who causes upheaval among people, or the destroyer of Maya: such is Shri Krishna.

_Janaan-arda yato yasmaat pralayo mahati dvikha, atah samprochyate Vede Janaardana iti Prabhuh_ ||18|| (O Naradji! At the time of the great dissolution, the Lord destroys the gross bodies of all beings and withdraws them into His own being; for this reason His name in the Vedas is Janardan.)

_Janaardanam bhutapatim jagadguru smaran manushyah satatam mahaamune, duhkhaani sarvaanyapahanti saadhayatya sheshakaaryaani cha yaanyabhipsate_ (O great sage! By constantly remembering Janardan, Lord of all beings and guru of the universe, a human being removes all his sufferings and accomplishes every undertaking that he desires.)

Janardan is the 126th name in the Vishnu Sahasranam; on it Shankaracharya has written this commentary:

_Janaan durjanaan adhayita hinasti Sanakadeen gamayateeti va Janaardanah. Janaih purushaarthamabhyudaya-nihshreyasa-lakshanam yaachyate iti Janaardanah_ (He is called Janardan because He crushes and destroys the wicked, or because He grants Sanaka and his brothers passage [to blissful states]; or because His devotees beg of Him the highest human goal, marked by both worldly prosperity and the supreme good — for this too He is Janardan. Because He also destroys the mockery of the wicked, God's name is Janardan.)

Devotees worship only the Lord; they need no other ritual observance, Vedic path, or path of yoga. Vishwamitra states this in the Pandav Gita, verse 43:

_Kim taasya daanaih kim tapobhih kimadhvaraih, yo nityam dhyaayate daivam Naaraayanam ananyadheeh_ ||43|| (For that person who, with an undivided mind fixed on nothing else, ceaselessly meditates upon divine Narayan, what need has he of charity, pilgrimage, austerity, sacrifice, and all such other means?)

Devotional remembrance and kirtan of the Lord are declared the very highest, as it is said:

_Gnaanaat parataram dhyaanam, dhyaanaat parataram japah, japaat parataram gaanam, gaanaat parataram nahi_ (Meditation is higher than mere knowledge; recitation is higher still than meditation; and singing the Lord's praise is higher even than recitation — nothing at all surpasses that singing.)

Therefore it is said in the Samagam, verse 54:

_Tirtham japastapo daanam vratam yagnastato-anyakam, Vasudevah param naam sarve vedyah pravartakaah_ ||54|| (Pilgrimage, recitation, austerity, charity, vows, sacrifice, or anything else whatsoever — all of it is Vasudev Himself; all the Vedas are but the proclaimers of that supreme name.)

In keeping with this 54th verse, it is likewise said in the Bhagavat, Skandh 1, Adhyay 2, verse 28:

_Vasudevapara Veda vasudevaparaah makhaah, Vasudevapara gnaanam Vasudevaparaah kriyaah_ ||28|| (The fulfilment of the Vedas, of all sacrifices, of all knowledge, and of every action lies solely in making people devoted to Lord Shri Krishna.)

In the commentary on this 54th verse, the Samagam states that even beyond crores of pilgrimages, crores of vows, crores of sacrifices, crores of acts of charity, and crores of austerities, the glory of the name of Vasudev is greater still.

Adhyaruji Maharaj says: without devotion to Vishnu, whatever else one looks upon is like reaching one's hand into deep darkness — one falls blindly into a pit. The ultimate aim of the Vedas and all such things is, in the end, only the path of devotion; hence Adhyaruji says:

_Jire amurat raja dhyaarue, ane roop arpe jaano de, ved maarag anusaro, bhakti bhaav man aano de_ (Worship that formless King in meditation, and know too that He offers form [that His true nature is both formless and with form]; follow the path of the Vedas, but bring devotional feeling into your mind.)

That reality of God which has no manifest form at all — such a God should be worshipped, knowing His nature to be formless; yet whether formless or with form, His true being exists in every mode. So, following the path of the Vedas — that is, the path of devotion to the highest reality — one should act; hold this thought in mind, for that alone is true devotion to God.

There is one flaw in the Vedas: through indirect, laudatory language they have tried to steer people toward worship performed with a desire for reward. Therefore, in the Gita, chapter 2, verse 42, it is said that from such flowery Vedic speech, bondage through action is incurred, because the Veda is composed of the three gunas; and so, in chapter 2, verse 45, Krishna tells Arjun, _nistraigunyo bhavaarjuna_ — that is, He instructs him to become free of the three gunas. With reference to this, Adhyaruji says that in following the path of the Vedas, the Veda, through ritual religion, has tried to make people forget devotion to Raghupati. Jivanji has stated this in Gurudev Ang, sakhi 13:

_Ola jhola Jivna, je sadguru diya bataay, karm dharmma raghupati, je vede dharyo chhapaay_ ||13|| (Jivandasji Maharaj says: so that one is not caught unaware and dragged about, the true guru has shown that within ritual religion the Veda has hidden and concealed devotion to Raghupati.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: so that we do not become entangled in the wandering maze of ritual religion and its ceremonies, the true guru — even while the Veda points toward ritual observance — has exposed how the Veda thereby threw a veil over devotion to Ram; this exposes the Veda's cleverness.

Before devotion to Ram and Krishna, every other kind of worship is like a slave, like a servant, to this devotion. In verse 55, showing the glory of devotion to Krishna, a shloka from the Mahabharat is cited:

_Ekopi Krishnasya kritapranaamo dashaashvamedhaavabhrithena tulyah, dashaashvedhi punaroti janma Krishnaapranaami na punarbhaavaaya_ ||13|| (Subhadra says: a single bow of obeisance offered to Lord Krishna equals the completion of ten Ashvamedh sacrifices. One who performs ten Ashvamedh sacrifices is born again, whereas one who bows to Krishna is not born again.)

This shloka was spoken by Bhishma Pitamaha to Yudhishthir in the Mahabharat, Shantiparva 47.91, describing the glory of bowing to God; a similar shloka occurs in the Shrimad Bhagavat also:

_Naam sankirtanam yasya sarvapaap pranaashanam, pranaamo dukh samanastam, namaami Hari padam_ (I bow at the feet of that Lord, the singing of whose name destroys all sin, and bowing to whom removes all sorrow.)

_Durgasansaarakaantaaraa kupaare vipradhaavayaam, ekah Krishne namaskaaro mukya taantaarayishyati_ (For human beings who run about trying to save themselves in this ocean-forest of worldly existence, so difficult to cross, a single act of obeisance offered to Lord Krishna is itself the means of protection — through liberation, it carries him across this forest of worldly existence.)

There are many kinds of obeisance to God. Among them, this shows how the dandavat, that is, the full prostration (sashtang) obeisance, is performed:

_Urasaa, shirasaa, drishtyaa, manasaa vachasaa tathaa, padabhyaam karabhyaam jaanubhyaam etad-ashtaanga-lakshanam_ (When the body's chest, head, eyes, mind and speech — and also both feet, both hands and both knees — these eight limbs, touch the ground, that dandavat obeisance is called sashtang, the eight-limbed namaskar.)

_Dobhyaam padaabhyaam jaanubhyaam urasaa shirasaa drishaa, manasaa vachasaa cheti, pranaamo-ashtaanga eeritah_ (With both hands, both feet, both knees, the chest, the head, the eyes, the mind and speech — with these eight, the sashtang obeisance is performed.)

Sarvaangai abhivadanam — to offer reverence with all the limbs of the body.

_Nidhaaya dandavad deham, prasaarya charanau karau, baddhyaa mukulvat paani, pranaamo danda-sangyita. Iti dandavat pranaamah_ (Laying the body flat like a rod, stretching out the feet and hands, and joining the palms together like a closed bud — this obeisance is called dandavat. This is the dandavat pranam.)

_Paadau shirasthaa hastau, nikunchya mukulaakriti, manobuddhabhimaanaishcha, pranaamo-ashtaangasangyitah. Iti vihitaih sarvair vandanam ityarthah_ (When the feet, the head, and the hands drawn together in the shape of a closed bud, together with the mind, the intellect and the sense of self, are all offered — this obeisance is called sashtang; that is, it is full reverence performed with all these ordained limbs and faculties together.)

_Mantroccharana-dhyaanaabhyaam, manasaa vachasaat kramaat, padashtaangena bhusparsha taddhai vandan muchyate_ ||1|| (That obeisance offered in due order, together with the utterance of a mantra and with meditation, with mind and speech, and in which the eight limbs touch the earth — that is called true vandana, reverent worship.)

_Baahubhyaam chaiva manasaa shirasaa vachasaa drishaa, panchaango-ayam pranaamah syaat poojaasu pravaraavimau_ (The obeisance performed with these five — both hands, the mind, the head, speech and the eyes — is called panchang, the five-limbed obeisance, because it is performed with these five limbs.)

_Ashtaanga vaapi panchaanga pranaamo purusha shcharet, panchaangam eva naari tu naanyathaa munisattama_ ||4|| (A man may perform either the sashtang or the panchang obeisance, O best of sages; but a woman should perform only the panchang, and not the sashtang.)

Thus pranam is itself a form of devotion that brings about one's welfare.

_Pranamya dandavad bhumau namaskaarena yo-archayet, sa yaam gatim avaapnoti na taam ritushatairapi_ (One who worships God by offering the dandavat prostration upon the earth attains a fruit that cannot be obtained even by performing hundreds of sacrifices — for sacrifices lead only to heaven, and that is subject to perishing, whereas the fruit that comes from devotion through pranam, namely the attainment of God Himself, is imperishable. For this reason the fruit of devotion through pranam has been declared greater even than the fruit of sacrifices.)

The Vaishnav Dharma Ratnakar, register no. 210, p.409, verses 17-18, likewise supports this statement. Adhyaruji Maharaj, in Bhavan Charan 26, speaks of namaskar with still greater fervour:

_Sukhe bhakt seva kare, ane bhakt paraayan dev, namo Vishnu em ochare, ehaj tamari seva_ ||26|| (That devotee who, with joy and love, renders You devotion, becomes wholly absorbed in devotion to his chosen deity, and utters "Namo Vishnu" — this alone is your true devotion.)

Whatever any being worships, and whosever devotion it may be, it ultimately reaches God alone — "all obeisance offered to any deity finally goes to Keshav." The final aim of the whole of the Vedas, the Puranas and all such texts is, in the end, only the attainment of God; but between the fool and the learned man, the difference lies only in understanding. The learned man does not err; but if the unlearned man errs and foolishly cries "obeisance to Vasudev," God forgives even that error and looks only at the sincerity behind it.

The shloka concerning "namo Vishnu" is that of Gargacharya, in the Pandav Gita, verse 63:

_Kim taasya bahubhir mantyair bhaktir yasya Janardane, namo Naaraayanaayeti mantrah sarvaartha-saadhakah_ ||63|| (For that devotee in whom devotion to Lord Janardan has already awakened, what need has he of many mantras thereafter? The mantra "Namo Narayanaya" alone accomplishes every purpose.)

For example, among the community of devotees there is a custom of offering pranam after the aarti. What sakhis our elders would recite in their minds while offering pranam, in earlier times, is recorded in the Gaddi Library, vol. 10, p.193:

_Aadne anek tun, sthaavar jangam taahaara tej, tun guruone taahaar, naam, sakal santsu tuj paranaam_ ||1|| (Sakhi) _Indri tana aparaadh, paranaame paachha fare, garath vaa laage kaain, moorakh man saanso kare_ ||1|| _Vinati hai nij daaski, suneeo deen dayaal, gaas aapno jaanke, sadguru hohu kripaal_ ||2|| _Bahu bandhanmein baandhiaa, ek bichaaraa jeev, apne bal chhoote nahin, jo na chhodaavo piu_ ||3|| _Main sevak hu samarthka, kabahu na haae akaaj, jo pativrataa naagi rahe, toh patiku laaj_ ||4|| (In the Aharnish Raas, Adhyaruji says: O Lord! From the very beginning until now, You alone pervade this entire universe; in every moving and unmoving thing, it is Your very essence that shines forth. You alone are great, and Your name is great; I offer pranam to You, together with all the saints. Whatever sins our senses may have committed, the whole burden of those sins is lifted from our heads by offering pranam, and the sins are erased. Offering pranam to God costs nothing at all, and yet foolish people, out of doubt and suspicion in their minds, remain unbelieving about the matter of pranam. O Lord, this is the plea of Your devotee: hear me, O God who shows grace to humble devotees — knowing me to be Your servant, O true guru, show Your grace upon me. O Lord! This one poor, helpless soul is bound by so very many bonds of karma, and therefore...

"If You do not release me, then by the strength of my own ego I cannot become free from the bondage of karma. I am a devotee of the almighty, all-powerful Lord, so no harm can ever befall me — for just as a chaste wife's honor being violated brings shame upon her husband, so the responsibility for my welfare must rest upon You."

Thus the mention of full prostration (sashtang pranam) points us toward surrendering our entire self to the Lord and handing over our whole responsibility to Him — it instructs us to adopt this spirit of taking refuge in God (bhagavad-sharanagati). For the devotee who has taken refuge, wandering through the eighty-four lakh species of life comes to an end. Moreover, verse 56 states that apart from devotion to God, every injunction and prohibition (vidhi-nishedh) is merely a servant of the path of surrender.

_Smartavyah satatam Vishnur, vismartavyah kshane na cha._
_Sarve vidhi-nishedhah syur etayor eva kinkarah. ||56||_
(Vishnu should be remembered always, and never forgotten even for a moment; all injunctions and prohibitions are but servants of these two — remembering Him and never forgetting Him.)

Explaining the sense of this verse, the Samagam says that the Lord's exclusive, single-minded devotees are such that their minds remain fully absorbed in His lotus feet. Not even for a quarter of the time it takes to blink an eye does their attention move away from the Lord's feet. It further says that Vaishnavas are so resolute that they reject the path of ritual injunction, that is, the path of karma. As for what "vidhi" means, the Samagam explains: by vidhi is meant the path of the Vedas, and these Vaishnavas treat this Vedic path as a servant of the path of devotion. Further, of the path of karma laid down by the Vedas, they accept only its essential element — devotion to God — so they regard the path of karma itself as a servant of the path of devotion. A servant is one who is bound to do; whatever work he is told, he does — such a one is his master's own messenger, and such a messenger cannot cause his master trouble. In the same way, the devotee, whose true master is devotion, is not bound to observe rites and rules simply because the Veda's commands of injunction and prohibition tell him so. Its sakhi is given in the Samagam.

_Kabir, Ved hamare het hai, aune ham Vedun ke manhi._
_Auro ku karm bataave, hamku bataave nahi. ||2||_
(Das Kabirji says: the Vedas work for our benefit, and we too, through the Vedas, secure our own welfare.)

This Veda can command people bound by the three gunas to perform karma through its ordinances, but for devotees like us, since it is our servant, it cannot command us to perform karma. Hariram Vyas, in the raga Sarang-Dhanashri, has described what kind of servant the Veda is:

_Shri Vrindavan ke raja Shyam, Radhika taki rani._
_Teen padarath karat majoori, mukti bharat jahan pani._
_Karmi-dharmi karat jevari, gharu chhavat hai gyani._
_Jogi, jati, tapi sannyasi, in chori kai jani._
_Paniha Ved Puran milaniya, kahat sunat yeh bani._
_Ghar-ghar prem-bhakti ki mahima, Vyas sabani pahchani. ||74||_
(Shyam, the King of the abode of Vrindavan, has Radhika as His queen. The three aims of life — artha, dharma, and kama — labor as His hired hands, while liberation itself fetches the water for their toil. All this is described further below.)

The Lord of the abode of Vrindavan is Shri Krishna, and Radhikaji is His queen. The three aims of life — artha, dharma, and kama — labor as servants, working, so to speak, as tradesmen for the Lord's sake, while Liberation performs the lesser task of drawing water to finish their labor. Rites and observances — the mental disciplines of japa, austerity, charity, and pilgrimage-vows — twist the binding rope; and on the roof of the devotees' house the men of knowledge lay the thatch. Yogis, celibates, ascetics, and renunciates came to recognize this dwelling. The Vedas and Puranas, like thirsty birds seeking devotion, kept repeating and listening to this teaching: that in home after home the glory of prem-lakshana bhakti (love-natured devotion) is proclaimed — such prem-lakshana bhakti has Vyas come to understand.

Kabirji, describing the Veda as a mere laborer, has said:

_Bani to pani bhare, charon Ved majoor._
_Karni to gara kare, rahani (Sahab) ka ghar door._
(The scriptural word only carries water; all four Vedas are but laborers. Right conduct makes the mortar, but the House of the Master lies far beyond them.)

Das Kabirji says: to build the house of the Supreme Abode, the scriptures and Puranas — the paths of karma, jnana, and yoga expressed as speech — perform the lesser task of carrying water for the labor, while all four Vedas, like hired hands, toil to assist. Right conduct makes the mortar for raising this house. But the true Supreme Abode of God lies far beyond the house built of these eighty-four lakh bodily forms — it is very slight and distant by comparison. The abode fit for our eternal, peaceful dwelling is something altogether different from this house made of the eighty-four-lakh bodily forms.

_Puran jaani Ved ki, sohat param anoop._
_Aadhi bhasha netra binu, ko lakhi paave roop._
(Das Kabirji says: the language of the Veda, taken in full, is beautiful throughout, but without the "half eye" — the understanding that guides one toward devotion — no one can perceive the form of love-devotion.)

_Bani to pani bhare, charon Ved majoor._
_Chooka, sevak bandagi, kiya chakri door._
_Chhin mein chooke chakri, to pal mein kije door._
(Das Kabirji says: the speech of the scriptures and Puranas toils hard to expound my devotion — that is, devotion to God — and the four Vedas labor hard at it too. But should any of them err in serving me, or grow careless in that service, I will dismiss them from my service at once.)

_Ved kahe main kachhu na jaanu, swasan ke sang aay._
_Daras het kar, bandagi, gun anek mein gaaya._
(Das Kabirji says: as the scripture states — "asya mahato bhutasya nihshvasitam etad yad Rig-Vedo Yajur-Vedah Sama-Vedah," this is the very breath of that great Being — so the Veda itself says: I have arisen from the breath of the Supreme Person. What is His form? How could I describe it? I know nothing of it; I only sing, in countless ways, of His qualities in the hope of glimpsing Him. The Vedas tried hard to describe the Lord's nature but could not, and in the end, exhausted, could only say of Him "not this, not this" — neti neti.)

_Bed hamara Bed hai, ham Bedon ke manhi._
_Jaun bhed mein main baasu, Bedon jaanat naahi._
_Jo maarag ham chale, so Vedon ku gam naahi._
(Das Kabirji says: hence devotees declare — the Veda is ours, and we too dwell within the Veda; but in the secret depth where we truly abide, the Veda has no knowledge. As it is said in the Taittiriya text, "yato vacho nivartante aprapya manasa saha" — that from which words, together with the mind, turn back unable to reach — such is the path of love-devotion that devotees like us have walked, a path of which the Veda has no understanding whatsoever.)

Criticizing the blindly superstitious and the religious fanatic, Kabirji says:

_Guru pashu, nar pashu naari, Ved pashu sansaar._
_Manush vaako jaaniyo, jaaka vimal vichaar._
(Das Kabirji says: in this world some foolish people are as brutish as cattle — slaves to their guru, cowed by their wives, or blindly Veda-bound. But truly, only one who discerns right from wrong, good from bad, one governed by reason, deserves to be called a real human being.)

_Nar pashu, guru pashu, Ved pashu, triya pashu sansaar._
_Kahai Kabir so pashu nahin, jaake vimal vichaar._
(Das Kabirji says: foolish people are like dull-witted cattle — some enslaved to other men, some to their guru, some unmanly and henpecked by their wives. But those who hold within themselves the discernment of right and wrong are, in the true sense, called human.)

_Balihari vah doodh ki, jaamein nikse dheev._
_Aadhi sakhi Kabir ki, char Vedka jiiye._
(Das Kabirji says: blessed is that milk — the four Vedas, the scripture of devotion — from which the ghee of Ram-nam emerges. Even half a sakhi of Kabir's carries the very life-essence of all four Vedas, since the Vedas themselves arise from that Name; thus this half-sakhi proves that Ram-nam is the origin of everything.)

_Aisa adbad jin katho, katho to raakho chhipaay._
_Bed katalbe na lakho, to kahe kaun patipaay._
(Das Kabirji says: do not declare the nature of God to be "this" or "that," as though wondrous and fully describable; and if you try, you will never manage to say it completely, for the telling will remain hidden and incomplete — who, then, would believe whatever you say?)

_Jyon paya madhya jheev hai, tyon Ramiya sab thaur._
_Kathta bakta bahut hai, math kaadhe te aur._
(Das Kabirji says: just as ghee lies within milk, so the nature of God pervades everywhere in this world. Many talk and prattle about what He is like, saying "it is this," "it is that" — but just as one churns curd to separate out its ghee, only a rare few are able to separate out the Supreme Brahman, seemingly mixed with maya, and attain the ultimate Truth.)

_Kabir, Bed Kataleb donun jug, joothi unki aash._
_Hindu Turak naarak mein padein, Vedon ku vishwaas._
(Das Kabirji says: both the Veda and the Qur'an are mistaken in expounding the nature of God and showing the path to reach Him. Both Hindus and Muslims fall into hell by placing their trust in the Veda and the Qur'an respectively.)

_Kabir, char Ved padhaayke, Harise na upajya het._
_Maal (laali) Kabira le gaye, pandit dhoonde khet._
(Das Kabirji says: though people have the four Vedas recited to them, love for devotion to God does not arise from it in the end. But whatever essential wealth of Ram-nam lay within the Vedas, the loving devotees have already taken it away. The real crop was that; and the learned pundits, after the harvest is already reaped, keep rummaging through the leftover stubble looking for grain — struggling amid the stubble of ritual, japa, austerity, and vow, searching for the genuine harvest of devotion, which is not to be found there, for the devotees have already carried it off.)

_Kabir, kathni kathe so poot hamara, Ved padhe so naati._
_Rahani rahe so guru hamara, ham rahani ke saathi._
(Das Kabirji says: those who merely speak as they please, whatever suits them, I regard as my own son, as a father keeps a son under his authority. Those who recite the Vedas, that is, perform ritual acts, I regard as my own kin — as it is said, "we are within the Veda," meaning devotees like us treat the Veda as our own servant. And those who hold within themselves the secret truth of God are my guru, my venerable saint-guru; I keep company with such secret-bearing saint-gurus, following the conduct they teach.)

_Kabir, Ved bada na Ved-si, nahi Gokul ki Brajnaar._
_Unhu sahaj paayi nahin, rahi pokaar pokaar. ||126||_
(Das Kabirji says: the Veda is not great enough to attain the Lord's love-nectar, nor can those learned in the Veda attain or bestow this supreme Truth; and even the standing of the women of Gokul, the Braj-nari, is not so great — for they did not effortlessly attain the full bliss of that love. When the circle of the rasa dance broke apart, they were left distressed and agitated, crying out in the pain of separation from the Lord.)

_Kabir, deepak joya gyaan ka, dekha aparam Dev._
_Char Ved ki gam nahin, tahan Kabira sev._
(I lit the red lamp of love-devotion and beheld the incomparable Supreme Lord. Where the speech of the four Vedas cannot reach — O Kabir, strive there for that divine Truth; practice devotion there.)

_Jot Julaho pragatchyo, kiyo naam prakaash._
_Ved mathi makhan liyo, pandit pive chhaash. ||2||_
(Maharaj Jivandasji says: a single flame arose in the form of the weaver-saint Sadguru Kabir, and he illumined the truth of God. By churning and analyzing the Vedas he attained the butter-like supreme essence of Ram-nam, while the learned pundits drank only the buttermilk — the recitation of Vedas and rituals, empty of the essence of God.)

_Ved van man Jeevna, bhoolya sab sansaar._
_Karam dharam phaansi bhayi, Kaazi Brahman kaal._
(Maharaj Jivandasji says: in the wilderness-forest of the Veda, O Jivan, the whole world has lost its way. Rituals, japa, and austerity have become like a noose, and Qazis and Brahmins have become the executioners who tighten it, agents of destruction.)

_Ved-Kabed doy haathiya, Kaazi Brahman maath._
_Tinke sir par Sevda, tahan na Kabira jaat._
(Das Kabirji says: the Veda and the Qur'an have become like two grasping hands holding worldly people fast, and the Qazis and Brahmins have become the authorities gripping us in those two hands. Worse still are the Sevadas — Jain monks who let their hair grow uncut, like sorcerers — so the community of Kabir's devotees will have nothing to do with them.)

_Kabir, Kaazi padhe Quran ku, pandit Ved Puraan._
_Taake peechhe sab jug chalya, e dozakh ka agwaan._
(Das Kabirji says: the Qazis recite the Qur'an, and the pundits read the Vedas and Puranas. The whole world follows behind them, acting as they say — thus these people are the leaders who take us down into hell.)

_Ajahun tera sab mite, jo guru-mukh paave bhed._
_Pandit paas na baithiye, baithi na suniye Ved._
(Das Kabirji says: even now, all your doubt can be dispelled if you receive the teaching of the true nature through the mouth of the Guru; but do not sit near Vedic pundits, and do not listen to their empty, wordy expositions of the Veda. Reference: R.ji 256/2, p. 603.)

_Vede bhoolya sakal jug, toon nahin apne saath._
_Took took karun Jeevna, jo chadhe hamare haath._
(Maharaj Jivandasji says: O Veda, you have led the whole world astray and deceived it, but you cannot come along with those of us who hold love-devotion — we will not keep you with us. But if you should ever fall into our grasp, O Jivan, I will tear you to pieces.)

_Bed bhed jaanai nahin, neti neti kahai bain._
_Ta Mohan son Radhika, kahai mahaavar dain._
(Devotees possessed of prem-lakshana bhakti neither know nor care for the convoluted commands of the Veda. To the Veda's teaching of ritual, japa, and austerity, such lovers keep saying, "we will not accept this, we will not do that" — even as the Veda itself, regarding the nature of God, can only keep saying "not this, not that." That very God, Shri Krishna, whom the Veda cannot capture, Radhikaji has brought so completely under her sway that she commands Him, "apply red lac-dye to the soles of my feet.")

_Kabir, Ram kaha tin sab laha, lahe safal shastra ka bhed._
_Ram na kahe so narke gaya, padhte charon Ved._
(Das Kabirji says: those who took the Name of Ram gained everything — they grasped the very essence of all the scriptures. Those who did not chant the Name of Ram had to go to hell, even though they recited all four Vedas.)

_Gharti to haandi bhayi, dhakkan bhaya aakash._
_Char Ved kaathi bhayi, jeev ka kahan nikaash._
(Das Kabirji says: this earth has become like a cooking pot in which the soul is trapped and made to suffer, and the sky above it has become its lid, while the four Vedas have become the firewood beneath it. In such a state of suffering, from where can this soul ever find its release, ever escape from that pot?)

_Kabir, dharti to haandi sahi, dhaapan sahi aakash._
_Guru (shabda) prataape bhakti pachha payi, jeev ka tahan nikaash._
(Das Kabirji says: let it be that the earth is like a pot and the sky its lid — that is no matter. But if, by the grace of the Guru's teaching, we attain love-devotion, then through it the soul will find its deliverance.)

In this world, the earth made of the eighty-four lakh bodies through which birth and death occur is that pot, and delusion (maya) is its lid; within it the four Vedas, in their fourfold form, torment this soul with the fire of rituals, japa, and austerity as though it were firewood. But the Guru shows us the way and means to escape from this bondage of worldly existence by teaching us devotion to Ram-nam, so that we may gain release.

_Ved mein bahu bhed hai, jaane virla koy._
_Sundar Sadguru mila vina, nirvaaro na hoy._
(Sundardas says: the Veda holds within it many hidden layers of meaning that only a rare few can know; unless, O Sundar, one finds a true Sadguru, deliverance from its deceptive snares cannot be attained.)

The Veda has been regarded as a servant — "we are within the Veda" means we have accepted the Veda in the capacity of a servant. If a servant errs, the master does not accept it and dismisses him; likewise, when the Veda, instead of prompting love-devotion, imposes only the contrary work of ritual, devotees do not accept it. Since the Veda's commands, bound up as they are with the three gunas, would break the wholehearted devotion required of devotees, they are not acceptable to that extent, and to that extent the Veda must be opposed — but this does not mean that the Veda disrespects devotion to God; rather, it has simply been granted the standing of a servant to the devotees. Nana Parekh, in the raga Velaval, has written beautifully of the Veda:

_Saheb mere Saiyan, vinti karun tohi._
_Ketik vaata atapati, samjhaavo mohi. (tek)_
_Bhai re Ved bada sab ko kahai, Hari mukh the aaya._
_Gopijan peechhe dharya, param pad paaya. ||1||_
_Bhai re Shukdev samaran kiya, maaya sab tyaagi._
_Vaikunth pedhan na diya, meri daajh na bhaagi. ||2||_
_Bhai re Parath ke tum saarthi, mohe achraj aave._
_Aisa bhagat ekaantka, Himaale kyun jaave. ||3||_
_Bhai re Aadhav Akrur aadhdehi, jan nikat kahaaya._
_Aise Harijan dekhtaan, shankh supach bajaaya. ||4||_
_Bhai re akath katha behad ki, boojhe mat mohi._
_Nana Sadguru bina mile, cheene nahin koi. ||5||_
(O Lord, my Master, I plead with You: many things about You leave me puzzled — explain them and grant me understanding. Everyone says the Veda is the greatest, that it came from Your own mouth and is uncreated; yet the gopis set aside its commands and still attained the Supreme Abode. Shukadev renounced all pleasure for knowledge and detachment, yet without love-devotion he was kept from entering Your Abode, and this grief has never left me. I marvel that You became the charioteer of Arjuna, Your own devoted soul, and yet he went to the Himalayas hoping to ascend to heaven. In the presence of Your closest devotees such as Uddhava and Akrura, it was an outcaste's conch that was sounded at the Rajasuya sacrifice. O Lord, of whom nothing can truly be said and who is without limit, no one can fully understand You; without a true Sadguru, says Nana the Vaishnav, no one can know how to love You, nor grasp Your wonders.)

Having quoted the sakhi "Ved hamare het hai" — the Veda works for our benefit — the nature of the path of karma laid down by the Veda has thus been explained through Kabir's sakhis. The following section now turns to exclusive, one-pointed devotion. A servant (kinkar) must observe due deference toward his master; but if the master instead defers to the servant, he would be counted a fool, an utter fool. In the same way, since the Veda is the servant, it is the Veda that must defer to the devotee, its true master — but should the devotee defer to the Veda instead, he would be counted an utter fool. Regarding this it is said:

_Bhane besi bhookho uthe, chaakarni raakhe maazha._
_Dharni baaydithi sharmaay, te murakhno raja._
(One who sits down to eat and rises still hungry, one who defers to his own servant, and one who is bashful before his own wife — such a person is the very king of fools.)

Ghost-Offerings (Pret Bhojan) and the Exclusive Devotee — pret bhojan is reckoned as company kept with Shakta and Salil worshippers. Once, in the Garuda Purana, what Shri Krishna said about pret bhojan is set out in verse 57:

_Varam halaahalam bhakshyam kaakamamsam shunastatha._
_Shvapachasya-annam bhunkshya pretabhojanam aatyaja. ||57||_
(Better to eat deadly poison, better to eat the flesh of a crow or a dog, better to eat food from an outcaste's house — but abandon pret bhojan, food offered to the dead, altogether.)

Garuda, son of Vinata, is the Lord's own carrier; only by eating pure food does he remain fit to carry Him.

_Hari-bhakti-vihitanam samsargo naraka-pradah._
_Udakam tu suraapaanam, annam gomamsa-sannibham._
(Association with those devoid of devotion to God leads to hell; the water in their house is like liquor, and their food is like forbidden cow's flesh.)

_Sant pade so langhna, aan-dasha nahin jaay._
_Jo kabahu bhookha rahai, ananya ke ghar paay. ||13||_
(The Vaishnav Nana Parekh, in the Sant Ang, says: even should a saintly devotee have to fast for a hundred days, he will not fall into wretchedness for it. If ever a time of hunger comes, he would rather stay hungry than eat — he will eat only in the house of an exclusive devotee.)

The Lord tells Garuda: by eating pret bhojan, tens of millions upon tens of millions of our births are ruined. What is to be counted as pret bhojan is described in verse 58:

_Deva-yajnaam deva-havyaam anya-devam-upaashritaah._
_Ekaadashyaam cha dvaadashyaam pretabhojyaath. ||58||_
(Food connected with sacrifices, oblations, and the worship of other deities, or eaten at the eleventh- or twelfth-day death rites, is pret bhojan, and it destroys the merit of one who partakes.)

Food from a yajna, homa, or havan; food offered to another deity; food from one not entitled to wear tilak and tulsi and who does not wear them; and food from the eleventh- or twelfth-day death rites — all these are counted as pret bhojan. Food offered before an image should not be eaten — from the commentary on the Parashar Smriti, chapter 11: scripture forbids eating food cooked and offered to deities in temples; only those of great austerity may eat it. Nowadays many people, thinking temple prasad sacred, eat it gladly, but the scriptures forbid eating food offered before images of deities. Food offered to Vishnu is counted pure, but only when worshipped within a private household shrine; in public temples, scripture forbids eating the food offered before the images, and whoever eats it incurs sin. It is also said in the Anusmriti:

_Samvatsarena patati patitena sahaacharan._
_Yaajanaadhyaapanaayaunaatraatu yaanaasanaashanaat._
(A man becomes fallen who, for a full year, travels in the same vehicle with a fallen person, sits on the same seat, or eats in the same row with him; but by officiating his sacrifices, teaching him, or exchanging daughters in marriage with him, one becomes fallen at once.)

Discussing pret bhojan, the Samagam gives this sakhi of Kabirji:

_Kabir, hom kanagat kaarto, saakut raandhyo khaay._
_Jeevat vishta shwaan ki, mooye narak le jaay._
(Das Kabirji says: one who eats food from homa, havan, shraddha rites, from the eleventh-day death feast, or food cooked by a Shakta, is, while still living, as impure as a dog's filth, and after death Yama's messengers carry him off to hell.)

Those who eat the food of the twelfth- or thirteenth-day death rites are counted of low standing, and Brahmins who do so are counted among them. Its sakhi:

_Brahman Bhangi ek hai, unki ek hi jaat._
_Vo kafan ko let hai, o teraahme khaat._
(The Brahmin and the sweeper are, in this respect, one and the same kind: the sweeper takes the burial shroud, while the Brahmin eats the food of the twelfth- and thirteenth-day rites.)

_Brahman Bhangi Rawka, chautha kahiye kaag._
_Kahe Kabir e chaaron janka, murda upar laag._
(Das Kabir says: Brahmins, sweepers, Rawal beggars, and, fourth, crows — all four keep watch over a corpse, ever ready to consume what belongs to the dead.)

Improper eating and drinking ruins one's reputation, and this is why Brahmins become disgraced. Its sakhi:

_Aambo phal pat raakhke, mahu phale pat khoye._
_Vaako paani je piye, tahan pat kahan te hoye._
(The mango fruit keeps one's honor intact, but whoever drinks the liquor made from mahua fruit — how can his honor be preserved?)

In this way, one who eats improperly loses his reputation, while one who eats and lives properly is highly valued. Food offered to another deity is of the lowest order, while food offered to God is the highest. It is said in the Gautami Tantra:

_Tulasi-dala-maatrena jalasya chulukena cha._
_Vikrinita svam-aatmaanam bhaktebhyo bhakta-vatsalah._
(The Lord is so compassionate and so affectionate toward His devotees that He gives away His very own Self to them for the price of a single tulsi leaf and a palmful of water offered with devotion.)

_Kabir, prasaad sohi kijiye, Hari arpit hoye._
_Aur bhojan nakhod hai, kahet Kabira soy._
(Das Kabirji says: one should take as prasad only what has been offered to God; all other food, say Kabir and the saints, is inauspicious.)

_Bin arpan bhojan kare, bin arpan jal paan._
_Bin arpan sumaran kare, ehi pret samaan._
(Whoever eats food, drinks water, or even remembers God without first offering it to Him — that act is counted as base as pret bhojan.)

In verse 59 of the Samagam, the same warning that the Lord gave Garuda about pret bhojan is given to exclusive Vaishnav devotees:

_Mrutakasya paavakash-chaiva shaaktasya mandire._
_Jalam pitvaa suraapaanam, annam gomaamsa bhakshanam. ||59||_
(Better to cook one's food with fire brought from a funeral pyre than to bring even an ember from a Shakta's house; water from a Shakta's house is as forbidden as liquor, and food from there is as inedible as cow's flesh.)

Shakta people consider impure whatever they dislike and pure whatever they like:

_Angamtu apavitra gani, gamtu ganyun pavitra._
_Chudo na ganyu haadku, jagat vichaar vichitra._
(Self-interested people consider impure whatever displeases them, and pure whatever pleases them — as when ivory bangles, though made of bone, are still counted an essential ornament for married women. Such is the strange, contradictory nature of such people.)

People regard women's natural monthly courses as unclean, while they regard the slaughter of animals in sacrifices, meat-eating, and the intoxicating drink of soma as sacred. People of such twisted, contrary inclination are as base as butchers, and association with such Shakta worshippers is therefore to be avoided. The Samagam advises staying far from such people, and how deeply wicked they are is stated in this fifty-ninth verse: it is better to cook with fire brought from a burning corpse in the cremation ground than to bring fire even from a Shakta's house, for that brings fault and sin upon us. It is said that fire itself is never tainted by what it touches, since fire reduces everything to ash — yet even so, we are commanded to stay far from the very fire kept in such a wicked person's house. Prescribing restrictions regarding Shakta and Salil worshippers, the Samagam gives seven sakhis:

_Kabir, Saakut keri sabha rachi, tahan jan baithan jaay._
_Ek gohaade kyun bane, rojh gadha aur gaay. ||1||_
(Das Kabirji says: devotees do not go to sit in the assembly of Shakta people, for just as chaos would come of penning wild nilgai, donkeys, and cows together in one enclosure, the same wretched fate would befall devotees there. People of every disposition — rajasic, tamasic, and sattvic — gather there and quarrel, and in such conditions the Lord's devotees are put to great difficulty.)

Shakta people worship other deities; Salil people keep a foot on both sides, worshipping both their chosen deity (ishta-dev) and other deities; but exclusive devotees acknowledge none other than their ishta-dev. Hence, in the quarrels between Shaktas and Salils, they are made to suffer.

_Kabir, had ke jeevsan, hit kari mukhai na bol._
_Jo laage behad son, tinson kachhu kachhu bol. ||2||_
(Das Kabirji says: O devotee, do not, out of affection, discuss the inner matters of love-devotion with those still bound within the limits of social convention and caste propriety; but with those who have left behind family custom and caste convention and become absorbed in love-devotion to the Supreme Being, speak freely and lovingly of devotion.)

_Kabir, had rahe so maanvi, behad rahe so saadh._
_Had behad se jo koi nyaara, taaka matta agaadh. ||3||_
(Das Kabirji says: "had," the bound, means one who performs the duties of caste and station strictly as the Veda prescribes — an ordinary human being; "behad," beyond bound, means one who rejects those duties entirely and follows the path of yoga — a sadhak. And those who dwell on the path of love-devotion, distinct from both the path of knowledge and the path of ritual action, hold a principle whose depth is beyond measure.)

_Mukh se rahe so maanvi, man se rahe so dev._
_Surat se rahe so sant hai, vidh jaano bhev._
(One who repeats the Name only with the mouth is merely a man; one who repeats it with the mind is like an exalted celestial; and one who repeats it with the inner attention is a saint — understand thus the mystery of such repetition.)

_Sant saath bahu antara, jyon dharti aakash._
_Sant chaahe Ramku, saadh santki aash._
(Das Kabirji says: there is a very great difference between the Sant and the sadhak — as great as the distance between earth and sky. Sants desire to attain God, Ram, directly, while sadhaks desire above all to attain a true Sant, since only through finding one does their own practice bear fruit.)

_Kabir, had mein Ram na paaiya, behad hai bharpoor._
_Had behad ki gam nahi, taasu Ram hazoor._
(Das Kabirji says: God is not attained within the bounds of caste convention and Vedic custom; He is found in full only beyond those bounds. One who has passed beyond all concern with either bound or unbound stands in the very presence of Ram.)

Devotion could not be attained through the limits of social custom and Vedic convention; one who breaks through those limits gains deep, direct experience. That state which lies beyond every limit — attained by one who breaks past social shame and pride to sound the banner of devotion — reveals the divine Truth to him directly.

_Kabisa, saadhu bahu antara, jyun dharti brahmaand._
_Saadhu odhaare aapku, sant odhaare khand._
(Das Kabirji says: there is a very great difference between sadhaks — knowers, meditators, yogis — and Sants, as great as the distance between earth and sky in their work. For sadhus practice for their own individual benefit, while Sants are well-wishers striving for the welfare of the whole universe — as the saying goes, "udaracharitanam vasudhaiva kutumbakam," for the noble-hearted the whole world is one family.)

Regarding the sadhu, Maharaj Gyaniji says:

_Mankun saadhe saadh so, raakho Saheb maanhi._
_Gyaani doojaa bhekh sab, saadh kahaave naahi. ||41||_
(Maharaj Gyaniji says: only those who strive to master the mind and keep their disposition fixed on God are true sadhaks; all others, he says, are mere costume-wearers, and cannot be called true sadhus or saints.)

_Saakutasu Jeevna, het kari mukhahi na bole._
_Salil bhagatsu munagrah, aninsu antar khol. ||5||_
(Sadguru Maharaj Jivandasji says: O Jivan, do not exchange loving words with Shakta people, nor deal warmly with them; keep your relations with Salil devotees firmly closed off. But with the exclusive, single-minded devotee, open your heart freely, without reservation or discrimination, and deal with him wholeheartedly.)

Trikamdas Gordhandas has composed a linked verse (kundali) upon this sakhi:

_Saakutansu Jeevna, tun het kari mukhahi na bol._
_Salil bhagatsu maun grah, aninsun antar khol._
_Anin sun antar bol, bol guru-mukh vaani._
_Salil Saakut sang chhod, bhataksho chaaro khaani._
_Kahun chhun vagaadi dhol, saambhale shishya Sadguru tana._
_Tun het kari mukh hi na bol, Saakutansun Jeevna._
(O Jivan, do not speak lovingly with your own mouth to the Shakta; keep silence toward the Salil devotee, but open your heart to the exclusive one. Open your heart to the exclusive devotee, and speak only the words that come through the Guru's own mouth; leave the company of both Salil and Shakta, or you will wander through all four species of birth. I proclaim this beating the drum, that the disciples of the Sadguru may hear it: do not speak lovingly with your own mouth to the Shakta, O Jivan.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: do not keep loving affection with Sakut people, nor keep their company; and have no dealings at all with a Salil devotee. But with those who practise exclusive (ananya) devotion, speak the thoughts of your heart openly, without hiding anything. Conduct yourself only according to the teaching received from your guru. Give up the company of Salil and Sakut, or else you will have to wander again through the four wombs of the eighty-four lakh species of life. I proclaim this loudly, beating the drum, so let the disciples of the true guru listen: Jivanji Maharaj has said that you must not associate with Sakut and Salil.

Salil people, along with their exclusive devotion, also worship Anadev (another deity, besides their chosen deity) — like a snake that keeps one hand in the milk and one in the curd, so that the curd spoils the milk as well; such is their conduct. True exclusive (ananya) devotees, however, are single-minded (ekanishtha) alone.

_manasyekam vachasyekam karmanyekam mahatmanam, manasyanyad vachasyanyat karye chanyad duratmanam_ (For noble souls, the mind, speech, and action are one and the same; for the base-minded, the mind thinks one thing, the speech says another, and the action does yet another.)

Noble, great souls behave the same way in mind, speech, and action, whereas base people think one thing in the mind, say something else with the mouth, and do yet another thing in action. Such people are counted as Salil.

_antar khole jarsu, kahe guruki vani, parsa patisu rusna, kahe ku kushalta_ (She opens her heart to an adulterous man, yet repeats the wise sayings of the guru's teaching — Parshuram asks: if she stays estranged from her own husband, how can any good come of it?)

Parshuram says: if a woman opens her heart freely before an adulterous man and behaves without restraint, yet also speaks the wise sayings of good saints, while remaining estranged from her own husband, then how can any true good come to her?

Salil and Sakut people have no single-mindedness, whereas single-mindedness exists among ananya devotees who are simple and guileless. Here is an illustration of this.

In a village of Vraj, an assembly of learned pandits was taking place. Everyone was describing their own exclusive devotion (ananyata), saying, "We do not accept any deity other than our chosen deity (Ishtadev)." (Some say they were describing the exclusive devotion of Shrimad Vallabhacharya Mahaprabhuji.) Just then a cowherd boy (gwalbal) arrived. He was told, "You people are ananya (exclusive), but I am fananya." Hearing this, the pandits fell into great confusion — everyone knows what "ananya" means, but what is "fananya"? Finally they all asked the boy for the meaning of "fananya." He said, "Listen — you people are ananya: you do not accept any deity other than your chosen deity, but you still know of the others. I, on the other hand, know of no one at all except my one and only Nanda's darling, dear Kanaiya (Krishna). As for believing or not believing in others — that is far too remote a matter for me even to consider." On hearing this boy's utterly truthful reply, the great brahmins bowed their heads before him and said, "Brother! You, who are fananya, are greater than us, who are merely ananya."

_to salilpe sakut bhalo, je kabahu pave par, salil duba kichme, jivan jal vina jaisi nav_ (So Sakut is better than Salil, for he may sometimes cross over to the far shore; Salil drowns in the mud — says Jivan — like a boat stranded without water.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that Sakut people are somewhat better than Salil people, because even though a Sakut worships Anadev, he may still (like Krishnadasji) sometimes get the chance to cross the ocean of worldly existence. Salil, however, worships many gods and also worships his chosen deity at the same time, and so, like a boat stuck fast in the mud for want of water, he ends up belonging nowhere. He falls from this side and from that, and wanders about ruined on every side.

In line 11, page 15, the revered Yadunath writes: "Salil — one who worships whatever deity he pleases, apart from the one appointed."

_salil bhagatku jivna, mat koi patiyay, kabahu sant sangat kare, kabahu sakutan mali jay_ ||7|| (Do not trust a Salil devotee at all, says Jivan — sometimes he keeps company with saints, and sometimes he goes and mixes with Sakuts.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: place no trust at all in a Salil devotee. At times he keeps the company of saints, and at other times he goes and mixes with the Sakuts.

A kavit by Chaturbhujdas, a cry of anguished appeal (gohai pokar):

_karm rat hari arpe, jani man anandvani jajai, karm krishnake ke to, kavan avkashaju bhajai, jyon sukh na lahat aru swad, nasikako udak pan kari, jadipi jathar-me jai, kahi gita ju avadhi pare, chaturbhuj moralidhar bhakti hit (var bajan), tanak salil nasht hi karat, jyon surasari jala kumbhme, suravrund kinchita parato_ (Chaturbhujdas says: only actions surrendered to Hari, done in devoted remembrance, are true; if one worships Anadev even while claiming great devotion to Krishna, calling that action "devotion to Krishna" makes no sense — like drinking water through the nose gives no taste or pleasure, and even if it reaches the stomach, it makes one retch and vomit before that. In the same way, if one worships Anadev while claiming devotion to Moralidhar, even a slight trace of Salil mixed in destroys the devotion entirely — just as a single drop of liquor dropped into a pot of sacred Ganga water spoils and defiles the whole pot.)

Chaturbhujdas says: one should act only after surrendering completely to God, becoming His refuge. Even though one knows that this alone is true devotion, if one still worships Anadev, then however much devotion to Krishna one may perform through one's actions, how can that worship truly count as devotion to Krishna? It is like drinking water through the nose — one gets no pleasure of taste at all, and even if the water does reach the stomach, a wave of nausea makes one retch and vomit before it gets there. In the same way, if one who is supposed to be a worshipper of Krishna-bhakti (devotion to Krishna) also worships Anadev, his state becomes just like that of a person drinking water through the nose. Chaturbhujdas says that if, without keeping one's aim fixed on devotion to Lord Moralidhar (Krishna), even the slightest trace of Salil-ness enters one's devotion, it destroys the whole of one's Krishna-bhakti — just as a single drop of liquor falling into a jar of Ganga water spoils and defiles the entire jar.

_pativratako dharm kahat ganika kahe kyon aavai, jor kahe to sharm(avar) karm kul nasht kahavai, jan ananya nij vrat karat (grahma) kaise salil sare, sakal dharm aru kul karm visare sevai jo ek hari, chaturbhuj kanchan aru kach jyon pheri shiar mrigraj jyo sam sare, kesar geru jyon ganiyo aru bhakt salil anin tyon_ (How can a courtesan ever be told the duty of a chaste wife — how could that duty ever come to her? If one insists on it, it is shameful, and it will only be called the ruin of one's family. In the same way, how can the practice of Salil-ness ever be reconciled with a devotee who upholds his vow of exclusive devotion? An exclusive devotee, holding fast to God alone, forgets and sets aside all other duties and family customs. Chaturbhujdas says there is as much difference between gold and glass, or between a jackal smeared in ochre calling itself the king of beasts, as between saffron and red ochre — that same difference exists between a true devotee and a Salil who calls himself an exclusive devotee.)

Chaturbhujdas says: even if a courtesan is taught the duty of a chaste wife, how could she ever actually become one? If she were called a wife, it would bring shame and would be said to destroy the honour of the family. In the same way, how could the practice of Salil-ness ever be accomplished by devotees who hold to the vow of exclusive, single-minded devotion? One who bears the vow of exclusive devotion and worships God alone forgets — sets aside — all other religious observances and family customs. Chaturbhujdas says there is as much difference between gold and glass as there is here. Just as it would be a sham for a jackal to smear itself with saffron-coloured ochre and call itself the lion, the king of beasts, so too it is when a Salil calls himself an exclusive (ananya) devotee.

Chaturbhuj has written the following kavit, laying stress on how one must give up the company of Salil.

_baru vichar man manjha, baru agni panjar kar, baru to byal avlamb, barut mrigraj ank (aalingan) bhare, baru barunalay kare pravesha, grasahi jala uksa, baru girivar chadhi shikhar, modpe (rudh) tahan deh adhah dhase, chaturbhuj moralidhar bhakt tav, bhul na sang salil kare, varu tan jo jay haribhajan jini haribhajan jat ravi tat dare_ (Better to enter a burning cage, or to be gripped in a serpent's coil, or to embrace the king of beasts, the lion — better to plunge into the ocean and be swallowed by its waters, or to climb the tallest peak of the Himalaya and hurl oneself down headfirst from its summit — than for a devotee of Lord Moralidhar to ever, even by mistake, keep the company of a Salil. Better that this body should perish while doing Hari-bhajan, says Chaturbhuj, than to give up Hari-bhajan; for even the sun, father of Yama, fears one who does Hari-bhajan.)

God Himself teaches and instructs His beloved devotee, so that the devotee understands that bad company disturbs one's devotion to God, and such company must be given up; one should not keep any companionship that creates an obstacle to remembering God. Whatever hardship it takes, one must bear it — even if bad company would bring some benefit, that benefit is worthless. Bad company must be given up. Whatever hardship must be borne, one should make every possible effort to escape it.

It is good for a devotee of Lord Moralidhar to resolve to act in just this way even towards his own worst enemy — with the thought: even if I must enter a burning cage, or be gripped in a serpent's coil, or come face to face with a lion, or plunge into the ocean, or climb to the summit of the tallest, highest peak of the Himalayas and be hurled down headfirst from there, I am ready to bear that suffering. But Chaturbhujdas says that even so, God's devotee will never, even by mistake, be ready to keep company with a Salil who would make him give up Hari-bhajan (devotional remembrance of Hari). Even if this body should perish while doing Hari-bhajan, that is better still. Even Surya, father of Yama, and Brahma, father of Surya, revere one who performs Hari-bhajan — so they can do nothing at all against a devotee of Hari.

Three kavits by Chaturbhujdas have been given here regarding giving up the company of Salil; let us also look at the kavit he wrote describing what a Salil is actually like.

_diksha mantra ju grahai, krishna kinkar ju kahavai, hari aaradhan karai, anadevan puni dhavai, karm dharm kul kaan, kaal kabahu na visarai, santan so ashraddha, kaam mati pasarai, aise salil sab nirakh ke, bhule na sang salil karai, haribhajan dar chaturbhuj na rahe, aru sahes maar jam jaal parai_ (Even one who has taken initiation and its mantra, and calls himself a servant of Krishna, who worships and adores Hari, yet still runs off to worship Anadev; who never forgets the ritual observances, customs, and family traditions handed down through the generations; who has no faith in the saints' teaching, and lets his mind run after selfish desire — having recognized such a Salil for what he is, do not, even by mistake, keep company with him. Chaturbhuj says: one who does not fear giving up Hari-bhajan will fall into Yama's snare and suffer his blows a thousandfold.)

Someone may have received initiation from a guru, taken the name of God and the name of Ram-Krishna, and let himself be called a devotee of Krishna, performing worship (aradhana) of Hari — and yet still worship Anadev as well; he clings to ritualistic works and observances, the customs and ways handed down through his family lineage across the four Vedic traditions, the customs of his caste and clan, and never forgets to celebrate the dark, worldly festivals and observances. Such a person, who places no faith in the teaching of the guru and the saints, and instead lets his mind run, sullied, after self-interested ritual — such a Salil, meaning one whose devotion lacks single-minded exclusivity — must never be kept company with, even by mistake, because his company will not let devotion to Hari remain steady within our hearts, and as a result we would fall into the noose of Yamaraj and have to endure his blows.

In the Samagam it is strongly urged that we give up both the food and the company of a Salil. There is a Sanskrit shloka on this subject as well.
