_avaishnavasya hastannam divya deshadupagatam, harei prasadam tirtha cha prayatnena vivarjayet_ (Food that comes from the hand of a non-Vaishnav, even if it has come from a divine realm, or even if it be the prasad of Hari or the sacred water from His feet, should be deliberately and carefully avoided.)

Food that has come through the hand of a non-Vaishnav should be carefully avoided, even if it has come from a divine abode, or is God's own prasad or the sacred water that has bathed His feet (charanamrit). The devotees have placed great emphasis on staying far away from the Salil, who has turned away from God.

_samarme laryo jahi, girihate giryo jai, gaganme phiryo jai pavakko dahisho, kananme rahyo jai, vyalkar gahyo jai, virahahu sahyo jai, aur kahya kahisho, halahal liyo jai, sarbas diyo jai, karvat liyo jai, varindhiko bahisho, aur duhkh yahute ju dusah kathin aiso jaiso kahun vimukh sang ekchhin rahisho_ (I could go and fight in battle, I could fall from a mountain, I could go whirling through the sky and be burnt by fire, I could go and live in the forest, I could let myself be seized by a serpent, I could bear separation — and what more shall I say — I could go and drink deadly poison, I could give away all I possess, I could be sawn in two, I could go and drown in the ocean, and I could bear any other suffering more unbearable and harder than these — but I could never bear to stay even for a single moment in the company of one who has turned away from God.)

If I must fight in war, I can fight; if I must fall from a mountain, that too is fine; if I must be whirled about in the sky, that too is fine; if I must be burnt in fire, that too is fine; I can live in the jungle, and even if a tiger devours me, that is fine; I can bear separation, and what more can I say — I could even drink deadly poison, I could be cut apart with a saw, I could drown in the sea — I am ready to bear even greater and more unbearable sufferings than these, but I could not stay even for a single moment in the company of one who has turned away from God.

In the Samagam, seventeen sakhis (couplets) are given to warn us against the Sakut.

_vyas sindh bhuja bhar bhetiye, sahiye tanki haan, salil bhagat nav bhetiye, vyase taji pahejaan_ ||1|| (Vyas says: I would rather embrace a lion with my arms and bear the injury to my body, but I would never meet with a Salil devotee — Vyas has given up all acquaintance with him.)

Vyasdas says: I would embrace a lion and bear whatever injury comes to my body, but I would not keep company with a Salil devotee, nor keep any acquaintance with him, nor have any dealings with him. Vyas, the exclusive devotee, has given him up entirely.

Trikamdas Gordhan has written a kundli (a chained-verse form) on this — see Diary (Samvat) 2025, page 74, on the kundli.

_vyasa vadhkun bhetiyo, sahiyo tanki haan, salil bhagat na bhetiyo, chhod dije pahijaan, chhod dije pahichaan, sangathi sukrit jave, adke vadhe abhadaat, paarkun paatak laave, samjo sadguru saan, garghav sam nav letiyo, sahiyo tanki haan, vyas vadhku bhetiyo_ (Vyas would meet even a tiger and bear the harm done to his body, but he would never meet a Salil devotee — give up all acquaintance with him. Give up acquaintance with him, for his company destroys good deeds; contact with him increases defilement and brings another's sin upon us. Understand the wisdom given by the true guru, and do not roll about like a donkey in that filth. Bear the harm to the body — Vyas would meet a tiger rather than meet a Salil.)

Vyasji says: it is acceptable to embrace and meet a tiger, and to bear whatever injury the body suffers because of it, but do not mix with a Salil devotee, and give up all acquaintance and dealings with him. Give up all relations with a Salil, for his company will destroy our merit and good deeds. Keeping contact with him will increase our defilement and untouchability and will bring another's sin upon us. Understand well the wisdom that the true guru has given. Do not roll about in the dust of Salil-ness like a donkey — that is, do not, like a fool, form any inward bond with a Salil. Vyasdasji says: if embracing a tiger injures the body, bear it — but do not, under any circumstance, keep company with a Salil.

_vyasa vadhkun bhetiye, sahiye tanki haan, salil bhagat no bhetiyo, chhod dije pahichaan, chhod dije pahichaan, sangate sukrit naase, chhodvi satsang gang, halahal vikhadan pase, salil sakutna chhanyade, bhulechukena besiye, sahiye tanki haan, vyas vadhku bhetiye_ (Vyas would meet a tiger and bear the harm to his body, but never meet a Salil devotee — give up acquaintance with him. Give up acquaintance with him, for his company destroys our good deeds and makes us abandon the Ganga of holy company (satsang, the fellowship of the devout), bringing us near the deadly poison of worldly desire instead. Never sit, even by mistake, in the shade of a Salil or a Sakut. Bear the harm to the body — Vyas would meet a tiger rather than meet a Salil.)

Vyasji says: it is good to embrace a tiger rather than to meet with, or keep acquaintance and dealings with, a Salil devotee, for his company destroys our merit and good deeds. His company makes us give up the Ganga of satsang and instead pours into us the deadly, powerful poison of maya — sensual desire and the like. So, even by mistake, one should never go into the shade or the ashram of a Salil or a Sakut. Vyasdasji says: it is good to embrace a tiger and bear the harm it does the body, but one must never make contact with a Salil.

The same essential meaning is stated also in the Sankhyayana Samhita.

_aalapaan daata samsparshaat nivasaat sah bhojanaat, santa charatiha paapaani taula bindu khimbhaasi. aalinganam varam manyo vyaal vyaghra jalaukasaam, na sangam shalya yuktaanaam naana devakai sevinaam_ (Better to embrace a snake, a tiger, or a leech than to keep company with those whose devotion is mixed with the thorn of worshipping various gods; for through conversation, direct contact, dwelling together, and eating together with such people, sin spreads within us, drop by drop, like a drop of oil spreading across water.)

It would be better to embrace a tiger, or even a whole group of tigers, and be caught in their claws, than to keep company with worshippers of the various Anadevs, whose company wounds us like a spear — because through conversing with them, through unguarded contact, through living with them, or through eating with them, sins spread within us just as a drop of oil spreads through water.

There is also a saying of Harivamshji on this.

_khanpan tahan kijiyo, rasik mandali manhi, jinke aur upasna, tako lijiye naahi_ (Take food and drink only within the company of fellow devotees who share your own loving devotion; never accept the food of those whose worship is directed elsewhere.)

Harivamshji says that we should eat and drink only in the company of those who share the same taste and language of devotion as we do; we should never accept food from those whose worship is different from our own — such food is not truly fit to be accepted.

_bhagati hai bahu bhaantki, jinke bohotek bhed, bina vivek milvo, tahan man pave ati khed_ (Devotion is of many kinds, with many different varieties within it; to associate with others without discernment brings the mind great sorrow in the end.)

Das Kabirji says: devotion to God is of many kinds, with different types — such as with desire, without desire, love-marked devotion, the mood of a servant, of a friend, of parental love, of the beloved, of sweetness, of enmity, of pure loving devotion, and so on. So, if one mixes with others without understanding what is fitting and what is not, then later, when differences of opinion arise in the mind, one is filled with deep regret.

_vyas sakut geheri chhandiye, gunka kije naar, hari dasi jo hoyegi, to kul na aape gaal_ ||2|| (Vyas says: give up a Sakut wife entirely, and instead make a courtesan your wife — for if she becomes a maidservant of Hari, she will bring no disgrace upon the family.)

Vyasdasji says that if one's wife is a Sakut, she should be given up; and, if it comes to it, one should rather choose to accept a courtesan — a woman who marries by virtue, or one who marries by outward attraction — as wife, because if she becomes a servant-devotee of God's devotees, our family and lineage will not be shamed or disgraced.

_triya jo va hoy haridasi, dusht mile aru man mile. varam shunya shala na cha varo dushtavrishabho, varam veshya patni na punaravinita kulavadhuh, varam vaso'ranye na punaravivekaadhipapure, varam pranatyago na punaradhamaanaamupagamah_ (If a wife is a servant of Hari, that is best; even meeting a wicked person and being of one mind with him is discussed here — better an empty cowshed than one occupied by a vicious bull; better a courtesan as wife than an ill-mannered, undisciplined wife of good family; better to dwell in the forest than in the city of an unwise king; better to give up one's very life than to associate with the base and the wicked.)

It is better for a cowshed to stand empty than for it to house a vicious bull. It is better to keep a courtesan as one's wife at home than to have a well-born wife who lacks humility. It is better to have to live in the forest than to have to live in the city of an unwise, indiscreet king. It is better to give up one's very life than to keep company with base, low people.

Harirayji, in the fifth verse of the Shikshapatra, has said:

_pratikulye yatha tyagah prabhvasambandhi vastutah, dhaneshu nisprihah sevopayogitvena rakshanam_ ||5|| (Just as one gives up any object that stands opposed to one's Lord, so too — though remaining free of any craving for wealth — one should protect and keep wealth only insofar as it is of use for His service.)

Just as anything that is of no use in the service of Thakorji (the Lord) is given up, so too, if wife, children, and the like are of no use in the service of Shri Thakorji, they are fit to be given up as well. One should not crave wealth; wealth should be kept and protected only by understanding it as something useful for the service of Shri Thakorji.

_kabir unche kulki kamini, na bhaje sarangpan, kulahi lajavai aapno, sudhi saapin jaan_ (Kabir says: a woman of high birth who does not worship Sarangpani, that is, Krishna, disgraces her own family — know her to be no different from a straight-fanged serpent.)

Das Kabirji says: a high-born woman who lives behind the veil, and who out of shame does not perform bhajan (devotional worship) of God, should be understood to be someone who disgraces her own family — exactly like a female serpent.

_duniyake dhokhe muzha, chale jo kulki kaani, tab kul phiska lajsi, jab le dharya masaani_ (Deceived by the world, one lives bound by the shame and honour of family and clan; but when at last one is carried to the cremation ground, it is then that the family's honour will truly turn pale with shame.)

This describes the anxious concern people have for worldly custom and family tradition, living their lives in accordance with the customs of the clan; but when your death comes and you must suffer torment in the abode of Yama, then it will become clear — whose family, and whose honour, will really have cause for shame.

_tulsi bhakt swapach bhala, jinke mukhme ram, uncha kulkun kya karun, jise satsang nahi vishwas_ (Tulsi says: even an outcaste devotee is better, if the name of Ram is in his mouth — what use is high birth to me, if that person has no faith in satsang?)

_jaj janma taani karmaani tadayus taan manovachah, nrinaam yoneha vishvaatmaa sevyate haririshvarah_ ||9|| _kim janmabhis tribhir veha shauklasaavitrayaajnikaih, karmabhir vaa trayi-proktaih pumso'pi vibudhaayusha_ ||10|| (Only that birth, those deeds, that lifespan, and that thought and speech are truly successful, O Prachetas, through which people worship Hari, the Lord who is the very Self of the universe, in this human form — all else is vain. What is the use, even of three exalted births as one born of the seed, through the sacred thread, and through the performance of sacrificial rites, or of a lifespan lasting as long as that of the gods, if the worship and knowledge of the God who bestows one's own being are not attained?)

Narad says: O Prachetas, that birth, that action, that lifespan, and that mind and speech alone should be considered fruitful and successful which are spent in the service of the Lord God, the Self of the whole universe — all the rest should be understood as fruitless. If one does not attain the service and knowledge of the God who has given us our very being, then what fruit is there even in the three exalted kinds of high birth — born of seed, of the sacred thread, or of sacrificial rites? None at all.

_yu bane nahi jivna, avala savli mel(sare), purusha puje ramku, sakut naari dher_ ||4|| (Says Jivan: it can never work out this way — a mismatched pairing cannot succeed — where the husband worships Ram, but the wife in his house is a Sakut.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that no good outcome can ever come from mismatched, roundabout arrangements. If a man worships Ram, but the woman in his house is a Sakut who worships Anadev, no true welfare can result.

_sharir sakutan parsate, gun gaanthko jai, raghupati risave jivna, to harijan kaise sahay_ ||5|| (If the body even touches a Sakut, the virtue we have gathered is lost; and if Raghupati (Ram) becomes displeased, says Jivan, how then can Hari's devotees come to our aid?)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: if our body even touches a Sakut, that is, if we keep any dealings with a Sakut, then whatever good quality of single-minded devotion we have gained will be lost, and God Himself will become displeased with us — so how, then, could the grace and help of the saints ever reach us?

_vyas sakut bhaiyaa, chhandiye aur kubere karan saman, taki paant na khaiye, nishche narak nikhaan_ ||6|| (Vyas says: even one's own brother, if he is a Sakut, must be given up, even if he equals Kuber or Karna in greatness; never eat in the same row with him, for it certainly leads to hell.)

Vyasdasji says: even if one's own brother rivals the greatness of Kuber or Karna, if he is a Sakut, all relations with him must still be given up. One should not even sit and eat with him in the same row (pankti). If we do eat with him, we will certainly fall into hell.

_vyas viveki bhagatsu, dradh kar kije prit, avivekiko sang tyaj, ehi bhagatki reet_ ||7|| (Vyas says: form a firm and unwavering love with the discerning devotee, and give up the company of the undiscerning — this is the true way of a devotee.)

Vyasdasji says: with a discerning, understanding devotee who truly grasps exclusive devotion, one should form a deep and firm love; but the company of an undiscerning person who does not truly understand should be given up — this is exactly the way that exclusive devotees have adopted for themselves.

_kabir sakut saga na bhetiye, apne kanth lagay, parmaarath bahe jai, paap rahe lapataay_ ||8|| (Kabir says: do not embrace even your own kinsman if he is a Sakut, clasping him to your own chest — the true purpose of your life will slip away, and sin will cling to you instead.)

Das Kabirji says that we must not keep close dealings with kinsmen and loved relatives who are Sakut. Keeping relations with them will destroy the essence of our single-minded devotion, and the sin of ill counsel and bad conduct will attach itself to us.

_sakut sakut sabko kahe jivna, kachhu sakutan sidhaan, ninda karveku shurma, nahi guru vachan pramaan_ ||9|| (Everyone says "Sakut, Sakut," says Jivan, yet few truly understand what marks a Sakut: he is a hero at slandering others, and does not accept the guru's word as authority.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: everyone keeps saying "Sakut, Sakut," but the chief mark of who a Sakut truly is, is this — such people are bold and fearless in slandering and reviling Vishnu-bhakti and Hari, guru, and saints, and they refuse to accept the authority of the guru's teaching.

_sakut sakut sabko kah, kachhu sakut subhav, harijanki ninda kare, anadevku dhaya_ (Everyone says "Sakut, Sakut," yet few know the true nature of a Sakut: he slanders the devotees of Hari, and runs after Anadev.)

The devotee says: everyone keeps saying "Sakut, Sakut," but what is the true, essential nature of a Sakut? It is this — he keeps slandering the saints, and he worships Anadev.

_kabir bhagat hazaari kapada, taame mal na samay, sakat kaali kaamli, bhaavai tahan bichhaay_ ||10|| (Kabir says: a devotee is like fine, costly cloth, in which no dirt can lodge; a Sakut is like a black woollen blanket, spread out wherever it pleases.)

Das Kabirji says: devotees and saints possess exalted virtues, like fine, costly, brilliant-white cloth, in which the dirt of bad company can find no lodging. Sakuts, however, are wicked in their deeds, like a black woollen blanket — and just as there is no harm in spreading such a blanket out anywhere at all, so too the Sakuts remain spread out everywhere, sunk in sensual pleasure and desire.

_yatha hi malinair vastrair yatra tatropavishyato, evam chalitachittastu chittaashesham na rakshati_ ||30|| (Just as a man wearing soiled clothes will sit down anywhere at all without discrimination, so too a man whose mind has once wavered no longer guards the rest of his conduct at all.)

Just as a man wearing soiled clothes will sit down anywhere at all, in dust or dirt, without a second thought, so too a man who has once fallen away from virtuous conduct no longer cares about maintaining any other good conduct — he becomes given over to every kind of misconduct.

Trikamdas Gordhandas has written sakhis about Salil and Sakut.

_sakut sang karva thaki, manushya ang abhaday, kabir sadguru kahi gaya, samajethi sukh thay_ ||1|| (Through keeping company with a Sakut, a person's very body becomes defiled — so said the true guru Kabir; understanding this brings true happiness.)

Trikamdas says that, through keeping company with a Sakut, our human birth falls into a condition as good as untouchable, weighed down with sin — so the true guru Kabir has said. So if we understand and follow this advice, our welfare will be secured.

_nachna kudna talku pitna, randiya khelki bhakti nahi_ (Dancing, jumping about, and beating out the rhythm — a widow's playful sport is not devotion.)

If we merely dance, leap about, and play the drums outwardly for show and call it devotion, such a feeble, pitiable, hollow display is not true devotion at all.

_salil sakutna sangathi, gun gaandhno jai, patit bani pachhaday jataan, vaaso narakmaan thai_ ||2|| (Through company with the Salil and the Sakut, the virtue we have gathered slips away; we become fallen and are thrown down, and end up dwelling in hell.)

Trikamdas says that through the company of the Salil and the Sakut, the good qualities within us are lost, and we become sinful; our condition becomes wretched, and in the end we must go to hell.

In verse 60, Mahadev has described the exclusive (ananya) Vaishnavs.

_jnana vairagya samyuktaah syur bhogino'pi param tapah, jivan-muktaash cha vijneyaa ananyaa vaishnavaah sada_ ||60|| (Those Vaishnavs who are joined with knowledge and dispassion perform the highest austerity even while enjoying worldly pleasures; the exclusive Vaishnavs are always to be known as liberated while yet living.)

Those Vaishnavs who possess knowledge and dispassion perform the highest austerity even while they enjoy worldly pleasures. Know that exclusive (ananya) Vaishnavs are always liberated while still living (jivanmukta).

Verse 60 describes the exclusive Vaishnav devotee. These Vaishnavs are liberated while living; they carry no burden of worldly entanglement connected with the body and such things. Outwardly they may appear to be enjoying luxurious pleasures, but inwardly they remain untouched by desire — their mind is fixed only on devotion to God. The word "ananya" breaks down as _na + anya_ — "that which is not other than oneself," that is, one who does not regard God as other than one's own self.

In Kalyan magazine, year 75, issue 6, it is written: _jis prakar shodhan kiya hua sankhiya anek prakarke rogonko mita deta hai, usi prakar dharmik bhavse bhoge hue bhog vasanase upar utha dete hain_ (Just as purified arsenic can cure many kinds of diseases, in the same way pleasures enjoyed in a spirit of religious devotion raise a person above desire, rather than binding them to it.)

In the life-story of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, there occurs the account of the hidden devotee Pundarik Vidyanidhi. His outer life was extremely luxurious. He would sleep on a costly couch, anointed with fragrant perfume, while servants waved fans over him and he used costly utensils — yet inwardly he was utterly free of craving. (Register 54, page 119.) An exclusive devotee has no attachment to the body and such things. It is said in the Gita:

_ananyaash chintayanto maam ye janaah paryupasate, teshaam nityaabhiyuktaanaam yogakshemam vahaamyaham_ ||22|| (Those who worship Me alone, thinking of nothing else, ever united with Me — for them, I Myself carry the burden of what they lack and what they already have.)

Those who, without worshipping any other deity, meditate on Me, the Supreme Self, and worship Me alone — for such people, who remain always single-minded and devoted to Me alone, I Myself carry, in every way and without even being asked, both their "yoga" (the attainment of what is beneficial but not yet possessed) and their "kshema" (the preservation of what is beneficial and already possessed).

Kabir has described what a true renunciant (tyagi) and ascetic (vairagi) is really like — he tells us what one endowed with knowledge and dispassion is like.

_apraapati chizka kya taje, praapti taje sohan tyaag hai, saraasi turang kau kya phaire, kathanath phaire soi vauji hai, jag bhavka gaavna kya gaave, anabhav gaave soi ragi hai, grahvanki vasna nash kare, kabir soi vairagi hai_ ||61|| (What is given up by giving up a thing never possessed? True renunciation is giving up what one has actually obtained. What is there in turning a horse that is already reined? True skill lies in turning back a wild, unbroken horse. What use is singing of the world's cycle of birth and rebirth — true song lies in singing of direct experience. He who destroys the very desire for home and forest alike — says Kabir — he alone is the true renunciate.)

Das Kabirji says: if you give up a thing you could never have had in the first place, what real renunciation is that? True renunciation is giving up what you have actually obtained. What great feat is it to turn a horse that already has a bridle and reins? Turning a truly wild, untamed horse — that is real horsemanship. What is the use of endlessly talking about the pleasures of this worldly ocean of birth and rebirth? He who sings, instead, the praises of that which lies beyond the ocean of birth and rebirth — he is the true lover of God. He who destroys the craving for both the household and the forest — he alone is the true renunciate.

_apraaptaku sab taje, praapti taje na koi, kahai kabir praapti taje, tyagi kahiye soi_ (Everyone gives up what they could never have gotten; no one gives up what they have actually obtained. Says Kabir: he who gives up what he has actually obtained — he alone should be called a true renunciate.)

Das Kabirji says: whatever we could never obtain in any case, everyone is quick to give up — but no one gives up what they have actually attained. So truly, only those who give up something they have actually obtained deserve to be called renunciates.

A sakhi of Kabirji is given here about saints and devotees whose minds are free of attachment, describing the strength of mind such devotees possess.

_gavan hi me rovna, rovan hi me rag, ek banaahi me ghar kare, ek dharahi me bairag_ ||1|| (Within singing itself lies weeping, and within weeping itself lies melody; one person makes his home even in the forest, while another lives in renunciation even within his own house.)

Das Kabirji says: what a strange spectacle this is — that one devotee, even while enjoying worldly pleasures within the household life, remains detached and free of attachment, and even in this state of detachment experiences the joy of loving devotion. On the other hand, those who have renounced the world and taken to life in the forest, even while living in the forest, indulge in pleasures and luxuries just like a householder. And the devotee who has taken up devotion right within his own household has begun to live, right there in the household, a life just like that of a true renunciate.

_vaneshu doshaah prabhavanti raginaam griheshu panchendriya nigrahastapah, akutsite karmani yah pravartate nivrittaraagasya griham tapovanam_ ||904|| (For one whose passions still cling, faults will arise even in the forest; controlling the five senses even while in the household is itself true austerity. For one who engages only in blameless action, and whose passions have truly ceased, the household itself becomes a forest of austerity.)

For a person who still has attachment to sensual objects, faults will arise even if such a person goes and lives in the forest. But for one who has cultivated restraint over his five senses even while living at home, that restraint itself is true austerity (tapa) in his mind. That is to say, for a person who remains occupied with good, blameless deeds and whose attachment to sensual objects has truly departed, the household itself becomes his forest of austerity.

One who disregards the householder life and goes to practise austerity in the forest — if such an ascetic later returns to the householder life, he is normally considered worthy of censure. Even though this is generally considered blameworthy, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu commanded Nityananda to give up his renunciate order (sannyas) and return to the householder life; yet he did not become an object of censure for it. Only hypocrites deserve censure.

_pahele dhar chhodya apna, pichhe paithe dhar maanhi, tulsi aise patitka, darshan kije naahi_ (First he gave up his own home; then afterwards he entered a home once more — Tulsi says: never even set eyes on such a fallen person.)

Tulsidas says: never even look upon a sinner who first, as an ascetic, gave up his householder's home, and then went back and entered the householder life once more.

_tulsi dharke dherme, dhadi dhadi tan chhin, kabahu ban banna phirai, kar karva kaupin, dharahi manhi ban kare, hari charane lauleen, tulsi aise santaaku, kaha karva kopin_ (Tulsi says: for such a false ascetic, moment by moment the body wastes away in worry over worldly household matters, though he wanders about with a water-pot and loincloth as if in the forest; but he who makes even his own home into a forest, absorbed lovingly at Hari's feet — for such a saint, says Tulsi, what need has he at all for a water-pot or a loincloth?)

Tulsidas says: there may be one whose body wastes away with worry in the whirl of the householder life, and who never actually wanders about from forest to forest holding a water-pot in hand, wearing a loincloth. Such a devotee, who lives out a forest-like life of devotion to God right within his own home — what need does such a saint have of a water-pot or a loincloth at all?

(In Raga Sarang.)

_kaha dar hai dharbaarko, jaake harde hariko samaran, dhokho naahi lagaarko. rahe dharmaanhe kaha ban maanhe, e to gyaan vichaarko, dhar chhodeki kaha bhalai, jutho khaaye sansaarko. tan vairagine man dharbaari, etu gyaan gamaarko, ek hi chhad anant hi laago, bhaar vahe sansaarko. hari chitaro harde dhaaro, gor gam gyaan apaarko, taaku karam kabhu nahi laage, sevak sarjanhaarko. sujha padhaavat gunka taari, vaaku vanaj vikaarko, ajaamel patit odhaariyo, naam liyo kartaako. seni dhana pipa aur napa, raanka jaat kumbharki, bhavna bhagatko khaando kaathkos pragat palat bhayo saarko. naanma kabira prem bhagat bhaye, aur rohidas chamaarku, dher betha govind grun gaave, bakhno sarjanharko_ (What fear of household bonds can there be for one whose heart holds the remembrance of Hari — no deceit of maya touches such a one at all. Whether one lives in the home or in the forest is merely a matter of thought and understanding; what good is there in leaving the home, if it only means living off the stale, cast-off food of the world? One whose body alone is renounced while the mind still runs after household matters — that is the foolish "wisdom" of an ignorant person; he leaves one home only to attach himself to countless others, and carries the burden of the world instead. Remember Hari, hold Him in your heart — this is the boundless wisdom the guru teaches; upon such a servant of the Creator, the bondage of karma never falls. He is taught the true worth of virtue; his trade is destroying vice. Ajamil, a fallen sinner, was delivered simply because he took the Name of the Creator. Seni, Dhana, Pipa, Napa, and Ranka of the potter caste were saved likewise; the devotee Bhavan's wooden sword was openly transformed into one of iron. Namdev, Kabir, and Rohidas the cobbler all became devotees of loving devotion — says Bakhno: seated right in one's own home, one may sing the praises of Govind, the Creator.)

Bakhnaji says: how could an exclusive devotee ever fear the illusion of household life, when the remembrance of Hari's Name is constantly running in his heart? Where that is so, no deceit of maya can remain at all. Whether one lives in a home or in a forest is a mere matter of imagination; what real benefit is there in leaving one's home, when the one who leaves must, in exchange, eat the leftover, tainted earnings of worldly people instead? Such people's bodies alone look like those of renunciates, while their minds remain exactly as worldly and household-bound as ever — this is the false understanding of such foolish people. They leave behind one single household and family, only to attach themselves to the company of countless worldly people instead, and take on the burdens and responsibilities of worldly life. Following the deep teaching of the guru, hold fast to God within your heart, as one worthy of your constant remembrance. A devotee of God, the Creator of the universe, is never bound by the fetters of karma. There was a courtesan whose trade was sensual indulgence, yet she taught her parrot to say the name of Ram, and God delivered her. Ajamil, who was a great sinner, took God's Name, and so God delivered him too. God rescued Seni Bhagat, Dhana Bhagat, Pipaji, and Napaji, as well as Ranka Bhagat, who was of the potter caste. For the devotee Bhagat Chavan, He turned a wooden sword into one of iron to help him. Namdev, Kabirji, and Rohidasji the cobbler became practitioners of loving devotion (prem-lakshana bhakti); staying seated right within their own homes, they practised devotion to God — and I, Bakhno, am likewise a devotee of the Creator of the universe, and a householder just the same.

(In Raga Desag.)

_sohi harijan grahi bhala, jaake harisu prit, raat divas visre nahi, aur harijan mit. kul karni sab bhetke, taje jug vahevaara, kshudha pramane udyam karai, aur taje pasaara. kanak kaamini kaalpana, parninda na jaane, bhaav bhagat hari pritsu, baana hi maane. kaam krodh mad matsar, abhimaan nivaarai, apna jiv sabhinka jaane, daya dharam vichaarai. kahat kabir kaljugme, harijan koi ek, aur sab swaangi sabai, jaake chit anek_ (That householder-devotee alone is blessed who has true love for Hari, never forgetting Him day or night, and who befriends only Hari's own devotees. Setting aside all family customs and worldly practices, he labours only enough to satisfy his hunger, and gives up all other display and excess. He harbours no thought of gold or women, and knows nothing of slandering others; his only mark and manner is loving devotion to Hari. He drives out lust, anger, pride, and envy; he regards his own soul as one with the souls of all beings, and reflects always on compassion and righteousness. Says Kabir: in this dark age of Kali, such a true devotee of Hari is one in a rare while — all the rest are mere pretenders, their minds scattered among countless things.)

_kabir sant samagam param sukh, aan alap sukh aur, maan sarovar hans hai, bagla thoro thaur. kabir sant sangat sabate saras, baana sat sab os, sant sabad parmaante, kaate kot adh dosh_ (Kabir says: fellowship with saints, satsang, is the highest happiness — all other happiness is little in comparison. As the swan lives on Man Sarovar lake, while the crane wanders here, there, and everywhere. Kabir says: the company of saints is sweeter than everything else; all worldly appearance is but a fleeting dewdrop. Through the authority of the saint's own word, crores of sins accumulated over past lives are cut away.)

Das Kabirji says: devotees who have true love for devotion to God within their hearts are excellent indeed, even if they are householders. They never, day or night, forget God and the company of Hari's devotees. They give up all worldly dealings bound up with family custom. They do not dwell on thoughts of gold or women, nor do they slander others. Their only fixed resolve is to practise devotion to God with loving feeling. They rid themselves of lust, anger, pride, envy, and arrogance. They understand their own soul as existing for the welfare of all beings, and they keep to the path of compassion and righteousness. Kabirji says that in this dark age of Kali, only a rare few such saints exist; all the rest are mere pretenders in disguise, whose hearts are filled with countless different desires.

Das Kabirji says: fellowship (samagam) with a saint is the highest happiness of all; every other happiness besides this is only slight, present in a very small measure. Just as the finest of souls, the swans, dwell in Man Sarovar lake, while hypocritical pretenders, like cranes, wander here and there...

...it is so. Das Kabirji says that the company of saints is the very best of all, while outward garb (the wearing of robes) is as trifling as hundreds of dew-drops. But if we properly heed the teaching of a saint, it wipes away the faults of millions of our sins.

God works in the world only through His devotee. Adhyaruji's own utterance on this is given below.

_Ghodli kar vina mande re vishva, pag vina sacharachar phire ||ghodli||
Ghodli mukh vina bole saar, lochan vina dekhe sahu ||ghodli||
Ghodli udar pakhe kare aahar, indi vina sukh bhogave ||ghodli||_ (Like a little horse, without hands He fashions the universe; without feet He moves through all that is moving and unmoving. Without a mouth He utters the finest words, and without eyes He sees everything. Without a stomach He takes food, and without senses He enjoys pleasure.)

The senses are this "little horse." In this way God has created the universe without hands. Without feet He can move everywhere, through the moving and the unmoving. Without a mouth He utters the finest words, and without eyes He can see everything. Without a stomach He eats food, and without senses He enjoys pleasure.

Just as God, being all-powerful, can do everything, so too the devotee can enjoy all pleasures without craving for them, and he can do so by resting his faith on the power of devotion to God.

_Kabir chakor bharose chandrake, jalta gale angaar.
Harijan maya khaat hai, dazhat nahi lagaar. ||4||_ (Trusting in the moon, the chakor bird swallows a burning ember; likewise the devotee of Hari partakes of maya, yet is not burnt in the least.)

Das Kabirji says that the chakor bird has firm faith in the coolness of the moon, and so it swallows even a burning coal without being scorched; likewise devotees too partake of maya, trusting in devotion to God, and yet they do not have to suffer the threefold afflictions and other such sorrows.

Trikamdas Gordhandas has written a kundali (a linked-verse composition) on the chatak bird:

_Samajhya jan sansarma, chup thai maun rahay.
Bole bijo thai jaso, samjhi chup rahay.
Samjhi chup rahay, vani par kabu karta.
Sahej samadhi janogh, dhumade bachka bharta.
Samjhel gurugam gaay, chakor chanch angarma.
Chup thai maun rahay, samajhya jan sansarma._ (Those who have truly understood remain silent in this world; speak, and one becomes something else — so, having understood, one stays quiet. Having understood, one stays quiet and holds one's speech in check; the multitude who understand attain effortless absorption, [while others merely] gulp at smoke. Those who have grasped the guru's teaching sing of it, as the chakor puts its beak into the burning coal; having understood, one stays silent in this world.)

Trikamdas says that people who have truly understood in this world become quiet and remain inactive, without giving voice to any kind of utterance, for if they were to stir up some other agitation it would lead only to harm — so, understanding this, they stay quiet. Understanding this, they withdraw within and keep their desires under check. But those who wish merely to observe a vow of silence (muni-vrat) without this natural, spontaneous one-pointedness are only laboring at a futile effort. Those, however, who have truly grasped the guru's teaching swallow the burning coal and its heat without fear, just as the chakor does — such people who have understood walk on trusting in the guru's command. Thus those who have truly understood in this world will live out their lives peacefully, free of [worldly] craving.

The chakor bird eats burning coals on the day of the full moon. Regarding this it is said:

_Lagi lagan chhute nahi, jibh chonch jari jaay.
Mitha kaha angarme, jahi chakor chabaay._ (Once a deep longing takes hold it does not let go, even if the tongue and beak get burnt. What sweetness is there, after all, in a burning coal, that the chakor should chew it?)

When there is intense longing for something, it cannot be given up, even if — as with the chakor — the tongue or beak gets burnt; whether it is tasty or not is of no concern. What sweetness could there be, after all, in the burning coal that the chakor goes for, that even though it gets scorched, it will not let go of it?

Those with single-minded devotion become absorbed in God alone and have no concern for anything else. As to what such devotion should be like, it is said:

_Chakoranam mathuranam tatha shubham, lakshananam dosh nirbhuktam dharya shri-nama-tatparaih. ||1||_ (One devoted to the holy Name should bear these faultless marks — the vow of the chatak, the gaze of the chakor, and the listening of the peacock.)

Like the chatak (a steadfast vow), like the chakor (meditation), and like the peacock (listening to the sound) — these faultless marks should be adopted by one devoted to the [divine] Name.

In separation from Sita, Ram wandered about the forest in great distress; seeing the forest birds calling out, His mind agitated, Ram said to the birds, "I am burning in separation," and cursed them: He told the cuckoo that her song would fall silent after spring. He told the deer and doe that when they mated, the hunter would kill them. He told the elephant and she-elephant that when they mated they would swoon for seven days. He told the peacock he would become impotent. He told the lion he would mate only once in his life. And He said to the chakwa and chakwi (the ruddy-shelduck pair):

_Chakwa chakwine kahe, thajo tamaro viyog.
Hu virahine dekhi kari, tame bhogvo chho bhog. ||8||_ (He said to the chakwa and chakwi: may separation come upon you too — for even seeing Me in separation, you go on enjoying your union.)

He said to the chakwa and chakwi that even though they saw Him in separation, they still enjoyed their union with one another; therefore they too would suffer separation.

Hearing this curse, all the birds and animals came seeking refuge, and He then softened it somewhat. To the cuckoo He gave her song only for the spring season. He said the deer and doe would be killed by the hunter only if they mated by day; the elephant and she-elephant would swoon for only two ghadis (about forty-eight minutes). He said the peacock's line would increase through tears. He said the chakwa and chakwi would be separated only at night. He said the lion would mate only once in his life.

_Kabir harijan aisa chahiye, udar samo ras leh.
Tame ganthe bandhasi, to jale pakhsu deh. ||5||_ (Kabir says: the devotee of Hari should be such that he takes only as much relish as fills his belly; if he ties up more than that for himself, his whole body will burn away.)

Das Kabirji says that a devotee should be such that he enjoys the taste of food only enough to sustain himself; but if he is tempted to hoard more than that, then he will be utterly destroyed, body and all — burnt away completely.

_Kabir parmeshwar te jan bades, taka kaha unmaan.
Hari maya aage dharai, sant rahe nivani._ (Kabir says: the devotee is even greater than God — what measure is there for this? Hari keeps maya before Himself, while the saint remains untouched by it.)

Das Kabirji says that the devotee is greater than God, and the measure of this is that God keeps maya present before the devotee, while the saint remains untouched by it.

Confirmation that Vasudevji and His devotees are one and the same in form — Divine Maya and the Ten Incarnations.

The devotee (harijan) is nirgun (attributeless) for the very reason that Vasudev too dwells in attributeless form within His devotees.

_Rup rekh kachhu vapu nahi, aise he Raghupati Raay.
Aise harijan Jivana, je naam nirmal jas gaay. ||1||_ (Raghupati Ray, the King, has no form, mark, or body at all — such too is the devotee, O Jivan, who sings the pure glory of His Name.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that just as King Ram has no shape or form of any kind, so too are His devotees, who sing the hymns and kirtans of the holy divine Name.

_Rup rekh jihi hai nahi, adhar dhari nahi deh.
Gagan mandalke vichme, nirkho purush videh._ (He who has no form or mark, who bears no body at all — behold that bodiless Being in the midst of the sky of the inner heavens.)

Das Kabirji says that the Supreme Being, the Paramatma, who has no form, shape, or kind whatsoever, who is bodiless, who has never taken on a body — behold that Lord in the empty sky of your inner soul.

In verse 61 of the Samagam, quoting Madri's words from the eleventh shlok of the Pandav Gita, the oneness of God and His devotees is described.

Madri Uvach (Madri speaks):

_Krishne rataah Krishnam anusmaranti ratrau cha Krishnam punarutthita ye,
te'bhinna-dehaah pravishanti Krishne havir yatha mantra-hutam hutasho. ||61||_ (Those devoted to Krishna remember Krishna at night, and on rising again remember Krishna; with bodies no longer distinct from Him, they enter into Krishna, as an oblation offered with mantras merges into the fire.)

Those who are in love with Krishna remember Lord Krishna at night, and the moment they rise, they remember Krishna again. Just as an oblation offered into the fire with mantras merges into that fire, so too they, becoming one in body with Him, enter into Krishna.

Explaining this shlok, the Samagam writes that the body of those who constantly remember Krishna is itself the body of God — there is no difference between them and God. Giving an example of this, it says that whatever we offer into fire itself becomes fire. Explaining this point, Revered Yadunath Maharaj writes in Lintiyu 38, page 14:

"There is an iron rod; when put into the fire it turns red. Now if you tell someone that fire is in this iron, he will say yes. Then tell him to separate the rod and the fire and show them apart — that is impossible. In the same way, it is also impossible to show Ram as separate from Kabir."

This chapter on the single-minded devotee comes roughly in the middle portion of the Samagam. In it, the divine Name "Ramkabir" given to us by Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj is presented here as the central theme. We become confused seeing the joining of the two names Ram and Kabir, and so the explanation of this has been given here at length; explaining it briefly, it is said that just as the devotee and God are both undivided, so too Ram and Kabir are one and the same — the Samagam gives two sakhis (couplets) on this.

_Kabir Ram Kabira ek hai, chinhe virla koy.
Antar mari kapatki, tathe dise doy. ||1||_ (Kabir says: Ram and Kabir are one, but only some rare one recognizes this; because a veil of deceit lies within, they appear to be two.)

Das Kabirji says that Ram and Kabir are indeed one and the same, but only a rare few can understand this mystery, because those whose inner heart has the veil of maya's illusion drawn over it feel that these are two separate beings.

_Kabir Ramkabira ek hai, kahan sunanko doy.
Do kari soi janai, jako sadguru mila na hoy. ||2||_ (Kabir says: Ram-Kabir is one; only in the speaking and hearing does it seem two. He who takes it to be two is one who has not met a true guru.)

Das Kabirji says that Ram and Kabir are one and undivided, but in speaking and hearing, for the sake of ordinary usage, their practical form appears as two, or as many; but only those who have not found a true guru take them to be two in ultimate reality.

Much has been said about the oneness of Ram and Kabir:

_Kabir Ram Kabira hoi rahya, kiyo kaljug mahi pravesh.
Sarv santan sukh karane, naam dharaya das doy._ (Kabir: Ram became Kabir and entered the Kali Yuga; for the well-being of all saints, He took on two names as devotee.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says in the Bhetka Ang that God, who bears the name Ram, became one in the form of Kabir and became known in the Kali Yuga as Ram-Kabir. To bring about the welfare of all saints, God took on these two forms — Ram-Kabir (Krishna-Kabir) — and assumed the title of being God's own devotee.

_Do aksharke antare, Ram Kabira ek.
So samjhat hai Jivana, jake sadguru diyo vivek._ (Only the two syllables differ — Ram and Kabir are one. This is understood, O Jivan, only by him to whom the true guru has given discernment.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that the only difference between Ram and Kabir is in these two sets of syllables. Otherwise, Ram and Kabir are one and the same form. But this can be understood only by those to whom the true guru has explained the mystery of this name and form.

_Ram Kabira ek hai, kahan sunanku doy.
Inme dushadha jo kare, maha narki hoy._ (Ram-Kabir is one; only in speaking and hearing does it seem two. Whoever creates doubt about this becomes the greatest of sinners.)

Das Kabirji says that the divine Name is a single reality; only in speaking and hearing does it seem like two. But whoever harbors doubt about this matter will be the greatest of sinners.

_Ram Kabira ek ai, ja ghatma pravesh.
Sharir dhare pan Jivana, adhar unka desh._ (Ram-Kabir is one, who entered this vessel [the body]; He takes on a body, O Jivan, yet His true realm is unsupported, beyond.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that Ram and Kabir are one and the same — it is that very Ram who entered into the body of Kabir (Ram dwells within every single body); God comes taking on a form with attributes, but God's true dwelling place is a unique one within the innermost self.

On this sakhi Trikamdas has written a kundali:

_Ram Kabira ek ai, ja ghatma pravesh.
Sharir dhare pan Jivana, adhar unka desh.
Adhar unoka desh, dekhe koi gurugam chela.
Manmati samajhat nahi, samje jene vivek hai.
Ja ghatnam pravesh, Ram Kabira ek hai._ (Ram-Kabir is one, who entered this vessel; He takes on a body, O Jivan, yet His true realm is unsupported, beyond. His unsupported realm — only a disciple who has received the guru's teaching can see it. One who follows his own opinion does not understand; only one with discernment understands. He who entered by name into this vessel — Ram and Kabir are one.)

Ram and Kabir are one and the same — it is that Ram who entered in body under the name of Kabir. This Ram-God does not, in fact, take on a body as one with attributes and form; rather, His dwelling place is a unique one within the innermost self. God's true abode rests on no support of any kind, and it can be understood only by those disciples who have received their guru's teaching. But those who are self-willed, who think according to their own whims, do not grasp this mystery — they are the sort of fools who cannot tell right from wrong. Those who can discern right from wrong understand that, for God, form-with-attributes and the formless-without-attributes are both one and the same — that God who has entered into the world of bodies is that very God, Ram-Kabir, one and undivided.

_Ram Kabira ek hai, naam dharaya doy.
Kahe Kabir do naam suni, bharam pado mat koy._ (Ram-Kabir is one; only two names have been taken on. Kabir says: hearing these two names, let no one fall into confusion.)

Das Kabirji says that Ram and Kabir are one and the same, but only two separate names have been taken on. Kabir says, let no one, on hearing two names, fall into the delusion that they are two separate beings.

_Virha virha sabko kahe, kachhu virhaka sidhaan.
Ram Kabira ek kare, Jivan jan pramaan._ (Everyone speaks of "separation, separation," but there is a true mark of separation. He who makes Ram and Kabir one, O Jivan, is proof of the true devotee.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that everyone keeps saying that the loving devotee is in separation from God, but the chief marks of a true virahi (one in longing) are these: just as Ram and Kabir are one and undivided, so too the true virahi is one who becomes wholly one in form with God.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has given an important sakhi in the section on separation (viraha ang) about this. In it he tells what true separation is like: a person who is separated from his beloved is indeed a virahi, but through contemplation of the beloved he becomes suffused with that beloved and becomes one in form with him. It is said:

_Je jenu chintavan kare, te temaj thai jaay.
Prabhu chintavi prabhumaya thavu, kir bhramvat nyaay._ (Whoever contemplates something becomes exactly that; by contemplating the Lord, one becomes suffused with the Lord — as in the logic of the wasp and the caterpillar.)

Whoever keeps contemplating something becomes one in form with that very thing he contemplates. Therefore if we contemplate the Lord, we can become suffused with the Lord — just as when a wasp stings a caterpillar, the caterpillar keeps contemplating the wasp alone, and thereby itself becomes a wasp.

This is such a law — thus when Hanumanji met Sita in Lanka, Sita said that she was in separation from Ram, and what afflicted her more was that she contemplated Ram continually, night and day; therefore it would be well if, taking on Ram's own form, she became Ram's — for greater than becoming Ram himself is the joy of loving devotion found in becoming Ram's devotee. If she herself were to become Ram, how would she attain the joy of loving devotion to Ram? One can know the joy of sweetness only in eating sugar-candy; but if she herself became the sugar-candy, how could she know what taste is in it? In the same way, Jivanji's sakhi tells us that a true virahi is like Kabir: just as Kabir became one with Ram-Kabir, so too, if one becomes one in form with the very mark of separation, that one is reckoned a true virahi.

_Ram jape nit santko, sant jape nit Ram.
Gyani palak na visare, aama saama naam. ||2||_ (Ram forever recites the saint's name, and the saint forever recites Ram's; O Gyani, not for a moment do they forget each other's name.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says that Ram forever chants the name of the saint, and the saint forever chants the name of Ram. Thus the two never forget each other's names, not even for a single moment.

_Swami sevakme vase, sevak swami mahi.
Gyani dono mil rahya, palbhar visare nahi. ||3||_ (The Master dwells in the servant, and the servant in the Master; O Gyani, the two remain merged and never forget each other for even a moment.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says that God the Master dwells within the devotee, and the devotee dwells within God; thus the two have merged into one another. Not even for a moment do they forget each other.

_Ye yatha mam prapadyante tams tathaiva bhajamyaham,
mama vartma-anuvartante manushyah partha sarvashah. ||11||_ In whatever way they come to Me for refuge, in that same way do I bestow Myself upon them — that is, I grant them their fruit; to one who worships Me desiring worldly fruit, I show grace by granting the fruit he wishes, and to one who worships Me without desire, I give him My own abode. O Partha, in every way, men follow My path.

_Virha bauri Jivana, aatur haal sharir.
Ram Kabira jab milai, tab paavai man dhir._ (Separation drives one mad, O Jivan; the body remains in an anguished state — only when Ram and Kabir become one does the mind find peace.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that the restless condition of a body made distraught by the pain of separation is such that its mind finds peace only when it becomes one in form with the beloved.

_Ram Kabir hi satya hai, aur sat hi Ram Kabir.
Paramatma Parameshwar hai, vohi din bandhu Raghuvir._ (Ram-Kabir alone is the truth, and truth itself is Ram-Kabir; He is the Supreme Soul, the Supreme Lord — He alone is the friend of the lowly, Raghuvir.)

In the Bhet Sakhi it is said that there is no difference in Ram-Kabir; Ram-Kabir is itself the true, real divine reality, and that which is the ultimate truth, the Parabrahma, is itself Ram-Kabir. Thus Kabir's supreme, highest soul is the Supreme Lord — He, born among men, is Ram, the benevolent friend of His devotees.

_Kabir dekho Ram hai, ek hi ras bharpur.
Jaise urvase sab bana, chini sakkar gud._ (Kabir: behold, it is Ram in everything — one single essence, brimming full — just as from sugarcane are made sugar, sugar-candy, and jaggery.)

Das Kabirji says: reflect deeply and see — Ram alone dwells in everything. This one essence in the form of Ram is fully present and pervading in each and every thing; just as from sugarcane are made sugar, sugar-candy, and jaggery, so too from this one Ram has this whole universe come to be, in its many varied forms.

_Raat dhola pila hai, koi kala hai aur laal.
Ram prabhuke sabhi to, bhinna bhinna hai ye baal._ (Some are red, some white, some yellow, some black — all of these are the children of Lord Ram, differing only in outward form.)

In the Bhet Sakhi it is said that in this world some are red, some white, some yellow, and some black — all of these are indeed the varied children of Lord Ram.

_Ram Ram japte japte, Kabir Ram ho gaye.
Aur Kabir Kabir kahte kahte, Ram Kabir ban gaye._ (Chanting "Ram, Ram" again and again, Kabir became Ram; and saying "Kabir, Kabir" again and again, Ram became Kabir.)

In the Bhet Sakhi it is said that by chanting Ram's name, "Ram, Ram," Kabirji became Ram, and in the same way, by saying "Kabir, Kabir," Ram took on the form of Kabir.

_Mera man nirmal bhaya, jaisa chokkha nir.
Piche piche Hari phirat, japat Kabir Kabir._ (My mind became pure, like clear water; behind me Hari now wanders, chanting "Kabir, Kabir.")

Das Kabirji says that when my mind became free of defilement, like clear water, God began following behind me, chanting "Kabir, Kabir."

_Prem rup Kabirji, aatam Raghupati naam.
Jan tarveku Jivana, kali kiyo vishram._ (Kabirji is the very form of love; the Name of Raghupati is his soul; to ferry devotees across, O Jivan, he took his abode in the Kali Yuga.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that Kabirji is the very form of love, and the Name of Ram is his soul; in this form of Ram-Kabir, he came into the Kali Yuga in order to deliver His devotees.

_Kabir marte marte jag mua, sut vit daara joy.
Ram Kabira ho raha, yo mua, ek barabar boy._ (The world dies again and again, looking upon son, wealth, and wife; but he who has become Ram-Kabir dies in this manner — sowing as one and equal with God.)

Das Kabirji says that the worldly soul, looking on maya such as son, wealth, and wife, dies over and over in delusion. But the loving devotee soul who is of Ram's own form keeps an equal vision toward the one Ram present in all, becomes free of bodily pride, and becomes one in form with Ram.

_Ram-Krishna Karima ek hai, naam dharaya doy.
Kahai Kabir do naam suni, bharam pado mat koy._ (Ram-Krishna and Karim [the Merciful] are one; only two names have been taken on. Kabir says: hearing these two names, let no one fall into confusion.)

Das Kabirji says that Ram-Krishna and the merciful Khuda (God) are one and the same God, but only these two names have been taken on. There is no need for anyone to make a distinction between these two.

_Sahjai sahjai sab gaya, sut vit kaam nikaam.
Ekmek hai Ram mil raha, das Kabira Ram._ (Naturally, effortlessly, all passed away — desire for son, wealth, and worldly aims; utterly merged as one, Ram remains united [with him] — the servant Kabir is Ram.)

Das Kabirji says that when the state of natural spontaneity (sahaj) is attained, the desire for offspring, the desire to give away wealth, and worldly desire naturally fall away on their own, and the devotee, merging together with Ram, becomes one and the same with Him.

In the shlok on Hari it is said that Hari and His devotee are one — this shlok is from the Niranjan Purana:

_Vaishnava Vishnu-dehash cha bhinnam janati ye narah,
te narah narakam yanti yavash chandra-divakarau. ||62||_ Those who consider the Vaishnavas and the body of Lord Vishnu to be separate — such people fall into hell (suffering) for as long as the moon and sun exist.

_Vaishnava mam dehastu tasmat pujyo mahamune,
anyatnam parityajya Vaishnavan bhaja shashvatam._ O great sage, the Vaishnavas are Myself, My very body — therefore worship them alone. Give up all other endeavors and forever worship, serve, and keep the holy company of the Vaishnavas alone.

_Harih sada vasottatra yatra bhagavata janah,
gayanti bhakti-bhavena harer namaiva kevalam._ Wherever devotees sing only the Name of Hari with a spirit of devotion, there God dwells forever.

_Kabir Shankar puchhe Brahmaku, ek akshar tattva-saar.
Je te bhakt bhomi par, te te Hari avataar._ (Kabir: Shankar asks Brahma about the one imperishable essence of truth — whatever devotees there are upon this earth, they are all incarnations of Hari.)

Das Kabirji says that Shankar asks Brahma about the one imperishable divine reality, and this true thing is that however many devotees there are upon the earth, all of them are incarnations of God.

_Harijan mile to Hari mile, man paaya vishwas.
Harijan Harika ansh hai, jyon phulanme vaas._ (If one meets a devotee of Hari, it is as though one has met Hari — the mind gains this conviction; the devotee is a part of Hari, just as fragrance dwells in a flower.)

If one meets a devotee of Hari, it has instilled in the mind the conviction that one has met God Himself, because just as fragrance is itself a part of the flower, so too the devotee is a part of God Himself.

In the Bhaktamal, devotion, devotee, God, and guru — all four are said to be one and the same.

_Bhakti bhakt bhagwant guru, chatur naam vapu ek.
Inke pad vandan kiye, naasho vidhan anek._ Devotion, devotee, God, and guru — these four bearing different names have but one and the same body. By bowing at their feet, many obstacles are destroyed.

Dayaldas too has written likewise:

_Dayala Harigur, santko ek mel bai, jyu dudhi madhye maakh chhut chhash.
Yu Hari gur harijanme, tathe harijan Haridas. ||20||_ (O merciful Hari, guru, and saint are a single mixed union, just as within milk lie butter, ghee, and buttermilk; in this way Hari, guru, and His devotees are all in one another — hence the devotee is a servant of Hari.)

Dayaldas says that Hari, guru, and saint are one combined mixture. Just as butter, ghee, and buttermilk are all present within milk, so too Hari, the guru, and His devotee dwell within one another — and therefore devotees are the servants of God.

_Sadguru sadhu Ramji, naam teen ang ek.
Gyani jinche ang lahya, tin paaya bada vivek._ (Sadguru, saint, and Lord Ram — three names, one body. Whoever has grasped this, O Gyani, has attained the greatest discernment.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says that Sadguru, saint, and Lord Ram — these three names are different, but their body is one and the same. Those who have understood this mystery have understood the very best of all.

_Harithe harijan bade, samjhi dekhu man mahi.
Kabir sabgaj Haru vishe, so Hari harijan mahi._ (The devotee is greater than Hari — see this and understand it well in your mind; everything is contained within Hari, and so Hari is contained within the devotee.)

Das Kabirji says: take it firmly into your mind that the devotee is even greater than God, because that whole world which is contained within God is, in turn, contained within the devotee.

_Sant sangatme Hari vase, unte duri nahi.
Gyani sab jag thaapke, aap basa in mahi. ||4||_ (Hari dwells in the company of saints; there is no distance from them. O Gyani, having established the whole world, He Himself dwells within these saints.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says that God dwells in the company of saints and is not far from them; having brought forth the creation of the world while remaining beyond it, God Himself dwells within that saint.

_Garbhvant Govindadi, saheb santo mahi.
Gyani dije ekku, dono pokhya jaay. ||30||_ (Govind dwells [within, as one who is] pregnant — the Master is within the saints; O Gyani, give to the one saint, and both are nourished.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says that God dwells within the devotee as a child dwells in the womb; in this way God abides within the saints. Therefore if we give food and drink to the saint alone, God who dwells within that womb also receives nourishment from it.

_Mai anahadme had hu, mai nirgun gun mahi.
Mai Ramnaam samool hu, jan bina duja nahi. ||97||_ (I am the bounded within the boundless, I am both attributeless and possessed of attributes; I am wholly present in the Name of Ram — there is nothing else apart from My devotee.)

Das Kabirji says: within the boundless reality, I also abide as the bounded; though I am beyond the three gunas and free of attributes, I also possess attributes. I am wholly and entirely present in the Name of Ram; and apart from the devotee (harijan) in whom that Name of Ram dwells, there is nothing else.

_Hadme behad mil raha, behad e behadke mahi.
Pala gal paani bhaya, yu harijan Hari mahi. ||60||_ (The boundless merges within the bounded, and the bounded is within the boundless; as frost melts and becomes water, so too is the devotee within Hari.)

Das Kabirji, in the Asasa Ang, speaking of the furnishings kept in the house that is the universe, says that within the bounded limits of creation, the boundless divine reality lies merged and present. In that boundless reality it lies contained in its boundless state. Just as ice melts and becomes water, so too do devotees (harijans) abide within God.

_Sadhavo hridayam mahyam, sadhunam hridayam tvaham.
Madanyat te na jananti, naaham tebhyo managapi. ||68||_ O Durvasa, what more can I tell you — My loving devotees are My own heart, and I myself am the heart of these loving devotees. They know nothing apart from Me, and I too know nothing apart from them.

_Kabir dil mila dayalasu, tab kachhu antar nahi.
Pala gal paani bhaya, chu harijan hai Hari mahi._ (Kabir: when the heart merges with the merciful Lord, then no distinction remains; as frost melts and becomes water, so is the devotee within Hari.)

Das Kabirji says that if our inner heart merges with the merciful Supreme Soul, then no difference remains between us and God; just as ice melts and becomes water, so too the devotee merges within God.

In shlok 63 it is said that one who remembers the divine Name gains everything.

_Sarva-dharmarjita Vishnor naama-matraika-jalpika,
sukhena triptim aapnoti jagat-sarva-prakashika. ||63||_ One who gives up all other observances and chants only the Name of Vishnu attains satisfaction easily, with happiness.

In the commentary on this shlok it is said that by remembering the divine Name, the entire universe becomes satisfied; God is satisfied only by the taking of His Name, and if His Name is not taken, God is not satisfied. Giving an example of this it says that just as watering the trunk of a tree nourishes all its leaves, so too by taking the divine Name there is no need for anything else in the whole universe — no sacrifices, rituals, or mantras.

_Yatha taror-mula nishechanena, tripyanti tat-skandha bhujopashakhah.
Pranopaharaash cha yathendriyanam, tathaiva sarvahunam achyuta-ijya._ Naradji had told the Prachetas that just as watering the root of a tree satisfies its trunk, branches, sub-branches, fruit, and leaves, and just as taking food into the mouth satisfies all the senses, so too the worship of God accomplishes the worship of all.

_Yatha hi skandha shakhanam taror-mula nishechanena,
evam aradhanam Vishnoh sarveshaam atmanashchahi._ Just as the trunk and branches are satisfied by watering the root of the tree, so too, through worship of Vishnu, the worship of all souls is accomplished.

_Vyas na sadhan aur sab, Hari seva mastul.
Patrani patrani jal bhidyau, sinche taruvar mool._ (Vyas says: no other spiritual practice equals the service of Hari; watering leaf by leaf is like watering the root of the tree.)

Vyasdas says that no other spiritual practice equals devotion to God. Just as watering the root of a tree reaches every single leaf, so too devotion to God fully accomplishes every other spiritual practice.

_Vyas bhaktiko van dhanau, sant lage phal phool.
Patrani patrani jal bhiyai, taruvar shakha mool._ Devotion to Hari is the trunk of the tree; the saints are its fruit and flowers; the guru, saints, and devotees are its branches and leaves. By watering the tree of devotion to Hari with the water of loving devotion, these branches and leaves receive the water of loving devotion.

_Ek sadhai sab sadhai, sab sadhai sab jaay.
Mali sinchai moolko, phulai phalai adhaay._ (Accomplish the one, and all is accomplished; try to accomplish all separately, and all is lost. The gardener waters the root, and it flowers and fruits abundantly.)

Das Kabirji says that by practicing devotion to Hari alone, every kind of devotion is attained. But if we pursue misdirected worship here and there, all of it goes to waste — just as a gardener waters the root and thereby nourishes the flowers and fruit, but if instead of the trunk he waters only the leaves, all his labor goes to waste; likewise, without devotion to Vishnu, all other practices — sacrifices, rituals, yoga, chanting, and so on — go to waste.

_Pahile nikh mool sinchate, jal pahonche sab gair.
Gyani Ram sambharate, sadhan rahe na aur. ||21||_ (Water the root first, without fail, and the water reaches everywhere else; O Gyani, hold fast to Ram, and no other practice is needed.)

Gyaniji Maharaj says that by watering the tree's own root from the very start, the water reaches every part of the tree; in the same way, by remembering and chanting Ram, nothing else needs to be done.

Revered Yadunath, explaining this sakhi, writes in Lintiyu 6, page 22: to keep a tree alive there is no need to water leaf by leaf; by pouring water on the tree's root it reaches every place. In the same way there is no need to serve every deity — Ramkrishna is Himself the embodiment of all deities; serve Him alone.

Kabirji tells us to practice devotion in the right way:

(Kahera)

_Mool sinch man, mool sinch man, mool sinch man maari ho.
Moolke sinche phal phool laage, aise phale teri baari ho. ||1||_ (O my mind, water the root, water the root, water the root, my dear mind. By watering the root, fruit and flowers will come — thus will your garden bear fruit.)

_Phalke laage anahad gaaje, khul gai bharm phivari ho.
Panch pachiso nikar na aave, surat kare rakhwari ho. ||2||
Gagan mandal bich aasan kiya, trikuri lagi hai tari ho.
Kahe Kabir naamka kahera, mahrami hoy so vichare ho. ||3||_ (When fruit comes, the unstruck sound resounds, and the gate of delusion opens; the five elements and twenty-five constituents can no longer come near, for the inner awareness stands guard. He has made his seat in the sky of the inner heavens, absorbed in trance at the meeting-point of the three inner channels. Kabir says this song of the divine Name — only a true intimate of this secret will reflect upon it.)

O my dear mind, water with the water of loving devotion the true and rightful, original divine reality. By watering this root reality, you shall attain the flower of taking refuge in God and the fruit of the supreme abode — thus will your devotion come to fruition. When such fruit appears, the unstruck sound (anahad nad) will resound; the true experience of the divine reality will occur, and the gate of maya's doubts will be thrown open; all uncertainties will vanish. The tangle of the five great elements and the twenty-five constituents of nature will not come near you, and absorption in God's own nature will protect and save you from this material nature. Having laid out a seat for God in the sky of the inner soul, you shall become absorbed in the tri-kuti (the meeting point of the three inner channels, between the eyebrows). Kabirji says that only one who truly understands this boundless, immeasurable reality that is the divine Name will desire to remember and chant it.

For those who set aside true devotion and pursue misdirected worship, Kabirji says:

(Vasant)

_Dekho dekho re aa narki bhool, sinchat sakhane takhat mool. De. tek.
Pragat niranjan ghat samaan, tahe chhand nar puje pashaan.
Jal pive pashan ghoy, so to aad ant pashaan hoy. De. ||1||
Pag paatal jaka shish asmaan, so kaise sampoot samaan.
Alakh niranjan aave na jaay, so kaise diyo re tihaaro khaay. De. ||2||
Ehi bhaanti sab gayo bit, kaahu na maani shabd reet.
Kahet Kabir nar kiya na khoj, bhataki muva jaise banka rojh. De. ||3||_ (Look, look at this folly of hell — watering the branches while leaving the root and trunk dry. The manifest, spotless Lord dwells within this body; forsaking Him, man worships lifeless stone — he washes this stone idol and drinks the water used to wash its feet, and such a person is, from beginning to end, as dull as stone. He whose feet are in the netherworld and whose head is in the heavens — how can He be contained within your small vessel of stone? That imperceptible Lord neither comes nor goes — how then does He partake of the offering you give? In this way everything passes by, yet no one accepts the true teaching. Kabir says man has never set out to seek the true reality, and wanders lost in this world like the ignorant wild rojh, the forest antelope.)

Das Kabirji says: O brothers, just look and see what mistakes these human beings make. These people water the branches of the tree and give up watering its root. The manifest Lord is truly present within our own body, yet forsaking this true presence, people worship lifeless stone. They wash this stone image and then drink the water used to wash its feet — such people are, from beginning to end, as dull and insensate as stone itself. That Lord whose feet are in the netherworld and whose head is in the heavens — how could He be contained within your small vessel, in a piece of stone? That imperceptible, spotless Lord neither comes nor goes anywhere — how then could He eat the offering you give Him? Yet in such delusions everything has passed away, and still no one accepts my teaching. Kabirji says that people have not set out to search for the true reality — they wander about lost in this world, unaware, like the wild rojh (nilgai antelope) of the forest.

_Bhakte tushto Haristushto, harau tushtai cha devata.
Bhavanti siktaah shakhaash cha, taror mula nishechanaat._ If the devotee becomes satisfied, then God also becomes satisfied, and if God becomes satisfied, then the deities too become satisfied — just as when the root of a tree has been watered, its branches and twigs are watered by that too.

Kabirji has said that the manifest Lord dwells within the living human body during life; Jivanji's sakhi relating to this idea is given in the Samagam.

_Sant dware Jivana, sabka hoy sanmaan.
Raghupati jajante jug jajo, jap tap tirath daan. ||1||_ (At the door of the saint, O Jivan, everyone receives honor; worshipping Raghupati is to worship every merit of every age — chanting, austerity, pilgrimage, and charity.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says that in the house of saints everyone receives honor and welcome; through devotion to Ram, service is rendered to the whole world. Whatever actions are performed in this world — chanting, austerity, vows, pilgrimage, charity, and so on — all of these accrue to the one who practices devotion to Ram.

Explaining this sakhi, the Samagam states that the dharma which Vaishnav devotees follow holds Ram-Krishna alone to be the true Supreme Lord; and when Sadguru Gopaldas met Jivanji Maharaj, he removed Jivanji's doubt as to what the divine reality is like — whether it is with attributes and form, or without attributes and formless — and gave the decision that the form of God as Morli Manohar (the enchanting flute-player) is indeed the true, rightful form of God, and that trying to understand God through His various incarnations is merely engaging with God's own maya. A pad (hymn) of Kabirji's on this is given: the visible incarnations are divine maya.

(Ashavari)

_Santo aavai jaay so maya, o pooran Brahma kalya hi kabahu.
O kahi gaya nahi aaya. ||1||_ (O saints, whatever comes and goes is maya; the perfect Brahma has never at any time been born — He has never gone anywhere, nor has He come.)

_Kaam kaso je machh kachh hove, shankhasur na vidare.
O pratipal saphalmein vyapak, kahahu konaku maare. ||2||_
(What need was there for Him to become a fish or a tortoise, or to slay Shankhasura? He who pervades all and sustains everyone as protector — tell me, who could ever slay Him?)

_Hari varaah bhayo nahin kabahun, dashan bhavan dhaari.
O to kaam nahin Ramke, jhunth kahai sansari. ||3||_
(Hari never once became a boar bearing the earth upon his tusks — that is not the work of Ram; worldly people speak falsehood.)

_O nahin Ram khambh jine phaara, Prahlad nahin re ugaarya.
O nirgun sabanse nyaara, nahin jeeta nahin haara. ||4||_
(It was not Ram who split open the pillar and rescued Prahlad. He, the attributeless one, stands apart from all, wholly different — He has never won nor lost.)

_Baaman hoi Bal nahin jaacha, jo jaachai so maaya.
O alekh lekhme nahin, o kaahu gaya na aaya. ||5||_
(He did not become a dwarf and beg from King Bali — whoever begs is bound by maya. He, the unaccountable one, is beyond all reckoning; He has never gone anywhere nor come from anywhere.)

_Parshuram hoi prithvi nahin deeni, kshatri koi na santaapya.
Bin bichaar sakal jug bhoola, maaye jug bharmaya. ||6||_
(He did not become Parshuram and give away the earth, nor did He torment any Kshatriya. Without reflection the whole age has gone astray — maya has deluded the age.)

_Sirajanhaar Sita nahi varne, jal paashaan nahin baandhe.
O Raam karta kar bujhe, (jo sumre) so aandhe. ||7||_
(The Creator did not marry Sita, nor did He bind stones upon water. Whoever takes Ram the Creator to be a mere doer (whoever remembers Him thus) is blind.)

_Karta Kahaan nahin re Gokul, karto Kans na maare.
O akal niranjan kala nahi kabahu, sab kachhu unke saare. ||8||_
(The Creator did not become Krishna in Gokul, nor did He slay Kansa. He, the unfathomable, stainless one, never took such a form — everything is His own arrangement.)

_Aisa samrath sab kaahu kiya, kari kari raha lokaanna.
Jal thal jeev sakalme vyaapak, aisa hai vardaana. ||9||_
(Such a Mighty One has made all of this and keeps sustaining the worlds; He pervades every being in water and on land — such is His boon.)

_Dash avataar ishwari maaya, taako karta kar boojha.
Kahat Kabir Raam avinaashi, aave jaaye so dooja. ||10||_
(The ten avatars are the Lord's own divine maya — do not take them for the Creator Himself. Kabir says: Ram is imperishable; whatever comes and goes is something other than Him.)

Das Kabirji says: O saints, whatever comes and goes is Maya-Brahm. That Purna-Brahm, the Parabrahm, no one has ever been able to fathom or estimate. That Parabrahm neither goes anywhere nor is given away by anyone. What need did this Parabrahm have to take the form of a fish or a tortoise avatar? He did not slay Shankhasura. Pervading everything, He is the Protector who nourishes and sustains all — tell me, then, who could possibly kill Him or destroy Him? This Lord never became a boar, nor did He bear the earth on His tusks. Worldly people lay this blame on Him, for such a deed is not the work of Lord Ram. This Lord Ram did not split open the pillar, nor did He rescue Prahlad. He is free of the three gunas, wholly set apart from everyone, entirely different — He has never known success or failure, has never won or lost. He did not go and beg deceitfully before King Bali — that is not the Lord's doing, that is the work of maya. He is unknowable, has never become something that can be known; He has never, in any age, gone anywhere or come from anywhere. Taking the form of Parshuram, He did not give the earth to anyone, nor did He torment any Kshatriya. Creator of the universe though Lord Ram is, if one takes Him — because of such deeds performed in avatar form — to be merely an avatar-being (avatari), and worships and serves the avatars as such, [that is a mistake, for] He whom none has ever fathomed or understood, who is free of all attachment — it is on Him alone that this whole world depends. Such a Mighty, All-Powerful Lord has fashioned, and keeps fashioning, all these twenty-one universes and fourteen worlds, and keeps them running; He pervades water, land, and everything else — such is that All-Powerful, All-Giving Lord. The ten avatars are His own wondrous, divine maya; people take these avatars to be the Creator-Lord of the world, but the Transcendent Ram, who never perishes, never comes or goes anywhere at any time — He is unmoving.

In the Samagam, the Bijak's very first rameni [devotional song] has been placed as the opening rameni, on the theme of the wish-born feminine avatar; and midway through the Samagam, the 8th rameni given is the one on the theme "Saints, whatever comes and goes is maya." But compared with the published Bijak texts, there is a slight difference of reading in these Samagam renenis — so the seventh line of this rameni differs somewhat in other Bijak texts. There it reads:

_Vai Raghunath ek kai sumire, jo sumirai so andha. ||7||_
(Whoever remembers Raghunath alone — whoever remembers thus is blind.)

In support of these words, the Bijak texts write that those who understand the Lord and Ram in this way [merely as an avatar-doer] are blind, without understanding. In the Samagam this seventh line reads instead:

_O Raam karta kar boojhe (jo samre) so andha._
(Whoever takes Ram the Creator to be understood as a mere doer — whoever remembers Him thus — is blind.)

People count Lord Ram and Krishna among the ten avatars and refer to them as "avatari" [avatar-beings], but there is no need to count this Ram and Krishna merely as avataris. What is said about Ram through Kabir's sakhi on page 98 of the printed Samagam we shall discuss in that chapter; but Kabirwani, Year 1, Issue 11, page 5, clarifies about this Ram as follows:

"In the above words of Kabir Sahib, in the passage where it says 'vai Raghunath ek hai sumire so andha' [whoever remembers Raghunath alone is blind], those who recall the name of Ram are called blind, that is, unwise. This statement causes distress to those who hold the incarnate Lord Ram to be the Supreme Being, and to Sadguru Kabir's own guru, Shri Ramanand Swami, and to the other great souls among his followers — but it is not the way of great souls to cause distress to anyone's heart.
