Devotees remain absorbed in devotion; the wise are unconcerned with worldly things; yogis are useless, of no practical service; and ritualists go about restlessly, like a hired pack-animal — as if none of it truly concerns them, yet they are ever anxious, hasty, and thrashing about to perform and have others perform the rites of ritual action.

Kabir indeed lashed out at the pandits, saying: _Dharti angar na hata, ko pandit tha pas. Kaun muhurat thapiya, chand surya akas._ (When there was not even the earth, what pandit was there present? Who fixed the auspicious moment for creating the moon, the sun, and the sky?) Das Kabirji says: when there was nothing like the earth or the sky in this creation, which learned pandit was there beside God to indicate an auspicious hour, day, or moment for the creation of the moon, the sun, the sky, and so on?

In roughly the middle portion of the Samagam, the central subject for devotion to God is the divine Name — we have already examined at length the divine Name ‘Ram Kabir’. Now, to establish the loving devotion that is the very support of our life-breath — the unique (ananya) devotion to Vishnu — eighteen sakhis (couplets) and a kavit (poem) have been given.

Jivanji Maharaj prohibited the muhurta, and Adhyaruji too gave this his support. In the marriage rite, Adhyaruji has gone so far as to say that devotees even digest Time itself — that is, they swallow Time whole as a single morsel — and he has said that the planets, the gods, and the guardians of the directions (lokpals) too remain subordinate to God.

_Kal pachine kansar nipayo, santo pirse santo pirse arogo var-rai._ (Having digested Time, a sweet dish [kansar] has been prepared; the saints serve it, the saints serve it — partake of it, O bridegroom-king.) O Supreme Brahm, O Master, the saint-devotees have, through devotion, brought Time under their control and cooked it like the sweet kansar dish — they now serve it before You; partake of it. Through devotion practised over the span of life, they have turned Time to their advantage. These devotees are so fearless that they are not prepared to flatter even the planets, though it was God who created those very planets. Why should one who has taken refuge in the All-Powerful flatter the powerless? Hence they do not perform ritual acts such as ‘grah-shanti’ (planet-pacifying rites).

Here are the sakhis (couplets) concerning the chief Vishnu-devotion that has been enjoined to be practised in this universe.

_Ramanandi sampraday men, Uda Jivandas. Kul karma karani taji, kari Ramcharanki aas. ||1||_ (1. In the Ramanandi tradition comes Uda Jivandas: having forsaken the deeds and duties of family custom, he placed his hope in the feet of Ram.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: within the teaching-tradition established by Ramanandji, Jivandas set going the practice of the Uda devotee. Giving up the rites of family custom and Vedic custom prescribed by the bounds of lineage, he practised a devotion whose desire was only to go for refuge to the feet of God.

_Kabir ko kulmen ko panthmen, mitat na asha koi. Dono tyaj nyara rahai, bhagat kahave sai._ (Kabir says: some seek status in lineage, some in a sect — in neither does hope of true fulfilment end. He who gives up both and remains apart is the one truly called a devotee, O Lord.) Das Kabirji says: some people keep to the bounds of lineage, hoping to gain standing and honour in the world; some others hope to gain their standing within a sect or creed. But whoever gives up the craving for both lineage and sect, and practises devotion to God, is the one to be called a true devotee.

_Uda jaat Hanumanki, dini ekaj phal. Hari phal lino Jivana, te Sadguruke upgar. ||2||_ (2. The Uda devotees’ leap is of Hanuman’s kind — a single mighty leap; Jivan[das] has obtained the fruit of Hari through this — it is the favour of the Satguru.) Satguru Jivandasji Maharaj says: the character of the devotees of the Uda community is like that of Hanumanji. The Uda devotees too, like Hanumanji, made one single great leap and, crossing clean over ritual action and family custom, obtained at once the fruit that is the attainment of God — and this they obtained by the grace of the Satguru.

_Tirath vrat sab parhare, Uda tako naav. Kul karma tyaj Jivana, je samre Sitaram. ||3||_ (3. Whoever gives up all pilgrimage and vows is named ‘Uda’; Jivan[das says]: having forsaken family duty, such a one remembers Sitaram alone.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: those who give up pilgrimage, vows, and the like are known by the name of Uda devotees. Giving up family custom and ritual action, they remember only the divine Name Sitaram.

_Lok ved sab jaan de, jaav de dharti akash. Sadguru shabde raho Jivana, jahan prembhakti prakash. ||4||_ (4. Let go of all worldly and Vedic custom, let go even of earth and sky; Jivan[das says]: abide in the Word of the Satguru, wherein shines the light of loving devotion.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: give up the deeds of the lokik (Smarta — worldly custom, family custom) and the Vaidik (Shrauta — Vedic custom, ritual action, and the like), and let go even of the philosophical knowledge that dwells on the distinctions and mysteries of the five great elements — earth, sky, and the rest. Practise devotion to God only according to the teaching of the Satguru — for in that alone is experienced the light and joy of prem-lakshana bhakti (devotion characterised by pure love).

Revered Yadunath, in his Lintiyu no. 46, page 6, writes: ‘Earth, sky — when one lets go even of the order of origination of the five elements, how much more should one let go of worldly rites of worship and adoration.’

_Kabir sant soi janiye, rahe lokved ten door. Kaam krodh vyape nahi, soi sant bad shur._ (Kabir: know him alone to be a saint who stays far from worldly and Vedic custom; in whom lust and anger do not take hold — he alone is a truly great and valiant saint.) Das Kabirji says: only he is to be called a saint who remains apart from worldly custom and Vedic custom. Moreover, one in whom lust and anger do not arise — such a one is to be called a great, mighty, and valiant saint.

The Narad Bhakti Sutra, verse 8, says: _Nirodhastu lok-ved-vyapar-nyasah ||8||_ (Restraint, however, is the abandonment of worldly and Vedic activity.) It means: ‘restraint’ refers to giving up all Vedic — that is, all ritual — actions along with worldly activity. Once the picture of the world has faded from the mind, that devotion is no longer suited to perform any lokik (Smarta/worldly) or Vaidik (Shrauta/Vedic) action — it falls away entirely of its own accord.

_Uda kudha Jivana, jap tap tirath daan. Ved marag pichhe raho, jai malyo Harinaam. ||5||_ (5. Jivan[das] leapt clear over japa, tapa, pilgrimage, and charity; the path of the Vedas was left behind, and he attained the Name of Hari.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: the Uda devotees leapt clean over the practices of japa (recitation), tapa (austerity), pilgrimage, and charity; thereby the practices of the Vedic path were left behind, and the devotee became engaged in the remembrance of Hari.

_Nal vanar ne kalje, aise Harike daas. Bhav sagar dake Jivana, naam sharan vishwas. ||6||_ (6. Such, with the daring heart of the monkeys like Nal, are the servants of Hari; Jivan[das] leaps across the ocean of worldly existence, in faith upon the refuge of the Name.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: just as a wild monkey has the daring to leap from one tree to another, God’s devotees have that same daring, like Hanumanji’s; moreover, the devotees, keeping faith in devotion to the divine Name, leap across the ocean of worldly existence.

_Dalki tuki vanari, shabdhka chukya hans. Sabhaka chukya pandita, tinoka nirvansh._ (The female monkey who misses her leap from the branch, the swan who fails to heed the Word, and the pandit who fails in scriptural debate in the assembly — all three of these come to ruin.) The female monkey who, in leaping, fails to grasp the branch; the disciple who errs in following the guru’s teaching; and the learned pandit who errs in a scriptural debate in the assembly — all three of these are utterly destroyed.

_Udit dharam Uda tano, nahi Anadev prasang. Samran Sitaramko, vali sant sangati nihshank. ||7||_ (7. Risen is the dharma of the Uda devotee — no occasion at all for worship of the Anadev; only remembrance of Sitaram, and further, fearless company with the saints.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: the dharma of the Uda devotees stands at a high level, in which no occasion whatever could arise for devotion to the Anadev [minor deities]; moreover, these devotees, without any doubt or hesitation, practise the devotion of remembering Sitaram together in the company of the saints.

_Mido valyo Jivana, jo karu Anadevki sev. Sadguru sat tattva kahyo, je saache Raghupati dev. ||8||_ (8. Jivan[das] has sworn off ever serving the Anadev; the Satguru has told the true reality — that Raghupati [Ram] alone is the true God.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: he has renounced outright the matter of ever worshipping the Anadev again. He has told the Satguru the plain truth — that Ram alone is the true Supreme Being.

_Nav liti ab Jivana, jo karu aiso kaam. Sitapatiku tyajke, le Anadevko naam. ||9||_ (9. Jivan’s name is as good as erased, should he ever do such a deed — giving up Sitapati [Ram] and taking the name of the Anadev.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: if I should ever now give up devotion to Sitapati and take to worshipping the Anadev instead, then, utterly humbled, I would surrender myself entirely to You.

_Nak liti ab Jivana, jo karu aiso kaam. Mudadaku maati kare, chhaki Raghupati Rai. ||10||_ [unclear in parts] Jivandasji Maharaj says: if I should now worship the Anadev, then, utterly humbled, I would surrender myself entirely to You. Why should one, giving up devotion to King Ram, go and marry — and take as one’s master — something that has not even a trace of consciousness in it?

_To Anadev sir khasado, sevakke mukh laat. Ramnaam vin Jivana, jo bole duji vaat. ||11||_ (11. Then a shoe upon the head of the Anadev, and a kick to the mouth of his servant — says Jivan[das] — should anyone speak of anything other than the Name of Ram.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: now I shall utterly disregard the Anadev, and if any of his worshippers speaks of anything other than devotion to the Name of Ram, I shall confront and oppose him to his face.

_Ab aisi karu Jivana, duniyasu virodh. Anadevne anusare, taki kadhu khoj. ||12||_ (12. Now, says Jivan[das], I shall so oppose the world — I shall track down and expose whoever follows the Anadev.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: now I shall act so forcefully that I shall confront the improper, harmful practices current throughout the whole world, and I shall seek out and expose those who, though calling themselves Vaishnavs, are worshipping the Anadev.

_Mel mukat bhai Jivana, jab Sadguru diyo updesh. Sarag narak vaikunthlun, jyun daar upade kesh. ||13||_ (13. Jivan[das became] freed of every taint, when the Satguru gave him teaching; heaven, hell, and even Vaikunth were let go, as one plucks out a strand of hair by the root.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: when the Satguru gave his teaching, our deliverance came about. We came to understand the true reality of devotion, and so, just as one forcibly plucks out a hair from the head and casts it away, we removed even our expectations of heaven, hell, or Vaikunth.

_Narvasak je Jivana, Harijan taka naam. Sarag narak vaikunth taje, je samre Sitaram. ||14||_ (14. Jivan[das says]: he in whom no worldly craving remains — his name is ‘Harijan’, God’s devotee; he gives up heaven, hell, and Vaikunth, remembering Sitaram alone.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: one in whom no worldly desire or craving born of maya remains at all — such a one is called a devotee of God. Such devotees do not even wish to enjoy the pleasures of heaven, hell, or Vaikunth, but engage only in the remembrance and worship of the Name of Ram.

_Narayana-parah sarve na kutashchana bibhyati, svarga-apavarga-narakeshv api tulyaartha-darshinah._ (All those devoted to Narayana fear nothing from any quarter; they view heaven, liberation, and hell alike, with equanimity.) A devotee wholly devoted to Narayana, unattached and selfless, does not fear hell, nor desire heaven, nor even long for liberation.

_Chhati phate Jivana, nahi Ram bhagati aasan. Tuk tuk kaleja ho pade, to pave pad nirvan. ||15||_ (15. Jivan[das says]: devotion to Ram is no easy seat — the chest breaks open; only when the heart falls to pieces does one attain the state of liberation.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: to practise devotion to Lord Ram is no easy matter. When the inner being of one who practises this devotion becomes so overwhelmed by intense feeling that the heart is pierced through by its own anguish — when, from the suffering of the heart, the inner soul is so stirred that it seems to break into pieces — then one attains the bliss of God’s supreme abode.

_Kabir khari kasoti Ramki, khota take na koy. Ram kasoti te sahe, je jivat mrutak hoy. ||16||_ (16. Kabir: true is the touchstone-test of Ram — no counterfeit coin passes on it; only he endures the test of Ram who, while yet living, is as one dead.) Das Kabirji says: when God tests the true and the false devotee — if a devotee is selfish and proud, wavering the moment hardship comes, such a devotee will not be able to bear the test of devotion to God. Only that devotee who, like one already dead, is free of any kind of pride or self-interest will be able to bear the test of devotion to God — even when hardship comes, he will not give up his devotion.

Revered Yadunath Maharaj, in Lintiyu no. 56, on the back of page 15, writes: _Kabir kardi kasoti Ramki, khori tike na koy. Kaam kasoti so tike, jivat mutak hoy._ (Kabir: hard is the touchstone-test of Ram — nothing crooked stands the test upon it; that alone stands the test which, while living, becomes as one dead.) The meaning of this sakhi is explained thus: ‘living-dead’ is the name for one who, though alive, can die to the self — just as though you garland a person with flowers, he feels no joy from the honour of the garland; and though you strike a corpse five or twenty-five times, it feels no pain. In the same way, one who, though known to be alive, maintains this same kind of bearing, is said to be in the ‘living-dead’ state — and it is he alone who endures the test of Ram.

_Kabir Ram kaho to mari kaho, jivat bahu na Ram. Jab lag jivat Ram hai, tab lag kacha kaam._ (Kabir: if you would say ‘Ram’, say it as one dying; while alive, do not much claim to have Ram — as long as one merely calls upon Ram while still living in the ego, so long the work of devotion remains unripe.) If one wishes to take the Name of Ram, one should take it without pride, in humility, and free of any desire. If you hold on to selfish desire and pride, God Ram’s grace will not increase for you. As long as you take the Name of Ram while still holding on to ego and attachment, your practice remains incomplete.

_Kabir mohi maraneka chav hai, maru to Ram darbar. Kabahuk deen dayalke, koi das muva darbar. ||2||_ (Kabir: I have a longing to die — but let me die in the court of Ram; then perhaps the compassionate one, merciful to the humble, will feel that some servant has died at his court.) I have a great desire to die — but I ask that I may die only in the court of Ram. Perhaps then it will seem, even to the gracious Lord, that some devotee has fallen in service for the sake of Ram.

_Milna to dil kholke, ladhna to shir phodke. Bhakti duheli Ramki, nahi kayarka kaam. Nisnehi nirghar ko, aatho prahar sangram._ (To meet God, meet with an open heart; to fight, fight breaking one’s own head. Devotion to Ram is hard — it is no work for a coward; for one who is loveless and without resolve, it is a battle through all eight watches of day and night.) Devotion to Lord Ram is very hard and difficult — it is no task for the fearful or the faint-hearted. For it, one who is entirely free of any kind of desire has to struggle unceasingly, confronting it constantly.

As to how difficult devotion to Ram is, Kabir has given a whole section (ang) on devotion concerning it.

_Kabir vipat bhali Harinaam let, kaya kasoti dukh. Ram naam bin kis kamki, maya sampat sukh._ (Kabir: adversity is good if it comes while taking the Name of Hari — even the body’s trial and pain; without the Name of Ram, of what use are the pleasures of worldly wealth and prosperity?) Das Kabirji says: however much hardship comes in the taking of the divine Name, it is still good and beneficial — even if the body must pass through trial, there is no harm in that. But without the Name of Ram, of what use is the wealth of worldly pleasures and enjoyments?

_Nanak Nana parakhu, chale chauta mahen. Khotko khota kahai, vaki nanda nahen._ (Nanak and Nana, the assayers, go about in the open marketplace; they call a false coin false — in that there is no fault of theirs.) Nanak says: assayers, who test currency coins, move about in the open marketplace, in the public square, and when they call a false coin false, they are not to be blamed for it.

_Jyun soni sona kasai, sab mal kadhe shodh. Gyani guru aise kasai, sab karma kadhe bodh._ (As a goldsmith assays gold and, examining it, removes all its impurity, so does the wise guru assay the disciple and, through understanding, remove all his karmic bonds.) Gyaniji Maharaj says: just as goldsmiths properly assay gold, examine it, and purify it by removing the mixed-in impurity and dross found in it, so too does the guru, in that same way, properly examine the disciple, remove his bonds of karma, and give him the teaching of devotion.

_Kach kathir adhir nar, kasa na upaje prem. Parasram kasani sahai, kai hira ke hem._ (Glass, base-alloy metal, and a restless man — when tested, love does not arise in them; Parashuram says: only a diamond or gold can bear the assay.) Parashuram says: glass, base metal (zinc alloyed with tin and lead), and a restless, impatient person do not succeed in the trial of love. Only a diamond or gold can endure such a trial.

_Kabir hansa bagla ek rang, maan sarovar jay. O bag dhundhe magh machhli, o hans mukta phal khaya._ (Kabir: the swan and the crane are one in colour, and both go to Man Sarovar; but the crane searches there for reeking fish, while the swan feeds on pearls.) Das Kabirji says: the swan and the crane are the same in colour, and if both go to Man Sarovar, this crane will search out from it the fish reeking of its smell, while this swan will feed on pearls.

Kavit — _Chugat hans nij naam, tahan bag karma kit na bhave. Khir nir niravar kare, so nad hans kahave. Bag machhi chug khaye, bag na mugta phal chug jane. Karat hanski hod, gat apni na pahichane. Maan sarovar hans ghar, bag chhilar sarbhar kare. Parasram jan hanski, kaha baglo sarbhar kare._ (The true swan pecks and feeds on its own proper food; there, the crane’s habit of feeding on worms does not suit it. That one who separates milk from water is called the true swan. The crane pecks and eats fish; the crane does not know how to peck at pearls. It vies in competition with the swan, yet does not recognise its own inferior state. Man Sarovar is the swan’s home; the crane makes do with a shallow puddle. Parashuram says: how could a crane ever compare with the true swan?) Parashuram says: the swan, true to its renown, feeds on pearls; and such a swan does not care for the work the crane does, of eating worms and fish. It is called the great swan because it separates milk from water. The crane, for its part, eats fish with its beak; the crane does not know how to pick up grains of pearl with its beak, yet still it tries to enter into competition with the swan, without recognising what its own conduct and understanding are really like. Man Sarovar is the swan’s dwelling place, whereas the crane keeps close company with ponds and puddles. Parashuram says: how could a crane ever properly be compared with swan-like people?

_Swang ek boho antra, koyal kagda joy. Pativrata aur punsali, bhelan bane na doy._ (The outward form is one, but the inward difference is great — see the koel and the crow; a chaste wife and an unchaste woman — the two can never become alike.) Nana Parekh says: the koel [cuckoo] and the crow are alike in their black colour and outward form, but there is a great difference in their qualities. A chaste, devoted wife and an unchaste woman — these two can never be alike in their qualities.

_Swang ek boho antra, jyo bagla aur hans. Ek bhekh pade bhramme, ek kate Kalko kans._ (The outward form is one, but the inward difference is great, as with the crane and the swan; one, in that guise, falls into delusion, the other cuts through the snare of Death.) Nana Parekh says: just as the crane and the swan are alike in colour and appearance, there is a great difference in their qualities. One, of the crane’s kind, falls into the delusion of maya, while the other, of the wise and understanding swan’s kind, cuts through the bonds of death (Kal).

_Kabir hariya jane rukhda, pani tana sneh. Suka kashth na pallave, jo keta uthe meh. ||2||_ (Kabir: it is the green tree that knows the love of water; dry wood does not sprout leaves, no matter how much rain may fall.) Das Kabirji says: it is green, living trees that know love with water; but on dry wood, however much rain falls, it has no effect whatsoever.

The devoted followers who compiled the Samagam have, in keeping with this occasion, included the following hymn.

(Raag Sarang.) _Chalo hansa desh sohamane (hansa), chalo desh sohamane. Yah sansar osko pani (moti), kirne chhute nahi pavano. ||tek|| Kaha Brahmalok kaha Shivlok, kaha Vishnulok thaharavano. Chalo hansa ve desh amar hai, jahan thai phir na avano. ||hansa||1|| Shunyakaal aur jot swarupi, e lokan man bhavano. Yoni sankashta mite nahi kabahu, bhram bhatki phir avano. ||hans||2|| Hansa hoy so va desh jai hai, kahat Kabir samjhavano. Jahan nahi Ram thagori aave, janam maran nahi dahano. ||hansa||3||_ (Come, O swan, to the beautiful land — come to that beautiful land. This world is but dewdrop water taken for pearl — its shine can never truly be attained. What is Brahmalok, what is Shivlok, what is Vishnulok, that one should settle there? Come, O swan, to that land which is deathless — whence, once there, one never has to return. Even the realm of the Void and of light-form is only a place dear to certain minds; the affliction of the womb is never removed there — one strays in delusion and comes back again. Only a true swan goes to that supreme land — thus Kabir explains it — where the deceit of maya never comes, and there is no more burning pain of birth and death.) O supreme devotee, let us go to that excellent abode. This world is as insubstantial as dewdrop water that only appears like a pearl — it is that false and fleeting. From the water of this dew, which merely looks like a pearl, we can never obtain the true lustre of a real pearl. So too, whether it be Brahmalok, Shivlok, or Vishnulok, all these realms are subject to destruction — of what use, then, is it to dwell there? But, O devotee soul, there is a land, an abode, that is deathless, from which, once there, one never has to return again to birth and death. Going into the false-time creation of the three-natured world of Omkar-light is the land dear to the worshippers of the Anadev. For such people, the suffering of coming and going through the womb never ceases — they wander round and round through such realms and come back again into this world. But it is the excellent devotee alone who goes to such a supreme abode — thus does Kabirji explain — a place where there is none of the deceiving maya fashioned by God, so that the pain of birth and death need never be borne.

The compilers of the Samagam have further included two more hymns in the Samagam.

(Raag Sarang.) _Hansa hans mile sukh hoi, jahan sahaj samagam hoi. ||tek|| Khat darshan pakhand chhanuva, bhekh banave loi. Char varan aur ved kateba, hans unthe nyara hoi. ||1|| Hansa to hai premka pyasa, sau vaikunth na hoi. Jahan mukat sakal mamtaki, hans taje jaise chhoi. ||2|| Hansa hamara shabad basera, shabad ahari hoi. So hansa sat lok pahucha, tahan jamra rahya roi. ||3|| So jamra jaay teen lok par, bandhe antariksh joi. Tahi chhod chale shabad hamara, tako aava-gavan na hoi. ||4|| Kahat Kabir pratit kijiye, hans na rahat bachhoi. Lei basavu me deev sagamag, hanse hans samoi. ||5||_ (When swan meets swan there is joy — where there is a natural, effortless coming-together. The six philosophical systems and the ninety-six sects put on their various guises. From the four varnas and from the Vedas and the scriptures of other faiths alike, the true swan stands apart. The swan is thirsty only for love — a hundred Vaikunths could not satisfy it. Where there is liberation from all attachment, the swan drops it just as one sheds a covering. Our swan’s dwelling is the Word; it feeds only on the Word. Such a swan reaches the True Abode, where even Yama is left weeping, unable to follow. Yama can go over the three worlds and bind beings even in the reaches of the sky; but our Word travels beyond even that, and for it there is no more coming and going. Kabir says: have faith in this — the true swan does not remain separated; I shall settle it upon the lamp aglow, where swan merges into swan.) When one saint-devotee meets another saint-devotee, there is great joy — where such a meeting occurs, a natural coming-together happens of its own accord, and an intense loving union takes place. People, following the six systems of philosophy and the ninety-six varieties of hypocrisy, put on various outward guises. Saint-devotees stand apart from the four varnas and from the Vedas and other scriptures alike. These saintly souls are eager only for love-natured devotion; such saintly souls are not to be found in Vaikunth, for they have no desire even for Vaikunth. In that state, they are untouched by any attachment or possessiveness — such saints are free of all these attachments, and they cast off possessiveness the way one casts off something untouchable. Our saints are ones who live according to the teaching of the Satguru — their eating, movement, that is, all their daily activity, is carried out according to that teaching. Such saintly souls reach the True Abode, the supreme realm, where even Yamaraj cannot go, and so he is left to lament. This Yamaraj can go into all three worlds and can even move through the paths of the sky; but those who, abandoning that three-world universe, live according to my teaching go beyond even him, to where they never again have to come back and move about in this world of death. Kabirji says that such saintly living souls never remain parted from this abode. I shall bring them and settle them in the most excellent, radiant, supreme abode, where these saints will be united together with the other saints. And further, Nana Parekh’s hymn too has been presented here.

(Raag Sarang.) _Harijan hans sulakshana santo, Harijan hans sulakshana. Nishadin preet nibhaye jaye, chhande nahi pan apna. ||tek|| Maan sarovar tachake vasi, aan sarovar avagana. Vake sant sangat hai pyari, salilsangsu risana. ||1|| Muhta phal bina chanch na bahe, karam kit nahi chakhana. Vake bade bade bhupati chahe, khit nitke parakhana. Vadgunthe nirgun kare nyara, Parbrahmke pyara dhana. ||3|| Bhayeg phale jo male jan aisa, prem bhagat paripurana. Nano kahe bali jau taki, pal pal leu ovarana. ||4||_ (The Harijan is of the swan’s fine character, O saints — the Harijan is of the swan’s fine character. Day and night he keeps love, never abandoning his own vow. He dwells at the shore of Man Sarovar; he disdains any other lake. To him the company of saints is dear; he is displeased with the company of mere water. Unless it is a pearl, his beak does not open — he does not taste the worms of ordinary deeds. Even great kings desire him; distinguishing pure from impure is his skill. Being of the great quality, he sets himself apart from what is qualityless; he is dearly beloved of the Supreme Brahm. Blessed and fruitful is he who meets such a person, one full and complete in loving devotion. Nano [Nana Parekh] says: I offer myself to him, and moment by moment I would wave an offering over him.) God’s devotees (Harijans) possess fine good qualities. O saints, the Harijans possess fine good qualities. They always uphold their loving devotion, and they never let go of their vow. They are like the swans that dwell at the shore of Man Sarovar — high souls who dwell at the shore of unique devotion. For them, other lakes and ponds — that is, devotion to the Anadev — hold no attraction beside the pure devotion that is like Man Sarovar. Only the company of saints is dear to them; they are displeased at keeping company with mere worldly water. Just as swans do not put their beaks into fish and the like, but only into pearls, in the same way these saints do not so much as taste the fish, so to speak, of ritual action — they do not accept ritual action at all — apart from the pearl that is the divine Name. Nothing besides the divine Name tastes sweet to them, or is pleasing to them. Therefore they do only the worship of the divine Name. Even the greatest of great men wish to love such excellent Harijans, who, like this swan, separate the water of maya from the milk of the Supreme Brahm. These Harijans are such as render themselves free of the three gunas (qualities of nature); they are thus the Lord’s most beloved devotees. If our good fortune should come to fruition, we too might obtain such Harijans, in whom there is complete and perfect love-natured devotion. Nana Parekh says: I am utterly devoted to such Harijans, and moment by moment I wish them well.

_Jage jad so jivani, mui na jage koy. Gyani sukha yon rah gaya, jivat hariya hoy._ (What sprouts though inert is truly alive; nothing dead ever sprouts again. Gyani[ji says]: it remains dry as it was, but what is truly living turns green.) Gyaniji Maharaj says: that whose roots sprout when given water is alive; but that which has died and dried up does not sprout. What has dry roots remains just as it is, unchanged, but what is living turns green with new growth.

_Kabir bhavatake bichhuda, dagh pare dil bich. Sukha kabdu na pallave, jo saat samudran sinch._ (Kabir: one parted from his beloved bears a burn-mark within his heart; dry wood never sprouts leaves, even if you were to water it with the seven seas.) Das Kabirji says: one who has been separated from his beloved bears a scar upon his heart; just as dry wood, however much you water it — even with as much water as the seven seas — never sprouts, so too does the lover’s heart remain wounded.

The Uda Vaishnavs are free of ritual action; they possess, like the swan, the art of separating water from milk — such Vaishnavs are said to separate maya from Brahm. This Samagam took place at Shahpura, where the code of this Uda dharma was set forth. This tradition of the Uda Vaishnavs is that of unique (ananya) devotion to Vishnu. What such unique conduct looks like, Kabirji has written a whole ‘ang’ (section) about.

THE SECTION ON THE UNIQUE (ANANYA) DEVOTEE

_Kabir kul adhar aur tan adhar, adhar vidya aur daam. E adhar taji nishchal rahe, sau pave agochar gam. ||1||_ (Kabir: support in one’s lineage, support in one’s body, support in learning, and support in wealth — one who abandons these supports and remains unshaken attains the unreachable, imperceptible state.) Das Kabirji says: those who consider themselves great because of a high lineage, or think their own body excellent — such bodily pride — or those who consider themselves great because of their learning or their wealth and possessions — whoever gives up all such kinds of pride and remains free of them can attain the supreme state.

_Kabir char aadharme eku rahai, tab lagi ananya sant na hoy. Ananya taku pekhiye, tan dhan vidya kul khoy. ||2||_ (Kabir says: as long as even one of these four bases of mind remains, one cannot be called a true ananya — single-pointed, exclusive — saint. Recognize the ananya one as the one who gives up pride in body, wealth, learning, and lineage.)

Das Kabirji says that if even one of these four egoistic tendencies (mano-vrutti) remains, then until it is gone one cannot be called a saint of ananya conduct. Only one who abandons pride in body, wealth, and lineage can truly be called an ananya saint.

_Kabir kul tajyo to dhan rahyo, rahyo jaavan aadhar. Hari ichchha jaako nahi, sau kaiso ananya nirdhar. ||3||_ (Kabir says: even if one gives up pride of lineage, the pride of wealth remains, and the pride of youth remains as a support; one who has no surrender to Hari's will — how can such a person be called truly ananya?)

Das Kabirji says: even if someone has given up pride of lineage, an alluring attachment still lingers in him, along with the pride of youth, and if the disposition of devotion to God or of attaining God is absent, then how, indeed, can he be said with certainty to be an ananya devotee-saint?

_Kabir hari ichchhame jo chale, chhaand sakal karma dharma. Sahaj vrat jin grahi, soi ananya nishkarma. ||4||_ (Kabir says: one who walks according to Hari's will, giving up all ritual acts and duties, and who has taken up the vow of the natural, effortless state — that one alone is the true ananya, untouched by karma.)

Das Kabirji says: one who remains content with however God keeps him, abandoning every kind of ritual and ceremonial conduct, and who has taken up the discipline of remaining in the natural (sahaj) state — that one, untouched by karma, is called an ananya saint-devotee.

_Kabir ananya taku pekhiye, je sabhi chhaande aas. Hari charane laaga rahai, jaaka sahaj shoonyame vaas. ||5||_ (Kabir says: recognize as ananya the one who gives up every hope and expectation, who remains ever attached to Hari's feet, and whose natural state dwells fixed in the void.)

Das Kabirji says: one who gives up every hope and craving should be understood as an ananya saint-devotee — one who remains always joined in surrender at the feet of Hari, and whose natural state abides steadily fixed in the state of emptiness (shunya).

_Kabir saat paanch sangi ho rahai, kathe ananyako desh. Rahani karani aave nahi, pakha pakhi updesh. ||6||_ (Kabir says: those who gather in small groups of five or seven and speak of the way of the ananya devotees, yet do not let any partisan bias enter their conduct and way of living.)

Das Kabirji says: those who come together in small groups of five and seven and discuss the ideals of ananya devotees, and who do not let any kind of sectarian bias or partisan dispute enter into their conduct and manner of life — such are these devotees.

_Kabir rahani karani naha vikat hai, adhar jaaki aas. Paau palakka sangrah kare nahi, soi ananya nij daas. ||7||_ (Kabir says: this way of conduct and living according to the rule of ananya-ness is very hard — one whose hopes rest on nothing, who hoards nothing even for the span of a quarter of an eyeblink, that one alone is the Lord's own ananya devotee.)

Das Kabirji says: living according to the principles of ananya conduct is extremely difficult — it belongs to one who holds no expectations at all within, and who does not gather or store even the smallest thing, even for the time of a quarter of an eyeblink; that one alone is called the intimate ananya devotee of God.

_Kabir nishkami nirmohita, eko na thaathe kaam. Taako ananya ham kahat hai, sohi hamara nij daas. ||8||_ (Kabir says: one who is free of desire and free of attachment, in whom not a single craving takes root — that one we call ananya; that one alone is truly our own devotee.)

Das Kabirji says: one who is without any kind of desire and without delusion or attachment, in whom not a single craving arises — him we call ananya; he alone is our own intimate devotee.

_Kabir karma dharma sabku tajai, tajai kul vahaivar. Khaanpaan aan sab tajai, tajai tan dhan vidya aadhar. ||9||_ (Kabir says: he gives up all ritual actions and duties, gives up the customs and dealings of lineage, gives up all eating and drinking with those of another persuasion, and gives up reliance on body, wealth, and learning.)

Das Kabirji says: he gives up ritual observances and religious duties of every kind, gives up the customary conduct and dealings of his lineage, gives up all eating and drinking together with other worshippers of a different persuasion, and gives up placing reliance on the pride of body, wealth, and learning.

_Kabir tanmad dhanmad gyanmad, vidyamad unmad. Aite mad jab dil mile, tab soone naad anahad. ||11||_ (Kabir says: when the pride of body, the pride of wealth, the pride of knowledge, the pride of learning, and the pride of self all dissolve away from the heart, then the unstruck sound, the anahad naad, is heard.)

Das Kabirji says: when the pride of the body, the pride of wealth, the pride of worldly knowledge, and the pride of learning and of the self all merge and dissolve within the heart, then one experiences the divine sound — the direct experience of God's presence.

At Bapu Vrindavan's manuscript folio, book no. 9, at the end, on page 142, in describing the marks (lakshan) of the Vaishnav, thirty are listed: 1) the company of saints (satsang), 2) Hari's bhajan (devotional singing), 3) devotion to Hari (Hari bhakti), 4) loving feeling (bhav), 5) faith (shraddha), 6) humility (dinta), 7) modesty (vinay), 8) the disposition of a servant (das-bhav), 9) discernment (vivek), 10) reflection (vichar), 11) forgiveness (kshama), 12) contentment (santosh), 13) detachment (vairagya), 14) trust (vishwas), 15) compassion (karuna), 16) right understanding (sumati), 17) mercy (daya), 18) modesty at wrongdoing (lajja), [item 19 is missing from the source], 20) non-duality (abhed), 21) self-reflection (atma-vichar), 22) helping others (par-upkar), 23) restraint of ego (aham-sanyam), 24) the disposition of silence (mauna-bhav), 25) constant bliss (sada anand), 26) detachment from worldly concern (udasi), 27) knowing the body to be transient (kshanabhangur), 28) [unclear] and eating sparingly (alpa ahar), 29) gravity of temperament (gambhirta), and 30) freedom from egotism (aham-bhav rahit).

Thus, ritual-free (karmakand-rahit) Vaishnav devotion is the art of the swan (hansa-kala) — devotion practiced by discerningly separating the pure from the mixed, as a swan separates milk from water. It was for this reason that Vaishnav Jivandasji declared, speaking of the Lord of the Kali Yuga, that Ram-Krishna is the Lord of the Kali Yuga, and that the dharma of the Kali Yuga is ananya bhakti (single-minded, exclusive devotion). This samagam (holy discourse) took place at Shahapar. On the way back, whichever devotee-souls of matching disposition came at that time to meet Vaishnav Jivandasji, he revealed that same dharma to them — that is, he gave them the experience of that dharma according to their own feeling — and they became fulfilled.

Dada Jasvantji Weeps

Jasvantji wept — for whoever separates a devotee of Vishnu from his devotion must suffer hell.

The date — the samvat, month, and day — on which the episode of Dada Jasvantji occurred has been recorded; likewise, in another chapter, the occasion of when Haribhai came from Aritha to Shahapar has also been recorded with its samvat and date. Of the two, the Shahapar episode occurred first, and the Dada Jasvantji episode occurred afterward. But the earnest and discerning devotees who transcribed the samagam preserved this sequence, placing the Shahapar episode first and the Dada Jasvantji episode after it. We, however, have made no alteration in transcribing it, even where the original samagam may itself contain some discrepancy; therefore we present the Dada Jasvantji episode here exactly as it stands in the original.

This episode of Dada Jasvantji, as presented in the samagam, is very difficult to understand. This event, which occurred on the 13th day of the dark half of Bhadarva in Samvat 1707, has been narrated together with its precise date. On this day such anguish arose within Dada Jasvantji that his soul cried out in pain — hence it is said that Dada Jasvantji wept. Seeing him in this state of anguish, his daughter Janakibai asked him why he was so distressed. Explaining the cause of his anguish, Dada Jasvantji said:

"If some person, on account of the influence of an exclusive Vishnu devotee (Vishnu bhakti — devotion to Vishnu) such as us, causes another to fall, through association with him, onto the wrong path of ritual action (karma-marg), and that person then becomes engaged in the worship of Anadev (aan-dev — worship of 'another,' a different deity, as opposed to single-pointed, ananya devotion), then his soul will not be received into the community of ananya devotees — his soul will not be accepted as an ananya devotee within that community. But whoever tries to stop such a person from proceeding by the path of karma toward the worship of Anadev — whatever suffering of hell that other person would have had to bear, that very suffering will instead fall upon the one who tried to stop him. For this reason, it cannot be borne to watch it happen, and yet it cannot be stopped by watching it happen either — this is the painful dilemma that arises for any person who feels emotional concern for another.

An example given of this is the sage Sandipani, who asked Lord Krishna for his dead son back [unclear — the source text is broken at this point]. For this reason, if a father and son, mother and daughter, father and son, or any siblings among themselves — brother and sister, or brother and brother — or father and daughter, being emotionally attached relatives, insist with stubbornness (hath) that one another practice Vishnu bhakti in a particular way, and try to stop the other from a different form of worship, then that person must bear hell in the other's place — he must bear hell on the other's behalf — and even the Vishnu bhakti that he himself has performed will go to waste. Such is the difficult situation that can arise. To make this clearer, a further example is given.

A snake bit and ate something, and the creature died; the snake was then killed for it. In this event, whatever karma there is attaches to the snake, but does not attach to the one who killed the snake. This is how it has been presented in the samagam — but this riddle is a difficult one; to help understand it, the earnest seekers who transcribed the samagam have set down their own views below.

Episode 1

On the 13th day of the dark half of Bhadarva, Samvat 1709, at a certain hour, Dado Jasvantji wept so that he might not be separated from his Guru — that is, his heart could not contain its love, and so he wept. His daughter Janakibai then asked, "Dadaji, why are you weeping?" He replied: "I weep because a certain soul, through the merit of Vishnu bhakti, took human birth. He was bhadra — that is, blessed by nature. But, dazzled by the sight of some worldly act, he became caught up in greed for worldly things. That soul has no ground left on which to fall [unclear] — that is, no basis left for it to fall, through ananya devotion, into surrender to God. If it should go under the shelter of Anadev, it will not be allowed to remain in surrender to God, because it has, again and again, turned away from the path of Vishnu bhakti — it has already seen and turned toward Anadev's worship instead. That soul has gone to hell. That soul now has work to do in the darkness of hell. Seeing this, I was moved to weep — because I am anxious about how I myself am to attain liberation, and it is out of the fear of being separated from my Guru that I weep — O Bhagavan!"

Episode 2

Sandipani's son had gone to hell. When the Lord became pleased with the sage, He established that son in Vaikuntha. At that time, Sandipani, out of his own longing, had the son called back to the mortal world. It is for this reason that, in the matter of Vishnu bhakti, Sandipani is said to have taken our own soul as the Lord's own, delivering it and rescuing it from the suffering of worldly existence. Therefore, if a wife and husband, mother and son, father and son, sister and brother, or any person among themselves, is practicing Vishnu bhakti, and someone causes it to be disrupted through stubbornness, superstition, or obstruction, then that person will suffer hell in the other's place, and — because he has obstructed that devotion — he himself will become disqualified and fall from grace. If he stubbornly restrains or obstructs another being from his devotion, misfortune will befall him. Moreover, however much disruption he causes, that other person will nonetheless go on practicing Vishnu bhakti and will, together with his whole family line, be sanctified — but the Vishnu bhakti of the one who caused the disruption will come to nothing, and he alone will suffer hell. Thus that being is affected in two ways. This is confirmed and upheld by scripture. If a snake bites someone, and before he dies he in his stubbornness kills the snake, the fruit of that killing attaches to the snake — for a snake never bites a person without provocation, or without some enmity carried over from a former life; yet because he stubbornly killed the serpent, the fault of that act will instead fall upon him as its fruit. In the same way, when a person practicing Vishnu bhakti, through the workings of karma, encounters happiness and sorrow, and becomes distraught and, through his own stubbornness, disrupts anyone's devotional practice — then, even though he himself continues practicing Vishnu bhakti, whatever ritual acts he performs will come to nothing. Therefore, whenever any person is engaged in the worship of God, one should remain accommodating toward him, and must never act against him in a way that disrupts his devotional practice.

There, the testimony of the Padma Purana — the same story is told at greater length in the Bhagavata, in the passage where the sage Kapilacharya instructs his mother; there the story is given in fuller detail. There, in the testimony of the Sahasranama, Mahadev spoke to Shri Vasudev the following corresponding verse —

_Brahmahatyaastoyapaapam shaamyodapi kathanchan, na punaatyasta krishnancha kalpakotishatairapi. ||64||_ (The sin of killing a Brahmin may perhaps, in some manner, be atoned for; but one who does not take the name of Krishna is not purified even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.)

Commentary: Shri Mahadevji said, "O Maharaj, no one is able to fully know the extent of your Vishnu bhakti. Although the scriptures hold that debt, enmity, and sin — these three — are never, at any time, released for anyone, so that even the Supreme Lord cannot discharge them on one's behalf [unclear] — yet if such sins as the killing of a Brahmin and others are committed unknowingly, through some circumstance of karma, by an unrighteous person, that person can free himself by circumambulating the whole earth in pilgrimage, by journeying to all the sacred places (tirthas) of the universe, and by performing austerities while chanting the name of Ram. But whoever disrupts a devotee in whom the qualities of Shri Vasudev are being glorified — even if that person performs austerities for as many crores upon crores of ages as he wishes, he is never delivered. A person who obstructs a devotee of Shri Hari, or obstructs devotion to Shri Hari, falls into the Shaurava hell, and there suffers the very greatest torments for as long as the sun and moon shine, remaining undelivered through many kalpas." This is described in the Bhagavata and in the Padma Purana.

There, Kabirji's sakhi (couplet) —

_Kabir harika bhagatimaan, je kathaa chalaave aur. Taa aparaadhi jeevaka, teen lok nahi ger. ||1||_ (Kabir says: whoever spreads unworthy talk regarding devotion to the Lord — that sinful soul finds no resting place in any of the three worlds.)

Das Kabirji says: whoever, in the matter of devotion to God, sets in motion some unfit or unworthy discourse — that sinning soul finds no place to dwell anywhere in the three worlds.

I now set down my own view, corresponding to the episode of "Dada Jasvantji Wept" as described in the samagam.

Seeing Dada Jasvantji weeping, his daughter Janaki asked the reason for his tears. Dada explained that if a person practicing Vishnu bhakti were falling into the worship of Anadev, and someone stopped him from doing so, then the one who stopped him would have to suffer hell in that other person's place. Thus, either way, a difficult situation arises for the Vishnu devotee. As an example — Sandipani asked Krishna for his dead son back. Likewise, because of relationships such as father and son, brother and brother, or wife and husband, if we create obstruction or act with stubbornness, we must bear hell on the other's behalf. If a snake has eaten a frog, the one who then kills that snake does not incur the sin of killing the frog — that sin belongs to the snake; and if a snake bites someone who then dies, the one who kills the snake does not incur the sin of having killed that person — that too belongs to the snake. For this reason, the account of Sage Kapil in the Bhagavata should be understood. Kapil's father, the sage Kardam, was a son of Brahma. When Brahma directed his son to assist him in the work of creating the universe, Kardam performed austerities for ten thousand years, pleased the Lord, and asked for the boon, "Give me a wife." At this, tears came to the Lord's eyes, and from them arose the lake called Bindu Sarovar, which exists today in Siddhpur.

Let me set out my own view regarding Siddhpur. The meaning of "Siddhpur" is this: the place where siddhi (spiritual attainment) is reached — that "city" (pur) should be understood as the body. Without a body, no work can be accomplished, nor can siddhi be attained; yet even having obtained a body, if one falls into craving for siddhi (supernatural powers) and riddhi (worldly prosperity) — that is, if the body given by God's grace as a blessing is used in pursuit of siddhi or of maya — then, on seeing this, tears come to God's eyes; and although that tear is but a single drop, it becomes as vast as a lake. Because you hold expectation for wife, son, and the like, the Lord has had to "come" — to respond to that longing — and a son is produced from just a single drop, yet the family that results grows as broad as a lake. Kabirji, in the following section, has said —

_Ek boondke khaali gai, rona sab sansaar. Anek boond khaali gai, tinke kaun vichaar. ||15||_ (Kabir says: for the loss of a single drop the whole world weeps; but countless drops have gone to waste, and no one gives that any thought.)

Das Kabirji says: great effort is made for the sake of a single body formed from one drop, but no one gives any thought to the many bodies, formed from countless other drops, that have gone to waste without devotional practice.

You weep at the death of a person born from a single drop, but you do not consider that many other bodies, born from countless drops, have likewise gone to waste without devotional practice. In truth, the world itself is produced only from the drop that enters a mother's womb. Any child playing in a mother's lap is itself a form of God — one should not think it was born for no reason. There are as many bodies as there are grains of stone, and into one such body falls a teardrop of God, and thus a son is obtained; this drop is received by the mother, which is why special weight is given to maternal faith (matru-shraddha) in that connection. But ananya devotees have no need to cultivate faith centered on mother or father in this worldly sense — we are not meant to fall again and again into birth from a mother's or father's womb. So when the question of stubbornness arises, it should be pointed out that if we become bound up in ritual action out of regard for worldly relationships — father and son, brother and brother, brother and sister, mother and son, and so on — that too is itself a form of stubbornness, and it touches us not in one way but in many ways. This stubbornness comes in an extremely subtle form, so that we remain wholly unaware of it.

Kabirji, in the following section, said: for one drop the whole world weeps; you offer faith to one mother or one father, yet so many other drops have gone to waste, and you cannot offer faith to so many generations. Moreover, you show favoritism, you take sides — and so Kabir said:

_Kabir harijan nahi, bahu kutumbko bhaar. Gadhdha hokar otare, bhaanda bhare kumbhaar._ (Kabir says: one who is not a devotee of Hari carries the heavy burden of a large household; he takes birth as a donkey, and the potter loads pots and vessels upon his back.)

Das Kabirji says: those who are not devotees of Hari carry upon their heads a very heavy burden of family and household. Because of this, they take birth as a donkey, and the potter loads the burden of vessels upon their back and makes them labor. Through this potter-like Brahma, one must bear, across the eighty-four lakh species, the burden of the body — like a vessel — of birth, again and again.

The potter is Prajapati — he is Brahma, and he is regarded as the presiding deity of Pitrulok, the realm of the ancestors. By performing deeds aimed at worldly attainment, one bears, many times over, the burden of the body of birth across the eighty-four lakh species. A devotee of Hari, however, does not carry the burden of being born into so many kinds of families. In this way, people generally remain inattentive toward karma that attaches to them in subtle ways; devotees of Hari, by contrast, remain ever vigilant.

Although Lord Kapil was himself, in essence, greater than his own father, he did not come forward on his own to instruct Sage Kardam. Kardam was spending the power of his austerities in pleasures with his wife, Devahuti, and Kapil made no attempt to stop him. Only when Kardam came to realize, "This one, in the form of my son, is God," and sought knowledge from him, did the Lord give his teaching. In the same way, when the mother too came to understand, "This one, in the form of my son, is God," he gave her the teaching of Sankhya philosophy. So the purpose of presenting this episode from the Bhagavata within Jivanji Maharaj's samagam is this: even though one may oneself be God, one must never — on the basis of any relationship, whether as father, mother, son, or otherwise — act with even the slightest stubbornness to restrain or stop another; nor should one do so. Even though Arjun was as close as a friend, Krishna — though called Jagadguru, the teacher of the universe — became his instructor, but did not become his guru in the sense of one who imposes authority.

This subject is a very subtle one. Just as a person's inner vital essence (sattva) diminishes when he begets a son, this same principle applies to any undertaking whatsoever. Indeed, even in giving an order to a servant, your merit (punya) is diminished, even though you may be paying him a wage. Thus, with each and every word we utter, the consciousness (chaitanya) residing within us is set into motion and expended. This is why sages strive, through silence, to conserve themselves. A guru who gives teaching transmits into his disciple a portion of the power dwelling within himself; thereby that guru's power comes to reside within the disciple. This transmission is called "paat" — a falling, or passing over. Just as a man passes semen into a woman, so too do we, in various ways, pass on our own inner essence. When we try to direct our son, our wife, or society in any particular direction, our own inner power is expended in the effort. This is why we cannot easily grasp so profound a subject; Jivanji has explained it very concisely. Even in telling someone, "Open the door," we lose some of our own vital force. A difficult problem arises on both sides — whether to restrain someone or not to restrain them — so the objection that the matter remains unresolved is not acceptable. Even where one does good, the possibility of wrongdoing does not disappear; the rule that good done by a person results in good for that person does not always hold true. So then — should one do good, or not?

_Duniya sab dhokhe muvaayaan, kare kutumbki kaan. Jab kul kiska laajasi, jab le dharaa masaan._ (Kabir says: the whole world dies deceived, caught up in concern for family honor; but when the body is carried to the cremation ground, whose lineage will then feel shame?)

Das Kabirji says: in the delusion of worldly pleasures and the like, people go about consumed with concern for the honor and reputation of family; but when the body is carried to the cremation ground, where then will the family's honor remain? The body is transient; pride taken in it is false.

Once the cremation ground is reached, whose lineage will feel shame — is there anything left to protect? Therefore, one should not, deceived by delusion, fall into concern for family reputation. At the time of death, it is your devotion that will be shamed if found lacking; therefore, having become a devotee, one should practice devotion by breaking free of concern for worldly reputation, family, and honor.

Stubbornness in the matter of Vishnu bhakti can be shown in many forms. For instance: (1) Once, the wedding procession of the world-guru Shankaracharya was passing through Dwarka on an elephant. He had the elephant halted on the way, got down, and, seeing a Brahmin bearing a Swaminarayan tilak on his forehead, tore off and took away his sacred thread, rebuking him harshly: "Shame and disgrace! Being a Brahmin, you wear a Vaishnavi tilak — Brahmins should apply only sacred ash." Even a powerful world-guru had to act in this way — and in this episode too, there is stubbornness. Whether for a Vishnu devotee or for a Shiva devotee, stubbornness is truly present; this creates a tangled situation even for religious authorities. Thus the presence of stubbornness persists in virtually every kind of conduct.

Whether someone smokes, gambles, drinks liquor, or performs any good or bad act — whether to stop him or not is itself a difficult question. (2) The consecration of the life-breath (pran-pratishtha) into an idol is likewise a form of stubbornness — an insistence on making God dwell within it. (3) Vows, petty religious disputes, sacred threads and charms, votive offerings, and the like are all forms of stubbornness. (4) Even the enjoyment of the pleasures created by God is enjoyed at the cost of one's own depleting merit (punya). If sin comes through stubbornness, then merit, too, has stubbornness as its cause. Whether we use water freely or use it sparingly, we shall still have to give an account of it to God — "How much of My water did you use? How much of My grain did you use?" — and so on. Just as a servant must give an account to his master, so too must we give our account.

_Kasugandha vanitaa vastram, geetam taambool bhojanam. Bhooshanam vaahanam cheti, bhogashatakamudeeriyatam._ (Fine fragrance, a woman's company, clothing, singing, playing music, chewing betel leaf, eating food, ornaments, and conveyance — these are the eight kinds of enjoyment; indulging in them causes the depletion of merit.)

This chapter concerns the event known as "Dada Jasvantji Wept," which took place in his life on the 13th day of the dark half of Bhadarva, Samvat 1709. As to who Dada Jasvantji was — the explanation is found by reflecting on the words used in the description given in verse 5 of the Bhaktamal of Jivanji Maharaj, composed by Haridas Nadiyada; considering those words clarifies who Dada Jasvantji was. It is recorded there, in verse 5. There are two variant readings of this verse — one as found in the guru lineage (guru-pranalika) recorded within the Bhaktamal in the samagam, and another as found in the lineage recorded in Handwritten Manuscript No. 44-Jha, page 31. The variant reading between the two is as follows:

Samagam, Verse 5 —

_Dvaadas jan apudeshmaan, sukhdaataa jethaa bhayaa. Taake shikh gopaalajee, jan joovan updesh diyaa._

According to this, among Ramanand's twelve disciples, the foremost, who gave the joy and bliss of loving devotion (prem-bhakti), was Kabirji. In his lineage came Gnaniji; his disciple was Dada Sukhji; and his disciple was Gopaldasji, who gave instruction to Jivandasji.

Handwritten Manuscript 44, Verse 1 —

_Dvaarakaadaas updeshmen, sukhdaataa jaag bhayaa. Taake shikh gopaalajee, jan jeevanku updesh diyaa._

According to this, Gnaniji's rajguru (royal preceptor) was Khojiji-Dwarakadas. Gnaniji's chief disciple, who gave the joy of loving devotion, was Dada Sukhji (Jasvantji); his disciple was Gopadasji, who gave instruction to Jivandasji.

Thus, according to what is stated in this text, in interpreting "Sukhdata Jetha," the view that Sukhdata Jetha refers to Dada Jasvant was put forward by Nazar Damodardas Purushottam, following the advice and opinion of the Revered Yadunath Maharaj; his account of this is as follows (reference: Jagdish No. 1465, page 206):

It appears that Jasvantji, the disciple of Gnaniji, must have had "Dado Sakhji" as another name. This seems evident because the name Jasvantji appears in the earlier verse, while in the guru lineage recorded in the samagam, we find "Dado Sakhji, of Pipavans, resident of Shukla Tirth." Weighing all this together — if each of these names belonged to a separate person, a great many years would need to have passed between them, which is not plausible; hence it appears that all these names belong to one and the same person. This is the view expressed by Puniyad Swami Yadunathji, and on reflection it seems the same to me as well. Between Jivanji Maharaj and Gnaniji Maharaj only two generations passed — Gopaldas and Dado Sukhji — this is a matter of common, well-known record; therefore, Dado Sakhji, Dado Jasvant, and the person addressed as Sukhdata Jetha are one and the same.

My own view is likewise that, in Jivanji's guru lineage, the guru of Gopaldas is called Dada Sukhji, and in this chapter it is said that "Dada Jasvantji wept." Thus the title "Dada" occurs in both cases, and Revered Yadunathji's view — that these two are one and the same — is, in my judgment, correct.

Thus, having noted the date on which this Dada-guru of Jivanji Maharaj experienced this event, mention has been made here of his devotion. This shows the depth of Jasvantji's feeling, and in support of it, a sakhi of Kabirji has also been given, declaring that whoever conducts himself wrongly in matters of devotion to Hari is as much at fault as one who acts with stubbornness. Kabir has said —

_Kabir khanchaataani mat karau, utaro bhav jal paar. Niranjan niraakaar au kahiye, sau raavan kumbhakarn sanharanaar._ (Kabir says: do not engage in excessive insistence and stubbornness; practice devotion, and you will cross the ocean of worldly existence. The one we call the formless, attributeless Brahman is that same Ram who destroyed Ravana and Kumbhakarna.)

Das Kabirji says: O brother, do not engage in excessive insistence and stubbornness — practice devotion to Ram, and you will cross the ocean of worldly existence. The one whom we call the formless, attributeless (nirgun-nirakar) Brahman is that same Ram who destroyed Ravana and Kumbhakarna.

_Kabir harikee bhakti bin, je kije aparaadh. Kahvo sunvo bolvo, sab karvo aparaadh._ (Kabir says: whatever worship you perform apart from devotion to Hari — speaking of it, hearing it, or discussing it — all of it is sinful.)

Das Kabirji says: whatever other worship one performs apart from devotion to God — speaking of it, listening to it, or discussing it — all of this is sinful and faulty.

The date of the episode "Dada Jasvantji Wept" is the 13th day of the dark half of Bhadarva, Samvat 1709 [unclear]. After this chapter, the samagam records, in several places, the dates on which certain further episodes occurred. The next episode given in the samagam took place fifteen days after Jasvantji wept.

Questions on stealing from the guru: 1 — of the acrobat (vadi); 2 — of the barber (khavas); 3 — of Naradji.

Second question — Shri Jivandasji said that once an acrobat (vadi) went out to display his skills. There he saw a lake in a great forest. Being thirsty, he sat down to drink water, and there he saw a crane catch a fish in its beak. The crane first caught the fish by the tail and tossed it high up; it tossed it in such a way that, turning it around, it caught it again by the head, in its mouth. The acrobat saw this. Then it occurred to his mind: 'I already know many skills, but this skill is new — let me master it and profit from it.' So he set about mastering the skill. He first practiced the whole technique with the bow and then with the spear. Having mastered the arrow, he then practiced the throw called jhang — catching the spear in his teeth and hurling it, then catching it again by turning and gripping it by the haft. Performing this feat, he played at many royal courts and grew infatuated with fame.

Once, before a certain king, another acrobat was performing, and this acrobat went and joined the contest. A rivalry arose between them, and the newly arrived performer began to show the feat he had newly learned. The very first time, the feat came off perfectly and he was overjoyed, and the other acrobat lost; the king, the ministers, and all the people were astonished. Then the defeated acrobat and the others asked where he had learned this feat, and he answered that he had learned it by his own wit — concealing his guru. At this the leader of the defeated acrobat said, 'There can be no skill without a guru — he has stolen [hidden] his guru. Make him perform again; this time he will not get away with it. If he wins a second time, we will accept it as proven' — so they told the king. So he was made to perform a second time, and this time he forgot the trick's timing. Because of that, the spear went from above straight into his mouth and passed clean through, piercing his whole body and going into the ground.

On this, Jivandasji said that because he stole [betrayed] the duty he owed his guru, he lost his own life — he gained a bad name in this world, and in the world beyond he was left belonging to neither side.

_Vigahamki vidya lai, bakhar barchhi jhil. Rajab guru gun chaurte, mukh mein paithi shil. ||1||_ (Having learned the art from the crane bird, [the acrobat] could catch the flung spear — but Rajab says: by hiding the debt owed to his guru, the spear went into his mouth.) The acrobat, having learned the skill from the crane, used to catch the thrown spear (sang) with the skill he had gained; but Rajabji says that by concealing the favor of his guru — the crane — the spear went into his mouth.

The second question is of King Bhoj. He knew all the fourteen sciences existing in the three worlds, but he was thinking of learning a fifteenth science, when at that time a sannyasi (renunciant) arrived. The king served and entertained him greatly, and as he was leaving, the sannyasi said, 'King Bhoj, tell me whatever wish is in your mind — you speak to me with such earnest requests that it seems you have a desire, so speak it.' Hearing this, the king submitted his request: teach him the fifteenth science, that of entering another's body (parkaya pravesh). The sannyasi said, 'Come to the cremation ground at night, and bring materials for the fire-offering (homa).'

As the king was about to go alone, Queen Bhanumati said, 'Take the barber (khavas) with you — do not go alone.' So the king set off, taking the barber along. He told the barber, 'You sit here,' and himself went on to the sannyasi's hermitage to learn. But the barber secretly followed and, hidden in the king's shadow near the hermitage, began to learn as well — without either the king or the sannyasi knowing, he stole the teaching for himself. Afterward the king came back to where he had left the barber, and the barber returned to his spot too. Both then performed the fire-offering and practiced the mantra, each on his own.

Now the thought arose in the barber's mind: when the king tested the power, he would enter the king's body and enjoy Bhoj's kingdom himself. Holding this thought, he went along with the king. On one occasion, to test the power, the king killed a deer and told the barber, 'Watch over my body.' The king then entered the deer, and at that the barber entered the king's body. The king, now in the deer, thought, 'The barber will kill me now,' and fled in the deer's form. The barber then had his own original body cremated, and, in the form of Bhoj, went to Bhanumati's palace.

When the queen offered him a pot of water, the king would always recite a particular verse at that moment — but this one, not reciting the verse, hurried straight into the palace. At that the queen understood that though the body was the king's, the spirit within it was a barber's. Resolving to punish him for this, she said, 'My lord, I am keeping a vow, so do not come to my chambers for six months.' Hearing this, he turned back and went instead to the house of the queen who was out of favor.

Now the barber thought: since the king was in the form of a deer, he should have that deer killed. So he ordered his attendants, 'Let us go hunting today.' They went to the forest, where the king was among a herd of deer; they surrounded the herd, recognized the king, and shot an arrow at him, so that the king fled with a lamed leg. He then told his attendants, 'Bring me the particular deer I have in mind, from among those that fled' — giving them the sign that it was the lame one — and they went on to kill many deer.

King Bhoj realized they meant to kill him; at that moment he left the deer's body — there lay in a thicket the body of a dead parrot — and made his soul enter that parrot, abandoning the deer's body. Then, in the form of a parrot, he came to the queen and, speaking in a human voice, told her everything, saying, 'You sent the barber with me, and because of that I have suffered terribly — he has stolen my art of entering another's body.' Hearing this, the queen consoled him, saying, 'I will get your own body restored to you; do not worry at all.' Comforting the king in this way, she kept him, in the form of a parrot, in a cage, and cared for him with great affection.

At that time, seeing among the deer killed by arrows one that must have been the king, and believing the king had perished, the barber came to Bhanumati. Seeing that the queen daily cared for the parrot in the cage and showed it the greatest, most loving regard, it occurred to that fellow's mind: 'She loves this parrot more than she loves me — if I enter this parrot's body with my soul, the queen's affection for me will grow.' Thinking so, he set about beguiling the queen in every way he could. Then the queen said, 'You have learned the art of entering another's body — teach it to me, and demonstrate it, so my mind may be satisfied; without that, I remain displeased with you.'

Hearing this, the barber, pleased, said, 'One can enter a dead body, but not a living one — so let a corpse be brought, and I will demonstrate it to you.' At that moment, looking out from a window, the queen saw at a distance the corpse of a dog that had just died in great agony; she had that corpse brought and said to the barber, 'First enter this dog's corpse with your soul and show me — only then will you teach me the art.' At the queen's word, the barber left the king's body and entered the dog's corpse. At that, King Bhoj, lord of men, made his soul pass from the parrot's body back into his own original body, and everyone then beat that dog severely and drove it away.

On this the Vaishnav Jivandasji said that one who turns against his true benefactor has no place even in the three worlds.

(This matter of entering another's body is also found in the Prabandh Chintamani, Canto 1; [unclear]-1, page 99.)

Once Vikram heard that without the art of entering another's body, even the powers of the yogi Bhairavanand were incomplete. To obtain that art he went to Shri Parvat and stayed near a yogi named Bhairavanand, serving that yogi for a long time. Before Vikram's arrival, a certain Brahmin had already been serving that same yogi in order to obtain this art, but up to then the Brahmin had not received it. This Brahmin said to Vikramaditya, 'You must not abandon me and take the art of entering another's body from the guru for yourself alone' — thus the disciple pressed him insistently. So the king began to petition the guru, who was preparing to give him the art, saying, 'First give the art to this Brahmin, then give it to me.' The yogi said, 'O King, this Brahmin is not fit for the art of entering another's body — he is utterly unfit,' and went on to say, 'If I give it to him, you will regret it.' Yet, because of the king's insistence, the guru gave the Brahmin the art as well.

Then both, having received the art from the guru, came to Ujjain. To test the art, seeing that the palace's finest elephant had died and the royal household was grieving over it, the king, in order to experience the art of entering another's body, entered the dead elephant's body himself.

Vikram already knew that once his own body lay empty, this Brahmin might enter it and take his kingdom; yet, since he was one devoted to relieving others' suffering, he took this risk without regard for his own body. Just as Vikram had suspected, the Brahmin did enter the king's abandoned body and began to rule the kingdom with a show of righteousness. The Brahmin also began to make use of Vikram's queen, so that an intimate bond formed between the two of them. One day a pet parrot that the queen loved dearly suddenly died. Vikram, in the elephant, thought: 'The queen's body has become the Brahmin's to enjoy; my chance of her touch is gone. Well, here is a good opportunity — if I enter the parrot's body, I will at least have the touch of the queen's gentle hands.'

Thinking so, the king entered the dead parrot's body, and the dead parrot suddenly came alive; because of this the queen's affection, which she had already had for the parrot, grew even greater. The Brahmin, who had become deeply infatuated with the queen, was constantly devising ways to please her, and he came to see that the queen loved the parrot even more than she loved him. So he thought, 'If the chance comes, I myself will become the parrot.' Vikram, residing in the parrot's body, discerned this plan. He was watching for a chance to leave the parrot's body, and just then he saw the empty shell of a dead lizard. Vikram quickly left the parrot and entered the lizard's body; seeing this, the Brahmin left the king's body and at once slipped into the parrot. The king then left the lizard's body and swiftly returned to his own original body. The unfortunate Brahmin, through his own deceit, in trying to gain the kingdom and the queen, lost his own body and, become a parrot, ended up shut in a cage. The queen and the king, having learned the whole matter from the king himself, treated that parrot with great harshness. In this way the accomplishment of the art of entering another's body came to pass.

Regarding entering another's body, Shankaracharya too made use of this art. When he defeated Mandan Mishra in philosophical debate, Mandan Mishra's wife said that he had won only half the victory, since a wife is the 'other half' of her husband [unclear], and so he would have to defeat her as well to be counted a complete victor; and she, as Saraswati, then put to him a question about the art of love.

_Prichchhami vad kamasya kala bhihato kimatmika. Kiyatyashcha kimadharastatha kamasya ka sthitih. Purvapakshe pare naryam nare tishthati va katham. Eteshamuttaram dehi savichary yatishvar._ (O lord of ascetics, what is the true nature of the arts of love, and how many are there, and on what do they rest? How does desire abide in human beings? In the bright and the dark halves of the month, where do these arts of love reside in man and in woman? Answer these questions after due reflection.) 'O lord of ascetics, what is the nature of these arts of love? And how many are there? And on what do they depend? In what manner does desire abide in human beings? In the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight, where do the arts of love reside in man and in woman? Please answer these questions after careful thought.'

Shankaracharya thought: if he did not answer, it would be a blot on his omniscience; if he did answer, it would be a blot on his vow of renunciation. So he asked for a month's time, and — there being a King Amarak who had died from the strain of hunting — in order to gain full experience of the amorous ways of that king's beautiful queens, he entered the dead king's body, and composed there an excellent treatise full of ever-fresh subjects on the science of love, which is today famous under the name Amarushatak.

In the Bhagavat, Canto Eleven, Chapter Fifteen, verses 23 and 24, it is said regarding entering another's body:

_Parkayam vishansiddha, atmanam tatra bhavayet. Pindam hitva vishetprano, vayubhutah shadandhrivat. ||23||_ _Pashnyarpidashcha gudam pranam, hriduh kanthanmurdhasu. Arohya brahmarandhrena, brahma nitvotsrijettanum. ||24||_ (A siddha wishing to enter another's body first contemplates the self within that body; then, leaving the gross frame behind, the life-breath, become as air, slips out effortlessly, as through six doors. To leave one's own body: pressing the anus with the heel, and raising the breath-conditioned self, that is, the subtle body, step by step through the heart, chest, throat and head, and carrying it out by the mind through the crown aperture, one abandons the gross body.)

When one wishes to enter another's body, the yogi first contemplates his own self within that body. Then he leaves his gross body behind and, carrying the subtle body (linga sharir) with him, enters effortlessly, just as a bee passes from one flower to another without labor; in the same way, by the path of the vital air, he enters the other body with ease. This accomplishment is called 'entering another's body' (parkaya praveshan). (23)

The method of leaving one's own body is then given: pressing the anus firmly with the heel of the foot, and raising the self conditioned by the vital breath — that is, the subtle body — step by step through the heart, chest, throat and head, and, through the door that is the crown aperture (brahmarandhra), carrying it by the mind into the other body, one abandons one's own gross body. This is reckoned the accomplishment called entering another's body. And when one draws the breath-conditioned self entirely out from one's own body through the door of the crown aperture without entering another body, that is reckoned the accomplishment called 'death at will.' (24)

Note — Bhagat Mohanbhai Motibhai of Tandalja tells me that a man of a lower-caste community in his village knew how to turn from a man into a tiger. When asked how this was done, that man said this is not an art anyone should wish to learn: when the change from man to tiger takes place, a tiger's tail emerges, and at that moment there is very great pain. This man used to take the form of a tiger [unclear] in order to go and meet his beloved. Dated 1 May 2006 — as of today, this bhagat, now 103 years old, is still living.

Giving the example of the acrobat, Jivandasji said that one who turns against his true benefactor has no place even in the three worlds.

Third question — Narad, son of Brahma, in his first incarnation was the son of a maidservant, and he lived in the town of Purajit. There the eight Vasudevs once came, and he served them with great devotion; because of this worthiness he came to be called Narad.
