Kripanath [the Lord] commanded this Narad, 'O Narad, go and take a guru, then come back.' Narad said, 'Whom shall I make my guru?' Then Kripanath commanded, 'Go to the town of Purajit; setting your own judgment aside, take a guru there — take initiation from whoever you meet first.'

Narad came and stood at the gate of the town of Purajit. A fisherman, going with a net over his shoulder to catch fish, came by. Narad fell at his feet and said, 'My lord, I take refuge in you.' The fisherman, pleased in turn, gave him initiation and said, 'When you fall into great suffering, remember me.'

Narad then came to Vaikunth. Countless devotees, Brahma, Rudra, and other gods were present there. The Sanakadi sages said, 'O Narad, whose teaching have you brought — name your guru.' Narad thought that 'fisherman' was too lowly a name to speak. At that Kripanath said, 'O Narad, go and undergo the eighty-four lakh births, and then return.'

Narad, weeping and lamenting bitterly, made his way back toward Purajit. Just then the fisherman, having caught his fish, was returning to his own home. He met Narad and found him lamenting, and asked, 'Who has caused you this suffering?' Narad said, 'My lord, when I spoke your name my heart did not feel glad — because of that I am being made to undergo the eighty-four lakh births.' The fisherman, growing angry, said, 'Who has the power to send my own disciple into the eighty-four lakh births?' Then he said, 'Tell Kripanath to set the eighty-four lakh forms before me, that I may pass through them all at once and be done. When Kripanath sets forth those forms, you go around them in circumambulation, prostrating upon them; and when Vasudev speaks, say: I undergo the eighty-four lakh births before your very eyes.'

Kripanath then came, called Narad, and embraced him, granting him the boon: 'I cannot manage even for a moment without you.' Regarding Naradji, Kabirji says:

_Guru duraya apna, to parharya kartar._ (When one keeps one's guru at a distance, the Creator abandons him.) When Narad kept his guru hidden and at a distance, God abandoned Narad.

_Kabir Narad haripad paiya, dhimarke updesh. Chaurasi fera mitya, bohor na kado bhes._ (Through the fisherman's teaching Narad attained the abode of God; the cycle of eighty-four lakh births came to an end, and he needed take no further birth.) Das Kabirji says that through the teaching of the fisherman, Naradji attained the abode of God, and the round of eighty-four lakh births came to an end for him, so that he never had to take another birth.

_Kabir Narad sarikha shishya hai, guru hvai machhimar. Ta guruki ninda kare, padai chaurasi dhar._ (Even if the disciple is as excellent as Narad and the guru as lowly as a fisherman, whoever reviles such a guru must fall into the eighty-four lakh forms of life.) Das Kabirji says that even if the disciple be of a lineage as excellent as Narad's, and the guru of a lineage as humble as a fisherman's, still, whoever reviles such a guru must fall into the eighty-four lakh wombs.

Just as Naradji received no honor in Vaikunth without a guru, the same happened to Shukdev; here is the couplet (sakhi) on that:

_Kabir garabh yogeshar guru bina, lage harki sev. Kahe Kabir Vaikunthate, fer diya Shukdev._ (Shukdev, a great master-yogi from birth, took up devotion to God without a guru — yet God sent him back out of Vaikunth.) Das Kabirji says that Shukdev, who was a great master-yogi (yogeshvar) from birth itself, began devotion to God without taking a guru; yet, without a guru, all his practice came to nothing, because God sent him back out of Vaikunth.

_Kabir Janak Videhi guru kiya, laga harki sev. Kahe Kabir Vaikunthme, ulati mila Shukdev._ (He then took Janak Videhi as guru and served with devotion, and this was accepted by the Lord; afterward Shukdev reached the abode of God.) Das Kabirji says that Shukdev then took Janak Videhi as his guru and performed devoted service, and this became acceptable to the Lord; afterward, having grown detached from worldly life, Shukdev reached the abode of God.

_Kabir Shukdev sarikha feriya, to ko pave par. Guru bin nigura jo rahai, padai chaurasi dhar._ (If even Shukdev was turned back for want of a guru, who without one can cross this world? The guruless must fall into the eighty-four lakh births.) Das Kabirji says that when even Shukdev, a master-yogi from the very womb, was pushed back into the world of the eighty-four lakh births for want of a guru, then who without a guru can hope to cross over worldly existence? So those without a guru will surely have to fall into the stream of the eighty-four lakh births.

_Lakhya mite nahi Jivana, je kachhu lakhiya lekh. Sadguru lekh mitaiya, tab paya aap alekh. ||2||_ (Whatever is written as fate cannot be erased — yet the true guru erased that writing, and then the unknowable Name was attained.) Maharaj Jivandasji says: O Jivan, whatever record of deeds destiny has written cannot be erased by anyone — but the true guru (sadguru) erased that writing of fate, and then we came to that Name of God which cannot otherwise be known.

_Likhita Chitraguptena lalatakshara-malika. Tanna chalayitu shakya asurais-tridashairapi. Na sapi chalitum shakya panditaih tridashairapi._ It is said in another Purana: the garland of letters that Chitragupta has written on the forehead cannot be moved even by gods, demons, pandits, or Shiva himself.

_Yaddhatra likhitam bhale tanmrisha naiva jayate. Rite Shri Ramdasanam prem nirbhar chetasam._ (What the Creator has written on the forehead never proves false — except for the true servants of Ram, whose hearts overflow with love.) Whatever the Creator has written on the forehead never turns out false — but this rule holds for everyone except the supremely loving servants of Ram, whose hearts are full of love.

_Kabir jo lakh supai alekhaku, adrishta akshar bij. To lakh rahe alekhaki, lakhu mite hi ghij._ (If we fix our aim on the God who cannot be shown, the seed of the unseeable arises in us, and that God's regard then rests on us; trust that the writing of fate will surely be erased.) Das Kabirji says that if we surrender our aim toward that God who can be shown by no one, a seed is sown from which that unseeable God arises within us; then such an unseeable God's regard rests upon us, and you may trust with certainty that whatever is written by past deeds will surely be erased.

_Alakh lakhayo Jivana, Sadguru Sitaram. Karma dharma vede kahyo, so chhand diyo bekam. ||3||_ (The sadguru made known the unseeable Lord, Sitaram; the rites the Vedas prescribed we abandoned as useless.) Maharaj Jivandasji says: O Jivan, the sadguru made known to us the unseeable Lord, the hidden Supreme Being who is Sitaram; and the ritual practices — japa, austerity, and the various rites the Vedas' karma-kanda prescribes — we have abandoned those useless labors.

_Kabir shishya hoy Narad sarikha, guru hoy machhimar. Tad guruku parhare, to vako var na par. ||4||_ (Even if the disciple be as high as Narad and the guru as lowly as a fisherman, if such a guru is abandoned no good comes of it.) Das Kabirji says that even if the disciple is of as high a standing as Narad, and the guru as lowly as a fisherman, still, if such a guru is abandoned, no good comes of it for the disciple at all.

_Kabir hem garam gau vipra ghan, e to paap aghor. E bache guru bandagi, par guru drohi nahi thor. ||5||_ (Stealing gold, or killing a cow or a Brahmin, are terrible sins — one is saved by taking refuge in the guru, but there is no refuge for one who betrays the guru.) Das Kabirji says that stealing gold, killing a cow, or slaying a Brahmin are extremely terrible sins; yet one is saved from them by taking refuge in the guru — but for one who betrays the guru, there is no refuge at all.

_Hem harn gau vipra vadh, e to paap aghor. Te chhute guru bandagi, guru drohi nahi thaur._ _Guru drohi nahi thaur, jagatman jakadai marto. Samje na kem nathor, sajjan vachan uchaarta. Trikam kahe chhe takor, samjan hoy to samaj sadya. E to paap aghor, hem haran gau vipra vadh._ Das Kabirji says that stealing gold, or killing a cow or a Brahmin, is a terrible sin, but one is saved by taking refuge in the guru — yet for the betrayer of the guru there is no refuge. One can never be saved from betraying the guru, and such people become entangled in worldly bondage; O shameless one, why do you not understand? Good people have spoken these very words. Trikamdas draws attention to this teaching: if you have the sense to understand, understand it quickly — to steal gold, or to kill a cow or a Brahmin, is indeed a terrible sin.

_Hem harn gau vipra vadh, e to paap aghor. Te chhute guru bandagi, guru drohi nahin thaur._ _Guru drohi nahi thaur, kahe chhe Kabir pokari. Samjat nahi nathor, jivan bhar rahe bhikhari. Samjan sadguru aur, guru karine samaj sadya. E to paap adhor, hem haran gau vipra vadh._ To steal gold, or to kill a cow or a Brahmin, is indeed a terrible sin, but one is saved by taking refuge in the guru — yet for the one who betrays the guru there is no escape at all. Kabirji cries out and declares that one can never be saved from betraying the guru, but the shameless, brazen person understands nothing, and so is ruined for his whole life; the sadguru has given us this excellent understanding, so make haste to understand it by taking a guru — to steal gold, or to kill a cow or a Brahmin, is indeed a great sin.

_Hem harn gau vipra vadh, e to paap aghor. Te chhute guru bandagi, guru drohi nahin thaur._ _Guru drohi nahi thaure, santo kahe pokari. Samjo nahi matimand, tethi fare bhikhari. Nugarane narakman thaur, sajjan shabdne samjo sadya. E to paap adhor, hem haran gau vipra vadh._ The fool does not understand, and so wanders about helpless, like a beggar. Those without a guru must fall into hell — so, virtuous brothers, understand these words quickly: to steal gold, or to kill a cow or a Brahmin, is a great sin.

_Kabir hari ruthe gati ek hai, je guru sharanagat jay. Par guru rithe gati ekau nahi, hari nav deve thay. ||6||_ (If God is displeased, taking refuge in the guru can save one — but if the guru is displeased, God will not grant shelter.) Das Kabirji says that if God is displeased, there is one remedy: going to the refuge of the guru, by which one may be saved; but if the guru is displeased, then God will grant that person no shelter at all.

_Hari ruthe hat ek chhe, guru sharanagat jay. Guru ruthe gat ko nahi, sant shastra sahu gay._ _Sant shastra sahu gay, guru droh gambhir ganay. Rau rau narak pahay, Ramayan path bhanay. Trikam sadguru kahay, guru drohi bahu dukh sahe. Guru sharanagat jay, hari ruthe gat ek hai._ If God is displeased, one is saved by taking refuge in the guru; but if the guru is displeased, there is no escape at all — so say the scriptures of the saints, [by which even God cannot save such a person]. The scriptures of the saints say that offense against the guru is reckoned a grave sin, and one must fall into the raurava hell — this is told in the account of Kag Bhushundi in the Ramayana. Trikam says that the true guru Kabir himself has spoken this: one who betrays the guru must endure much suffering, but if it is God who is displeased, then there is this one remedy — that one is saved by taking refuge in the guru.

_Kabir guru mahila guru bavaya, guru devan ka dev. Jo tu chelu kharo shayano, to karle guru ki seva. ||7||_ (Even a guru who seems mad or bewildered is still the god of gods — a wise disciple serves the guru all the same.) Das Kabirji says that even if the guru seems mad, deranged, or utterly bewildered, still the guru is the greatest, the very god of the gods; so if you are truly a wise disciple, render service and care to the guru.

_Kabir guruke avagun ankho dekhe, so to hove andh. Chhot kare parsadki, so kude bhav sindhu._ (Whoever looks with his own eyes for the guru's faults becomes blind; whoever spurns the guru's grace as untouchable drowns in the ocean of worldly existence.) Das Kabirji says that whoever looks with his eyes for the guru's faults becomes blind, and whoever treats the guru's grace as untouchable drowns and dies in the waters of the ocean of worldly existence.

_Guruki karni chit dhare, shikh sohi chandaal. Taki sangat parasram, nishche gase kaal._ (Parshuram says: whichever disciple keeps dwelling in his mind on the guru's conduct and finds fault with it is like an untouchable; keep company with such a person, and death will surely devour you.)

_Guru je avagun kare, shikh so dekhe naahi. Gyani jaane Ramroop, dubdha dilme naahi._ (Gyaniji Maharaj says: whatever fault the guru may commit, the disciple should not dwell on it in his mind; rather he should regard the guru as a form of Lord Ram himself, and hold no doubt or suspicion in his heart.)

_Ekah eva paro bandhur-vishame samupasthite, Gurusakaladharmatma, yatra-akinchanago Harih._ (Shridhar says of the guru: in a terrible calamity like death, the one true friend who comes to help is the guru alone. The guru is righteous in every way, for Shri Hari, who loves the poor and destitute, dwells within the guru's heart.)

_Yasya sakshad bhagavati tranadeepapade gurau, martyasaddhih shrutam tasya sarva kunjharashochavat. ||26||_ (The guru who lights the lamp of knowledge in the heart is God himself, present before us. If a foolish person regards him as merely human, then all the scripture that person has heard is as useless as an elephant's bath, which only covers it in dust again.)

**Sugar-Candy Food**

The parable of how faith was ruined by eating sweets from the hand of a sakut (a self-serving, worldly-minded person, as opposed to a true devotee).

Once, at a time of famine, a Smarta (worldly, self-interested) Brahmin, his Brahmin wife, and their son were travelling along and came to Shri Gokul. There, the parents deceived their seven-year-old boy and abandoned him on the bank of the river Yamuna, then went away. The child began to wail. Shri Gosainji happened to come to that spot. When he asked the child who he was, the boy said, "I am a Brahmin's child. My mother and father have left me and gone." Gokulnath Gosainji felt compassion. He had the boy's head shaved, gave him a mala and tilak, placed his hand upon his head, and named him Govardhan. He entrusted him with the seva of Shri Govardhannathji and put the keys of the storehouse in his hands. He instilled in him the spirit of a servant among the Vaishnavs, and the boy came to love the path of devotion to God very dearly.

Some days later, his parents returned to that same bank of the Yamuna at Gokul, to the very spot where they had abandoned him, and both of them heard the child. He was crying loudly, so the people of Braj living in Gokul came and told the Smarta Brahmin the news that his son's name had been made Govardhan, and that Shri Gosainji had entrusted him with the seva of Govardhannathji. Just then that Vaishnav boy came carrying a golden pot on a yoke to fetch water, and the people of Braj pointed him out to his parents. His mother and father broke down weeping, but he did not even look at his own parents. They stayed there like this for five days, grieving constantly, but the boy, being a Vaishnav bound by such strict vows, would not let even their shadow fall upon him. One day, at the bank of the Yamuna, his mother came and fell at his feet, since Govardhan Thakorji's water-carrier had come there to fill water. His father then tied up a lump of sugar-candy and gave it to him, saying, "Please take this sweet; let our anguish be relieved." Knowing their sorrow, the boy put the sugar-candy in his mouth twice, and as soon as it entered his mouth he said, "Now your wish is fulfilled" — and went on his way. But once that sweetness had gone down into his stomach, he said, "You are grieving for my sake; I will come with you." He made a promise to his mother and father, saying, "I will bring some wealth with me." Then he took all of Hari's ornaments — the diamonds, pearls, and jewels — locked up the temple, handed over the storeroom, took the keys with him, and set off with his parents. The three of them walked a distance of three, five, ten kos. Meanwhile, in Shri Gokul, all the Vaishnavs were crying out in great distress because a theft had occurred in the temple. They sent Vaishnavs out in all directions to search. At that time, Shri Gosainji said, "He will not go anywhere and leave the seva of Nathji's temple. His parents were self-serving, and he has taken sweets from their hand; that sweet will remain in his stomach, and only once it has passed through and its effect wears off will he come back. Since Shrinathji's chamber is locked, he is bound to return — that is what I say." After some time, when all the Vaishnavs were sitting together in assembly, that boy came in, weeping and wailing loudly. He told the whole story at length: "As long as the wicked portion of that sweet remained in my stomach, I was carried away by it, and once that unoffered, impure portion had passed through me, I became blind to the truth and could not see the way ahead. That is why, Maharaj, I have left that wickedness behind and have come to take refuge at your feet. I have brought back all the ornaments, the diamonds, pearls, and jewels." Saying this, he handed the keys to the guru and bowed at his feet, weeping loudly. Then Vyasji spoke this sakhi in that assembly —

_Vyas bohot meethai vipraki, taame lago ju aag. Shri Vrindavanke swapachke, rahiye sevak hoiye maag. ||1||_

_Vyas Vrindavanke swapachke, rahiye sevak hoi. Taathe bhinna na aaniye, peeje pagraj ghoi. ||2||_

(Hariram Vyasdasji says: however great a Brahmin may be, if his sweets — being the sweets of a non-Vaishnav — are bound to spoil, let them spoil; give them up. But one who dwells in Vrindavan-dham, the realm of devotion, even if he is of the lowest caste, a bhangi, is still to be preferred — become his servant and beg from him if need be. Vyasdasji says: one who dwells in Vrindavan, even a devotee of the bhangi caste, should be served; do not think of him as different or lesser — rather, wash his feet and drink that water, that is, welcome and honor him with the greatest respect.)

**The Crow that Perched on the Ship — A Parable of the Bond between Guru and Disciple**

Jivandasji said: Once there was a ship with its helmsman. While it was under way it anchored partway along its route. A crow then flew and settled upon it, and after a while the ship set sail again. The crow began flying about, looking in all four directions, and then came and settled right back on the ship. "Now tell me, of the two — the ship and the crow — which is the better?" Hearing this, none of the other Vaishnavs answered, so Vaishnav Jivandasji himself said: the nature of the ship is that of the guru, and the nature of the bird is that of the disciple. In this world one sees only the water of worldly craving; if there were somewhere else to go, one would go there, but where can one go in the water? That is why the crow keeps returning again and again to perch upon the ship.

_Sitapati Raghunathji, tum lagi meri daur. Jaise kaag jahajko, soojhat aur na thaur._ (In this doha it is said: O Sitapati Ram, my striving can carry me only so far as reaching your shelter, with whatever strength I have — just as a crow, clinging to the ropes of a ship, has nowhere else to go besides the ship, so too I find no refuge anywhere besides you. A person can exert only the strength that lies within his own capacity.)

_Kabir mere sahab aap ho, tum lagi meri daur. Jaise pankhi jahajka, aur na soojhe thaur._ (Kabir says: O my Lord, you alone are mine; my striving reaches only as far as you — just as the ship's bird finds no other refuge in sight besides the ship.)

_Kabir jal kaasht boodai nahi, kaha bhai kahaanki preet. Oopna seencha jaanke, eh badaanki reet. ||1||_ (Das Kabirji says: a log of wood does not sink in water — tell me, brother, what is the nature of this love? The answer: "I have watered and nurtured this wood, knowing it as my own," and it is out of that knowledge that one does not let it drown; such a noble sentiment belongs only to the great and elevated souls.)

_Pathar pabedo naakhtaan, kalpa vriksha phal det. Aise Harijan Jeevna, bhaage jaateku det. ||2||_ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: even when a loose stone is hurled at it, a wish-fulfilling tree still gives fruit in return; in the same way, the devotees of Hari shower their grace even upon those who trouble them and run away.)

_Kabir mein seenchyo het jaanke, o hoi neem kaath. Dekho gat sansaarki, sheesh par paadi baat._ (Das Kabirji says: "I have watered this, knowing it as my own" — even should it turn out to be bitter neem wood, that very wood, out of love, makes a path for the water over its own crown; such is the way love runs in this world — understand it well.)

_Poot pithaara baapko, gohan laaga jaay. Lobh mithai haath de, aapan gaya bhoolaay. Deenhi khaand padtikikar, man mein ros upaay. Rovat rovat mili gaya, pita piyaare jaay._ (Das Kabirji says: a son is dear to his father, to his guru; he keeps running along in his father's, his guru's, embrace. The devotee went for shelter to the Lord, to the guru; then the father put a sweet in the son's hand — the mistaken notion that the soul is meant for worldly enjoyment — and lured by greed for that sweet, the son let go of the guru's hand and forgot his own true self. But then he threw away the packet of sugar-candy, anger rose in his mind, and weeping, weeping, he went and was reunited with his beloved father, his guru. Once the devotee gave up the objects of the senses, he attained Hari.)

**Kundali**

_Gordhan gaando thai gayo, maat taatni khai khaand. Hakk vanu santjan khaayna, khaay te to jan bhaand. Khaay te to jan bhaand, khaataan jag haansi thashe. Kahun chun laai het, na samajya maaraj khaase. Trikam lakhe kritaghnanun kaand, samajaavva vichaar thayo. Maat taatni khaand khai, Gordhan gaando thai gayo._

(Trikamdas Govardhandas Suryodhoda writes: the Smarta Brahmin's son Gordhan lost his senses after eating sugar-candy from his parents' hand, and so committed theft in the temple and fled together with his parents. This is how true saints behave — they never accept anything beyond what rightfully belongs to them, and those who obtain and enjoy things in this improper way are nothing but clowns and buffoons. Anyone who indulges in this way will only bring shame and disgrace upon themselves before the world. I say this with pure love and affection; if you proceed without understanding it, you will only suffer for it. Trikamdas [says]: I am writing this account of the wretched state to which an ungrateful person, one who harms his own benefactor, is reduced. It occurred to me to explain this through the example of how the son Gordhan lost his senses after eating the sugar-candy given by his mother and father.)

**Kavit**

_Gordhan gaando thai gayo, sakut ni khai khaand. Maat pita hova chataan, mati thai gai ti bhaand. Mati thai gai ti bhaand, daagina laine naatho. Thaishna swami haandh, kaadhish nahi jaraay laantho. Thaish na swami haanth, kaadhish nahi jaraay laantho. Thai fare chhe sevak raand, sakut sang hadghoot thayo. Sakut ni khai khaand, Gordhan gaando thai gayo._

(Trikamdas Govardhandas Suryodhoda writes: because Gordhan ate the sugar-candy from the hand of his self-serving parents, his mind grew as corrupted as a clown's, even though his own real parents had given it to him — because they were sakut, his understanding, being fed on that food, turned as base as a buffoon's. His intelligence became as spoiled as a clown's, so he took the temple's ornaments and fled together with his parents. So, O worthy soul of high standing, do not become as proud and unruly as an overfed bull; nurturing such pride will bring you to nothing [text unclear/incomplete in the source at this point].)

As the Chandogya Upanishad, 7.26.2, says:

_Aahaarashuddhau sattvashuddhih, sattvashuddhau dhruva smritih. Smritishuddhau sarvagranthinaam vipramokshah._

(This is explained thus: when purity of food — that is, the purity of one's perceptions and understanding gained through it — is attained, purity of the inner faculties follows, and one gains the benefit of the quality of sattva. When the inner faculties are purified, steady remembrance is attained; through that, one is able to grasp true principles, and such discerning wisdom awakens. From the resulting attainment of true remembrance, all the knots of bondage are completely loosened, and the bondage of worldly existence is destroyed.)

On the theme "as the food, so the belch; as the water, so the speech," Trikamdas Govardhandas wrote Kundali No. 618 — Diary 2.32, page 200.

**Kundali**

_Anna tevo odkaar chhe, anna tevun man. Sakut anna khaava thaki, adham bane chhe jan. Adham bane chhe jan, khaand khaai Gordhan gaando. Sutradhaar samaaj, trirashi jaldi maando. Kahe Trikam sudharel jan, oont sam par upkaari chhe. Anna tevun mand, anna tevo odkaar._

(Trikamdas says: as the food one eats, so the belch of wind that follows; likewise, as the food one eats, so the mind becomes. By eating the food of a sakut, a person becomes base and sinful — as base as Gordhan's intelligence became corrupted after eating the sugar-candy of his self-serving parents. So, O saints and mahants who bear responsibility for guiding society, quickly work out the lesson from this example: even though this sakut's son was eventually redeemed, still, if eating a sakut's food could corrupt his intelligence, then the intelligence of people like us could just as easily be spoiled. Therefore, Trikamdas says, those who call themselves cultured and refined people often present themselves as being of the highest order, like a camel, claiming to do good to others, while remaining careless and indifferent toward the ordinary, lower classes, like a jackal — such people are hypocrites. So, whatever food you eat, that same corruption will enter your mind and intellect.)

_Deepo bhakshayate dhvaantam, kajjalam cha prasrayate. Yathaannam bhakshayet nityam, jaayate taadrshi prajaa._ (A lamp consumes darkness, and in doing so produces soot; likewise, whatever food a person eats every day, offspring of that same nature are born to them.)

_Kinchidvedamayam paatram, kinchit paatram tapomayam. Paatraanaam uttamam paatram, shoodraannam yasya nodare._ (Some vessel may be precious for being learned in the Vedas, some vessel may be radiant with austerity, but the best vessel of all is the one within whose stomach there is no food from the house of a base or unworthy person.)

_Avaishnavasya hastaannam divyadeshaadupaagatam. Hareh prasaadam teertham cha prayatne vivarjayet._ (Even if food from the hand of a non-Vaishnav has come from a divine and holy place, and is Hari's own prasad or holy water, one should nonetheless make every effort to avoid and give it up.)

_Mero man anatahi sachu paavai, jaise udat jahaajko pakshi, phiri jahaaj pai asai. Jo nar kamal nainko tajikai, aanadevko dhyaavai. Vidyamaan Gangaatat pyaaso, durmati koop banaavai. Jin madhukar antuj ras chaakhyo, taahi karil na bhaavai. Surdas prabhu Kaamdhenu taji, chheri kaun duhaavai._

(Surdasji says: my mind finds no true peace anywhere else. Just as the ship's crow flies out over the ocean and then comes back to settle on the ship again, so too my mind does not stray anywhere else. In the same way, a person who abandons the lotus-eyed Lord and worships other gods is like a foolish man who digs a well for himself while standing right at the bank of the Ganga, dying of thirst. One who has tasted the lotus's nectar as a bee will never find the castor-plant's flower pleasing. Surdas says: why, then, would anyone abandon the wish-fulfilling cow Kamdhenu to go milking a goat?)

In the diary from Samvat 1984 (the Adhadhiya notebook), pages 34–33, is written the following account by the revered Yadunath, dated Samvat 1984, Magsar Sud 4, Monday, 28-11-1927, and also on page 33, Magsar Sud 3, Sunday, 27-11-1927: "Today, some portion of the conversation that took place with Bhagat Garbadbhai Ramdas of Kandari, Taluka Karjan, is recorded below."

Originally, the first seat was not at Puniyad. A government official had once come to inspect the temple, at a time when the swami was away from the residence. When the official arrived and looked, it turned out that he had received his answer from the swami and gone away. On the strength of this, the seat upon which Ishwar, that is Jivanji Maharaj, had sat while manifesting the swami's form, came to be regarded as worthy of worship and was kept for veneration; the founding of the gaadi is counted from that time. Regarding the greatness of that seat, he related another account, as follows. Chhagan Krishnaram, a resident of Kandari, who was the moneylender — and also the friend — of Jagannath Swami: Garbadbhai says from his own experience that once, when they had gone there to settle a matter of money owed, and began to sit near a pillar at the fair, they were stopped and told, "Do not sit here," because that spot belonged to Bhai Jagannath Swami, as he was addressed by that name. Garbadbhai then asked, "Do you yourself not sit here either?" The reply was, "No" — meaning that the seat and bolster near the pillar where Jagannath Swami used to sit, no one else made use of.

He also told an account regarding food, as follows.

At the same Krishnaram's house, they had adopted Ambalal, the son of his sister-in-law, whose own father's ancestral home lay on the bank of the Narmada. On one occasion, provisions had come to Krishnaram, as a patron, for a feast for the Bhoi caste; on that occasion a Dandi Sanyasi also arrived and asked for food. Since the meal was to be served late, food was given to him quite late, and by then night had fallen. The sannyasi stayed there overnight and was given a blanket to sleep under. In the morning, his mind turned to covetousness over the blanket, and he took it and left. Further on, he had a change of heart over having taken it, and after going two or three kos, he repented and came back to return it; and when he inquired whose food he had eaten there, and reflected on how his austere discipline had been broken, he was overcome with remorse. This incident, it is said, occurred in the winter of Samvat 1983.

A similar incident had occurred that was reported in the Kalyan monthly magazine, and I have mentioned it in my discourse too. At the house of a certain sheth, a sadhu-mahatma had come as a guest. The sheth attended to him and fed him, then had him lie down to rest in his own office, while the sheth himself sat counting money. In the meantime, someone suddenly called for the sheth, so he left the money just as it was and went outside. The sadhu, his eyes turning covetous, picked up a bundle of ten thousand rupees and made off with it. The next day, when the sheth's money was found missing, the sadhu was struck with remorse, thinking, "I gave up my mother, I gave up my father, I gave up wife, son, and wealth — so why did my intention turn corrupt over this money?" Fearing that the sheth would beat all his servants over it, the sadhu returned; and indeed, the sheth was scolding all his servants at that time. The sadhu then said, "Sheth-ji, do not beat anyone — I am the one who took the money." The sheth said, "I never suspected you at all." The sadhu then asked, "Sheth-ji, what kind of grain did you feed me, that my mind turned so corrupt?" The sheth replied that sacks of rice used to come to his warehouse from a railway godown, and it was from that rice he had fed him. The sadhu then said, "It was from eating stolen food that my mind became corrupted."

The Muslim community, too, places great importance on honesty (iman). Regarding the ascetic Ahmad Harsh, it is written in Kalyan magazine, Year 7, Issue 9, page 1165, Registration No. 18, as follows: One day his mother cooked food and brought it to him, saying, "Son, this food has been cooked from the grain of our own house, so eat it without any hesitation." Ahmad said, "No — one day I saw that our neighbor's grain was also mixed into ours. This neighbor gathers his wealth unjustly. Since his grain is mixed into ours, I feel great reluctance about eating this food."

Muslims do not believe in alcohol or gambling. That is why, in America, stores owned by Muslims do not sell liquor or lottery tickets — whether or not they themselves drink, they do not engage in the business of selling liquor.

It is written in Hand-written Manuscript No. 330, page 146, that devotees once asked Jivanji Maharaj whether God truly partakes of the offering placed before the garlanded image or not. Jivanji Maharaj said he would tell them at some point. Once, Vaishnavs had brought thals of prasad; all the plates were gathered together except one devotee's plate, which was kept separate. Then a garland was offered upon that separately-kept plate, and at that moment a bead of the garland burst. From this Jivanji Maharaj explained that this particular plate had been prepared with someone else's, unearned money, and that was why the bead had burst — thereby proving that God does indeed partake of the offered plate. In that manuscript, the account is recorded in the old dialect of the time, to this same effect: the devotees asked Jivanji whether the Lord truly eats the offered food; Jivanji told them he would explain. All the Vaishnavs were asked to bring their plates; all were gathered together except one Vaishnav's plate, which was kept apart because it had been made with someone else's money. When the garland was placed upon it, its bead burst — and from this everyone understood that the Lord does not accept anything not rightfully earned; and by this sign, everyone came to know that God does indeed partake of what is offered.

_Saat paanch sangi mile, surabhi bhadai uthaay. Jeevan man atakyo Shaamsun, sau neek na it ut jaay._ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: seven or five saintly companions come together and lift this wish-fulfilling cow of loving devotion up out of the mire of worldly delusion. With such a spirit, Jivandasji says, my mind has become so firmly fixed and absorbed in loving devotion to Lord Krishna that it does not stray even a little from it.)

There is also an episode recorded among the miracles of Jivanji Maharaj: a certain woman once invited Jivanji Maharaj for a meal. But when he sat down to take the prasad, Jivanji Maharaj remained seated without having offered the garland first. When everyone asked him the reason, Jivanji Maharaj said that this prasad was already impure, because the woman had cooked it using fire carried hand to hand directly from her neighbor's house. In this way, one must maintain the utmost caution and keep no dealings whatsoever with a sakut in matters concerning food and prasad.

There is the example of Upamanyu, or of Shvetaketu, who agreed to eat another's leftover food in order to have a violent sacrifice performed.

(From the Pranavidhi text, pages 16–17:) Whatever a person eats or drinks — whatever substances, creatures, or people come into contact with him — and finally, whatever thoughts he keeps his mind absorbed in, the nature of his life-force is shaped as a result of all these. From every object, whether inert or living, whoever remains close to it keeps absorbing the effect of its subtle influence; that is to say, one who stays near any given object cannot help but absorb the effect of that object's subtle influence. Clothes once worn, water once drunk, food once eaten, a book once touched — all of these become imbued with the subtle influence of the one who wore, drank, ate, or touched them, and before enough time has passed for that influence to fade, if someone else then uses that same item, this hidden quality absorbed into it is transferred to the new user. It is with all of this in mind that such rules have come into practice: not to drink water someone else has already drunk from, not to eat food someone else has already eaten from, not to eat from the same vessel as another, not to wear clothes someone else has worn, and rules about what may or may not be touched, and what may or may not be eaten. Bronze absorbs such subtle influence more quickly than copper or brass and does not release it again for a longer time; that is precisely why it is regarded as a metal that becomes unusable if touched by a person of another caste.

In Samvat year 1709, on Vaishakh Sud 5, Haribhai came from village Mauj Aritha to Shahapura. He took Vaishnav Jivandasji along and went himself to the fields; all the other Vaishnavs went along into the field as well. There they saw abundant rasal (sugarcane produce). Haribhai then said, "Vaishnavji, how is there such rasal in this month of Vaishakh?" Vaishnav Jivandasji answered by quoting the twenty-first saying of Bhakta Biradavali, of Bajid (Hand-written manuscript No. 5, page 242):

_Dharti ambar aadya dei, ravi shashi paani pavan. Sant jaan e to rachyo, nahitar kaaran kavan. ||1||_ (Having first given the earth and sky, and then the sun, moon, water, and wind — know that all this was created for the sake of the saints, for what other reason would it have been made?)

In the world, God first created the five great elements — earth, sky, and so on — and likewise created the sun, moon, water, and wind, knowing that the saints and devotees are all his servants; he made all these creations for their good. Otherwise, God says, what need would there have been for him to create all of this?

Jivanji Maharaj also says the same:

_Main sabras keeno Jeevna, so apne janke kaaj. To peechhe joolan leeno, tab paayo naam Brijraaj. ||32|| Das._

(Jivandasji Maharaj says: I have prepared every kind of flavorful dish, and I did it for the sake of my own devotees; and it was only after taking the portion left over from their eating that I attained the name Brijraj, Lord of Braj.)

Then, sitting beneath a mahuda tree, he spoke a parable: just as the one who operates the water-wheel at a well causes the water of the well's grace to flow, and makes channels to water the sugarcane — yet weeds and wild grasses also spring up in those very channels — so is this entire universe merely such a field. The devotees of Hari are the sugarcane; the self-serving, like a forest of weeds, have grown thick and overgrown. That is why the sugarcane saplings grow only slowly, little by little. On this, he gave this sakhi —

_Ek palakmein sab kiya, trilok ekvees brahmaand. Harijan kartaan Jeevna, laage din dashvees._ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: the all-powerful Lord created the entire three worlds and the twenty-one universes in a single blink of an eye. But, mighty as he is, it takes him ten to twenty days to make a single devotee.)

(Tri.Go. Diary 2032, page 81:)

**Kundali**

_Ek palakmein sab kiya, lok ekvees brahmaand. Harijan kartaan Jeevna, laage din dash vees. Laage din vees, patitne punit kartaan. Sahejmein sudhare nahi, prayatna karine martaan. Kahai Trikam padho addaavees kon kon kaho, tar gaya. Trilok brahmaand ekvees brahmaand, ek palakmein sab kiya._

(Jivandasji Maharaj says: the all-powerful Lord created the three worlds and the twenty-one universes in a single blink of an eye. Yet, mighty as he is, it takes him ten to twenty days to make a devotee; it takes ten to twenty days to purify a sinner. A sinner does not reform easily; one must labor at it even to the point of exhausting oneself. Trikamdas says: read Adhyaruji's twenty-eight kirtans, and see for yourself who among the saintly and the base was redeemed first — "_Kaashta klevar vipla niramla kidha neer, adhan enipar osharyaa pachhi sant sharir_" [unclear, an archaic quoted line — roughly: the impure body, made pure by water, gives way; only after such lowliness is refined does the body of a saint follow]. Thus, though the three worlds and the twenty-one universes could be made in a single instant, the making of a saint takes a very long time.)

In this episode with Haribhai, Jivanji Maharaj gave a glimpse of his own way of life. Whomever he placed his hand upon — that is, whomever he made his follower — he never held out his own hand beneath that person's hand, meaning he never accepted anything from him; instead, he supported himself through his own farming. That understanding comes through here. Haridas Nadiadao, referring to this matter, wrote in the Bhaktamal: "_Jeeva ja shir kar dharyo, ta kar tar odyo nahi_" — meaning that whomever Jivanji Maharaj placed his hand upon and accepted as his own, he never stretched out his own hand beneath that person's hand to take anything from him. It was when Haribhai came here from Aritha that Jivandasji Maharaj sat with him beneath the mahuda tree in his own field where the mahuda trees grew, and they had this conversation there. Speaking with reference to farming, Jivanji Maharaj said that God made things like the five great elements — earth, water, air, fire, and sky — for the sake of his devotees; but just as a farmer works the water-wheel to bring water for his sugarcane, weeds and other grasses also spring up along the channel. From this example, it is implied that the self-serving too are nourished by the merit of true devotees. Hence he said —

_Gau santanke kaaran, Hari varsaavat meh. Taake peechhe Parasuram, duniya paale deh. ||1|| Gau sant bhookhe mare, duniya lap lap khaay. Parasa taa paap the, sooka pad pad jaay. ||2||_

(Parashuram says: for the sake of the cow and the saints, God sends down the rain, and behind them, all the people of this world are nourished and sustain their bodies. Meanwhile the poor cows and saints go hungry, while the people of the world eat their fill greedily; because of this sin, famine keeps falling upon the land, again and again.)

_Uge tahaan vaave nahi, aur vaave tahaan jal jaay. Tulsi aa sansaarmein, maal mashkara khaay._

(Where it would grow, no one plants it; and where it is planted, the water simply drains away — so, Tulsi says, in this world it is the wicked and the mocking who reap the wealth. This means: if sound teaching is given to a worthy person, it bears real fruit; but if, without discernment, one waters the seed of teaching upon the unworthy, then whatever benefit results will only be enjoyed by rogues and cheats, while good people gain nothing from it.)

God produced costly things like dried fruits, cashews, and almonds in Kabul, while in Vrindavan he grew only thorny clusters of wild ker. Yet even a humble thing, appearing in the right place, can prove to be of good use.

_Kabir kahaa kahun us Raamko, mile to deun shikh. Nigura maanas raaj kare, Harijan maage bheekh._

(Das Kabirji says: what shall I say about this Ram, how strange he is; if I could only meet him I would give him a piece of my mind — asking why such an unfair arrangement exists, that people with no guru, far removed from devotion, live in comfort and rule, while your own devotees, poor souls, suffer hardship and go begging.)

_Kabir Harijanku main raaj gau, to sab Harijan ho jaaye. Narak kund khaali padai, Vaikunthmein na samaaye._

(Das Kabirji himself answers: if I were to give power and sovereignty to my devotees, then everyone would become a devotee, following their example — and then the pits of hell would stand empty, while heaven would overflow, unable to hold everyone.)

_Sabka daata Ram hai, raaja parja bheradaa. Uparse paani na pare, to kaun kisiku det._

(God is the giver of all — be it king or ordinary subject, whatever form they take. But if rain does not fall from above, then neither king nor subject would be able to give anything to anyone.)

_Mani maanek moghe kiye, songha taran jal anaaj. Tulsi taathe jaaniye, Ram bade garib nivaaj._

(Tulsidas says: God made precious stones like jewels and rubies costly, while making grass, water, and grain cheap and abundant — such is the plan of creation. From this, know that Lord Ram is a great benefactor and friend of the poor.)

In Hand-written Manuscript No. 98, page 29, there is an account of how the rasayan (the produce, that is, the watermelon) grew lush and green in Shahapura: it uses the parable of a man who makes a garden by irrigating it with water from a well, in which grasses and other things also grow, and explains the point in a kind of mystical, parable-language — the one who draws the water from the well is the Compassionate Lord, the young plant is the saint, and the weeds and wild grasses are the world; God made this rasayan for the sake of the saints. In this Manuscript No. 98, the account of how God made this rasayan for the saints is written as follows —

"Ram Kabir Question," the second: In the village of watermelons, Shahapura, Vaishnav Jivandasji resides. In Samvat 1709, in Vaishakh, from Sud to Vad, Vaishnav Haribhai came from the village of Aritha and visited the garden and field there. There the Vaishnavs brought and offered the rasayan, Tarbuch Maharaj (the watermelon). "In the month of Chaitra, how did this rasayan come about?" — so the Vaishnav asked, and Vaishnavji answered, saying: "There is a certain well. From that well, he made a garden. There the saplings grow, and countless weeds and wild grasses are also nourished within it. The well-drawer's attention is on the saplings, though the weeds within also get nourished. This is a parable; the principle to understand is this: the well-drawer is the Compassionate Lord, the sapling is the saint, and the weeds and wild grasses are the world. This rasayan was made for the sake of the saints." This is the testimony of Parashuramji. Sakhi —

_Gau santanke kaarane, Hari varsaavat meh. Taake peechhe Farasuraam, duniya paale deh. ||1|| Gau santan bhookhe mare, duniya lap lap khaay. Taa kaaran the Farasuraam, sooka pad pad jaay. ||2||_ (The same meaning as before: for the sake of the cow and the saint, God sends rain, and through them the world is fed, while the cow and the saints go hungry as the world eats greedily; because of this sin, famine keeps recurring.)

The saying of Bhagat Biradavali: _Dharti ambar aad dai, ravi shashi paani pavan. Sant jaan eno racho, nahi to kaaran kavan. ||3||_ (Having first given the earth and sky, then the sun, moon, water and wind — know that all this was created for the sake of the saints; otherwise what reason would there be for it?)

_Main janki nidhi, jan nidhi meri. Main janki nidhi, jan nidhi meri. Main so mamjan, mamjan so main. Sun Kamla saachi so teri. ||tek|| Sindhu suta bilag jin maano. Toon jan te kachhu naahi ghaneri. Ashta siddhi nav nindaa chatur mugat, so mere bhagatanki cheri. ||1|| Main saakaar bhayo janke hit, Brahma paar na paave heri. Main ek paav gadho kar jori, bhakta aadheen deen vrat leri. ||2|| Teen lok aur bhuvan chatur das, bhakta vatsal mero birad aheri. Sukh saagar senike saaiyaan, bhagatanke vash Ved kaheri. ||3||_

(God says: I am the treasure of my devotees, and my devotees are my treasure. I am my devotees' own self, and my devotees are my own self. Listen, Kamala, I speak this truth to you, and you must accept it as true: O daughter of the ocean, never think of my devotee as separate from me; you yourself are no greater than my devotee. The eight siddhis, the nine nidhis, and the four kinds of liberation are but handmaidens of my devotee. I took on a form with attributes for the sake of my devotees — a mystery even Brahma cannot fathom. I stand ready, on one foot, hands joined, submissive before my devotee, bound by a humble vow. In the three worlds and the fourteen realms, it is my very nature to hold deep affection for my devotees. I am the ocean of happiness, the Lord of all, and, as the Vedas themselves declare, I remain under the control of my devotees.)

Having written the above, it is further stated in Manuscript No. 98, page 31, that this Prashna (question) of the Samagam belongs to Vaishnav Jivandasji, as recorded in the register kept in the Parthara of Dalidas Vala, of Vayda Pol; it has been copied from what Vaishnav Sitaram wrote out in full at Agra, in Samvat 1796, Magha Sud. If any letters appear faint or unclear, please read them with correction as needed.

_Sadguru sandesa mokala, kachaabachaa sab aap. Naam chintaaman Jeevna, je bhaave so paave. ||1|| Been asthaan kul kaachli, drishti pokhe parvaar. Hari janki sevak roodaan, kriyaa kataaksh aadhaar. ||2|| Nirgun re kaahaan pekhiye, lai chakh hridayaa vichaar._

(Jivandasji Maharaj says: the Sadguru sent word inviting everyone, young and old, small and great, to come to him, saying that his Name is like the wish-fulfilling jewel Chintamani; whoever desires anything of it, receives it. So take from that jewel-like Name whatever peace and joy you seek. Napaji Bhagat, in his chopai, says that just as a tortoise's young are nourished purely by the glance of the mother's compassionate gaze, without any touch, so too God is like that mother, and his devotees are like young ones sustained by his compassionate gaze; his devotees, his good servants, rely on the support of his glance and grace. Why, then, should one go looking elsewhere for the Formless? — O Lord, you yourself, through the eyes of your gracious gaze, hold and contemplate us within your own heart.)

Considering what is written above, in Hand-written Manuscript No. 98, pages 29 to 31, it can be understood that when Haribhai came from Aritha to Shahapura, it must have been in the hot season, around the month of Vaishakh, and he must have brought watermelons for the devotees to eat, watermelons he had grown in his own field named Vadiya. That field is presently Survey No. 201, measuring 5 vighas, 8 vasa, 3 acres, and 7 guntha, and is now in the possession of Bhagat Gunvantbhai, alias Jashbhai Vitthalbhai, of Baroda. From this it can be inferred that Haribhai...

In summer they saw much rasayan (a miracle-abundance) in the field, and among it there would also have been watermelons; Maharaj Jivanji must have welcomed the saint-devotees with these watermelons. There is another legend that at Aritha, Maharaj Jivanji made a field of vaal-papdi (a green bean) turn lush and green; that field is at the edge of the village, and nowadays, because of the polluted atmosphere, the devotees' minds are drawn toward worldly amusements rather than toward it, so it is known by the name "the field of vaal-papdi," and it is regrettable that the devotees have built a Shiv temple there. There is yet another confusion: whether Maharaj Jivanji showed Haribhai this great rasayan at Shahapura or at Aritha -- this question arises, but if we think it over sensibly, it can be said that seeing the way Maharaj Jivanji used to carry on the business of farming at Shahapura, Haribhai too must have been inspired to farm in the same way; so whatever vaal-papdi and other greens he grew in his own field, he must have given it the name "Maharaj Jivanji made the field of vaal-papdi turn green," expressing his gratitude to Maharaj Jivanji in that way. Whichever of these is true, one thing is certain: Maharaj Jivanji used to farm, and he must have inspired the devotees to live by earning through their own labor. To become self-reliant is Maharaj Jivanji's principle.

**KARMA PANJAR -- The Cage of Karma**

_Nar tatha ghodana kalbut rachi kripanathe atmane bandaginu puchhu te_ (Having fashioned the molds -- kalbut -- of man and horse, the Merciful Lord asked the soul about devotion.)

Compared to a devotee, it takes the Merciful Lord ten to twenty days. God did not fashion sensory pleasures (bhog) for those of tamasic (dull, dark) disposition, but this universe imagines that all pleasures were made for its own sake; in truth, the Merciful Lord made all pleasures for the sake of His saints. On the day the Merciful Lord created creation, He arranged and built the universe in just such a fitting way, and set it going.

The Vaishnav Jivandasji said: at one time, the Merciful Lord fashioned the kalbut (the wooden foot-shaped mold that is hammered inside a shoe) of a number of souls -- that is, so that the tamasic disposition of His own creation might not manifest within their own pure form, He fashioned these molds out of that tamasic tendency. Among them He made some into horses and made some souls into men.

Then the Merciful Lord first asked the men: "Will you do devotion, worship, and hymn-singing, or will you take on riding -- that is, enjoy sensory pleasures?" Some said, "We will do devotion, worship, and hymn-singing." And some others said, "We will take riding" (that is, enjoy pleasures). Those who agreed to take riding He made into horses; and those who had earlier been made horses He now made into men. Then the Merciful Lord spoke to those He had made men, asking: "Will you do remembrance, worship, and devotion, or will you take riding" (that is, become sadhus, mendicants, renunciants who sit and are fed)? Of these, a few said, "We will do remembrance and worship," and half said, "We will take riding" (become sadhus, renunciants, and so on). Then those who had agreed to devotion and worship became householders -- men and women living in the world -- and those who had agreed to riding (sadhus, mendicants, renunciants, yogis, ritualists) were made into horses. He made them the burden-bearers of sadhana, meditation, concentration, tantra, mantra, ritual, pilgrimage, vows, and so on.

A kalbut is the wooden mold, shaped like a foot, that cobblers make in order to fashion shoes; they wrap leather around this mold and make the shoe. This wooden mold is called a kalbut. In order to create the universe for souls, God made 8.4 million kinds of kalbut-molds for the 8.4 million species (yonis), and He filled souls into bodies of that shape; and so, whatever action the souls dwelling in that cage made of a body perform is called karma panjar, the cage of karma. Adhyaruji has spoken of the "victory cage" (vije pinjar).

_Harini sharanagat vije pinjar dayanidhi, riddhi akshaypad dataro._ (Sharanagati -- surrender: for the soul that lives in surrender to God, the cage that is its body is a victory cage, O treasury of mercy -- and it grants that soul a happiness greater even than riches and supernatural powers, riddhi-siddhi.)

Kabirji has called the soul like a parrot in a cage, and gives it this counsel.

**(Mangal Aarti)**

_Ram kaho panjarke suva, Ram kaho re panjarke suva.
Haju lagi khabar padat nahi andha, dhandho karat sakal jag muva. (Tek)
Ghadi re sutare kahero kino, haju lagi saaj nishchal nahi huva.
Anta kaal ripu hot manjari, haari chalyo jaise juvari juva. (Ram)
Asha met paanch panihari, khutat naahi karam la karva.
Kahe Kabir jene hari ras chakhyo, vaahike mukh amritras chuva. (Ram)_

O soul, like a parrot shut up in the cage of the body, chant and remember Ram. O unwitting, blind soul, you still have not understood that all the world dies away doing worldly deeds. God the carpenter has hollowed out the trunk of the human body -- like a palm or date-palm tree -- that is, He has fashioned it into a boat; but you, sitting in that boat, have not yet decided what provisions of devotion and worship you will carry along with you. So, at the final hour, it is like gamblers who play dice by balancing a lamp on a cat's head as a wager -- at the very moment of the decisive win, the cat, seeing a mouse, leaps, the lamp falls, and so the gambler loses. As that cat becomes the gambler's enemy, so too will you, like that gambler, lose the game that is human birth, and go to Yama's abode. In this world, giving up cravings, one draws out through the five senses -- like women drawing water -- the water of sensory pleasure from the well that is worldly existence; yet the water that is the bondage of karma never runs out. But Kabirji says: those who have tasted the flavor of devotion to Hari have had the good fortune of drinking, from their own mouths, the ambrosial flavor of supreme happiness.

Revered Yadunath has written, in Lintiyu no. 105, page 11: "Only when the cage becomes victorious does one come to chant Ram." The body indeed came to be prepared through the working of destiny (prarabdha), but you have not yet decided what to do with this human body. The soul is shut up in the cage that is the body; if it is not protected, the cat that is time (kaal) will devour it.

Karma is of two kinds: enjoined (vihit) karma and forbidden (nishiddh) karma. The kinds of enjoined karma are: nitya (daily, obligatory), naimittik (occasional), kamya (desire-driven), and prayashchit (expiatory). Those who follow the path of karma analyze karma in this way, but we ourselves are entirely untouched by karma. Maharaj Adhyaruji, too, says that devotees are not bound by karma.

_Abhakta janpe karma karave, karma bhogvava deh dharave, sevak karma kashano? Hari Hari. ||8||_ (You, O God, make non-devotees perform actions, and make them take on a body in order to reap the fruits of those actions; but for Your servant, what karma can there be?)

_Atmape tu karma karave, karma bhogvava deh dhaveraro, pamya sharan Hari Parbrahm Rai. ||7||_ (You make the soul perform actions and make it take on a body to reap the fruits of karma; but I have found refuge in You, O Hari Parbrahm, the King.)

Thus Adhyaruji has shown these words twice. Further, regarding the devotee and the non-devotee, Adhyaruji says:

_Sevak janne dayal tu, kaal tu bhagat vihin. ||4||_ (To the devotee You are merciful, but to one without devotion You are death itself, kaal.)

Thakkar, in his book on the doctrine of karma, has tried to prove that we must take birth according to our karma. But for those of us who are devoted to God, even though we perform actions, karma does not touch us. This principle holds both spiritually and, by ordinary worldly conduct, in that a master is held responsible for the wrongdoing of his servant. The law, too, follows this very same rule; hence it is known by the name of the master's liability for the servant's wrongdoing. Nor is there anything wrong in that -- it holds in divine law as well. On this basis Adhyaruji argues, on the strength of this legal principle, that for the servant, what karma can there be? Your servant performs actions only in Your service, so You alone are responsible for his actions. Indeed Adhyaruji states:

_Heli re nirbhay tuhaj ek, kijtan karma laage nahi e. ||25||_ (O Lord, You alone are wholly without fear of any kind, and so whatever act You perform, You are never bound by the karma of doing it.)

By this same principle, since the devotee and God are held to be one, whatever the devotee does, he does with the intent of offering it up to God, and so he too is not bound by karma. Not only that -- through the Name of God the devotee becomes entirely free of karma (nishkarma).

_Deh dhare nishkarmapanu nathi, pan naa mahelu Hari naam, paamesh naam sharan vade, nishkarmapanu nirvan. ||8||_ (Even though souls take on bodies in order to be free of the bondage of karma, freedom from karma is not thereby attained. But the devotee says: I shall never give up the Name of God; therefore I am certain that through refuge in the Name of God I shall in the end attain the state free of karma.)

He further says, in the Vadughol, verse 7:

_Karma tano bhay tahan lagi huto e, Hari Hari jahan lagi tuj thaki veg loe, prakruti narke jeev sanchariyo, Hari Hari bhatiyo narkani kodand kod._ (For as long as the soul stayed apart from devotion to God, for that long alone did it fear the bondage of karma. For, from the moment the soul entered into material nature -- prakriti-maya -- it has been buried in hell crore upon crore of times.)

_Karma bandhan chhediyan, sanjhori chare khan, antak maarag lopiyo, Hindola re Parbrahm bhakt paran, Hindola re yog adhyatam saar. ||7||_ (He cut away the bonds of karma, and out of the four wombs He fashioned a rattle to shake for God, who lies cradled in the swing; thus He erased the path to Yama's abode. In such a cradle-swing, Parbrahm holds His devotee dear, and keeps love for him.)

_Gyan vairag toran karya, ane sthambh Shankar Brahma, nishkarma bhakti hindoldo, Hindola re hinche hinche Hari Parbrahm. ||8||_ (He made a cradle of knowledge and dispassion, with Shankar and Brahma as its posts. Such a cradle-swing is made of karma-free devotion, and in that swing God Parbrahm swings and rocks.)

Adhyaruji, giving counsel, says:

_Karam vishwanu talva, ane galva gun beej, sansar paar utarva, jaachne Jugdish. ||4||_ (In order to overcome the karma of the whole world, and to bury -- that is, destroy -- the seed of the three gunas, and to be delivered from the ocean of worldly existence, make your plea to God devotedly.)

Umavlo means an eager surging, an overflowing, a foaming rush of enthusiasm -- a state in which repeated upsurges keep occurring. In such a state, sometimes false upsurges of maya arise, and the soul makes a mistake and gets swept off onto the wrong path. Speaking of this in the Umavalo, Adhyaruji says:

_Padhiyo padhiyo re lahyo chare Ved e, karam marag re bhulyo bhamyo e, na janiyo re lahyo bhaktino bhed e, hun anek ranto sir aani e._ (Having studied the four Vedas, the soul went astray on the path of ritual karma and kept wandering in the bonds of karma, because it did not grasp the secret of the path of devotion to God; and so it kept holding in its mind attachments of many kinds, such as "I" and "mine." Therefore, O yellow-robed Parbrahm Padmanabhji, my God, I have come to the refuge of Your feet.)

Practice devotion with such eager fervor for remembering His Name. Regarding souls in the cage of karma, Maharaj Jivanji says in the Samagam:

_Ek alla (matika) the do bhaya, ko ghoda ko mir, aato saato Jivna, nar samajhat nahi bepir. ||149||_ (Out of the same clay -- the five great elements -- God fashioned souls of two kinds of nature. Among them He made some like horses, laboring to enjoy sense-pleasures, and He made others victors who gained mastery over sensual desire.)

But he who enjoys the pleasures of sensual desire in this way can only enjoy those pleasures if, like a horse, he bears the burden of the world; whereas those who do not care for sensory pleasures can become like victorious generals who enjoy supreme happiness and peace. Thus, in place of laboring to enjoy sense-pleasures, one may instead enjoy such pleasures directly, and if one does not care for sense-objects, one may enjoy supreme happiness -- in this way, such enjoyment comes about through an exchange of labor. Foolish people such as these do not understand this.

**Entry into the Cage of Karma -- Its Release: Guru and Sadguru Are One**

Third Question -- Jivandasji said to Haribhai: In creating this creation, He made a cage for the soul. With the five elements and three gunas -- these eight aspects -- the soul entered into the cage. And again the Merciful Lord said: "Soul, enter this cage." Then the soul awoke and said: "Maharaj, You are sending me into this entry of karma-yoga -- then by what means shall I now attain You?" When it said this, the Merciful Lord said: "Brother, count the food and movement of the senses as little; enjoy your wife but once; and take subtle food, not much more than one ser -- five hundred grams -- of grain; and thereby conquer the eleven senses (the five senses of knowledge and the five organs of action)." -- A sakhi (couplet) follows:

_Kabir tanki bhukh alpa hai, teen paanv ke sher, manki bhukh agaadh hai, gal jaay Mer Sumer. ||1||_ (Das Kabirji says: the hunger of the body is of only a very small measure -- it is satisfied by three-quarters of a ser, about 375 grams, or a full ser of about 500 grams, of food. But the hunger of the mind is exceedingly deep; in it, even great mountains like Meru and Sumeru could sink, so vast is its depth.)

For this the Merciful Lord said: "Consider the five elements and three gunas as dwelling with Me; you will not thereby fail to become My devotee. Wherever you stay and remember Me, there I am present before you. By your own good will, even in the stationary and moving beings, in insects and birds, I shall not let you keep any attached share in the three gunas and five elements -- that is, hold no attachment there. This is My true word." Thus, at that gathering of creation, the Merciful Lord gave His word to the soul.

In your tradition, in the seventh verse (aad) of the fourth kadvu of Adhyaruji, the word is spoken:

_Have rakho re have rakho re, Swami aapan mahen, aapno vol sambharajo._ (O Master, now keep this soul in Your refuge. Keep it in Your refuge -- for You Yourself have said:)

_sarva-dharman parityajya mam ekam sharanam vraja, aham tva sarva-papebhyo mokshayishyami ma shuchah. ||66||_ (Abandoning all duties, come to Me alone for refuge; I shall release you from all sins -- do not grieve.)

For that reason, when this attention is lost, great greed befalls the soul as well. The Merciful Lord has said, "Wherever you dwell and worship, there I am" -- yet it is the soul itself that keeps holding on to its own attached share; not taking heed of this, it must wander in the round of birth and rebirth. If it understands, its wandering ceases, and it attains contentment and merges into the form of God. "Knowing Me to dwell in the stationary and moving," He says, "consider well your original share in the eight aspects." The three gunas and five elements that the Merciful Lord has spoken of -- forgetting these and disregarding them, the soul, having forgotten the form of God, still goes about seeing Vasudevji in the stationary and moving world, yet still does not understand. And so it has drifted from birth to birth. In this way it has, of its own doing, led its own soul astray. For this reason no soul attains God. On this, the word from the fifth verse (aad) of the first kadvu of Adhyaruji:

_Sacharachar jene bholvyu, bholvyu vividh vichar, prakruti tane gune vahiyo, mohiyo bhame re sansar._ (The one who has deluded all stationary and moving beings -- He has deluded them with manifold thoughts. Carried along by the strands of nature, the deluded soul wanders in the world.)

All beings in the world, stationary and moving, have been deluded through the foundation of the three gunas, deluded into all sorts of separate thoughts and intentions. In this way, subjugated to the qualities of maya, they keep wandering in the wheel of this world amid so many kinds of thoughts and counter-thoughts.

For this, the Vaishnav Jivandasji said to Haribhai that the soul, by becoming subject to material nature-maya, has erred in discernment; but Vasudevji has not deluded it. That day, in that same way, under the mahuda tree, the question-and-answer session, with its illustrations and occasions, was thus completed.

The Vaishnav Jivandasji further said: the soul is void -- caught in the noose of infatuation with material nature, its heart made empty, cut off from its own true duty, without a guru. Without a guru, how can one's inborn tendencies and the disorders of the senses be given up? And without a sadguru, who will carry one across? Jivandasji said: the soul that does not attain God is the one that, by its own doing, keeps treating guru and sadguru as two separate things; but on the day these two come together as one, it attains God. There is an illustration for this. The soul, having gone round through the eighty-four lakh species, has come to stand in a human body. It stands at the court that is the heart, at the door of the Lord, and lodges its complaint. What the first guru tells it is called the "complaint" -- but as long as the Master has not heard and granted redress, the matter remains unresolved. When that Master hears the plea and comes forward eagerly to meet it, then the sadguru is found -- that is called "redress heard."

For this, the word of the [first] verse of the first kadvu:

_Hari Hari samarath Parbrahm anusaryo e, bhagyo ati sandeh, bhay saghala have nirdalya e._ (Ah! When I began to practice devotion to the all-powerful Parbrahm and to live accordingly, my great doubt of falling life after life vanished, and every fear of the bondage of karma fled and was destroyed.)

This same sentiment also appears in a verse from the aarti kirtan:

_Bhale aaviya Parbrahm Ram, samarath dhanine sante seviya e._ (O Padmanabhji, form of Parbrahm, it is very good that You have come. Saints such as You are all-powerful, and so they release the disciple from the bonds of the karma of many lifetimes.)

Maharaj Jivanji says:

_Likhya mite nahi Jivna, je kachhu likhiya lekh, sad-sadguru lekh mitaiya, tab paaya aap alekh. ||39||_ (Maharaj Jivandasji says: whatever record of karma the Ordainer has written cannot be erased even by more karma; but the Sadguru has erased such a written record of karmic bondage -- and then, O Lord, we were able to attain You, whom otherwise none could come to know.)

_likhita chitraguptena lalatakshar-malika, tan na chalayitum shakya asuraih tri-dashaur api._ (It is said elsewhere in the Puranas: the garland of letters that Chitragupta has written on the forehead -- neither the gods nor the demons have the power to move it.)

_yad yatra likhitam bhale tan nrishtham naiva jayate, rite Shri Ramdasanam prem nirbhar chetasam._ (Whatever the Ordainer has written on the forehead never becomes false -- except that this rule applies to all others, but not to Ramdas devotees whose hearts are full of supreme love.)

For this, the word of Kabir's kahera (couplet-refrain) has been quoted in the Samagam, and its refrain-verse (abhog) has been written down there. Here we shall look at the whole of that pada (hymn). The sentiments contained in this pada are very much worth understanding. In Handwritten Manuscript no. 8, page 125, the raga of this pada is given as Godi, but it can also be set to the raga Bilaval.

**(Raga Godi)**

_Rehta mera jarjara, kaantu jhina soot re. (Tek)
Jal jaai thal upni re, aai nagar aap.
Ek achamba mein suna, betdiye jaaya baap. ||1||
Bava mera byah karo, koou tumsa var laayo.
Jab lagi var paaun nahi, baba tab lagi tumhi bihayo. ||2||
Ek badiya jin karo, dooja mari mari jaao.
Jine mera raihera dhada, main to taahike sang rahaao. ||3||
Kahat Kabir sohi nar gyata (jaaga), is padka kare vichar.
Pahele parche guru kiya, sadguru le utare paar. ||4||_

In a hidden, profound sense Das Kabirji says: this frail, worn-out spinning-wheel of mine is this body; with it I spin a very fine, delicate thread -- that is, through this body I spin, as it were, the fine thread of knowledge and wisdom, my fancies and imaginings. This body, born from the water that is a drop, has appeared in the form of an earthly body, come forth into this city that is the world. I have heard one truly astonishing thing: a daughter has given birth to her father! This is a matter of surat-nirat (inward attention and absorption). When absorption (tallinata) comes, that is the "daughter"; and once absorption has come, the vision of God (bhagavad-darshan) occurs -- so it is only the daughter that is fine thread and absorption who can make manifest the Supreme Father as "Father." That is, only once a son or daughter is born can a man be called that child's father; before the birth of the son, no one can be called "father." So it is a wonder indeed that the son has given birth to the father. O elder, now arrange my marriage -- to such a bridegroom as is as powerful as You. Until I attain such a husband, keep me betrothed to You alone. Do one thing so great: never give me such a husband that, should one die, the next would die too. Rather, I shall stay only with that Creator who has fashioned this body of mine, wheel-spun through the eighty-four lakh births. Kabirji says: that man alone will be truly awake and wise who is able to reflect on the deep meaning of the words given in this pada. Such a person will have taken as guru the one who, through a first acquaintance, gives him understanding; and through a second, deeper acquaintance, the sadguru will carry him across the ocean of worldly existence.

A pada related to this one appears in Kabirvani, Year 10, Issue 114, page 1. This pada is also found in Najar Note no. 13, page 177; its explanation has been presented very beautifully in Kabirvani -- let us look at it.

**(Raga Sorath)**

_Mere piyu to base re agampuri, milna kaise hoy? (Tek)
Haanji dhundhat dhundhat jarjarya, khevat mat baal.
Dhundha mara jajara.
Virah rupi (behal) nadiya vahe, kis bidh utaru paar? ||1||
Haanji patiya likh likh bhejti, koi na kahe re sandesh.
Jis nagarimein Halam base, kaun kahe re sandesh. ||2||
Paap punya dou vaniya, vishaya lagi re (rachyo re) bajar.
Ketke soda kar gayo, ketek aavanhaar. ||3||
Kahe Kabir suno sadhuva, sab mili karo re vichar.
Pahelo parche guru mile, dooje sarajanhaar. ||4||_

Das Kabirji says: my Husband dwells in a hidden city beyond comprehension -- how, then, can I meet Him? Ah, searching for Him, my very body has grown worn and frail; and my ferryman, that is, my guru, is utterly blissful. The river that makes for such a wretched state -- the river of separation -- flows on; how then shall I cross to the far shore? Ah, I write letters and send them, but no one brings back word. In which city my beloved Husband dwells, what country that is -- no one tells me; no one gives any message about it, no one brings word. Sin and merit are two merchants who have set up the marketplace of sensory desire, and some have already done their trading in it, while still others' trade in karma is yet to come. Das Kabirji says: O saints and sadhus, listen -- gather together and reflect on this matter, that with this my Husband, at the first meeting I found the guru, and at the second encounter I found the Creator-Lord.

[Glossary:] khevat (boatman) = guru; patiyan = letters; vaniya = merchant; ketke = some. A detailed exposition of the above pada has been given in Kabir Vani, Year 10, Issue 114, from page 1 onward, as follows: This pada is extremely well known among us.

In the scriptures, devotion (bhakti) is recognized as being of two kinds: primary (mukhya) devotion and secondary (gauna) devotion. Primary devotion is the devotion practiced by forming a bond of love with God; in it, there is only the longing for the vision (darshan) of the Lord. In secondary devotion, on the other hand, desires of many kinds are mixed in; sometimes God is even set aside altogether. Even without acquaintance with God, and without love for Him, devotion is practiced by adopting some fixed ritual procedure in order to fulfill some desire of the mind; such devotion is therefore also called vaidhi (ritual, rule-bound) devotion. Thus, in secondary or vaidhi devotion, importance is given to some desire or procedure other than God Himself; whereas in primary devotion, nothing other than God is even considered -- only love and passionate attachment (raag) toward God alone arise. The saints therefore call it ragatmika bhakti, devotion born of passionate love. In this pada we see ragatmika bhakti, or primary devotion. God is regarded as the Beloved, and the soul as His beloved lady. The beloved lady remains absorbed in the sweet remembrance of her Beloved. The soul has an intensely fervent longing for the vision of God; yet the possibility of that vision does not appear to be forming, because the soul is in ignorance. It has no acquaintance with the abode of God, nor any knowledge of the path to reach it; yet, all the while, its longing for that vision grows more and more intense -- and it is this very state of the soul that is described at the very opening of this pada.

In such a state, the soul looks for help. It hopes that some assistance might come. It becomes convinced that only if it meets someone who truly knows the secret can it reach its destination. But no such knower is met with. Without a boatman-guru, or such a knower of the secret, it seems extremely hard for the soul to cross the river of separation flowing in between; still, it keeps trying by every means to obtain help. Whoever offers help offers it, but only superficially, because God remains beyond reach -- the soul has neither experienced God nor beheld His abode. All it knows is that the abode of God is called Agampuri (the unreachable city). And so the soul, seeking God, wanders here and there without rest. If someone says He will be found in the Himalayas, it runs off to the Himalayas. If someone says He will be found at a place of pilgrimage, it goes on pilgrimage after pilgrimage. If someone says He will be found in a temple, it goes to temples and performs every ritual there too. Yet no one can satisfy its hunger for the vision of God. If, in this moment of longing, the soul finds no help, its state becomes like that of a spring drying up in the desert.

Therefore, in the closing lines, Kabir Saheb, instructing the sadhus, puts this message before the world. An appeal is made to the sadhus to gather together and deliberate; but that sadhus are unable to gather together is the greatest tragedy of all. Envy, malice, and enmity are all to be found among sadhus. Sadhus have not been able to free themselves from the very faults of ordinary people; hence the question arises -- whom should one call a sadhu? Should one who preaches religion and morality in public while practicing unrighteousness in private be called a sadhu? Or should one who merely dons saffron robes and renounces the world be called a sadhu? Should one with long hair and beard, smeared with ash, begging for alms, be called a sadhu? Kabir Saheb says to the sadhus: gather together and deliberate -- the true sadhu is the one who labors to move from untruth toward truth, or who is ever moving from darkness toward light. Not only that, but the garb of a sadhu can rightly be worn only by one who continually holds good thoughts, forms good resolves, behaves well, and inspires others toward good as well. Such sadhus are true sadhus, and only such sadhus, gathering together, can truly deliberate and can lead the world onto the path of well-being.

But today there is a dearth of people capable of guiding society. Who today, breaking free from the center of self-interest, can think of others? The condition that existed six hundred years ago is the very same condition that exists in the present age. Sadhus become "sants" and then become masters of a gaddi (a seat of religious authority). A web of scheming keeps being woven. Like any householder, such a person too remains absorbed in preserving his gaddi. As a result, though living within society, he remains distant from it. To preserve a gaddi one needs a following; to gather a following one needs wealth; and to gather wealth one must deceive society. In this way, the welfare of society cannot come about through such a corrupt path. Instead, he fills a marketplace of sense-objects and lures people. When collecting donations, he says, "We will have your name engraved on a marble plaque." A man's ego is thereby fed; the desire for honor and fame is stoked. As a result, even a competition in giving donations gets arranged -- people take part in it so that their own fame may increase. Meanwhile, in this flowing river of donations, the gaddi-masters enjoy their own pleasures and live in comfort and indulgence. Such a vicious cycle keeps turning; from time immemorial, people have come and gone, been born and died. In that marketplace of sense-objects, each departs after having struck his bargains. What does he carry away with him? Only the impressions (vasanas) of sin and merit. Since the days of Baba Adam, the soul has kept its journey going, carrying along a store of greed and infatuation.

This is exactly the point to reflect on. All have come in darkness -- come with their eyes shut. And when they go, they too go in darkness with their eyes shut. Where did they come from? Where have they ended up? Who sent them? Who kept them alive while they were in the mother's womb? Who filled the mother's womb with nourishment? Such questions never even arise in the soul.
