When such questions do arise, know that one's good fortune has dawned; only when the grace of God comes about do such questions awaken in the mind -- and from the very moment such questions awaken, that soul's journey toward the good (shreya-yatra) is reckoned to have begun. Within its inner being, a wind of transformation begins to blow; little by little, the tamasic forces diminish, and the inner self grows steady in a sattvic disposition. Bad qualities fall away, and a continuous process of purification goes on. Such progress is what we call the shreya-yatra, the journey toward the good.

Before the journey toward the good begins, the experience of a love-triangle inevitably occurs. The soul wishes to form a bond of love with God, but before its wish can be carried out, it enters into a relationship with maya. A close, entangled dealing with maya begins. Maya keeps manifesting before the soul in the form of objects and sense-pleasures. The soul truly comes to revel in the enchantments of the world. At that time, the soul does not even remember God, because maya's colorful, decorated, enchanting form, full of objects and sense-pleasures, never departs from its mind.

Once this special, distinctive attraction of maya has taken hold, talk of God begins to seem like idle chatter to the soul. Thoughts of God feel pointless. Those who speak of Him, those who preach Him, come to seem like bitter poison. Yes, sometimes a flash of lightning does occur -- that is true -- but only when calamity strikes. Then the soul makes do with a makeshift lamp and wick: it sings a bhajan or two, gets into the habit of visiting temples, and observes a vow or two. But as time passes, these too are forgotten, one after another, and by whatever reckoning, the soul settles into a merely mental sort of contentment. Even if a flash of God's grace has occurred, the soul is unable to make use of it. Once again, in the marketplace of sense-objects, the soul goes on striking ever new bargains in fresh acts of karma.

This whole saga of the love-triangle needs to be reflected upon carefully. What is the nature of maya? Where does maya reside? The scriptures and the saints say that maya belongs to God Himself. It is especially necessary to recognize the relationship between maya and Maya's Lord, God. If we form a bond of love with the Lord of Maya, then maya no longer torments the soul; rather, it tries to become favorable to the soul on its journey toward the good. Maya then becomes a maidservant and turns into a help.

Some call material nature (prakriti) maya; some call ignorance (avidya) maya. Maya exists in many different forms; yet its true dwelling place is in the mind alone. In the form of desire, in the form of craving, in the form of thirst, it keeps arising in the mind like bubbles. Whatever object comes before one's eyes, that object begins to be liked. Liking and disliking are the manifest form of maya. Once an object is liked, the wish to obtain it arises, and one tries, by whatever means, to obtain it. In this way, the wheel of maya keeps turning. Infatuation and possessiveness are maya's companions; the attraction toward them keeps forever growing. As a result, the soul forgets God and becomes engrossed in striking bargains over sense-objects in maya's marketplace.

Therefore it is beneficial that those in society who call themselves sadhus should first fully grasp the reality of this love-triangle, because becoming a gaddi-master is itself to be reckoned as falling into maya. How can one who remains sunk in maya remember Maya's Lord? So it is well if one tries to keep apart from maya. As for the idea of withdrawing from the world altogether, that is of no use -- every soul will have to take birth into this world, and so there is no benefit in disregarding the world. The soul must indeed come into the world; it will just as surely have to resolve to live rightly. When hungry, one must eat; when thirsty, one must drink water. Whatever is necessary for the nourishment of this body must indeed be done, and one must act according to one's destiny (prarabdha). Even so, what is wrong in that?

Once born, one will naturally have relationships with mother, father, brothers, and sisters; once one becomes a householder, one will naturally have sons and daughters too. Mother, father, brothers, sisters, sons, and daughters are, in themselves, not any form of maya at all -- it is the desire and craving one holds for these people that is maya. Since the form of maya is, in this way, born of craving, it is from that standpoint that such cravings ought to be uprooted from the mind. Just as a boat floats on water, so one must learn to float across the ocean of worldly existence. If water fills the boat, the boat sinks and can never float again; likewise, if worldly cravings begin to fill the mind, one sinks into the ocean of worldly existence. If one wishes to cross the ocean of birth and death (bhavsagar), it is necessary to root out worldly attachments from the mind -- and that alone is what is meant by "becoming separate from maya."

That husband and wife should love each other can be understood; but if that love is born of infatuation, it drowns one. One ought really to reflect on whether a husband's love for his wife is for her body, or for the consciousness dwelling within that body. If the love were for the body, then after she dies he ought not to take her to the cremation ground; yet, in fact, the body must be taken to the cremation ground, for otherwise it begins to stink and to rot. From this it is necessary to understand that it is the conscious principle (chetan tattva) alone that the soul holds most dear; even after death that consciousness continues to be remembered. Therefore the soul ought to form a bond of love with that consciousness and become steadfast in it. Only if sadhus themselves cultivate this kind of understanding can they explain it to others in society.

The soul in whom sudden love toward God awakens -- to that soul, God certainly sends help in one form or another. When such a soul becomes utterly overwhelmed with feeling for God, God Himself sends a guru to meet it. Without the grace of God, one does not attain the vision (darshan) of a guru. In our own land there lived Paramahansa Yoganandji. On his guru's instruction, he went to America and propagated the science of yoga there. From 1920 to 1952 CE he carried out the finest possible propagation of Indian culture in America. Even today, the ashrams he established are still there and continue to direct yoga-related activities across the whole world. One wonderful episode from his life comes to mind here.

He was studying in Calcutta at the time, a student in college. His boundless love for God had grown so great that he made many efforts to find a guru. In those days, in Calcutta, the name of Master Mahashay was well known -- Master Mahashay was a disciple of Shri Ramakrishna Paramahansa. Yoganandji felt drawn to him and would meet him again and again. One day, intending to install him as his guru, he made a garland of flowers and went to him. Before he could even say a word about his own feelings, Master Mahashay already knew what was in Yoganandji's heart. After Yoganandji had paid his respects and was about to place the garland upon him, Master Mahashay stopped him, saying: "I am not your guru. Your guru will meet you very soon." Some time then passed. Yoganandji kept feeling an eager longing for his true guru to appear. He went from Calcutta to Banaras for his studies; there too he continued longing for his guru --

...was in his service. One day he had gone out to buy vegetables for the ashram kitchen. On the way, some distance off, he saw a saint standing there — the saint simply stood in that same spot. He felt as though his own feet had become locked in place; his feet would not move at all. They would move to go toward the saint, but they would not move to go toward the market. When he reached the saint, he could not help but bow to him. Placing a hand on his head, the saint said, "So you have come at last. My child, I was waiting just for you — now you will not be able to remain apart from me." This saint was Shri Yukteshwar Giri. With the help of Shri Sadguru Yukteshwar Giri, this disciple was able to rise to the stature of Yoganandji Paramahansa, and served as India's representative at the world's parliament of religions. Hence Kabir Saheb rightly says:

_Pahele parche guru mile, duje sarjanhaar ||_
(First, through direct recognition, one attains the guru; through him, second, one attains the Creator.)

If one obtains a guru, one attains the vision of the Supreme Being. He who is the Creator, who is the lord of the world, is that very Parmeshwar; he alone takes care of everyone. Whatever any soul longs for, he brings to that soul sooner or later, in one way or another. When souls feel a spiritual hunger, that same Paramatma sends a sadguru to bring the soul the help it needs. Through the guru's grace, the deep secrets of the spiritual world then open up before that seeking soul. The soul comes to recognize its own true nature. Only after winning the guru's love does the seeking soul obtain the good fortune of the guru's grace; through that, its journey toward the highest good keeps advancing. Then, on some blessed day, through the sadguru's grace, a glimpse of the Supreme Being is attained. It is a well-known fact that Kabir Saheb, too, came to know his sadguru Ramanandji in just this way.

For this reason, experienced and wise men keep singing the glory of the guru. In the guru's company one gets the good fortune of plundering an inexhaustible spiritual treasure. The memory of one's births across many lifetimes stirs and awakens. Within the body a continual sacrifice of purification (shuddhi yajna) keeps going on. Futile activity comes to an end. Thoughts find a definite direction. The mind increasingly takes on wholesome resolve. Restraint over speech keeps growing. The senses come under control. The inner faculty (antahkaran) becomes pure. In this way the ground for the vision of the Supreme Being is laid through the guru's company.

[Kabirvani, Year 10, Issue 114, Bavaji, Kapura, pages 1-5.]

Jagdish of Ravapura had an experience just like this.

Regarding guru and sadguru, the Vaishnav Nana Parekh has written a pad (hymn) in the Sindhudo raga.

_Sindhudo

Bhajat mugat tano swami chhe sahelo | Goheló hoy te shu re aape |
Jaachak hoy te jaacho tehne jai | Dukh daaridray sarve kaape ||tek||

Shuk Samkaadik Aadinaarad dai | Saadh sarve mali mugat maage |
Bhagatinaa bhogiaa sant viralaa koi | Teh kahiye motaa param bhaagi ||1||

Jire guru sadguru biche vaharo atidhano | Guru to vegne mukh bole |
Sadguru bhed bataave samjhaave igam tano | Kot mugat nahi teh tole ||2||

Jire jehne jevo guru male tene tevi ugrataa | Kije udyam tevo laabh lije |
Bhaare halvaa tanu nathi jene paarkhu | Tene dosh te kem dije ||3||

Jivanchaa Prabhu mugat morlidharaa | Gopi tanaa var garuaa kahaave |
Naano sevak kari sant ne sopie | Bhagat daataar bhalaaj bhaavo ||4||

Saakhi
Kabir sadguru guru bich bahu antadaa | Jyon divas aru jaam |
Guru bataave vaikunthaku | Sadguru de nij dhaam ||1||_

(Devotion's very master is gracious and easy of approach — what can a niggard lord give? If you are a fit beggar, go and ask of him — he cuts away every sorrow and every poverty. [refrain] Shuk, Sanakadik, Narad, and all the rest — every seeker joins together and asks for liberation, but rare indeed is the saint who longs to enjoy loving devotion itself; call such a one the greatest of the fortunate. [1] Between guru and sadguru there is a very great gulf: the guru merely speaks urgently with his mouth, while the sadguru shows the hidden secret and explains what is unfathomable — millions of liberations cannot equal that. [2] Whatever kind of guru one obtains, that intensity of practice must be taken up, and the benefit gained accordingly; one who cannot tell heavy from light should not be blamed for it. [3] The Lord of life wears the peacock-feather crown and holds the flute; he is called the great, honored husband of the gopis. Make me the lowliest of servants and hand me over to the saints — devotion is the true giver, may this be granted with grace. [4] Sakhi: Kabir says there is a vast gap between guru and sadguru, as between day and night. The guru shows the way to Vaikunth; the sadguru gives his own abode. [1])

The master of loving devotion and liberation is himself supremely gracious and worthy, but how could a wretched, miserly lord give us happiness? If you are a fit beggar, then go to such a one and ask of him what can cure your sorrows and your poverty. Shukdev, Sanakadik, Narad, and the rest — all seekers alike gather together and, with one mind, ask for liberation; but those who wish to enjoy Hari's loving devotion are only a rare few saints. Them alone shall we call the truly fortunate. Ah, but there is a very great difference between a guru and a sadguru! One who is merely a guru gives instruction only by speaking with his mouth, whereas one who is a sadguru gives understanding of whatever hidden mystery one is unable to grasp on one's own — even millions of liberations cannot equal that. Hence, whatever kind of devotional practice (upasana) a person's guru follows, that guru shows him that same kind of practice with great intensity; but even after millions of labors spent on it, one may still fail to receive the benefit of one's own deliverance through it. As for one who has no discernment of what a superior or an ordinary devotional practice is — for such a one there is Lord Krishna, who wears the crown of peacock feathers and holds the flute, who is called the great, honored husband of the gopis. Surrender yourself, becoming his lowly devotee-servant, and place yourself under the shelter of the saints, for they carry the virtuous, gracious nature that gives loving devotion.

The Sakhi — Das Kabirji says that between guru and sadguru there is a very great difference: just as there is a great distance between day and night, such is the difference between guru and sadguru. A guru merely shows us how to attain a liberated realm such as Vaikunth, while a sadguru shows us how to attain his own divine abode (Bhagavad-dhaam).

Trikamdas Gordhandas has written a kundali (expanded verse) on guru and sadguru. [Diary of Samvat] 2032, page 15.

_Guru sadguru bahu aantaro | Jyu divas jharu jaam |
Guru bataave vaikunthaku | Sadguru de nij dhaam ||
Sadguru de nij dhaam | Talee jaay janamnaa feraa |
Shaa ith aan | Akhand Vrundavan heraa |
Trikam sadguru vachane aaraam | Ghar bethaan chhe jaataraa |
Jyu divas aru jaam | Guru sadguru bahu aantaro ||_

(Between guru and sadguru there is a vast gap, as between day and night watch. The guru shows the way to Vaikunth; the sadguru gives his own abode. The sadguru gives his own abode, and the rounds of birth are removed. [unclear — one short phrase in this line could not be rendered with confidence from the source.] One beholds the unbroken Vrindavan. Trikam finds rest in the sadguru's word; the pilgrimage is attained while sitting at home. As between day and night watch, so is the vast gap between guru and sadguru.)

Just as there is a gap between day and night, such is the difference between guru and sadguru. A guru shows us only how to attain a liberated realm such as Vaikunth, while a sadguru — [as the source repeats here] shows how to attain a liberated realm such as Vaikunth. The sadguru, however, shows us his own state, and because of this our rounds of birth and death come to an end. That is, the God who dwells forever, everywhere, as the one, undivided Ram — who dwells in the unbroken Vrindavan — is all that then remains. Trikamdas says that thus, through the sadguru's teaching, we shall enjoy complete peace, and the pilgrimage-place that is the sadguru comes to us while sitting at home itself; hence, just as great as the difference between day and night, that great is the difference between guru and sadguru.

According to the three gunas, whichever of the three types of quality (guna) a given guru possesses, he gives instruction of that same kind; but a sadguru gives instruction in supreme devotion that transcends the three gunas (trigunatit).

Jnani — Knowledge is nothing but a collection of information. (Knowledge itself is nothing other than a mere collection of pieces of information.)

Sant — Apply the information in a known situation; that is understanding. (One who takes whatever knowledge he has and puts it into practice in an available, familiar state or circumstance — such a person is called a sant, a wise and understanding one.)

Guru — Application, diligent and thorough application: to apply the information in an unknown situation. Explication — to develop, to open up, to bring out. (One who applies whatever knowledge he has to unfamiliar circumstances is called a guru — one who gives understanding to the ignorant.)

Sadguru — Skill: to create new information for any situation, whether known or unknown; able to draw up a blueprint. (One who possesses the skill to devise entirely new knowledge suited to any state or condition whatsoever, whether manifest or unmanifest, and to draw up its blueprint — such a one is called a sadguru.)

The sadguru has no need of scriptures, Vedas, Puranas, or bundles of old texts; he himself can bring about wholly new creation, can compose wholly new works, and has no need to search anything out. Searching and seeking is something the knowledgeable, the ignorant, the inquirers, the seekers of some end, and the distressed all have to do. The sadguru, however, need not search for anything at all — he already knows a very great deal. Thus the sadguru is a fully realized being possessing complete power and sovereign glory. Among gurus, some are religious teachers (dharmaguru) and some are teachers of worldly knowledge (vidyaguru); gurus, in this way, each carry a particular quality according to the three gunas. There are base, lowly gurus as well.

If a difference remains between guru and sadguru, one does not attain the Supreme Being; only if the two are brought together as one is the Supreme Being attained. This point is an important one. By way of illustration it is said that the soul, after wandering through the eighty-four [lakh species of birth], finally arrives at God's own court — that is, when true understanding dawns, it lodges a complaint. That complaint concerns the suffering endured in the womb and the torment of the wheel of the ocean of worldly existence (bhavsagar); at that point it says a guru has been obtained, because the soul has now come to true understanding, but God had not yet come to its aid. However, when God himself comes forward of his own accord, in the form of the sadguru, to help it, then all worry over its sufferings comes to an end. After that, the delusion of the world, or the fear of the ocean of worldly existence, begins to fade —

...comes to an end. A hymn (pad) relating to this illustration has been given in order to make guru and sadguru understood. Further, in order to show guru and sadguru as one and the same, a special exposition has been given in this chapter, Nitya Pralay (Daily Dissolution).

Nitya Pralay

The Example of Shurpanakha — The States of Daily Dissolution and Great Dissolution

As an illustration of how guru and sadguru are counted as one in this matter: at Panchavati, Shurpanakha came to seek Ram in marriage, having come there in a deceitful disguise; from this it was known that she was a rakshasi (demoness), yet in her own mind there was no deceit — she had come with a pure mind. What follows is the teaching of guru-dharma, in the words of Gurua Ganpati's raas.

_Ramakuli nishachari aavi | Shurpankha Lakshmane sambhaavi ||
Shravan naakshikaa chhedyaan | Hari Hari ||_

(The demoness enamored of Ram came; Lakshman took note of Shurpanakha. Her ears and nose he cut off — Hari, Hari.)

When the lust-stricken demoness Shurpanakha came to seek him in marriage, Lakshman cut off her nose and ears.

In this way Ram gave her the teaching of guru-dharma, and so became her guru. Later, in the Krishna incarnation, in Mathuraji, that same woman had to marry the Lord of Grace as Kubja — that was her attaining a sadguru. When she touched the sacred body (vigraha) of Shri Krishna Paramatma, at that very moment she was freed from all worldly desires and, in a state of utterly pure feeling, attained fixity in her own true self (swaatma-nishtha); thus, in the form of Krishna, she attained her sadguru.

Thus, through these words [unclear — a phrase referring back to the earlier doha on 'first recognition of the guru' could not be rendered with confidence from the source], the concept of guru and sadguru has been conveyed. [unclear — the following clause, concerning 'the wheel, the body, and the daughter born to the father,' could not be rendered with confidence from the source] — its hidden meaning being surat-nirat (indrawn attention). This pad has been presented in order to make guru and sadguru known as one.

In this very incarnation, the lust-driven Shurpanakha first made Ram her guru, but Ram did not accept her; in the next incarnation, Krishna married that same Shurpanakha, who had by then come as Kubja. Hence it is said that the lust-driven Shurpanakha, taking God as her chosen husband, held toward him a strong and innocent devotion; because of this, Shurpanakha became infatuated with Ram, and even though she died, her longing and her indrawn attention (surat) to marry him remained unfulfilled. So, when she was born as Kubja, God then spins the thread of her desires and, turning us round in that very wheel of birth and rebirth, grants a new birth in another place, and so fulfills those unfulfilled desires. Such is the turning wheel (rehatmala) by which this happens. Hence, if one's indrawn attention (surat) is fixed upon the guru, then, even in another birth, that same guru comes to one, having become a sadguru.

It is worth understanding that in her previous birth she was Shurpanakha. It is not fitting that Manthara should be born as Kubja — even though Kubja was a hunchback, how could the ill-natured Manthara wish for Ram to become her own husband? Therefore Kubja could well be Shurpanakha, who, demoness though she was, had come to feel a true love for Ram.

Register No. 230, page 1517, writes: Who was this Kubja before? In the Ram incarnation, in Dashrath's palace, Kaikeyi had a maidservant named Manthara who was a hunchback, and so her name was Kubja. Before that she was a bird, and before that a gandharvi (celestial musician). In this incarnation her form was beautiful, but she was bent in three places — head, chest, and legs — so her name was Trivaka. Shri Krishna too is Tribhangi, standing bent at three points while he plays the flute.

Scholars who interpret this from a spiritual viewpoint say that Kubja means a mind bent in three places. What are those three places? Mind, speech, and body. According to Maharaj Jivanji's view, Shri Krishna is the one who, from being bent in three places (trivakta), becomes tribhangi and plays the flute. He is tribhangi. If we look at the deeper meaning of his standing bent at three places while playing the flute, it is this: Shri Krishna, breaking through the three gunas (qualities of nature — sattva, rajas, tamas) while he plays the flute, is the one beyond the three gunas. He who breaks through the three gunas while playing the flute is that same Shri Krishna who is beyond the three gunas. Because he is beyond the three gunas, the flute-charming Lord who is the true divine cowherd of Gokul is established as such — this is the conclusion Jivanji reached after discussing and deliberating with Gopaldas.

Register No. 251, page 276, writes: When Namdevji meditated and looked, he found that she (Janabai) had been Kubja in the Krishna incarnation. If we think along these lines, we could say that Harmabai, who was disabled from birth, could likewise have been Kubja in the Krishna incarnation, and just as Krishna healed her, Jivanji too removed Harmabai's disability and was united with her. We do not wish to make any claim of this kind, but it is shown in Jivanji's hagiography (parchari) that just as Maharaj Jivanji was Krishna's companion in the Krishna incarnation, Harmaba and the other fellow devotees were the gopas and gopis. That is fitting.

In the matter of guru and sadguru, Shurpanakha's incarnation as Kubja is consistent from the viewpoint of Samagam. Many speculations have been made about Kubja.

Shamal Haribhai's notebook no. 1, part 1, page 80 (Jagdish's no. 258):

The union of Kubja and Shri Krishna should be seen purely from a spiritual viewpoint. It is like the setting of the sun — each person interprets its meaning according to what suits them. For instance, one who performs the evening (sandhya) worship takes it as the sign for sandhya. A traveler on the road takes it as a signal to reach his destination quickly. A thief or a lustful person takes it as a signal to prepare for theft or seduction. Those who eat before sunset take it as a sign that eating is now forbidden — many such inferences (implications) can be drawn. In the same way, various meanings have been drawn about Kubja and Shri Krishna.

There is a Kubja-like disposition even in the ninefold devotion (navadha bhakti), because the goal is the attainment of Parabrahm. To atheists, devotion appears to be a sham. To those of other faiths, it appears to be [unclear] deliberately faulty. To those driven by desire, it grants enjoyment according to their disposition, and for the desireless it purifies the inner being (antahkaran) and leads to the attainment of God — just as Kubja received the Lord's grace. Likewise, one who practices the devotion described in the scriptures also attains God. (Based on Bhagvat, Canto 10, Chapter 42, Shridhar's Ganesh edition, pages 88-89.)

Shurpa-karna — ears like a winnowing fan (shurpa): the winnowing fan separates the grain from the bad husk. The quality of the winnowing fan is that it separates Brahm from Maya.

Shurpanakha — one with nails like a winnowing fan: her nails perform the work of scraping and digging, like a hoe into the ground. Shurpanakha tried to win over Ram and Lakshman through her large nails. Maya presents her claws before Brahm, and, being unable to attain the love that resides in Brahm, she tries using her claws. But Maya's effort is not capable in that field of action, and so her nose and ears get cut off. Maya may be a portion of Brahm, but when Brahm wishes to remain within a limit (maryada), Maya's forceful attempt to merge with and attain it fails — this longing of hers was fulfilled in the Krishna incarnation, when she was wed as Kubja. When Brahm behaves not as one bound by limits but as Purna Purushottam (the complete Supreme Being), he cannot keep Maya separate from himself; if he did, Maya would be considered to have a separate existence of her own. Shurpanakha is consumed by desire (kama). Those consumed by desire regard even day as night — that is why they are counted among creatures of the night (nishachar).

_Diva pashyati no uluko, kako ratrau na pashyati; Apoorvah kopi kamandho, diva naktam na pashyati._
(The owl cannot see by day, the crow cannot see by night; but the one blinded by lust is unique indeed — he cannot see either by day or by night.)

The owl is blind by day, the crow by night, but one blinded by lust is blind both by day and by night. In broad daylight she went right up to Ram. Krishna is dark-complexioned, so for him it is easy to wed Kubja even in broad daylight. For one consumed with desire, night alone is considered suitable — she made even night into a six-month night, [unclear] and thus took the gorasa (milk-curd) of daytime.

Shamal Haribhai's notebook no. 4, part 2, page 194 (Jagdish's no. 265), writes:

It is mentioned in the Mathura Harivansh that Kubja, in her previous birth, was a king's daughter. Hearing Narad sing, she became enraptured with the Lord and desired to marry him. When the king spoke to Narad about a groom for his daughter, Narad said that the girl's own wish should be consulted. The girl said, "The one whose praises you constantly sing — him alone I wish to marry." Narad said that this could not happen. The girl said, "Even if it takes millions of births, I will marry none but him. Know this as certain." Seeing her unshakeable resolve, Narad showed her a way to attain the Lord. Seeing her austerities (tapa), the Lord's seat trembled, and a voice from the sky declared: "In your next birth you will become Kubja, and the one whose touch makes you beautiful will marry you." She was born in the house of Kansa's minister, and Kansa gave her the task of bringing sandalwood paste. The Lord says, "In whatever form one worships me, in that same form I meet them" — and it was owing to her own devotion that he had to meet her in this way. According to another version of the story, it is found elsewhere that Kubja was a partial form (amsha) of Satyabhama — she was the Earth, who had become bent under the weight of wicked kings. The Lord, with natural ease, straightened her and indicated by gesture that the Earth's burden was now about to be lifted. To think anything else about Kubja is ignorance. (Kalyan, page 785.)

Bhagvat, Canto 10, Chapter 44, verse 15, says:

_Kamam krodham bhayam sneham aikyam sauhadam eva cha; nityam harau vidadhato, yaanti tanmayataam hi te._ ||15||
(Those who constantly direct desire, anger, fear, affection, unity, or friendship toward Hari — they verily attain absorption in Him.)

Those who direct toward the Lord — in whatever way — desire, anger, fear, affection, unity, and the bond of fellowship, certainly become absorbed in the Lord.

Bhagvat, Canto 7, Chapter 1, verse 25, says:

_Tasmadvai ranushadhena, nivairan bhavena va; snehat kamena va yunjyat, kathanchin nekshate prithak._ ||25||

Canto 7, Chapter 1: "Oh! How did Shishupal attain a state that even good devotees do not attain?" When King Yudhishthir asked Narad this, Narad answered that God does not become disturbed by anyone's slander and the like. Therefore, through any of these five means — enmity, devotion, fear, affection, and desire — one should fix one's mind on God.

_Kamat dveshad abhayat, sneha-dyatha bhaktatyoshware manah; aavesya tadagham hitva, bahavastadgatim gataah._ ||24||
_Gopyah kamad bhayat kanso, dveshacyaidyadayo nripah; sambandhad vrishnayah sneha-dhuyam bhaktya vayam vibho._ ||30||

Just as the mind is fixed on God through devotion, so too by desire, hatred, fear, and affection, many have become freed from sin and attained the state of God. The gopis attained Shri Krishna through desire, Kansa through fear, kings like Shishupal through hatred, the Yadavs of the Vrishni clan through kinship, you [Yudhishthir] through affection, and we through devotion.

Register No. 449, page 217, writes: To become enraptured by the Lord's divine glories (vibhutis) is itself a form of devotion. Even in the present age, though the Lord is Maryada Purushottam (the Supreme Being who upholds propriety), one who becomes enraptured by him will certainly attain a good end (sadgati). Even if someone reaches the Lord through a base desire, good still comes of it. The women of Janakpur became enraptured, and many of them looked upon him with the feeling of a husband, yet may the Lord be blessed. The women of Janakpuri became enraptured, and many looked upon him with the feeling of a husband, but the Lord did not look upon them with that same feeling. In the Ram incarnation he did not wish for additional wifehood. Those women who became enraptured desired only the state of a female companion (sakhi) — they became the gopis; those who desired wifehood became his queens.

The Garga Samhita, pages 181-182, writes: After her nose and ears were cut off, Shurpanakha performed austerities to Shiva so that Ram might become her husband; Shiva therefore told her that in the Krishna incarnation she would become Krishna's beloved. Register 449, page 218, writes that Ram himself told Shurpanakha: "In this incarnation I cannot accept you; I will fulfill your wish in the next incarnation." Shurpanakha became Kubja in the Dvapar age.

The couplet in Samagam telling how Kripanath (the Merciful Lord) had to wed Shurpanakha, who had come in the form of Kubja, is as follows:

_Saath varasni dokri, sol varasna Kahan; Chandan base Jeevna, kidhi aap saman._ ||1||
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: Kubja was an old woman of sixty years, while Shri Krishna was a youth of sixteen. Yet, on the pretext of bringing sandalwood paste, he made her as beautiful as himself and sixteen years young.)

In the 107th couplet of the Naam-rupi Sakhi it says:

_Saul varasni sundari, panch varaske Shyam; Kharak dekhavat gaye Jeevna, tab pure manke kaam._ ||10||
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: the beautiful Radha was sixteen years old, and Shri Krishna was five, yet when he went out to graze the cows, he fulfilled the desires of her heart.)

_Krishnavatar kamini, Raghupati kino jog; Ved vachan kahe Jeevna, naari leeno bhog._ ||18||
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: In the Krishna incarnation, Raghupati achieved union in love with desirous women — this is what those who truly understand the words of the Vedas have declared: that the Lord enjoyed the company of women in this way.)

Everyone in the whole universe talks of "guru, guru," but among gurus there exist countless kinds and endless views. So Samagam says:

_Guru reejo vichaarke, johi bataave Ram; Sarayu toore Jeevna, je nagar Ayodhya gaam._ ||1||
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: choose your guru with understanding and thought — one who directs you to worship the King who resides in the city named Ayodhya on the banks of the river Sarayu.)

Even when we go to buy a few paisa's or a rupee's worth of tooth-twig (datan), we check it carefully before taking it. When we go to buy grain, we hold the sample in our hand. When we go to buy cloth, we check its weave and width before taking it. Do we make such a careful examination when choosing a guru? Samagam has written that everyone in the universe says "guru, guru," but there are endless views about who a guru is — why did this need to be written? Because a single idea has become fixed in the minds of everyone in the universe: that if one is to take a guru, it should be someone who is shrotriya (learned, versed in the Vedas) and brahmanishtha (established in Brahm, absorbed in meditation on Brahm, a knower of Brahm). But see how remarkable Maharaj Jivanji's own view is: he says one should take as guru whoever leads one to the darshan, bhajan, and bhakti of Ram of Ayodhya on the banks of the Sarayu. Thus, in discussing Ram of Ayodhya, a conclusion has been reached about what kind of Ram Jivanji Maharaj had in mind, so we will not go into a lengthy discussion of that here.

In Samagam it is said that there are many kinds of gurus, so one is advised to become alert and cautious before taking a guru. A cunning guru who misguides us, leading us onto the wrong path and deceiving us, is called a "ghant guru" (a hollow, sham guru). Such hypocritical gurus live in VIP-like pomp and grandeur.

_Kabir sain hamara Ramji, jaka Dashrath baap; Duniyaku dojakh diya, hamku apna jaap._ ||2||
(Das Kabirji says: Many engage in great disputes over the name of Ram. Such scholars remain absorbed in disputation alone and become unhappy — that is, they fall into hell. But for us there is only the one name of Parabrahm, which is Ram, and it is that name we chant and remember.)

The world knows Dashrath as the father of Ram, and this misleads worldly people. The Ram whom people call the son of Dashrath is, for us, a different Ram — not the Ram counted among the ten incarnations (dashavatar), but the primal (adi) Ram, the Parabrahm who has no mother or father, who takes incarnation of his own accord. That Adi Ram is our chosen deity of worship.

_Sabke sadguru Kabirji, mamat karo gat koy; Aur duniyaku Jeevna, sadguru gharki joy._ ||3||
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: Kabirji is the sadguru of all Vaishnav devotees, so no one should insist stubbornly on claiming anyone else as sadguru. But for all others caught up in the entanglements and reputation of worldly life, it is their own household wife who is their sadguru.)

_Bhav bhanjan dukh parharan, amak karan sharir; Aad jug aadi aap ho, guru charo ju Kabir._
(O Kabirji, to remove the suffering of the ocean of existence (bhavsagar) and to save the soul from the body, from the womb, and from birth and death — you alone, from before the beginning of the ages and throughout all four ages, have eternally been the guru-sadguru of all.)

_Sabka sadguru Kabirji, durmat bhanjanhar; Bahar beetar ekasa, sadguru vasne paay._
(Das Kabirji alone is the sadguru of all; he is the destroyer of our ill intellect. Being the same both outwardly and inwardly, that is, unchanging in every way, such a sadguru remains ever steadfast and free from blemish.)

_Bhakti heeno gurustyajyo, mithyavaadi vidambakah; Swashanti na janaati, patra shanti karoti kim._
(A guru without devotion is to be abandoned; he is a fraud and a mocker who spreads falsehood. One who cannot bring about his own peace — how can he bring about another's peace?)

Guru and sadguru: one's mother and father are also gurus, one's parents-in-law are also gurus, an elder in the family is also a guru, the schoolteacher is also a guru, anyone who trains one in a trade or profession is also a guru, the priest who performs religious rites is also a guru — these are all gurus, but a guru who does not free one from the bonds of worldly existence (bhava-bandhan) is not a sadguru. [unclear] It is only the one who gives Name-remembrance (naam-smaran) who is the true sadguru — that is why we call Kabirji, Namdev, and Kabir the sadguru.

The various kinds of gurus mentioned above come to a person at different stages of life. Therefore the Vaishnav Jivandasji said that the soul (atma) undergoes constant dissolution (nitya-pralay), which the Gita also affirms. The soul passes through these states:
Waking, dream, deep sleep, and turiya (the transcendent fourth state) — these are the soul's states.
Birth, old age, and death — these are the soul's three sorrows.
Sattvik, rajasik, and tamasik — these are the soul's three gunas.
Adhyatmik (pertaining to the self), adhibhautik (pertaining to material beings), and adhidaivik (pertaining to the divine) — these are the soul's three afflictions (taap).
Childhood, youth, and old age — these are the soul's states of life.
But when one takes refuge in a guru, one's birth becomes fulfilled; without taking refuge in a guru, one cannot truly be called human.

In "Tattvamasi" (Thou Art That), the word "Tat" (That) [unclear] belongs to both Ishwar (God) and Jiva (the individual soul), and is therefore all-pervading and beyond perception.

In the Beejaswa Ang, in the 22nd couplet, it is written:

_Kabir ang sakaarka, baare ang niraakaar; Baare ang niranjani, aur avastha chaar._ ||22||
(Das Kabirji says: the Lord's form-with-attributes (sakar swarup) has twelve limbs, and his formless (nirakar) aspect also has twelve limbs. These twelve-times-twelve divisions belong to the attributeless Brahm (nirgun Brahm), and it has four kinds of states. The next chapter, on the Brahm within Jagat (Maya), gives the names of these twelve kinds.)

In the Panchratnamala, 3rd edition, page 662, in Kehra 6, Kabir describes the four states:

_Jagrat swapna sushupti kahiye, turiya maahi herana ho; Chaar avasthame hoi vatate, chaitan naam thaharna ho._ ||5||
(The Lord's conscious principle passes through and merges within the four states — waking, dream, deep sleep, and turiya; having passed through these four states, its name is fixed as "Chaitan," pure consciousness.)

To show that without taking refuge in a guru one cannot be called truly human, this couplet is given:

_Kabir Harki bhakti bin, raja kutta hoy; Gali gali bhusat phire, par tuk na daare koy._ ||1||
(Das Kabirji says: without devotion to the Lord, even a king must undergo the birth of a dog, wandering from street to street barking, yet no one throws him even a scrap of food.)

_Kabir Harki bhakti bin, raja bhi khar hoy; Maati laade kumbharki, ghaas na daare koy._
(Das Kabirji says: without devotion to the Lord, even a king attains the birth of a donkey; potters load clay upon him, yet no one throws him even grass to eat.)

_Kabir Harki bhakti bin, paada hoy Patel; Dashrake din maarahi, dede ghoda gail._
(Das Kabirji says: without devotion to the Lord, even a Patel (village headman) must take the birth of a male buffalo, and on the day of Dashera he is shot and killed, sent on the path of death.)

For this reason the body of the individual soul (jivatma) undergoes constant dissolution — at night dissolution occurs and by day one awakens again. But there is said to be a great difference between the sleep of a Harijan (a devotee of Hari) and the sleep of a worldly person:

_Ek suto Jeevna, Kumbhkaran nishchint; Ek nidrae Ahalya sui, gade dhari Kamalkanth._ ||1||
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: on one hand, Kumbhkaran sleeps without any care whatsoever; on the other hand, Ahalya too lies asleep, become inert like stone, yet with her heart set on attaining the Lord, the lotus-eyed one.)

The state of a Harijan's sleep was thus shown to be of true worth, whereas the waking state of a selfish person was found to carry no worth at all. The distance between a moth and the sun is as great as the distance between the waking of a base creature (sakut) and the sleep of a Harijan. This is the couplet on the waking state, showing what happiness a Harijan gives when in the waking state:

_Kabir Harijan suta jagaiye, jape Ramko naam; Teet suta na jagaiye, saakut shukar saap._
(Das Kabirji says: if a devotee is sleeping, he should be woken, so that he may remember the name of Ram; but three creatures should never be woken from sleep — the jackal, the dog(?), and the snake.)

_Kabir kalika ramjan, mata jaisa dhing; Keval gyan dradhavate, sahama mande sing._
(Das Kabirji says: the wicked people of this Kali age are as strong and unruly as a rutting bull. If one tries to instill pure knowledge in them, they become provoked against us, as if charging with lowered horns like a bull.)

_Kabir Ram rahya je khijai, kaudhi vai gal jaai; Shukar vai kar avatarai, naak baduta khaai._
(Das Kabirji says: those who become angry when we speak to them of Ram's name become lepers, rot away, and die; then, taking birth as a pig, they thrust their snout into the mud and eat filth.)

_Kabir saapku na sarahiye, paya aur sakkar paay; Taku kabahu na dheejiye, daav pade tab khaay._
(Das Kabirji says: never praise or feed a snake milk and sugar, and never trust it — whenever it gets the chance, it will bite and devour us.)

_Kabir Harijan to suta bhala, uthkar jape jaap; E teeno jaaga bura, saakut nahar saap._
(Das Kabirji says: it is good to wake a devotee even from sleep, for on waking he will remember Ram's name; but waking these three — the jackal, the tiger, and the snake — is a very bad thing.)

sections.title_en: With Whom One Should Not Make Enmity
sections.translation:
Ramayan: the episode of the dialogue between Ravan and Marich.

There are nine [with whom one should not make enmity]: 1) Shastri, 2) Marmi, 3) Prabhu, 4) Sath, 5) Dhani, 6) Vaidya, 7) Bandi, 8) Kavi, 9) Kovid.

1) Shastri — one who carries weapons. 2) Marmi — one who knows [another's] merits and faults. 3) Prabhu — a master. 4) Sath — a fool, who watches for a chance to strike alone, to set a fire, to give poison, and the like. 5) Dhani — a wealthy man can do whatever he pleases [against you]. 6) Vaidya — a physician can prescribe what is harmful. 7) Bandi — a bard/flatterer spreads heavy slander. 8) Kavi — a poet [unclear] can bring harm through verse. 9) Kovid — a learned pandit can destroy [one] through spells of death and delusion (marana-mohan vidya). One should not make enmity with these nine enemies as described above.

_Kabir sant sohagi ramke, shabde uthe jaag, salil shabdse nahi, jar uthe ban aag._ (Servant Kabir says: saints who are devoted lovers of Ram become alert and awaken on hearing the sound of Ram's name; but the wicked/worldly person [salil], hearing that same sound, blazes up in anger like fire.)

_Pathato nasti murkhatvam, japato nasti patakam, mounina kalaho nasti, na bhayam chasti jagratah._ (One who studies has no foolishness in him. One who does namasmaran [recitation of the divine name] carries no sin. One who keeps silence has no quarrel. And one who remains alert and watchful has no fear.)

_Kshudhitastrishitah kami vidyarthi bahuposhakah, bhandari rakshakashchaiva sapta suptanprabodhakah._ (The hungry one, the thirsty one, the lustful one, the student, one who supports many, the storekeeper, and the watchman — these seven should be awakened if found sleeping.)

_Ya nisha sarvabhutanam tasyam jagarti sanyami, yasyam jagrati bhutani sa nisha pashyato muneh. ||69||_ (Gita, ch. 2) (That which is night for all beings — in that the self-controlled one keeps awake; and that in which [other] beings are awake [to sense-pleasures] is night for the sage who beholds the Supreme.)

Rekhta (page 180, Volume No. 62).

_Sovta hai to jagya hai bapda, jagta sovta kahan jage. Mani man mahi gyani huva, sabad avdhutaka kaha lage. Kahat aru sunat sab avadhi hui, anapayani bhakti nahi hath aai. Kahat Kabir ih gyan sab thothra, jivka bhala kyun hoi bhoi._ (If a person is truly asleep, poor fellow, he will wake at a shout; but one who feigns sleep while actually awake — how can he be woken? One who has, in his own mind, taken himself to be a knower — how can the teaching of a soul absorbed in God have any effect on him? By merely speaking of it and hearing of it, while his allotted span of life runs out, he never attains unshakeable, unchanging devotion. Kabir says: all such [pretended] knowledge is hollow — how then can such a soul ever find its welfare?)

A Harijan (devotee of Hari) who has thus risen and awakened from this daily dissolution (nitya pralaya) is, as it were, born anew. One should embrace and meet a Harijan warmly, for that brings about a second birth; therefore, through one saint meeting another, and through uttering "Ramkabir," that devotee becomes fulfilled — but only if he also sings the glories of Govind; without that, that is, without the kirtan (hymn-singing) of Keshav, merely passing the time brings no success. A sakhi (couplet):

_Kabir harijan aavat dekhkar, uthkar so maliye sadh, mansa vacha karmana, mite koti aparadh._ (Servant Kabir says: on seeing a Harijan approaching, rise and go meet that saint; by meeting him in thought, word, and deed, our millions of sins are erased.)

In turn, Jivandasji said that this has been called the daily dissolution. Now, in the great dissolution (mahapralaya), when the individual soul escapes from the mouth of Time — if it does not then attain Vasudevji, it falls once more into the mouth of the Time of the great dissolution. The words of Adhyaruji:

_Kshanu kshanu janme ne kshanu mare, (swami) chadhe kaalne hath, thaam thaam kare maaheru, te nahi aave saath, payelagi kar vinati._ (The body is born and dies at every single moment, and falls into the grip of Time. The life within it keeps claiming "mine, mine" over this place and that, but none of it goes along with it [when it departs].)

So Vaishnav Jivandasji said that this dissolution is such that, in the three worlds, Time has devoured the whole world except the Harijans. Every moment [beings] were born, and every moment they died; from one kalpa (cosmic age) to the next, right up to [the final] kalpa, they kept dying and being born, yet they never worshipped the Lord. A sakhi:

_Kabir chinta to harinamki, or na chitpe daas, je kachhu chitve ram bina, sohi kaalse paas._ (Servant Kabir says: O devotees, be concerned only with the remembrance of the Lord's name; devotees should be concerned with nothing else. Whoever gives thought to anything other than Ram falls into the grip of Time.)

Thus Adhyaruji says:

_Aharnish sant sangat karo, pahor ghadi anumesh, dhyan dhariney joiye re, dise tara vesh._ (Keep the company of saints day and night; do not give up their company even for a watch, an hour, or the blink of an eye. For if we look with deep reflection, our own true self is seen manifest in those saints.)

Kabirji further said, in Mal Godi (Sarang):

_Rameiya hari gun gaiye, paiye param nidhan, Rameiya hari gun gaiye. ||Tek||_
_Akare jug upaje re, tikare jug jaay, anahad ben bajai le, prabhu mahara rahyo re gagan math chhaay. ||1||_
_Juthe jug dahekyo ghanu re, kaha jivanki aas, ram rasayan je pie, taku bohor na duji pyaas. ||2||_
_Adakshanu jivyo bhalo re, hoy hari bhagtansu het, kot kalp jivyo vritha, taathe nahi mere harjisu het. ||3||_
_Kaha bhasam lepan jata re, kaha guphame vaas, man jite jug jitiye, taathe vakhya fare re udaas. ||4||_
_Kaha jap tap sanjama re, kaha tirath vrat asnaan, ene joge jugat na paiye, taathe bhaav bhakt bhagvaan. ||5||_
_Sampat dekhi na harkhiye, vipat na mariye roe, jaanhaan sampat taanhaan vipat here, raja ram kare so hoy. ||6||_
_Sarag vaas na vanchhiye re, na dariye narak nivaas, honaar so hoega, taathe juthi e mankee aas. ||7||_
_Shunya mandalme shodhi le re, hari prem jot prakaash, jaako roop na rekh he re, bin phule phalo re akaash. ||8||_
_Kahet kabir hari shodhi le re, sant rudia manjhaar, jaanhaan sevak seva kare re, ta sang rame re moraar. ||9||_

(O soul, sing the praise of Ram's divine glories, and thereby attain the supreme treasure — sing the praise of Hari. [Refrain]
1. From the manifest form [sagun-sakar] this world arises, and through transformation the world passes away; so keep sounding the unstruck word ceaselessly — my Lord abides, pervading the inner, celestial abode.
2. The soul has been deceived a great deal by this false, illusory age — what trust is there in this life? One who has drunk the elixir of Ram no longer thirsts for any other taste.
3. Better to have lived even half a moment in this world with loving affection for Hari's devotees, than to have lived for millions of kalpas in vain, without love for my Lord Hari.
4. What use is smearing oneself with ashes, or growing matted locks? What use is dwelling in a cave? If one conquers the mind, one conquers the world, and thereby [worldly] desires themselves grow weary and depart.
5. What use is japa, tapa (austerity), or self-restraint? What use is pilgrimage, vows, or ritual bathing? By such practices alone one does not find the right method — through them, loving devotion to God is not attained.
6. Do not rejoice on seeing prosperity, nor weep and wail on seeing misfortune; for wherever there is prosperity, misfortune lurks there too — remain content in whatever King Ram ordains.
7. Do not long to dwell in heaven, nor fear to dwell in hell; whatever is destined will happen — so the mind's hopes and cravings are false.
8. Seek out, in the empty, uninhabited expanse, the manifest radiance of Hari's love — He who has no form or mark, who blossoms and fruits without flower or fruit, pervading the whole sky.
9. Kabir says: seek out this Hari within the heart, there where saints dwell — wherever a devoted servant renders service, there Morar [Krishna] plays alongside him.)

Thus the soul, confined within the body which is like a cage of karma, dissolves moment by moment in this daily dissolution; but if it finds a Guru, the Guru shows it the way to be freed from bondage to the qualities of the senses, and by meeting one's true Guru (sadguru), through the company of saints, it attains the realization of God.

sections.title_en: The Brahma of the World of Illusion (Maya)
sections.translation:
The Brahma of the World (Maya)

The Children Were Brought Back — In the satsang, on the tenth day of the bright half of Chaitra in Samvat 1710, Jivanji Maharaj discussed the episode of the Brahmin's children as it appears in the Bhagavatam.

The satsang held on the tenth day of the bright half of Chaitra in Samvat 1710 told of a Brahmin near Dwarka whose children, one after another, would not survive birth. The child would be born, live only long enough for its mother and father to see its face, and then it would vanish. This caused the Brahmin great sorrow. Then one day Arjun came there. Hearing the story, Arjun said, how could this be? Growing angry at Shri Krishna and Balbhadra, Arjun declared that some demon, gandharva, or yaksha must have carried the child away. If Death (Kaal) had taken it, the Brahmin would have seen the corpse; since no corpse was seen, someone must be carrying the child off whole. In front of Kripanath (Krishna), Arjun declared in the assembly that the duty of a Kshatriya no longer stood. "O Brahmin, your wife now carries her seventh child — when she is about to give birth, call for me," he said, and thus consoled him. Then when the time of birth came, Arjun was sent for. Arjun built such a fortress of arrows — with countless arrows fitted with astras, crosswise, above and below — that he made a cage of arrows around the birthing room in all ten directions, so tight that not even the wind could enter. Yet after the child was born, Arjun did not see it at all — it vanished. Then the wife and husband began to wail in great anguish. "Because this sinner came to watch, we did not even get to see our child's face," they said. "The other children had at least lived a moment, but this one we did not even see." Arjun was crushed in spirit. He then built a pyre and prepared to burn himself upon it. The fifty-six crore Yadavs of Dwarka gathered. Shri Krishna came and gave much counsel, but Arjun would not accept it. Arjun said, "Lord, bring back the Brahmin's children, or I shall burn myself to death on this pyre." Shri Krishna had the chariot yoked; Shri Kripanath himself became the charioteer, and they set out. They pierced through the Himalayas and rose beyond them, passed Lake Manasarovar, crossed Mount Meru and the other great mountains, went past the earth with its seven continents and beyond the realms of the gods and demigods — the oceans and mountains themselves making way for the chariot —

— and thus Arjun and Shri Krishna, crossing Mount Lokalok, reached the great radiant abode of the Lord. At that time, Arjun came to the vicinity of a mountain. From there he saw a great radiance — there was no moon, no sun, no fire. He saw a great effulgence, and there he saw a luminous city of radiant heat. Shri Krishna said, "Halt the chariot here." They stopped the chariot there and walked on. Kripanath took Arjun by the hand and led him there. There stood a fortress, with winding, reversed passages branching out. There, such light emanated as if a thousand veils had been hung. At that doorway it seemed to Arjun that, though looking and looking, he could not see that form at all — but he heard a voice speaking. He saw Shri Krishna speaking, and heard that voice. This form of light, of which one can speak but which cannot be seen because of its intense radiance — no one can truly describe it, such is this incomparable form, it was said. Then, beholding the form of the Parabrahm, they began, with reverence and humility, to bow and offer prayer. Shloka — the words spoken by the mouth of Shri Brahma:

_dadarsha tabhyog sukhasanam vibhum mahanubhavam purushottamottam | sandambudabham supishangavasasam prasannavavratam ruchirayatekshanam ||65||_ (Brahma said: I beheld the Supreme, the greatest of the exalted Purushottamas, seated at ease upon Sheshnag — radiant like a rain-laden cloud, clad in yellow garments, with a serene countenance and beautiful, wide eyes, that form of the Supreme Being who is like the great Kaal.)

Lord Purushottam, reclining upon the body of Sheshnag, was beheld — he was of immense majesty and all-pervading. His radiance was like that of a dense monsoon cloud. He wore beautiful yellow garments; his face was serene, and his eyes were lovely and long.

Brahma said: O Purushottam, you who are the best of all beings, you have done wondrous deeds — you swallowed the forest fire, you humbled Indra's pride. Thus Brahma spoke in wonder — you have accomplished the tasks of many devotees.

_mahamanivratakiritakundalaprabhaparikshiptasahasrakuntalam | pralambachaveshtabhujam rukaustubham shrivatsalakshmam vanamalayavritam ||66||_ (whose hair shone with the radiance of a crown and earrings set with great clusters of gems, whose eight arms were long and beautiful, who wore the Kaustubh gem, bore the mark of Shrivatsa, and wore a garland of forest flowers — such was the Lord I beheld.)

His mass of hair gleamed with the radiance of a crown set with many great gems and of his earrings. He had eight arms, long and graceful. He wore the Kaustubh gem at his throat, and was adorned with a forest garland that enhanced the beauty of his Shrivatsa mark.

The Vedas have sung your great praise, O treasure of mercy (Kripanidhan). Your name is that of the being of a thousand radiant powers. Maharaj, you have accomplished great deeds — you slew Trinavart, Pralambasur, Bakasur, Vatsasur, Dhenukasur, Aghasur, Shankhasur, Mushtik, Chanur, Keshi, and Kansa; you have performed mighty feats of valor. You bear these marks in fullness, Lakshmi serves you, and you wear a forest garland at your throat. To you, who are such a Lord, I bow.

_sunandapramukhaih svaparshadaishchakradibhirmurtidharainijayudhai | pushtya shriya kirtyajayakhilardhibhirnishevyamanam parimeshthinam patim ||67||_ (I beheld the Lord of all the exalted ones, attended by his own companions headed by Sunanda and Nanda, by his own weapons — the discus and others — which had taken bodily form, and served by Pushti, Shri, Kirti, Ajaya, and all manner of divine prosperities.)

His companions, chief among them Sunanda and Nanda, his own embodied weapons such as the discus, and Pushti, Lakshmi, Kirti, Maya, and the eight siddhis all attended upon him in service. Beholding this Lord reclining upon Shesh, Arjun and Shri Krishna grew awed, and stood with joined hands, bowing to the Lord who is the master of all great souls and their own very source. To them, that all-pervading Lord — the Lord even of lords — spoke in a grave voice as follows.

_vavanda atmanamanantamachyutam jishnushcha tadarshanajatasadhvasah | tavaha bhuma parameshthinam prabhurbaddhanjali sasmitamurjaya gira ||68||_ (Krishna and Arjun, who had grown awestruck at the sight of the Lord, bowed with devotion to that Infinite, Imperishable One. To the two of them, standing with joined hands, the Great Being, the Lord of the exalted ones, spoke smilingly in a majestic voice.)

_dvijatmaja me yuvayordidakshuna mayopanita bhuvi dharmaguptyai | kalavatirnavavanerbharasuran hatved bhuyastvarayetamanti me ||69||_ (These sons of the Brahmin were brought here by me for the sake of protecting Dharma in the world — the reason being that I desired to see the two of you. You who have descended as partial incarnations, having slain the demons who had become a burden upon the earth, come to me quickly, both of you.)

The Purna Purushottam (the Total Being) said: Out of my desire to see you, I brought the Brahmin's sons here. Both of you have incarnated from a portion of Myself to relieve the earth of its burden and to protect Dharma. Now, having finished the task of slaying the demons who burden the earth, come to me.

O Maharaj, your divine play is here on this earth. Having taken leave of me you departed, yet that bound of order is never broken. When he fell into deep sorrow, you went and brought back the Brahmin's children. Showing great mercy toward me, you left that play behind and came here. O Maharaj, I who am your very portion — how am I? I fill all three worlds, and yet I had become diminished, for that portion of me which separated when you took incarnation had gone apart from me. So by coming here you have done a great deed. Do come again soon — my heart ever dwells upon you.

_purnakamavapi yuvam naranarayanavrishi | dharmaacharatam sthityai rishabhau lokasangraham ||60||_ (Though you two, Nara and Narayan, are ever complete in yourselves and desire nothing, being the foremost of sages, you must continue to practice Dharma for the sake of upholding the world's order — for the guidance of humankind.)

_ityadishtau bhagavata tau krishnau parameshthina | omityanamya bhumanamadaya dvijadvarakan ||61|| nyavartatam svakam dhama sampradrishtau yathagatam | viprya dadatuh putran yatharupam yathavayah ||62||_

Thus commanded by the all-pervading Purna Purushottam Bhagavan, both Shri Krishna and Arjun, gladly accepting his command, took the Brahmin's sons, bowed to the all-pervading Purna Purushottam Bhagavan, and returned by the same path they had come, back to Dwarka. There they gave the Brahmin his sons, restored to exactly the same form and age as before.

_nishamya vaishnavam dhama parthah paramavismitah | yatkinchitam paurusham pusam mene krishnanukampitam ||63||_

(Having beheld the abode of Vishnu, Arjun was struck with the greatest wonder, and he came to understand that whatever valor or achievement a man possesses is entirely due to the grace of the Lord.)

The Lord's radiance, like that of ten million suns, resides in his lotus feet themselves.

Then Arjun asked Kripanath, "What was that conversation about?" Shri Krishna replied, "He told me, 'You are welcome; I am waiting for you — come soon.' And I told him, 'I am still attending to the work of creation, and will come.'" Thus did the gentle Kripanath conduct himself in this matter concerning Arjun. Such was Arjun's fraternal intimacy (sakha-bhaav, the disposition of treating the Lord as an equal companion) toward Krishna that it undid him entirely, root and all — it did him harm. Because of the arrogance that arose in Arjun, Krishna had to undergo the trouble of bringing back the Brahmin's children in order to save him.

_vishvasah samatanityam sakhyatam bhava uchyate_ — (Trust that is always accompanied by a sense of equality is called sakhya-bhaav, the disposition of friendship-as-equals.)

Jivandasji said: whoever holds such a disposition does not fare well. Because Arjun held this sakha-bhaav toward Shri Krishna, this misfortune befell him.

_kabir paarath shooro me sunyo | jaake saarangpaan sahaay | baaher veri bohot hune | ek na maarya maanhi ||1||_ (Das Kabirji says: I have heard that Parth was such a great warrior that the Lord himself aided him. Yet though he slew many outer enemies of the world, he did not slay even the one inner enemy — the ego.)

_paarath shoora me sunya | krishna arjunki saakh | harikee paarakh na padi | gaya himalaya dakh ||_ (Prem Bhakt says: I have heard that Arjun was such a great warrior, and that there was a sakha-bhaav between Krishna and Arjun. Yet, because he failed to recognize that Krishna was truly Bhagwan, he went to the Himalayas to bury his bones. Behold this example of what happened between Krishna and Arjun.)

_kabir dehithe dehi mili | suno krishna arjunki saakh | shabd ki paarakh na padi | gaye himale dakh || shabd vichaare baahare | sadguru shabd jaanya vina ||_

(Das Kabirji says: an embodied soul met an embodied form of God — hear this example of Krishna and Arjun. But he failed to recognize the teaching of the World-Guru Krishna, and so acted contrary to Krishna's teaching; behold, therefore, he went to the Himalayas to bury his bones.)

Arjun was an embodied being, and Krishna too had manifested by taking on a body, but Krishna was God himself — so although he had a body, he was beyond the body. Yet Arjun regarded Krishna merely as an embodied being, and so could not accept him as his Guru. In the Gita, chapter 2, verse 7, though Arjun did say, "Shishyaste'ham shaadhi maam tvaam prapannam" (I am your disciple; instruct me, who have taken refuge in you, in whatever is good for me), still he went to the Himalayas to bury his bones — thus his conduct turned away from Krishna's spoken teaching. Therefore, one should not regard the Guru as merely a bodily being.

_je sajaniya sukh podhate | so jan gaye kedar | guru shabd bin jivana | mile na dooji vaar ||157||_ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: those Pandavs who once enjoyed the comfort of being close kin to Lord Krishna nonetheless went to Kedar in the Himalayas to have their bones ground down. This was because they had not received the teaching of a true Guru; hence, in the Himalayas, a World-Guru like Shri Krishna, one who could give them teaching such as the Gita again, was not to be found there a second time.)

Poojya Yadunath, in Litiyu No. 67, page 10, writes concerning this episode that Jivanji Maharaj said of Arjun: Arjun, who used to sleep in the same bed as Lord Krishna, went to Kedar to die at the time of his death without ever having recognized the Lord — and this itself shows that he had not known Krishna for who he truly was.

_krishna sameepi pandava | gale himalaya jaay | loha ko paaras mile | kaahe kaayi khaay ||26||_ (In the Bijak, Das Kabirji says: even though the Pandavs lived close to Krishna, they went to the Himalayas and had their bones ground away. For if iron has truly touched the philosopher's stone, it turns to gold — and how then could rust consume it? In the same way, since these Pandavs failed to recognize Krishna, they fell into the ocean of worldly existence.)

In a composition named Sharanlila, Bhagwandas has written:

_maara vahaala sevak jan | ek sajyaaye sen kare | ekatha kare bhojan | ek ekane kautuk kare | maahara vahaala_ (Bhagwan says: My devoted servants are very dear to me. I sleep together with them in the same bed, I take meals together with them, and I even engage in playful roughhousing with them. Thus did he behave with the Pandav Arjun.)

Among the Pandavs who set out on the great ascent toward heaven to have their bones ground away, when Arjun's body finally gave out, Bhim asked Yudhishthir: according to the law of the wheel of time, even Arjun Parth has fallen — how could such a famed archer, the wielder of the Gandiv bow, leave us and go? Yudhishthir replied that he was a proud and willful archer, and that was why he fell. Thus, the pride he displayed in the episode of bringing back the Brahmin's children was shown here.

This is discussed in Gujarat Samachar, 24 January 2002, page 11.

It was stated in the satsang that because Arjun held sakha-bhaav toward Krishna, no true good came of it, for he went to Kedar to be ground away — a place considered to be Shivji's domain. Jivanji Maharaj himself went there and, upon returning, concluded that this was no fit place for any devotee of the Lord to dwell; and so he turned back from there. Shivji is the form of Omkar, while the saints and devotees are the rightful heirs of the Lord's realm beyond the three gunas. Hence, a sakhi is quoted here describing Omkar.

_manasa devi upani | taathe bhaya omkaar | ghat ghat vyaapak jivana | so khele nandadwaar ||1||_ (Jivandasji Maharaj says, in the section named Garbhavati, concerning the soul entangled in the wheel of 8.4 million species: at the beginning of creation, a goddess named Mansa, of the nature of Maya, arose, and from her the Omkar-bound creation came into being. That very essence of the Parabrahm Paramatma pervades every single body in this world — and that Supreme Being sports in the courtyard of Nandji.)

_ichchha (manasa) roopi naari avatari | taaka naam gaayatri dhari | taake teen bhaye jo pootaa | brahma vishnu mahadev suta ||_ (In the Ramaini of the Bijak, Das Kabirji says: a woman in the form of Desire, that is Goddess Mansa, came into being, and she was given the name Gayatri. She bore three sons — Brahma, Vishnu, and Mahesh. Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj instructed us to practice bhakti toward Vishnu, but this is not that Vishnu born of Gayatri — rather, it is the beginningless, endless, complete Parabrahm Paramatma, through whom this creation of the illusory world was made.)

Reference: Hindu Dharmakosh, page 493 — "Among the many forms of the Mansa-shakti, worship of the goddess named Mansa is very prevalent in Bengal. A good number of songs in her praise have also been composed, known collectively by the literary name 'Mansamangal.' She is regarded as the mother of serpents, and her worship is believed to ward off trouble from snakes." Mansa-vrat: Goddess Mansa should be worshipped on the ninth day of the bright half of Jyeshtha when conjoined with the Hasta lunar asterism, or, absent that conjunction, on the tenth day, upon a branch of the Snuhi tree. According to Hemadri, in the Chaturvarga Chintamani, part one, page 621, the worship of Goddess Mansa should take place on the fifth day of the dark half of Ashadh. Mansa is also worshipped on the eleventh day of the dark half of Shravan. (From a book titled Bhasha tatha Sahitya, pages 257-276.)

Mansadevi — a goddess of this name has her temple atop the mountain behind Har-ki-Pauri in Haridwar. She is the mind-born daughter of Sage Kashyap, and the wife of Jaratkaru (Mahabharat, Adi Parva, chapters 45-48 and 160): sister of Vasuki, she is the queen of serpents. She is also called Jagadgaura, Nitya, and Padmavati. She is regarded as a portion of the root Prakriti and a beloved disciple of Sadashiv. She is worshipped as the goddess who protects against fearsome crawling creatures. Her nature is jealous — if she is not worshipped first, she sends snakes to take revenge.

Kabir has mentioned her in a pad, in Raga Asavari:

_santo bhai dhokha sabku maare | ko niramal gyaan vichaare ||tek|| koi khoje shiv shaktiku | koo khoje kaaya | koo khoje shoonya mandalku | aise jug bharmaaya ||1|| koo mansa khojai | ko ulata pavan chalaavai | koo khoje jantra mantraku | koo kaashi chal jaavai ||2|| koo jangam jalme naahaavai | koo shekh shayaana | koo desh deshaantar dolai | koo tap teerath lapataana ||3|| bharam karamki saankal kaatau | paarabrahmaku sevai | kahat kabir so harikaa daasaa | maathe boj na levai ||4||_

(Das Kabirji says: O brother saints, delusion and deceit destroy everyone; only a rare few of truly pure understanding grasp this. Others strive to find the Supreme Reality through the practice of Shiv-Shakti; some strive to search for it within the body through knowledge of Brahm; some try to find it through Goddess Mansa; others practice yoga, holding the breath through pranayam; some seek it in tantric rites and mantras; some go off to the region of Kashi; some bathe in the water of a Shiva-linga; some become clever dilettantes; some wander from land to land; some are lured into the trap of austerities and pilgrimage. But whoever breaks the bonds of superstition, delusion, and karma and worships the Parabrahm Paramatma alone is called a true devotee of the Parabrahm Paramatma — such a one no longer accepts the bondage of karma.)

The hidden, subtle form of Desire is Vasana (latent craving), and the subtler form of Vasana is Sanskar (impression); that is to say, the manifest form of Sanskar is Vasana, the gross form of Vasana is Desire, and the gross form of Desire is sorrow and delusion.

In Raga Asavari:

_manchha maalani re | tu soorat chhaabari leh | jal ban koop bhom ban baari | aradh uradh beech kyaari || ihaanke phool uhaan pahonchaaye | so maalan piya pyaari ||1|| moj dei maalan paheraai | baso apana bheeraa | shoon shikhar gadh leeo mukaate | gaave daas kabeeraa ||2||_ (Das Kabirji says: O Mansa, you flower-seller woman, you go about carrying a basket of attentive, focused meditation. Your flower-garden has neither water nor well; there is a bed of flowers set in the space between above and below. You take the flowers grown there and deliver them elsewhere, O beloved gardener-woman of the Beloved. Delighted, the flower-seller garlands everyone with her garlands and then, in fear, withdraws to abide in her own place. Das Kabirji, having settled in the highest state of effortless samadhi, sings the praises of the Lord's qualities.)

Parth and the Pandavs, too, were destroyed by just such delusion and deceit. A sakhi is now given, introducing the Parabrahm — the source from whom this delusion arises.

_kabir antariksh ida agamka | adhar raha niraadhaar | nitya vikase nirmaan phal | trigun vriksh vistaar ||2||_ (Das Kabirji says: the sphere of the unfathomable Brahm-essence of the Lord's nature cannot be known; it abides fixed without any support at all. It ever unfolds and continually produces fruit. Such is this tree, whose spread has extended into the three gunas.)

Ida means one egg — one portion out of the infinite cosmos.

_kabir sava lakh niramaan | uthe nitya avaaz | lakh sabad samata same | rahat anaamat gaaz ||3||_

Niranjan (Dharmaray) performed austerities and demanded sovereignty over the three worlds, the ocean of worldly existence. Growing arrogant because of this, he received a curse: from now on you shall no longer have sight of Me; and every day you shall swallow up a hundred thousand souls and give birth to a hundred and twenty-five thousand. The Lord's supreme devotees, roaring their defiance and confronting Niranjan's challenge every day, go on to the Lord's abode; crossing over Niranjan's dominion of the ocean of worldly existence, they proceed on to reach the Lord.

A Shabd:

_chetho re cheto nar baavare | kaha achet rahaai | kaal daga hai sir oopare | sabku dhar khaai ||1|| lachh jeev nit khaat hai | sava lakh oopai hau | kaahuku chhede nahi | aise kaal anyaai ho ||2|| jagat chavena hai kaalka | sabko khaat yugaai ho | chun chun khaaye shoormaan | khaate na adhaai ho ||3|| kul marjaada metake | karo tum sad sagaai ho | kahai kabir tab bancho | kaal daga mit jaai ho ||4||_

(Das Kabirji says: Oh, you bewildered mortals — how can you remain so unconscious? The treacherous Kaal circles above your heads and seizes and devours everyone. Every day he devours a hundred thousand souls and produces a hundred twenty-five thousand more, yet he spares no one — such a deceiver he is. This whole world is merely a snack for Kaal to munch on, and even so, he is never satisfied. Therefore, cast off the flowery bonds of the Vedas, ritual works, and the like, and bind yourself instead to the true relationship with the Lord's own Name. Only then, Kabir says, will you be able to escape, and the fear of Kaal's treachery will vanish.)

Das Kabirji says (reference: manuscript No. 8, page 228; No. 28, page 191) — a Ramaini:

_kalime niranjan bade anyaayi | ochhe bade jeev sab khaai ||1|| laakh jeevaka kare aahaaraa | sava laakh jeev jug vistaaraa ||2|| aap gapat hoi raho chhipaai | laakh jeev tahaan le maagaai ||3|| apana naam niranjan keena | thakuraai jin aapahi leena ||4|| moorakh jeev kachhu samajata naahi | kahaansu aavai kahaan chal jaavai ||5|| agam panthaka khoj na karahi | phir phir parchaame par hi ||6|| ghatame karataa kaun kahaavai | taahe chhaandi yon dhyaan lagaavai ||7|| man hi vibhram ghatake raajaa | taate saryo na eko kaajaa ||8||_

_man ramataa sab ghatame | suranar muni karo vichaar | kahai kabir tahaan puras hai | jaho shabd takasaar ||64||_ (Sakhi)

(Das Kabirji says: in this Kali Yug, the Nirgun Brahm, the false Niranjan, is a great tyrant, destroying beings both small and great. He kills a hundred thousand souls, and spreads a hundred and twenty-five thousand more into the world. He himself remains hidden, concealed, and from that hiding place summons a hundred thousand souls. He has taken for himself the name Niranjan — free of Maya, the Nirgun Brahm — and has kept lordship over all for himself. Foolish, unwitting souls understand nothing; they do not understand where they have come from nor where they must go. They do not seek out the hidden, unfathomable path, and so fall again and again into the cycle. Abandoning the One who truly governs within the body, they fix their attention here and there instead. Since the mind, the ruler and governor of the body, wanders in delusion, no true good is ever accomplished in any way. Sakhi: the mind revels within every body. O gods, men, and sages, reflect upon this — Kabirji says the Soul dwells right within this very body, where its voice, its sovereign presence, its dwelling, resides and moves.)

Four more sakhis regarding this Niranjan are given below in this ramaini —

_kabir teen chori bhi | sab kaahuka sarabas leen | binaa moodaka chokhaa | paraa na kaahu cheentu ||2||_ (Das Kabirji says: theft has occurred in all three worlds — everyone's all has been taken away. Yet no one could ever recognize that headless — that is, having a head, yet without mercy — thief.)

The headless thief refers to Omkar, the Formless Brahm — the mind, Maya, and Desire in the form of a thief. Hanumandas has said of this thief: "Just as, without a head, a trunk cannot be recognized, so too in that binding-free Omkar-essence, the ultimate reality, all worlds dissolve away — yet no one could understand it." The three worlds mean Rajas (the devotee), Tamas (the yogi), and Sattva (the man of knowledge) — theft occurred among all three of these, robbing them entirely, souls and all. By the syllable "U", devotees were robbed; by the syllable "M", yogis were robbed; and by the half-syllable, men of knowledge were robbed — all were deluded. Yet that headless thief, Omkar, was recognized by no one. This Omkar is nothing but a false imagination. Because it went unrecognized in this way, it devoured the whole world. Or else, the headless thief is Desire, who committed theft in all three worlds and took away the understanding of gods, demons, and men alike, subduing them all and imprisoning them in the dark cell of the womb. Bound in this desire, all — Brahma and his kind, Vishnu and his kind, Shiva and his kind — dance to its tune. Yet this thief in the form of Desire was recognized by no one.

Rivanaresh writes: "The headless thief is the formless Brahm, whom no one could recognize; or else, the headless thief refers to the worshippers of the goddess Chhinnamasta, who hold no devotion for anyone else, saying, 'We ourselves have no head — for what reason? Because it is written that one must become the deity to worship the deity.' These Shakta worshippers are recognized by no one; casting all souls into Maya, she keeps them all deluded." Rivanaresh regards either the Formless Brahm, or the goddess whose own head has been severed, as this headless thief. This Shakta goddess is one who takes sacrifice by cutting off the heads of all.

In the text Bhavtaran, it is stated in a chaupai concerning Niranjan:
