_dharamdaas suno sant sujaanaa | niragunkaa ab karahu bakhaanaa | niragun naam niranjan bhaai | tin saari utapat banaai || niragunse bhayo ohankaaraa | taaso teeno gun vistaaraa | trigunse man bhayaa prachandaa | taako baas sakal brahmandaa || vo onkaar man aap niranjan | naanaa vidhake kiye veejan | bhaanti bhaatike ghaat sanvaaraa | kahaan lagi kahu vaar na paaraa || taake ansh sakal avataaraa | paraam krishn taame saradaaraa | pooran aap niranjan hoi | iname pherphaar nahi koi || niragun niragunki karai sevaa | bhakti karai aur poojai devaa | karai aachaar vichaar na jaanai | sau mere man kabahu na maanai || man bodhe man maanhi samaavai | nij padakun koi nahi paavai | manakun bodh karai jo koi | man pahuchaavai pahuchai soi || jaay niranjan maanhi samaavai | aage gaman kaahu paavai | aise teen lok sab atakai | khare sayaanai te sab bhatakai || rishi muni gan gandharv devaa | sab mili karai niranjan sevaa | siddh saadhak saadhu jo bhayeu | eenake aage koi na gayeu || bahut preetsu bhagat vichaari | milat milat milai adhikaari | jaay niranjan so hoy bhetaa | kaal roop dhar kare sameta || ehi niranjan ker pasaaraa | taame urajho sab sansaaraa | jaahaan taahaan raakhe vilamaai | rachanaa anant apaar banaai || dharamdaas tum bhakt sanehi | iname jin atakaavau dehi | janam dhare nahi bhaai | taato aayo kahu gauhoraai || bhagat gupat jaane nahi koi | surat dharamdaas sujaan ||_

(O wise saint Dharamdas, listen — now I shall describe the Nirgun. O brother, Nirgun's name is Niranjan; he has fashioned the entire creation of this world. From the Nirgun arose Omkar, and from that the three gunas spread forth. From the three gunas the mind became fierce and forceful, and it dwells throughout the entire cosmos. That Omkar-mind is itself Niranjan; he has produced seeds of many different kinds, fashioned forms of every manner — how far shall I go on describing them, for they have neither end nor limit. All the divine incarnations are but portions of him; among these, Ram and Krishna are foremost. They themselves are the complete Niranjan; in this there is no difference at all. Yet, in their manifest form, they render service and devotion to the Nirgun principle, and worship the gods — they perform such rites and worldly reasonings, but my mind never accepts this. The mind, once instructed, settles back within the mind itself; no one attains their own true state this way. Whoever instructs the mind is carried only as far as the mind can carry him, and no further — he goes and is absorbed into Niranjan alone; none can attain passage beyond that. Thus all three worlds remain stuck there; even the truly wise all wander lost in it. Sages, munis, the hosts of gandharvas and gods — all together render service to Niranjan. Whatever siddhas, sadhaks, and sadhus there have been, none has ever gone beyond him. With great love the devout one reflects, and by meeting again and again, the one who is worthy attains him; he goes and has his meeting with Niranjan, but Niranjan, assuming the form of Kaal, gathers him up. This is the vast expanse of Niranjan, in which the whole world lies entangled; he keeps beings delayed here and there, having fashioned a creation that is endless and boundless. O Dharamdas, you are a loving devotee — do not let your embodied self get caught up in this. [The following line is obscure in the source.] No one knows the secret, hidden devotion — attend closely, O wise Dharamdas.)

Sakhi — _inate gupat bhagat hai | suno dharamdaas sujaan | bhagati karai bhav aavai nahi | soi bhagati pramaan ||_ (There is a truer, hidden devotion beyond this Niranjan — hear it, O wise Dharamdas: that devotion which, once practiced, keeps one from returning to this ocean of worldly existence — that alone is the proof of true devotion.)

_kabir aad purush to ek vriksh hai | niranjan vaaki haar | trigun roop hi shaakhaa bhai | paat bhaye sansaar ||3||_ (variant reading: "Brahma and Vishnu become branches") — (Das Kabirji says: the Original Being, the Supreme Self, is like a single tree, and Niranjan is like a branch of it. The three-gunas forms — Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva — become its branches, and this creation becomes its leaves.)

Kabir has said in a Ramaini (reference: Kuvarpura Grantha No. 7, page 4 / No. 28, page 173):

_niragun pedh aad banvaari | niragunki saragun haari | taa daariika e vistaaraa | raajaa rank sakal sansaaraa || raj veerajaka keenhaa melaa | taatai bhayaa guru aru chelaa | jaamane ek sab jaamaa | ghar beru aru baahar naamaa || ek dehakaa eh anusaaraa | na koo bhayaa kaahute nyaaraa | paanch tataka sab hi bhaande | nahi koi shoodra nahi koi paande || haad chaamakaa ropyaa thambhaa | taamai duniyaa karai aarambhaa || ek hi deevalaa ekahi joti | pandit karau kaunki chhoti ||_

_kabi pandit chhot na keejie | dekho soch vichaar | ham tum ekahi jaat hai | gharani amar mojhaar ||1||_

(Das Kabirji says: the root tree of the Garland-Bearer, the Lord, is the Nirgun; the sagun devotion serves that Nirgun. The branches of that tree have spread out, and within them lies the whole world — kings and paupers alike. Through the union of seed and blood, guru and disciple alike have come into being. All the bodies held within the womb-fluid are bodies of this kind; one's household and one's separate outer lineage all conform to this same single kind of body — none has been made different from another. All are pots molded from the same five elements; among them there is no Shudra, and no Pandit-Brahmin either. These pillars of bone and skin have been erected, bodies have been fashioned, and it is dwelling within them that the world begins its work. Since it is thus all of one and the same kind, then why, O learned Brahmins, do you practice this defilement of untouchability through touch? O Pandits, do not shrink back in this fear of pollution — reflect deeply, just for a moment, and see that you and we belong to one and the same kind, dwelling together upon this same eternal earth.)

_kabir chor ham bhal olakhiyaa | chor keenahu na keen | chor paramodhe jagataku | choraku hamahi dakhyaa deen ||4||_ (Das Kabirji says: it is good that we recognized the thieves, for the thieves have not been able to do us the slightest harm. These thieves go about giving the people of the world instruction and understanding. But we have taught such thieves a proper lesson. They have, through the four Vedas, the four Upanishads, the four scriptures, the six shastras, the eighteen Puranas, the sixty-eight pilgrimage sites, vows, rules, homa and havan sacrificial rites, ritual conduct, the seven days of the week, the fifteen tithis, the twelve months, the four Yugas, the deeds of karma and dharma, the nine planets, the four states of liberation, the four kinds of knowledge, mantra-recitation, hell, heaven, and so on — woven a net of ritual works in this world, and through it have lured the innocent, simple-hearted souls of this body with false charm and attachment, casting them into a trap, and their...)

...the five deities beyond (Niranjan, the primal power [Adya Shakti], Brahmaji, Vishnu, and Shankarji) run the kingdom. All the world worships, bows to, praises, and performs yajnas and homas for them. Because of this, no soul can pass from their ocean-of-existence-like kingdom into the ocean of bliss (the supreme abode) — that is, no soul can escape their grip. (Register No. 2078, p. 124.)

Niranjan (Dharmaraya) obtained the kingdom of the three worlds (the ocean of existence) from God by performing austerities (Register No. 2078, p. 80). Through the power of his austerities he became arrogant, so he was punished: in future he would not have the Lord's darshan; each day he would devour one lakh souls and create one and a quarter lakh souls. Such was the curse Niranjan received (Register No. 2078, p. 16). Niranjan forcibly demanded from Karma-Kachhap (the Tortoise of Karma) the materials for building the three worlds, the ocean of existence (Register No. 2097, p. 92). Ritualists (karmakandis) hold that Niranjan received a curse, so that his head was cut off — God cut it off, that is, rejected him. For this reason the saints and Harijans (devotees) do not accept Niranjan; but the ritualists believe that Niranjan, by his own authority, does not let souls leaving the ocean of existence pass beyond him. So they take the coconut as the symbol of Niranjan: taking a pot as his torso, placing on it leaves of creation such as mango and ashopalav [a decorative tree] as if they were his limbs, and setting a coconut on those leaves as Niranjan's head, they imagine Niranjan's body in this way and worship it, accepting it thus in auspicious ceremonies. But the Harijan saint-devotees, having taken refuge in God, have no need to flatter or serve Niranjan.

_Kabir ind trisama bhagka, bhalka chhuta ek,
tin tin lok mariya, varpar nahi chhek ||4||_
(Kabir: out of the whole cosmic egg one strand out of thirty parts broke loose, and it struck down all three worlds; the destruction it wrought has no end.)

Das Kabirji says: out of the whole cosmic egg of the Perfect Parabrahma, one strand out of thirty parts broke loose, and through it the threefold-gunas maya struck down all three worlds; the destruction it has wrought has no end.

In the Samagam, among Kabir's sakhis, in the Bij anga, in Anga sakhi 15, he says:

_kabir bund athah jalhar, thak mag kachhu nahi,
ind trisame bhagme, sab jag upji vilay ||14||_
(Kabir: the drops of this cosmic egg are like a boundless, fathomless lake; from one thirtieth part of this egg the birth and destruction of all this world takes place.)

Das Kabirji says: the drops of this cosmic egg are like a lake without shore or bottom — their extent cannot be estimated. From one such thirtieth part of this cosmic egg, the birth and destruction of this entire world takes place.

Revered Yadunath writes, in [unclear], p. 105, that is, that a single spark flew out from a great blazing fire.

||Kedaro||
_tis bhan ek thaur dekhe, mai tis bhan ek thaur,
ta upar ek chand biraje, yathe chhabi nahi aur ||tek||
dharan so gagan gagan so dharani, ta par kiyo vistar,
kot kot arun bhari shobha, bin ravi bhayo ujas ||1||
hai nirgun sargun bhayo sagar, ta par adhik bhar,
bas jaye sur tihare darasaki, pandit arath vichar ||2||_
(O mother, I have seen the light of thirty suns falling in a single place; above it sits a moon, and there is no beauty greater than this. His form spans from earth to sky and from sky to earth, spread over both; his splendor has become like the reddish glow of crores upon crores of suns, so that his light shines forth even without the sun. He is the Absolute beyond gunas, yet he has become a vast ocean of qualified, embodied being besides — O scholars, reflect and consider the meaning of this.)

Surdasji says: O Mother (Radha), I have seen the form of God, radiant as if the light of thirty suns fell in a single place. Above that form a moon sits. No other form in the world can surpass it. His form extends from the earth to the sky and from the sky to the earth; his brilliance has thus spread over both earth and sky. His splendor has become like the glow of ten million suns' reddish dawn-light, so that his light shines forth even without the sun. Though he is, in this way, the Parabrahma Paramatma beyond the gunas, he has yet become like a vast ocean of qualified, embodied (saguna-sakar) form, and depends greatly on that embodied aspect. Surdas says: it is my wish that a vision of your form of this kind should become fixed in my mind. O scholars, consider and reflect on what this form must be like.

_kula jat kubharki, chapna ghadchan tris,
nam kiya shri ramka, tansaran banyan tris_
(The potter's caste is by nature like a creator: he made thirty small clay saucers, and gave, as their maker, God's — Shri Ram's — own name; and as he went on shaping those small saucers, they grew as large as great platters of Ram.)

The potter's caste is by nature like a creator. He made thirty small clay saucers (chappan), and as their maker was given God's, Nature's, own name; and while he went on making these small saucers, they grew as large as great platters of Ram.

Kabirji has regarded the Id-Anda (cosmic egg) as maya; he wrote of it in the Id-Maya anga (chapter).

_kabir adhar ind ajmal hai, adhar kare vepar,
kala sankeli saiya, tab sab ekakar ||5||_
(Kabir: the divine Id, unfathomable and wondrous, conducts its affairs suspended in space without support; when the Lord withdraws his device, all this creation becomes one.)

Das Kabirji says: the divine Id (cosmic egg), the Lord, is unfathomable — exceedingly beautiful, strange, and wondrous. It conducts its affairs suspended in space, without any support or prop. When it withdraws and shuts down its device and power, all this creation merges into a single form.

Krishna went with Arjuna to fetch back the Brahmin's children who had been carried off; showing who that Parabrahma was who carried the children away, and why, Jivandasji has described him in the sakhis above, and, explaining it, said: that same enchanting flute-player, the Lord who is Namdev and Kabirji's God, who came to Dwarka and rose to the children's rescue, is one and the same; and the Lord of the world's cosmic egg who carried off the Brahmin's children is, in his original form, that very same Lord. For this reason the names of Brahma are: Omkar, 1. Brahma, 2. Mansa Devi, 3. Jyot Swaroop (form of light), 4. Vishnu Gun, 5. Hiranyagarbha, 6. Tej (radiance), 7. Gudhi, 8. Mahakali, 9. Niranjan, 10. Gayatri, 11. Id, 12. Mahatattva — these are the names of Brahma. That is, he is the Lord of the cosmic egg, while the enchanting flute-player is the Lord of infinite crores of cosmic eggs.

Inquiring students of the Samagam who have made copies of it have, in them, noted down the Vallabh Sampraday's view of this supreme reality as follows. Vallabhi Gosainji Hararayji, in his Shikshapatra, page 38, gives a fairly full explanation: 1. the Lord of the imperishable abode, 2. the cosmic form of the unmanifest Brahma [Akshar Brahma], 3. Rama together with Vaikuntha's Lakshmi. In this way the Vallabh Sampraday has described the nature of God under three aspects.

Kabirji, however, has said that this reality has become known under twelve names, and that these twelve names belong to Brahma, that is, to maya (Kuvarpura Handwritten Manuscript No. 1, page 135; also Panchratnamala, Anga 3, page 660, verse 4). There too Kabir says: _maya brahm bhinna mat jano_ (know Maya-Brahma to be a separate doctrine).

_kabir jar darpan nirmal liya, jine dekha agam apar,
jau deu maya muchchha, to pragat na hoy didar_
(Kabir: the Harijans took up a mirror-clean inner faculty, free of maya's stain, and beheld the boundless reality no sense can know; but were I to make this embodied Brahma-maya swoon senseless, how could I then see the divine reality at all?)

Das Kabirji says: the Harijans (devotees) took up a mirror-like inner faculty (antahkaran), free of the stain of maya, and with it beheld the boundless divine reality that cannot be known through the senses. But if I were to make this saguna-sakar (qualified, embodied) Brahma-maya swoon and lose consciousness, then how could I see the divine reality at all? This is mentioned in Krishnadas's Parachari Charam, pages 44–45.

_bar namki prasiddhi kari, sab sansar soi ur dhari ||544||
chaud lok tahe the bhaye, koy sant yati vichitra bhaye ||545||_
(He made the twelve names well known, and the whole world took them to heart; from them the fourteen worlds came to be, and some saints and ascetics turned out without real substance.)

Because the true understanding of the illusory world that God created was not grasped, people of the path of knowledge — the followers of the six systems of philosophy — declared, according to their own understanding, that Brahma-maya should be understood through twelve names, and all the people of the world took this to heart. From this divine reality of twelve names the fourteen worlds/realms came to be, and some saints and ascetics turned out to be without real substance or truth.

_kabir bara nam pare, kiya rai lon,
jisahi chalave panth tun, tisahi bhulave kaun ||3||_
(Kabir: he made the twelve-named reality regal and beautiful; O Lord, whomever you lead in whatever way, who then can mislead him and stop him?)

Das Kabirji says: to conceal his true nature, and to lead unwise people into confusion about him, God, through these twelve names, made this twelve-named reality appear regal, supreme, and beautiful. O Lord, whomever you lead, and however you lead him — who then can mislead and stop that one from following it?

_kabir bar ang sakarka, bar ank nirakar,
bare ang niranjani, aur avastha char ||22||_
(Kabir: the embodied aspect of the divine reality has twelve parts, and the formless aspect too has twelve parts; but all these twenty-four parts, and the body's four states besides, are portions of the Nirguna Brahma.)

Das Kabirji says, in the Bij-swara Anga: the divine reality's saguna-sakar (qualified, embodied) aspect has twelve parts, and the nirguna-nirakar (unqualified, formless) aspect also has twelve parts; but all these twelve-and-twelve parts, together with the body's four states, are portions of the Nirguna Brahma.

In this way Kabir has referred, in two sakhis, to the twelve names of Brahma-Maya (Id).

Parvati desired to see the form of Vasudevji, but no one is capable of seeing it. In a second episode, Parvati asked: "Mahadevji, what is the nature of your Vasudevji's form?" Rudra replied: "Look at the sun's form — it is truly the form of the Purusha, but because of its extreme brilliance it appears in the shape of a disc; that is only a portion of maya. If you wish to see his true form, you must give up maya and, in proper union, look toward the indwelling Self (Antaryami Atma) seated in the heart — giving up infatuation with maya, possessiveness, pride, impurity, anger, greed, lust, betrayal of trust, addictions, and wrongdoing, and, with the senses mastered and a calm disposition, through the power of pure feeling. The saints and Harijans (devotees) are able to see him in this way. If, instead of the fleshly eye's fleshly sight, you look at the Self in the form of the solar orb, you will see the formless-and-formed [nirakar-sakar] form of your own chosen deity (Ishtadev), and attain supreme contentment." Hearing this, Umiyaji (Parvati) said, "Make my sight pure."

Hearing this, Mahadevji uttered the name of Ram, placed his hand on her head, and firmly established her mental meditation. Because of this she first saw the sun's form, though incompletely — seeing the sun's crown upon its head, earrings in its ears, its chest adorned and filled from every pore with many garlands of splendor, and its extremely radiant hands, feet, body, and lustre, she felt very great joy. Then she said to Mahadevji: "O Lord, I understand it to be so that your Govindji's form cannot be seen with sight — I have understood this much, but now describe it and tell me." Rudra said: "Umiya, listen — let me tell you the form of my Lord. The brilliance of this sun is but the twenty-first part of the radiance of the nail of the little toe of Vasudevji's blessed foot. That is why the sun does not come fully into your sight — so how could you possibly be capable of knowing Govindji?"

_namo narayanadastu sarasaya mahatmane,
vishuddhagyanavikshyaya kotisuryasamarchishe ||71||_
(Salutations to Narayana, the delightful great soul, who can be seen only through purified knowledge, and whose splendor is like that of ten million suns.)

Salutations be to Narayana, the delightful great soul, who can be seen only through purified knowledge and whose splendor is like that of ten million suns.

Umiya said: "O Lord, I have understood Vasudev just as you have described him. The form of Govindji, whose lotus feet hold the splendor of infinite crores of suns, cannot be seen by me; therefore I have today come to know that Govindji as being of the nature of light (Jyoti Swaroop)."

_kabir parbrahmke tejka, kaisa hai unman,
kahevekee shobha nahi, dekha hi praman ||1||_
(Kabir: no estimate can be given of the radiance of Parabrahma Paramatma; there is no worth in describing its splendor — only by seeing it can one know what it is like.)

Das Kabirji says: what the radiance of Parabrahma Paramatma is like — no estimate or inference of it can be given. There is no worth in describing and telling of its splendor; only by seeing it with one's own eyes can one know what it is like.

_kabir dekhya ek agam hi, mahima kaha nav jay,
tej bund parasmani, nayane rahya samay ||2||_
(Kabir: I have seen the one profound reality; its glory cannot be described — a single drop of its radiance is as magnificent as the touchstone, and it has come to dwell in my eyes.)

Das Kabirji says: I have seen the one profound divine reality; its glory cannot be described. A single drop of its radiance is as magnificent as the touchstone (Parasmani), and it has come to dwell in my eyes.

So how could that Vasudev come within the sight of this world? (Now, the ascertainment of Brahma.) For this reason foolish people take it that Brahma is of the nature of light, and radiant only; but he does in fact possess form. Like a tortoise, he too has withdrawn his senses, and for this reason (some holy men call Brahma) formless. But when one considers from what place these senses, the three gunas, and the five elements have developed, one will understand that such is the nature of his true, essential form. Having known this, one should give up the distinction between formed and formless and remain absorbed only in one's own devotion (bhajan) — so said Mahadevji. Hearing this, it occurred to Parvatiji's mind that, since God is embodied (sakar), one ought to become a worthy, qualified person to see him, because without the darshan of Shri Krishna one cannot attain happiness; and since she had not attained that darshan at this time, she wondered what to do, and began forming devotional reflections in her mind: "If he were not embodied, how could he have taken away the Brahmin's sons without hands, how could he have come to Dwarka without feet, how could he have spoken to Arjuna without a mouth? And if Parabrahma had no eyes, how could he have seen Shri Krishna? And if he had no mouth, how could he express an opinion, and how could he have said to Shri Krishna, 'By my power of maya I have summoned this Brahmin's son here, in order to bring you here'? And how did it come about that, beholding Vasudev, Shri Krishna, the great yogi and teacher of the Gita scripture, prayed to his own embodied form?"

For that Parabrahma has the activity of all the senses, yet he does not come into anyone's vision unless full qualification (adhikar) is attained. He who has, within merely one thirtieth part of a single portion of himself, fashioned the whole cosmic egg — the sun and moon, the moving and unmoving universe, the nine planets, the garland of constellations, yoga, maya, and all else — even so, what people describe is only the radiant form arising from his powers. The remaining twenty-nine parts remain intact, and no one's sight can reach them; therefore people go on saying of him, "He is light, he is light." It is only because they fail to attain the direct experience of his embodied nature that they call him formless — for if there were no form at all, the very word "formless" could not arise.

Only through the grace of the Merciful Lord (Kripanath) does one gain the benefit of attaining his darshan; therefore one should simply keep remembering his name, so that through his grace we shall gain the benefit of his darshan. Just as a farmer, in order to store grain, keeps aside a moshitu (moshayo — the clean grain that falls below when winnowing grain in a sieve), so the Merciful Lord has, within his own true light — that which is called Nirguna — tied up and set aside that portion called Brahma as his moshitu. From one part of it the Merciful Lord did, as it were, the farming of the cosmic egg, and has kept the remaining twenty-nine parts tied up as the moshitu.

Such is the immense capability of Shri Krishna, the flute-holding Lord. Who, without his grace, can know that Govindji, who upon each single hair of Vasudevji's body has fashioned crores upon crores of Virats (cosmic forms), and within every single pore of each of those Virats there dwell countless cosmic eggs. Heaven, the mortal world, and the netherworld — these three worlds together form a single Virat form. Here Surdasji bears witness. (A kirtan follows.)

(Raag Sarang) ||Malgodi||

_chosi sarup jagannath jagat guru, jagat pati jagadish,
jog jag jap tap vrat dulambh, pyare lalso grahe gokul ish ||tek||_
(That Lord of supremely excellent form, guru and master of the world, the lord of the universe, unattainable through yoga, sacrifice, japa, austerity, or vow — that beloved darling, Lord of Gokul.)

_jake jathar trailokya jala thal, panch tattva chaukhan,
balak hoi jhulat bij palane, pyarelal jashomati bhovan nidhan ||2||_
(In whose belly rest the waters and lands of the three worlds, the four quarters made of the five elements — that same one, having become a child, swings in the cradle; O beloved darling, treasure of Yashomati's house.)

_ek ek rom kot vairat tan, anant kot brahmand,
lie ochhang mat jashoda, pyarelal apne nij bhuj dand ||3||_
(On every single hair of his cosmic body dwell endless crores of cosmic eggs; yet mother Yashoda takes the beloved darling onto her lap, and lifts him up in her own arms.)

_anurin shravata sudharas pancham, chintamanisi dhen,
vai taji jashomatiko pay pive, pyare lala bhagatanku sukh den ||4||_
(Though the wish-fulfilling cow ever yields sweet nectar, leaving that aside, the beloved darling, giver of joy to his devotees, drinks the milk from Yashomati's breast.)

_ravishashi kot kala bamb lochan, trividhi tap mir jat,
anjan det het sut ve chakh, pyarelal lekar kajal mat ||5||_
(His wide eyes hold the splendor of crores of suns and moons, by whose power even the threefold afflictions are removed; the mother, out of love, applies kohl to those eyes of her beloved darling son.)

_kshiti map tripad gunit karunamay, bal chhali diyo re patal,
dehori olang sakat nahi so prabhu, pyarelal khelat nandjike dwara ||6||_
(The merciful one who, measuring the earth in three strides, deceived King Bali and pressed him into the netherworld — a Lord whose threshold none can cross — that same beloved darling plays at Nandji's door.)

_kamalanayak vaikunthsayak, sukh dukh jake hath,
khandh kambal kar lakuti nagna pad, pyarelal bandhe hai nandjiki rani ||8||_
(The lotus-eyed Lord, the resort of Vaikuntha, in whose hand lies the power to give happiness and sorrow, a blanket on his shoulder and a staff in hand, going about barefoot — that beloved darling, for stealing butter, is bound fast by Nandji's queen, Yashoda.)

_ved vadat upanishad khat ras, urpe bhagata nahi,
gopi gop povalki mandalime, pyarelal hasi hasi juthan le khat ||9||_
(The Vedas, Upanishads, and the six systems of philosophy speak of him at great length, yet devotion to him is not in their hearts; while the company of gopis, gopas, and cowherd boys laughingly and joyfully eat the beloved darling's leftover food.)

_baka baki bakasur sakat trinavat, agh dhen vrishbhas,
kans keshiku gat dini, pyare lal rakhe hai charan nivas ||10||_
(Having slain Baka, Bakasur, Shakatasura, Trinavarta, Aghasura, Dhenukasura, Vrishabhasura, Kansa, and Keshi, and delivered them, the beloved darling has granted them abode at his own feet.)

_bhagat vachhalo prabhu patit odharan, rahe sakal bharpur,
marag rok padyo hath dware, pyarelal patit shiromani sur ||11||_
(The Lord, loving to his devotees, deliverer of the fallen, remains fully present everywhere; O beloved darling, I, Surdas, the greatest sinner among sinners, stand blocking your path, fallen at your very door.)

Surdasji says: what great merit these residents of Vraj must have, that even the great Brahmaji speaks of them in a spirit of devotion — of that supremely excellent Lord of radiant form, the greatest guru of the world, the master of the world, whom one cannot attain through yoga, sacrifice, japa, austerity, or vow, that beloved Lord who is the God of Gokul; in whose belly rest the waters and lands of the three worlds and the four quarters made of the five elements, and who, having taken the form of a child, swings in the cradle. O beloved Lord, you are the treasure-house of Yashodaji's home. In every single pore of this cosmic (Virat) Lord's body dwell endless crores of cosmic eggs; yet that very one Yashodaji plays with in her lap, and lifts up the dear, beloved Lord in her own arms. For that Lord the wish-fulfilling cow always yields sweet, delightful nectar; yet leaving that aside, the beloved Lord, for the happiness of his devotees, drinks the milk from Yashodaji's breast. The radiance of his eyes exceeds that of crores of suns and moons combined; by its power even the threefold afflictions are removed. His mother, for the good of her dear, beloved son, takes kohl and applies it to those excellent eyes. Counting three strides and measuring the earth, he deceived King Bali and pressed him down into the netherworld; no one can withstand the force of such a mighty Lord — yet that same dear, beloved Lord plays in Nandji's courtyard. The beloved husband of Lakshmiji, the resort of Vaikuntha, in whose hand lies the power to give happiness and sorrow — with a blanket on his shoulder and a staff in his hand, barefoot, the beloved Lord goes about. This Lord is the doer and sustainer of his devotees; his vow is to nourish the world. Because butter was stolen from his head [i.e., he was caught stealing butter], the beloved Lord was bound by Nandji's queen, Yashodaji. The Vedas, Upanishads, and the six systems of philosophy speak a great deal, yet in their hearts there is no devotion toward this Lord; while the company of gopis, gopas, and cowherd boys eat this beloved Lord's leftover food, laughing with joy. Having slain Bakasura, Shakatasura, Trinavarta, Aghasura, Dhenukasura, Vrishabhasura, Kansa, Keshi, and others, he delivered them, and this same beloved Lord granted them a place at his own feet. Such a Lord, gracious to his devotees, deliverer of sinners, remains fully present everywhere. O beloved Lord, I, Surdas, the greatest sinner among sinners, stand blocking your path, holding fast at your door.

Such is Vasudev, who dwells in the hearts of the Harijans (devotees).

_kabir mor mugat pankaj nayan, kundal makrakar,
so murat mere nayan baso, chitme karat bihar ||2||_
(Kabir: may that form — wearing a crown of peacock feathers, lotus-petal eyes, fish-shaped earrings — dwell in my eyes and move joyfully in my mind.)

Das Kabirji says: may the form of the Lord Shri Krishna — who wears a crown of peacock feathers, whose eyes are like lotus petals, and who wears fish-shaped earrings — dwell and remain in my eyes, and move about in joy and delight within my mind.

Vaishnav Jivandasji said that the Lord's greatness and majesty come into no one's sight except a Harijan's; and if such a one beholds him with love, it becomes a source of great auspiciousness and well-being — that is, one attains the fulfillment of human birth and comes to a state of supreme bliss (paramanand) whose very nature is love.

(Raag Sorath)

_santo bhai re ulajhan bhari, pathafer — achraj ek bau bhari,
kahat sunat kachhu samaj na aave, avigatki gat nyari, santo ||1||
koi kahai ham nirgun sove, par nirgunka gun kaisa,
koi nirgun koi sirgun (kahavat) bhai, ye (vame mohi) bada andesha ||san||2||
nirgun kahiyo nam mahatam, sirgun santa biraje,
nirgun sirgun ek rup hai, koi ek nij jan nirkhai,
pani pavan bhaya jab mela, tab ek rup hoi barkhai ||san||4||
(shabd surati jab doy milave, tabahi amirasa barse ho ||)
kahat kabir antarki karni, pragat hoy tab sachi,
apne piyajike sukh karan, nagan magan hoi nache ||san||5||_
(O saints, brothers, a great tangle has arisen — a great wonder in this variant reading; nothing can be understood by speaking of it or hearing of it, so strange is the way of that unmanifest one. Someone says, 'we dwell on the Nirguna' — but what special quality does the Nirguna have? Some call him Nirguna and some Saguna, brother, and this raises great doubt in me. The Nirguna is called the glory of the Name, while in Saguna form he is present among the saints; Nirguna and Saguna are one and the same form, and only a rare soul beholds this himself — when water and air come together in union, then it rains down as one single form. When the Word and one's inner attention (surat) meet, then the nectar-rain falls. Kabir says: the working of one's inner devotion becomes true only once it is made manifest; for the sake of one's own beloved's joy, one becomes lost and immersed, and dances in ecstasy.)

Das Kabirji says: O saints, a great tangle has arisen — no understanding of it comes whether by speaking of it or by hearing of it; such is this strange matter of the eternal divine reality. Someone says, "We worship the Nirguna (attributeless) reality" — but what special quality can the Nirguna reality have? Ah, friend, some call him Nirguna and some call him Saguna, but this raises a great doubt in me. For the greatness of God's Name itself is called God's Nirguna aspect, while in the form of the saint he is present and shines forth in Saguna form. The Nirguna reality cannot be understood without any shape, form, or manner whatsoever, and yet whenever any form comes before it, that Nirguna reality withdraws and moves away. But when a meeting takes place between Nirguna and Saguna, the two together take on a single form and rain down as grace; when the Word — God's Name — and one's inner attention (surat) meet, then the nectar-essence of this divine reality rains down. Das Kabirji says: it is genuine only when such a feeling awakens in the working of one's own inner disposition — like a bride's dispositions becoming guileless, joyful, and absorbed, rising up in eagerness, in order to please and gladden her husband.

||Sakhi||

_kabir nav man sut arujhijhya, kabira ghar ghar dwar,
tahan surujhaya bapra (ramji), jahan jani bhakti murari ||1||
kabir balihari guru apna, arujhjhaya sarujhjhod,
nav man sut arujhijhya, so palme kiya nimed ||2||_
(Kabir: nine maunds of thread got entangled, in house after house, at door after door; there it was untangled, poor thing, by Ram, where devotion to Murari became known. Kabir: great is my own guru, who took what was entangled and untangled it — the nine maunds of tangled thread he resolved in a single moment.)

Das Kabirji says: by forgetting the original, true reality, every embodied soul becomes entangled, in the dealings of the body, in nine maunds of thread — the four inner faculties [mind, intellect, chitta, and ego] and the five sense-organs [of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell]. There, whoever was thus helplessly entangled had their confusion untied by God, the Guru, at the point where devotion to Murari-Hari became known to them.

Das Kabirji says: great is the grace of our guru, who untied the tangle in which a body bound by nine maunds of thread-like entanglement — the four inner faculties and five sense-organs — was caught, and who resolved and settled it in a single instant. (Kam Pustakalay No. 393, p. 55.)

On the soul, the Nyaya school's view (Vichar Sagar, page 461): the Nyaya doctrine holds that [1.] pleasure, [2.] pain, 3. knowledge, 4. desire, 5. aversion, 6. effort, 7. dharma (merit), 8. adharma (demerit), 9. mental impressions (samskaras) of knowledge, 10. number, 11. change/result, 12. distinctness, 13. conjunction, and 14. disjunction — these fourteen qualities pertain to the soul (jiva) as atma. (No., Ne. 1, p. 50 — see note.) An attempt has been made, as above, in the Vichar Sagar, to reckon how many difficulties the individual soul (jivatma) runs into by exercising the intellect.

||Kafi||
_nahi vako varpar, saheb nyara hai,
jo kahiye so nahi tahi, aisa akal pasara hai ||tek||
nahi jiv shiv bhi nahi, nahi purush aur nar,
nahi nirgun nahi (nirakar) akar ||1||
nahi lekh alekh bhi nahi, nahi ko akar,
rajot sarup vahi te nyara, soi sarjanhar ||2||
nahi sthul sukshm bhi nahi, nahi rup arup ||3||
aave na jay mare na jive, nahi gam aur tham,
kahat kabir suno bhai santo, aisa hai so ram ||4||_
(There is no end to him; the Lord is unlike anything else — whatever you say of him, he is not that; such is his ungraspable extent. He is not the soul, nor Shiva; not male, not female; not Nirguna, not formless, not possessed of form. He is not written, nor unwritten; he has no shape at all; his form of splendor is beyond even that — he alone is the creator. He is not gross, nor subtle; not with form, nor without form. He neither comes nor goes, neither dies nor lives; he has no village, no place. Kabir says: listen, brother saints, such wondrous is that Ram.)

Das Kabirji says: the divine reality has no end; that Lord is unlike anything else. Whatever you might say of him, he is not really that — such is his inconceivable, ungraspable extent. He is not the soul-principle (jiva), nor formless, nor possessing form; nor is he female. He is neither Nirguna nor formless nor possessed of form. He is neither visible nor invisible, nor does he have any shape. His form of light is beyond even that; he alone is the creator of creation. He is neither vastly great nor minutely small; neither possessing form nor without form. He neither comes nor goes, neither dies nor lives. For him there is no village or place. Das Kabirji says: O saints, listen — such is the wondrous nature of that Ram.

A pure mind: _ulajhanoko sulajhaneke liye aur dharm sankat upasthit hone par samuchit vyavastha deneke liye parishkrit (safe karelu) aur nirmal mastishk ki avashyakta hai_ (to untangle confusions, and to give the proper resolution when a dilemma of dharma arises, a refined and pure mind is needed). — Najar, No. 1, p. 25.

_ghar sutarne fadke, ghani gunjavan vir,
tani tode akalo, dhire ukele dhir_
(In the household — a ball of thread — many knots arise, brother; the impatient one tugs and breaks the tangle, while the patient one slowly unravels it.) — Register 231, pp. 1939 and 2144.

A household is like a ball of the thread of worldly existence: however many knots arise in the life of a householder struggling in the world, when it comes to untangling them, one who grows impatient and angry simply breaks off the knotted part, while a person of calm nature slowly and patiently unravels it.

Keeping silence is best. Between husband and wife, parents and children, brothers and sisters, and other such close relations, wherever there is a close bond, if one of the two becomes harsh, the other must become gentle. If, instead of staying calm, the other also grows heated and starts flinging harsh words, it is like pouring ghee onto fire. In such a conflagration all one's close relatives get burned up, while others merely get a spectacle to watch. Enemies gain the pleasure of gloating over it without even trying. Even one's own work cannot be done properly because of the mind's agitation. Excess cleverness will only create confusion in matters of true, ultimate welfare (paramartha) — that is exactly why it is said: _nav man sut ulajhiya, ghar ghar bar_ (nine maunds of thread got entangled, in house after house, at door after door).

In this chapter, "The Brahma of the World (Maya)," by showing the divine reality that carried off the Brahmin children of Dwarka, and Shri Krishna, who brought those children back, an attempt has been made to clarify the matter of the original, true Supreme Being, the Parabrahma. The followers of the path of ritual action (karma-margis) have tried to understand, by means of twelve names, the Lord of the cosmic egg who carried off those children. The Parabrahma Paramatma is of the nature of light (jyoti swaroop) — that is the original, true light of God, whom even one such as Parvati is unable to see; and the light that people try to know as the Supreme Being through twelve names is, in fact, the light of the Maya-Brahma form. In this way a confusion has arisen between the true Brahma-reality and the illusory (mayavi) Brahma-reality. Through this chapter the Samagam has made known the very twelve names by which those who try to know God through twelve names have themselves created this confusion. Such confusion has also been created by the Vedas, and it has come about through great pronouncements (mahavakyas) such as _aham brahma_, _prajnanam brahma_, and the like; and the Vedas, growing weary, stop short by saying "neti [not this, not this]." The Brahmanical scriptures and the Upanishads too have struggled to understand Brahma, but no conclusion has been reached. Japa, tapa, vows, pilgrimage, and the like have led people into error in this world.

Having held this Samagam at Shahapur, the true dharma of Vaishnav devotion was shown to all Vaishnavs; devoted Vaishnavs of one's own household were called into refuge, the Vaishnav dharma was set going among them, and they were led to attain the supreme benefit.

Speaking further about lands, Vaishnav Jivandasji said that there is a certain merciless land, without compassion, where great violence is done to living beings — one should not go there. (This is mentioned on page 126 of the Vasana samagam; it is not found in the original samagam.) Baba Kabirji forbade it:

_Kabir jahan daya tahan dinta, dinta tahan hoy prem, daya dinta jahan nahin, tahan janeka nem. ||1||_ (Where there is compassion there is humility, and where there is humility there is love; but the rule kept is: never go where neither compassion nor humility is found.)

Das Kabirji says: where there is compassion, there is no humility, and where there is humility, there is love; but wherever one goes and finds no humility, one should never go there — this is the rule he has kept.

_Kabir sakutki sabha rachi, tahan mat baitho jaay, ek guvade kadi bade, roj gaddha aur gaay. ||2||_ (Servant Kabir says: do not go and sit in an assembly of the worldly-minded; for if a nilgai, donkeys, and a cow are kept together in one cowshed, a quarrel will surely break out at some time.)

Das Kabirji says you should not go and sit in the assembly of worldly (saakat) people, because if a nilgai, donkeys, and a cow stay together in one cowshed, a quarrel will certainly happen at some point; in the same way, people of every disposition — rajasic, tamasic, and sattvic — gather there and quarrel.

The devoted seekers who copied out the samagam, while narrating the episode of Bhoja Gujar's misfortune, mentioned this forbidden, merciless land. Even one who dwells in the sacred land of Vraj and is pure and holy may unknowingly incur a fault; even then God comes to his aid. This forbidden land is also called, in the Bhagwat and other texts, the land of Kikat:

_Yatra yatra cha madbhaktah prashantah samadarshinah, sadhavah samudaraste pooyantyapi keekataah._ (Reg. 413, p.47; Reg. 1606, p.383) (Wherever my devotees dwell — who are prashant [free of any desire for enjoyment, liberation, or mystic powers, and free from passion, anger, and greed; that is, self-controlled and endowed with calmness and restraint], who are samadarshi [seeing the presence of God equally everywhere and in everyone], who are of saintly nature, and who happily observe right conduct — that place, even were it the land of Kikat [that is, a most impure land], becomes purified.)

The names of the Kikat lands are also listed in a verse:

_Anga bangakalingeshu saurashtramagadheshu cha, tirthayatram vina gatva punah sanskaram arhati._ (Reg. 413, p.47; Reg. 53, p.11) (In Anga desh, Bang desh, Kalinga desh, Saurashtra, and Magadha — should one happen to travel there for any purpose other than pilgrimage, one must, on returning, undergo the purification rite once again.)

Anga desh, Bang desh, Kalinga desh, Saurashtra, and Magadha desh — should one have to pass through them for any reason other than pilgrimage, one must have the purification rite performed again. It was formerly believed that a Brahmin becomes impure the moment he enters Bengal; the Mahabharat mentions this in many places. In the dictionary, Kikat is named as one of the ninety-eight ancient non-Aryan lands — now the province of Bihar, or the land of Magadha.

_God bangal kamarun, poorab aur gujarat, parasram ya jeevakun, rajak maut le jaat. ||44||_ (H.Li.-5, p.228) (In Gaud, Bengal, Kamarudesh [Assam], the East, and Gujarat, Parashuram says, it is death's own destiny that carries this soul away.)

In the lands of Gaud, Bengal, Kamarudesh (Assam), the East, and Gujarat, Parashuram says, death's destiny takes this soul away.

The brothers who copied the samagam have written this discussion about the lands mentioned above. In the original samagam there is no mention at all of this forbidden land, but loving devotees, in keeping with the episode of Bhoja Gujar, have introduced this discussion into the samagam.

After the sakhi "Navaman Sut Ulajhiya," the chapter concerning Bhoja Gujar begins. After such satsang discussion of Navaman Sut and the rest, he came to Mangaleshwar and remained seated daily in the assembly of Vaishnavs for six months, granting to all the joy and blessing of devotional celebration. On that day —

In the year Samvat 1716, on Magshar Sud 2, Jivandasji arrived at Mangaleshwar; on the way he spoke this sakhi:

_Dase dish bandhu jivana, deu Raghupatiki aan, vaat ghaat raksha kare, chhodve chaare khaan. ||1||_ (Maharaj Jivandasji says: In all ten directions everywhere I invoke the authority of Raghupati [Ram], asking that protection be given at every place and in every condition, and praying that God release souls from the four wombs [forms of birth].)

Maharaj Jivandasji says that he calls upon the authority of Ram in every direction, asking that protection be granted at every place and under any circumstance, and prays to God to release beings from the four kinds of birth.

He returned again to reside at Mangaleshwar. In Samvat 1716 (also written 1916 in the text, evidently the same year), on Magshar Sud 2, Gujar Bhojo, a Vaishnav, came before Jivandasji and offered great praise (mahastuti). Vaishnavji then asked him: tell your name, tell your place — for what reason have you come in the preta [ghost] form? He replied: Maharaj, I was with you in Gokul; I was among the companions (sakhas) of Shri Krishna — Arjun, Bhoj, Ban, Vishal, Sabal, Gang — and among them, Bhoja Gujar was my name. I had a daughter named Dhanbai; Kripanath [the Lord] engaged in amorous play with her, and so, from a worldly point of view, a fault of lustfulness was seen in Dhanbai — for this, God commanded that I remain in the preta form for two ages, the Dvapar and the Kali yuga. Its shloka:

_Dvapare'tha yuge prapte bhojo pretatvam apsyati, lilaganena krishnasya pretamuktir bhavishyati. ||72||_ (When the Dvapar age arrives, Bhojo will attain the state of a preta [ghost]; and through the singing/kirtan of Krishna's divine plays, he shall be freed from that state.)

When the Dvapar age comes, Bhojo will attain the condition of a preta, and through the singing (kirtan) of Krishna's divine plays, he will be freed from that condition of ghosthood.

The meaning of "Bhoja" in the Vinit dictionary is given as "a caste of people." Krishna's principal companions are counted as eight: 1) Krishna, 2) Tok, 3) Rishabh, 4) Subal, 5) Arjun, 6) Vishal, 7) Bhoj, 8) Shridama. (Notebook no.1, p.146)

Devotees of the Vallabh sect state that the eight devotees of the Ashtachhap of the Vallabh sect were themselves the eight sakhas [companions of Krishna]. A chhappay [verse] gives the names of those who sang of the eight companions' divine plays:

_Surdas so to Krishna, Tok Parmanand jano, Krishnadas so Rishabhe, Chhitswami Subal vakhano, Arjun kun Kumbhandas, Chaturbhujdas Vishala, Vishnudas so Bhoj, Swami Govind Shridama, Ashtachhap aatho sakha Shri Dwarikesh parman, Jinke krut gun gaan kari nij jan hot suthan. ||1||_ (Know that Surdas represents Krishna, Parmanandadas represents Tok, Krishnadas represents Rishabh, Chhitswami is called [the poet] for Subal, Kumbhandas for Arjun, Chaturbhujdas for Vishal, Vishnudas for Bhoj, and Swami Govind for Shridama — these eight, the Ashtachhap, accepted the faith of Shri Dwarkesh; through composing and singing His praises they attained their own true, blessed abode.)

Krishnadas (Rishabh), Kumbhandas (Arjun), Surdas (Krishna), Parmanandadas (Tok), Nandadas (Bhoj), Chhitswami (Subal), and Govindswami (Shridama) — these eight companions of Krishna accepted devotion to Dwarkesh Krishna, and by singing His praises and performing kirtan, they attained the blessed abode of the Lord's own intimate devotees. Every sect sings the praises of its own devotees; even though Bhoj may be reckoned as an incarnation of Nandadas — who lived in the sixteenth century — while it was in the year Samvat seventeen-hundred-sixteen that Bhojagujar's liberation took place; he [Nandadas] may indeed have been born as a supreme devotee, but who was who in an earlier birth cannot be said with certainty. In any case, Bhoja's liberation was accomplished by Jivandas Maharaj in Samvat 1716.

Among the eight companions there is also this listing: 1-Madhu, 2-Mangal, 3-Subal, 4-Subahu, 5-Bhoj, 6-Arjun, 7-Shridama, 8-Vishal. (Nani notebook no.8, p.59)

Another list: 1-Shridama, 2-Madhumangal, 3-Bal, 4-Subal, 5-Arjun, 6-Stok, 7-Krishna, 8-Anshu. (Nani notebook no.15, p.31)

Yet another list: 1-Shridama, 2-Subal, 3-Stok, 4-Krishna, 5-Arjun, 6-Anshu, 7-Vishal, 8-Rishabh. (Nani notebook no.15, p.30)

The samagam records that from the Dvapar to the Kali yuga there was a command to remain in the preta form — the question was when it would be lifted. In the Kali yuga, taking human birth, the manifest divine play would be sung; thus it is fitting that Bhojo should come in this way, as a devotee, in the Kali yuga. Having perceived a fault in the Lord and turned away from Him, Bhojagujar, upon taking refuge with Jivanji, was freed from the preta form.

Sadguru Jivandasji Maharaj had to take incarnation specifically for the liberation of Bhojgurjar. He came to this earth for Bhoja's sake alone, and along with Bhoja's deliverance, our own work too was accomplished. Through the medium of ourselves, of Kanman, and of Keshavdas and Krishnadas and others, he also brought about the liberation of Surat district and of Kothi district.

Pu. Yadunath writes, in notebook no.60, on the back of page 20: I have no doubt about the account given in the notes of the Ram Sanehi (saint) sadhu (H.Li. Granth no.98, p.26); the story of Bhojagujar is true — reading it with one's own [overactive] intellect will only create more confusion, this is my opinion. Excessive cleverness creates confusion in matters of ultimate truth — that is exactly why it is said: "Navaman Sut ulajhiya, ghar ghar baar" (the thread of the ninth spindle got tangled at every household's door).

Regarding Bhojgujar, the following is written on the basis of the notes of a sadhu named Ram Sanehi and of the copy of the samagam made by Nazar:

In the year Samvat 1716, on Magshar Sud 1, Gujar Bhojo, a Vaishnav, came before Jivandasji and offered great praise. The matter that had occurred at the time of Krishna's incarnation in the Dvapar yuga now came to light. Now, regarding Gokul — Vaishnav Jivandasji had been present in Gokul as a devotee during the Raslila, and it is Vaishnav Bhojagujar who bears witness to this; his account has thus been set down. It was for the sake of this Bhojagujar that Vaishnav Jivandasji had to come into this incarnation; that account is recorded here. Now, the daughter of Vaishnav Bhojgujar was named Bai Dhanbai, who used to serve Vaishnav Jivandasji; at that time her father, Bhojagujar, arrived at that place — the hymn (pad) of that occasion:

_Santo bhai ghar mah jhagra bhari, raat divas mohe(mili) uthi uthi laage, panch tota ek naari. Tek. ||1|| Pancho ku bhojan juda juda chahiye, pancho aap(adhik) savadi, nyaro nyaro bhojan chaahe, gharko kutumb kahyo nahi maane, (pancho) aapuhi aap muraadi. ||2|| Hai koi aisa dev devalme, panchoku pakat chapet, durmati keri duhaagini hai, dhorahi chaapi chapere, kahet Kabir soi jan saacho(mera), dalki duvidha mete. ||3|| Gharki raari nivere._ (O saintly ones, a great quarrel has broken out within this house [the body]; day and night those dwelling in it rise up again and again to fight — the five senses are like five children, and the soul is the one wife. Each of these five wants a different kind of pleasure, each finding its own most delicious; each wants its own portion kept separate. The household is told not to, but it will not listen — each of the five is bent only on its own satisfaction. Is there some deity in this temple [of the body] able to seize and restrain all five at once? A wretched, ill-fated wife named Durmati [perverse intellect] provokes and drives these children by force. Kabir says: that person alone is truly worthy who resolves this crowd's confusion and settles the household's quarrel.)

Das Kabirji says: O saintly ones, a very great quarrel has begun in the house that is the body. Those who dwell within it, day and night, become provoked and start to fight. The five senses are like five children, and the individual soul (jivatma) is like one wife. These five want to enjoy different kinds of pleasures; each of the five is intensely absorbed in its own particular relish. The members of this bodily household, the senses, are told to remain restrained, but they do not obey; each of the five has its own separate desire. Is there some deity of good understanding (sadbuddhi) in this temple that is our heart, able to hold all five of these in check and keep them restrained? The wretched, ill-fated wife that is Durmati (perverse intellect) forcibly incites these children that are the senses. Das Kabirji says that, in truth, the only person fit for this task is the one who removes the suffering of the inner self.

Having seen that divine play, a fault of vision (drishti-dosh) arose. After that, Bhoja Gujar's body began to fail. When his allotted life came to its end, Shri Krishna commanded: O Bhoja, go now into a state of downfall (avagati). Then Bhoja Gujar entreated Shri Krishna: Maharaj, why is this? I am but your servant. Shri Krishna said: you have incurred a fault against a great one, and therefore, O Bhoja, this is your fate. Bhoja Gujar again begged for grace: Maharaj, when will I be delivered? Shri Krishna answered: it will happen in the Kali yuga. After that, the Vaishnav against whom Bhoja Gujar had incurred fault was Vaishnav Jivandasji, residing in the village of Mangaleshwar; Bhoja Gujar came there in this manner, as a token of this: he entered the body of Bai Rambai, wife of the goldsmith Vaishnav Keshavdas Zadeshwariya. Vaishnav Jivandasji then inquired: who are you? At that, the spirit said: Maharaj, you do not recognize me — my name is Bhojo Gujar. Vaishnav Shri Jivandasji then asked: what is this to you? Bhoja Gujar answered: I have incurred a fault regarding Dhanai; Maharaj, now free me from it. Vaishnav Jivandasji then asked for a token, saying: how can this be believed? Bhojo Gujar was asked to give the token from that place; and after some hesitation, Bhoja Gujar gave the token concerning Brahma: Brahma had come to receive your prasad but had not obtained it. In the land of Vrindavan, wishing to receive your prasad, Brahma came deceitfully in the form of an insect, and you all then spread a blanket on the ground and took your meal there. That attempt of Brahma's was thwarted. Shri Krishna said, "this bird is deceitful," and after that a bower of creepers was made, and the meal was taken there. Then Brahma, thinking further, came in the form of a fish; and after the meal you wiped your hands upon a blanket. Again, once, Brahma stole away the calves, and on that day you all became the calves. I will give a second token concerning the group of cowherds — I will name the cowherds: Arjun, Bhoj, Vishal, Bal, Sabal, Gang, Madhumangal, Shridama, Stok, Krishna, Anshu, Rishabh, Subahu — and among them, Bhoja Gujar was my name. These tokens, all belonging within Gokul, Vaishnav Jivandasji then accepted; after that he said to Bhoja: will you take prasad?

Bhoja replied: I have come into your refuge; give me prasad. Then the Vaishnav woman who was mother and sister to Raghu Kahanji sang Mehtaji's [Narsinh Mehta's] kirtan.

Raga Ashavari:

_Mathurama mahi vechavane thaayan taan, ko najie palav zaalyo re, maa maa kartaan aalingan didhun, chumban vaali lidhun re, aa jone adhar dank laagyo, aa sho kidho anyaai re, Bhoja gujar tani hun beti, maru naam Dhanaai re. ||1|| Ughaadi jaat aahir hamari, bol kuhuni nav saankhu re, patine gamtaan vaar na laage, laaj tamari raakhun re. ||2|| Dahiyaan mahiyaan vechine jeevun, dithade maarag jaaun re, bese kar te Kansne aapun, javaab kahone na deun re. ||3|| Maara re kulmaan kaaval nahotun, ratan si dehahi vagoi re, Narasaiyaacha swami sange ramtaan, sansaar vaat jaanaai re. ||4||_ (When we [gopis] had gone to sell curd at Mathura, someone caught hold of my hem; and though I kept saying "no, no," he embraced me and pulled me close and kissed me. Look — my lower lip bears the mark of his bite; why has he done such wrong to me? I am the daughter of Bhoja Gujar; my name is Dhanai. We Ahirs are of an open, unashamed nature — I do not endure anyone's taunting words. If this were to please a husband it would take him no time at all to be displeased with me, yet I preserve your honor. I earn my living selling curd and buttermilk, going along my straight, honest road; whatever toll I owe I give to Kansa alone, and to no one else do I give any answer. There was no blemish in my family, but this jewel-like, unblemished body of mine has now been disgraced. Playing together with Narsinh Mehta's Lord, this matter has become known to the whole world.)

Narsinh Mehta says: the gopi Dhanbai told Krishna, speaking as if to the people of this world, that when we milkmaids went to Mathura to sell curd, Lord Krishna caught hold of my hem, and though I said no, no, still he embraced me, took me into his arms, and kissed me. Oh, look — there is now the mark of his teeth upon my lower lip; oh, why did he do such an unjust thing! I am the daughter of an Ahir named Bhoja Gujar; my name is Dhanbai. We Ahir folk are of a shameless nature that does not tolerate anyone's taunts or reproach; I am not one who would put up with anyone's mockery or abuse. If a husband did such a thing he would soon be displeased by it, but out of regard and shame before you I say nothing. I make my living selling curd and buttermilk and go about on my own straightforward, honest path; whatever toll is owed, I pay it to Kansa, and I refuse to pay tax to anyone else besides him. There was no stain of any kind upon my family, and now this precious, jewel-like, unblemished body of mine has been made to bear a stain. All of this became known to everyone through Narsinh Mehta's Lord Shri Krishna's sporting with the gopis.

Narsinh Mehta composed another hymn as though the gopi were saying: do not leave a tooth-mark upon my lips —

Raga Vasant (H.Li. no.9, p.341):

_Dant maa daish duraj dekhe, vaat kare vistaari, aakho dan nihaalti hinde, ehti nanandi amaari. Tek. Parnaarini sangamaa ramtaan, eku chihin na kije, amo vahuaaru maansadamaan, sam khaataan sahije. ||1|| Jan janne uttar so dije, amo chhe abla baali, Narasaiyaacha swami sarve taharu, adhur mehel ek taali. ||2||_ (Do not leave the mark of your teeth, for others watch to find fault and spread exaggerated tales; our sister-in-law watches us all day with a sharp eye. While sporting with another man's wife, leave no such mark; we are like ordinary married women who so easily have to swear our oaths [of innocence]. What answer could we give to every single person, being as we are weak, helpless women? O Lord of Narsinh Mehta, everything we have is yours — spare only this one thing, my lower lip.)

Narsinh Mehta says that the gopis tell Lord Krishna: do not leave the mark of your teeth upon us, for wicked people are always watching for faults and exaggerating small matters into big ones; my sister-in-law watches us with a sharp eye the whole day long. While sporting with another's wife, do not make any such mark; we are like ordinary married women of this world, and we bear the shame [of suspicion] while swearing to our purity. If any mark were to appear, how could each of us defend our honor before everyone? We are helpless women; O Lord of Narsinh Mehta, everything of ours is yours to give — only spare this one exception, our lower lip.

Another hymn concerning Bhoja Gujar of similar sentiment is recorded among the Harmala hymns (Nani notebook no.4, p.6; Panchratna, ch.4, p.742; Bapu Vrindavan, book no.1, p.48; R.H. Vachakopothi, Mesaru's cover, p.241):

Raga Sorath:

_Vahaalo gokulmaan raheto, tahaan navneet chori leto, gujar dhanaine gher jaato, tahaa taadho thubro khaato. ||1|| Dhanaai baandhati gaanthe taani, tahaan mukaavta saarangpaani, tamo te vela sambhaalo, ehvun jaanine ugaaro. ||2|| Maaho maahe motai na aano, mune potaani kari jaano, hala maare rude taaru rudu, maara bhunde taaru bhundu. ||3|| Naagar batka bolaa kahiye, tun to kaain na aane hooiye, par aadhin thai pet ja bharato, gujarnaan dhaan re leto. ||4|| Maari pat jaataan taari jaase, tyaare vaikunthmaan nahi rahevaas, am sanghaate vaad na kije, mune haar taantano dije. ||5|| Lok varkhaan bole maaraan, dhaank maaraan ughaadis taaraan, haan tun konaa rudemaan baitho, valti maari mite nahi ditho. ||6|| Tune vrikshabhaansuta rahi raakhi, tene aanandthi joto zaankhi, ehvi ved vade chhe saakhi. Saakhi — Shukdev Narde chhupaayo, Parikshitne shravane samaayo. ||7|| Taaraan varkhaan pooraan na thaay, pad ek Narasaiyo gaay, taare Narasaiyo rise bharaay, muj vinaa jas kon gaay. ||8||_ (My beloved used to live in Gokul, stealing butter there; he would go to Gujar Dhanai's house and eat her stale, cold bread. When Dhanai bound him up tight, I would plead with the Lord and set him free — remember, O Lord, your own plight then, and knowing this, deliver us likewise now. Do not maintain any superiority between us — know me as your very own. My friend, my good is your good, and my harm is your harm too. One who is clever, witty, and plain-spoken would take such words to heart, but you remain unmoved; you filled your belly dependent on others, eating Gujar's own grain. If my honor is lost, yours is lost too, and then you could not remain in a place as high as Vaikunth. So do not quarrel or contend with us — give us the wager. People speak ill of me — conceal my faults, or I will expose yours; your heart has still not yielded. In whose heart are you now so absorbed that you do not even glance my way? You have kept Vrishabhanu's daughter as your beloved, and gaze at her joyfully in secret — the scriptures themselves bear this witness. Witness: even Shukdev and Narada kept this hidden, yet a faint account of it reached Parikshit's ears. Your praises can never be exhausted; Narasaiyo [Narsinh Mehta] sings but one such song — and should Narsinh Mehta grow angry with you, who but I will sing your renown?)

Narsinh Mehta says: devotees, Shri Krishna, the beloved of the gopis, used to live in Gokul, stealing and eating the gopis' butter. He would go to the house of Gujar Dhanbai and there eat her cold, plain bread. When Dhanbai would tie him up tightly, I [the devotee-poet] would plead with the Lord and free him from her bonds. O Lord, remember what a helpless plight you were then in, and now, knowing this, deliver and save wretched souls such as us. There was, between us, this mutual practice of binding and releasing one another — so let there be no distinction of who is small and who is great between us; rather, know me as your own beloved devotee-maidservant. My friend, my good is your good, and my harm is your harm; if my honor is lost, your honor too will suffer along with it. One who is truly clever — witty, teasing, plain-spoken — would take such words to heart, but nothing seems to affect your mind at all. Yet you lived dependent on others for your food, and ate Dhanbai's grain — so if my honor goes, yours will go with it, and then you could no longer dwell in a place as high as Vaikunth. So do not quarrel or contend with us, but give us plainly whatever ordinary due is owed. People speak ill of me, so keep my honor hidden, or I too shall make your faults known to all. Ah, truly — whose heart have you become so infatuated with, that you no longer even show affection toward me? Knowledgeable people give proof that you keep Vrishabhanu's daughter Radha as your beloved through this illicit bond, and that you gaze at her lovingly in secret. This matter of your loving bond with Radha was kept concealed by Shukdev and Naradji within the Bhagwat itself, and Parikshit, on hearing the Bhagwat, gained only a faint, partial sense of it. So your virtues and faults together cannot be told in full — yet Narsinh Mehta, composing this hymn, sings your praise; and it is for the sake of the wager of these Harmala hymns that Narsinh Mehta is moved to such passion — for who besides me, he says, will sing such praise of you?

A second hymn of the same sentiment appears in the Harmala as follows:

Raga Dev Gandhar (Ashavari) (Najar notebook no.28, p.420):

_Maahare mandalik su padi chhe hod re, mune tahara charan joyaana kod re, mune bhav bandhanthi chhod re, tamo jakh maarso mune haar aapo. Tek. Mune tamo vecho to vechau re, kaache taantne baandhi jaau re, hun gun govindnaa gaau re. ||1|| Tune gujar dhanai baandhati taani re, tyaare hun mukaavto saarangpaani re, men to pothamtaa tahaari jaani re. ||2|| Lok varvaan bole chhe maharaan re, dhaankya maharaan ke ughaadis taharaan re, taharaan manadaan haju nathi haaryaa re. ||3|| Tune vrikshabhaansuta rahi chhe raakhi re, te to mahara manmaan rahyo chhun saankhi re, men karnaa taraahi bhaakhi re. ||4|| Amo naagar batak bolaa kahaae, kahyaa kathan na raakhie hooiye re, taam vinaa sharan amo kone rahiye re. ||5|| Taharo narasaiyo rosh bharaay re, mujh vinaa jas taaraa kon gaay re, tun van vaahaare maharaari kon dhaay re. ||6||_ (I have made a wager with [King] Mandalik regarding you; my only longing is to behold your feet. Free me from the bondage of this worldly existence — though it may cost me, give me the wager. If you sell me, I will be sold; I will bind myself with a fragile thread, and still I will go on singing Govind's praises. Gujar Dhanai used to bind you up tightly, and I would free you, O Sarangpani; I have come to know your very helplessness. People speak ill of me — shield my faults, or I will expose yours; your heart has not yet softened. You keep Vrishabhanu's daughter as your beloved; this I bear silently within my own heart — this much mercy have I shown you. We Nagars speak plainly, and we do not withhold what is said or done — without you, in whose refuge should we remain? Your Narsinh Mehta grows angry — without me, who will sing your praise, and without me, who will run to my aid?)

Raghu Kahanji's mother, Baheniba, sang the hymn concerning Bhoja Gujar — "went to sell curd at Mathura" — thereby recalling this episode of Bhoja Gujar's life. Vaishnav Jivandasji then said: Bhojo, that is you, and Dhanbai, that is her. Vaishnavji then accepted this account. (Note — I, Jagdish, expressing my own view, say that since it was by the grace of Sadguru Jivandasji that I was given the strength and inspiration to write this account of the samagam, it seems to me that this Dhanbai is, at the present time, none other than Baheniba, Raghu Kahanji's mother, who sings Narsinh Mehta's hymn — the very same one who served Jivanji during the Krishna avatar is the same one who is serving Jivanji now. Ram-Kabir's Dhanbai has come here as Baheniba; my respectful [pranam] to them — Ramkabir.)

Vaishnav Jivandasji then asked Bhoja: will you take prasad? Bhoje said: Maharaj, whatever we take there [in that manner], that I will take — bring that [milk-food]. Then the lady brought gorasa [a milk-based offering]. The elder [Jivanji's son] Vasandas then rose to fetch a leaf-plate. Vaishnav Jivandasji asked: Bhoja, in what will you take your prasad? Bhoje answered: Maharaj, in whatever manner we receive it there, in that manner I will take it. So the elder Vasandas did not go to fetch a leaf-plate. That same day, at Vaishnav Jivandasji's temple, Harmabai gave Bhoja the curd-prasad, which Bhoja received by cupping both hands together. Then Bhojo said: now I am satisfied. After that he sought leave and made this plea: erase all my faults, whatever they may be. Vaishnav Jivandasji then said: Bhoja, your faults — whatever they were, from the past and up until this present day, have all been removed by the grace of Shri Kripanath. Having received that prasad, and having taken leave and blessing from Vaishnavji, Gujar Bhojo made his pranam to his own place. The very moment he made that pranam, Bhoja's release and deliverance took place, and he then reached Shri Kripanath. Thus was the episode of Bhoja Gujar completed. After this, the Vaishnav proceeded to reside at Dhanora.

Pu. Yadunath writes, in notebook 67, page 38: I heard the account of Bhojagujar from my mother, Gangaba, sitting in her lap. She would demonstrate the "cupped hands" gesture — interlocking the little finger of the right hand with the little finger of the left hand, forming a cup-like shape with the hands — and would say that this is how Bhoja drank the curd-prasad.

I, Jagdish, have likewise demonstrated to devotees and to Najar, with my own hands, what this cupped-hand gesture looks like. I have seen this with my own eyes, and I remember it.

Before Jivandasji Maharaj, Bhoja established proof of having been Krishna's companion during the Dvapar-age Krishna-lila, by reminding him of the episode of Brahmaji stealing the calves. That this same soul, who had once been Krishna's companion during Krishna's lila, should meet with Jivanji Maharaj, is a matter of pride for us; it is our great good fortune to meet one who had direct contact with Shri Krishna. Bhoja recalled the episode of Brahma and the calves of Krishna; Kabirji sang of this matter in a hymn in Raga Bhairav, as follows:

_Kaag kit hoi brijme aayo, avigatki gat aap bhulaayo._ (Becoming a crow and an insect, [Brahma] came into Braj — he himself forgot the true nature of the Imperishable [the Lord].)

Brahmaji took the form of a crow, and also the form of a fish, and tried in this way to obtain the Lord's prasad, yet the Lord never gave him the opportunity to receive it. Narsinh Mehta, too, has described this divine play:

Raga Gaud Malar Thal:

_Aa jone govalamaan game, govindaraay re dado re jame, jagan kare tahaan nikat na aave, jai aahiradamaan rame. ||1|| Aap aapnaan maathaan sahu laine, prabhujini aag daakhe re, shaak paak naahna vidh athaanaan, joi jaadav raache re. ||2|| Tyaare brahmajie man vichaaryun, meen tanun roop lije, jamunajimaan chalu lese, chaturbhuj mahaa prasaad paamije. ||3|| Antarjaamie tatkshan jaanyun, brahmaa meen tanun roop laavyo re, Narasaiyaacha swami chatur shiromani, kaamlie kar loharaavya. ||4||_ (See how much the Lord loves being with the cowherds — Govind eats their simple, humble fare there. Where a great sacrifice is performed, he will not even go near it, and yet he goes and plays among the lowly Ahir folk. Each one brings his own bundle of food and offers it before the Lord; seeing the vegetables, dishes, and various pickles, the Yadava [Krishna] rejoices. Then Brahmaji thought to himself: let me take the form of a fish, so that when the Lord comes to rinse His hands in the Yamuna, I, the four-armed one, shall receive that great prasad. But the all-knowing Lord instantly perceived that Brahma had come in the form of a fish; so Narsinh Mehta's Lord, foremost among the wise, had his hands wiped instead upon a blanket by the cowherds.)

Narsinh Mehta says: ah, look how much the Lord loves being with the cowherds; he eats the finest food together with them. Even if someone performs a great sacrifice (yajna), the Lord does not go near it, yet this same Lord goes and plays among the cowherd folk. Everyone brings his own bundle of food and offers it before the Lord; seeing the vegetables, dishes, and the various kinds of pickles, Shri Krishna becomes delighted. At that time Brahmaji thought to himself that he would take on the form of a fish, so that when the Lord came to wash his hands in the Yamuna, he could obtain that great prasad. But the Lord, who knows the innermost heart, instantly knew that Brahmaji had come in the form of a fish; therefore the Lord, most clever among the clever, had his hands wiped instead upon a blanket by the cowherds — and did not allow Brahma to obtain his prasad.

In discussing Bhoja Gujar, the Ram Sanehi sadhu wrote out Kabirji's Bijak hymn, Shabd 3, referring to the body and its senses as a household; this hymn was presented in Kabir Pani, year 1, issue 4, page 6, and its meaning was beautifully explained there. In it, the king of Riva is said to have counted, among those given over to durmati [perverse intellect], those who take the self [ego] to be the ultimate truth — reckoning among them the followers of "I am Brahman" as well as the atheists.

The spirit of Bhoja Gujar, which had attached itself to Rambai, wife of the goldsmith Keshavdas Zadeshwariya, was delivered by Jivanji Maharaj in Samvat 1716. That goldsmith became the devotee Uda, and established the Uda faith in Surat district. In the lineage of the mahants of the Surat seat, Naranadas is named as the first acharya of the Surat seat; this Naranadas is [also known as] Vasantdas, the eldest son of Jivandasji. Thus, through the propagation carried out by Naranadas as well as by the goldsmith Keshavdas, the Uda faith spread in Surat district. Not much particular information is available about Keshavdas; but when the devotee Narsinhbhai Ramji, of the Naaria Khadki quarter in Vadodara, was working in Vadsad, a goldsmith lived next to his residence. One evening, when Narsinh the devotee (bhagat) began to recite the evening arati, that goldsmith, on hearing the arati of Padmanabh, began to say: Bhagat, where did you get this arati of ours from? Then Narsinh Mehta

[The account breaks off here at the close of page 237 of the source; the sentence continues on page 238, which begins the next section of the samagam and falls outside this unit's assigned pages.]

He said, "This is our aarti," and the goldsmith said, "No, this is our aarti." Then, once the matter was clarified, the goldsmith said, "We are of the line of Uda Soni — the Uda Soni who [served] Narsinh — we are Uda Soni, and we recite the aarti of Padmanabh." Then that goldsmith once had a handwritten manuscript come to Narsinh Bhagat. Narsinh Bhagat showed it to me, but I did not ask to keep it, and so that manuscript has since gone missing from their collection. I did not examine the manuscript very closely, and I regret that. But this much is certain: today the heirs of the new generation may not know whether we are, or once were, Uda Soni. Even so, up until about Samvat 2025 a descendant of Uda Soni was still living. It is true that the devotees of Surat district are in no position to investigate such an Uda Soni further. But the goldsmiths who gathered in Valsad had kept alive the memory of Jivandasji's faith — that was the last trace of it.

## In the Presence of the Compassionate Lord of Dwarka

_Dwarka padharya leela joi, manav dehi malvana marag kaha_ (Having gone to Dwarka and beheld His divine play, the path by which an embodied soul may meet the Lord is told.)

In Samvat 1726, on the eleventh day of the bright half of Bhadarva, after coming to Dhanor, Jivandasji Maharaj set out for Dwarka. To attend upon him in service he took his son Shyamdasji along. Having asked leave and taken farewell of the whole Vaishnav community, he set out for Shri Dwarka. On the way a village came — the name of that village is Patdi-Bajanu. The whole company lay down to sleep there; at that time the Vaishnav Jivandasji had gone to sleep, and his son Shyamdasji was pressing his feet, when Maharaj had a dream in which he seemed to be conversing with Kripanath (the Compassionate Lord), and some words were heard being spoken. After he awoke, the Vaishnav Shyamdasji asked Swamiji, "What conversation did you have with the Lord in today's dream?" Maharaj said, "I asked, 'What fruit will You give to the children who come to me in dream [i.e. who turn to me in devotion]?'" Then Vasudevji (the Lord) said: "Whoever wears the tulsi-tilak and walks in it, and keeps to it — for him I shall clear away every fault of karma, and, so that he need not fall again into the wandering of the eighty-four lakh species of birth, I shall grant him, so that he may worship once more, one human birth in which to worship Shri Krishna. The tulsi-tilak is the very sign of Namdev and of Kabirji." Here follows the testimony of Kabirji's own birth-horoscope:

|| Bhekh ||

_Aayo re man sarovar-ko hansa, jinke shrunkhale niranjan vasa ||1||_ (Here has come the swan of Man-Sarovar lake, in whose chain of deeds the Pure One himself dwells.)

_Aayo re malayagiri-ko vasi, kaate karma laage nahi paasi ||2||_ (Here has come one who dwells on the sandal-scented Malaya hill; no bond of karma can ever touch him.)

_Aayo re Sinhal dvipa-ro haathi, aadya purush-ko nirantar saathi ||3||_ (Here has come the elephant of the isle of Sinhal; he is the constant companion of the Primal Being.)

_Aayo re ban kankar-ki jyoti, seep samudra bin jesa moti ||4||_ (Here has come a light out of the forest pebbles — like a pearl formed without sea or shell.)

_Aayo re paras kanchan kaaran, dahekyo kaal dekhyo bhav(jug) taaran ||5||_ (He has come as the cause that turns [base metal] to gold, like the touchstone; having seen and burned away time, [he has come] to carry the age across.)

_Aadya purush-ko sahodar aayo, tulsi tilak naam dhan laayo ||6||_ (He has come as the very brother of the Primal Being; he has brought with him the wealth of tulsi, tilak, and the [Divine] Name.)

_Bast ajuaari so gai re chhapaai, ta kaaran vahalo bhaye sahaai ||7||_ (The bright, shining thing [true devotion] had gone into hiding; for that reason the Beloved became its helper.)

_Udanme aaye das Kabira, bagat kaaran man rakhyo dheera ||8||_ (Into the garden came the servant Kabira; for the sake of the devotees he kept his mind firm and patient.)

_Udyanme dali paayo dhare, marag maanhe julaahe nihaare ||9||_ (In the garden he was found resting on a bough; on the path a weaver caught sight of him.)

_Aap aap maanhi kare vichaara, sundar baalak eh apaara ||10||_ (Within himself the weaver began to wonder — "this is an exceedingly beautiful child.")

_Ke tajiye ke lije uthaai, kartaki gat kali na jaai ||11||_ (Should I leave him, or should I pick him up? The Creator's way can never be fathomed.)

_Ko kahuka larka hoi, hamku aap larega soi ||12||_ (He must be someone's child; that someone will himself come and fight me [for taking him].)

_Jhaar puchhkar jab godo lina, saheb moku beta dina ||13||_ (Setting aside his hesitation, he then took the child into his lap, saying, "The Lord has given me a son.")

|| Sakhi || (a devotional couplet)
_Kabir Kashi khet padhariya, khodya karmana mool.
Chaar charan hoi hari bhajo, bhit gai sanso sool ||1||_ (Kabir went forth to the field of Kashi and dug up the very root of ritual karma. He said: as long as your four limbs stand, sing of the Lord — [do this and] the thorn of doubt melts away.)
