At Jagannath Puri, no pilgrim lights a hearth of his own; only Jagannath's own prasad is eaten -- yet the Uda community has the freedom to prepare their own prasad without such restriction.

Thus the Uda devotee community truly stands apart, distinguished from every other community; yet, on the matter of the rajasvala taboo, the followers of the Pushtimarg, because of their exclusive devotion, have obtained an exemption from the taboo -- which resembles, to some extent, our own practice. Our own womenfolk, however, have never at all accepted the notion of impurity attached to the menstrual state, and so on -- and it is indeed true that our way of life appears to those bound by ritual to be of quite a different kind. The Vaishnavs of the Pushtimarg practise a devotion bound up with the three gunas (trigunas), whereas we practise a devotion that transcends the three gunas altogether. At Shahapura, the sannyasi Maheshvaranandji once told me: "Vaishnavah panchamo varnah" -- Vaishnavas stand apart from all four varnas. Where eighteen kinds of varna are reckoned, we, the Uda devotees, say that ours is the nineteenth varna, and the feeling behind it is that we are distinct from all of them.

Narsinh Mehta has said, in a kirtan (hymn) set to the raga Sindhudo:

_Harinaam vina nar sootki re, mahapaataki re tene aabhadvano adhikar nahi, evi Ved Puraane vaani ja kahi._ (Tek.) (Without the Name of Hari, a man remains in a state of sutak, ritual impurity -- he is a great sinner, and no one has the right even to touch him. Such is the word declared in the Vedas and Puranas.)

Without devotion to God's Name, every human being remains in a state of sutak; therefore no one has any right to touch, that is, to have social dealings with, such a person. Such is the pronouncement made in the Vedas and Puranas. Women are dubbed untouchable when they are in the state of menstruation. The only real point behind this is that, in such a state, sexual intercourse with a woman ought not to take place -- such restraint is what ought to have been observed; but instead of that, women themselves have been made out to be utterly polluted. That women undergo the menstrual state is a natural law, but the scriptures and Puranas have given it the form of stories and legends and thereby made it seem an acceptable rule; the chief reason for this is simply that ordinary people will keep to moral codes of discipline only if they are shown some fear or superstition of this kind.

With this purpose in view, the story of a killing committed by Indra is given in the Bhagavata, Canto 6, Chapters 7-8. The arrogant Indra, on one occasion, did not rise to honour his guru Brihaspati, and so the guru departed from there. Thus, deprived of their guru, the gods' radiance was destroyed; Brihaspati's rival Shukracharya then helped the asuras, the demons, and thereby won heaven for them. The gods, having lost their lustre, then entreated Vishvarupa, the son of Tvashta, asking him to accept the role of guru and become their priest (purohit), but Vishvarupa said that the office of purohit is a very lowly one.

_Pitharhitam dharmashilai brahmavarch-upavyayam._ (The work of a purohit consumes and wastes away one's brahma-tej, spiritual radiance; for this reason, righteous, dharma-minded sages have condemned it.)

Tulsidas has said, in the Ramayana:

_Uparohitya karma ati manda, Bed Puran sumrati kar ninda._ (The work of the priesthood is a very base one; the Vedas, the Puranas, and the Smritis all condemn it.)

_Adhikaari stri-maasau, mathapatyas tribhir dinaih, shidhram narakam avapnoti, dinam ekam purohitah._ (An officiant attains hell in three months, and the head of a monastery in three days; but if one wishes to attain hell most swiftly of all, let him become a family priest for even a single day.)

Despite knowing this, Vishvarupa still accepted the office of guru; and to Indra he gave the Narayana-kavach, a protective mantra-armour of Vaishnava devotion. By virtue of this Vaishnava knowledge, Indra achieved victory over the demons; but at the time of a yajna, Indra grew suspicious of him. Since Vishvarupa was the son of a mother of demon lineage, he would secretly offer oblations to the demons as well, and so Indra cut off all three of his heads. With one mouth he used to drink soma-rasa, with the second mouth he drank liquor, and with the third he ate ordinary food. By slaying him, Indra incurred the sin of brahma-hatya, the killing of a brahmin. Indra bore this sin for a year, and then divided it among four benefactors who each accepted a share on his behalf. The earth accepted a quarter share, and because of this, part of the earth became desert wasteland; Indra then blessed the earth, saying, "Whatever pits and hollows form in you shall, in the course of time, fill up again." The trees accepted a quarter share, and this is why gum forms in them -- as a result of that portion of the killing; and since gum is thus a product of that killing, the Vaishnavs of the Pushtimarg do not eat it. But for the Uda devotee community, there is no objection at all to eating any kind of gum. Indra blessed the trees, saying, "Even when you are cut down, your branches will sprout again." Water accepted a quarter share of the killing, and this is why bubbles form in water; Indra blessed it, saying, "You shall go on increasing" -- and this is why, however much water is drawn from wells and the like, it never runs dry. Women accepted the fourth quarter of the killing, and this is why they must undergo the state of menstruation. In compensation, Indra granted them the boon of being able to enjoy intercourse without restriction.

Prabhudatt Brahmachari writes, in Bhagwati Katha, Part 41, page 40: "The Lord said: women's monthly flow, the bubbles in water, barren wasteland, and the gum of trees -- these four portions of the killing of a brahmin turn out to be of great use as well. Everything is stuck together using gum. Resin and guggul are themselves a form of gum, from which incense is made. Baroza is a gum used to condition the strings of the sarangi. Asafoetida, too, is a gum, and it is used to temper dal, vegetables, and other such foods."

Indra's sin of brahma-hatya was thus removed; but Tvashta, the father of Vritrasura, then brought forth, by means of a mantra, a son named Vritrasura for the very purpose of killing Indra. But in the recitation of the mantra a mispronunciation occurred, so that instead of the mantra bringing about Indra's death, it turned out that Vritrasura would die by Indra's hand -- and so Indra slew Vritrasura. In devotion to Vishnu, even if an error occurs in the pronunciation of the sacred syllables, importance is given to the devotional feeling of the one reciting them; so even if "Mara" is uttered instead of "Rama," it is still counted as the remembrance of Rama alone. It is only worshippers of a tamasic disposition who must be careful about correct pronunciation. Because of this killing, the sin of brahma-hatya again fell upon Indra; but since Vishvarupa had earlier given him the Narayana-kavach, by the power of remembering that Name he escaped from the sin. Indra had committed an offense against the Name, and that offense was removed only through remembrance of the Name. Thus, the fault of an offense against the Name is removed only by remembrance of the Name. So it was that, once again, by the power of the Narayana-kavach, Indra regained the kingdom of heaven. Such is the account. But those bound by ritualism regard the state of menstruation as a defilement, and make efforts to remove the resulting sutak, ritual impurity.

In the Samagam it is clearly stated that a woman (abala, "the powerless one") is bound by the bonds of her husband; her duty is to follow after her husband. Therefore, whatever karma the husband performs, its fault must be borne by the husband himself; the woman does not incur the fault of karma performed by her husband. For women, no new karma is generated. Men, however, must perform many kinds of karma without any such exemption -- charity, meritorious acts, vows, pilgrimage, study, teaching, fire-offerings, the accepting of gifts, circumambulation of the earth, and so on -- countless millions of blows of karma of this kind fall upon ritualistic brahmins, but such karma does not attach to women. Having given this instruction on the removal of karma for women, Jivandasji, overcome with emotion, said: "Father, the Lord of Mercy, cherishes all with fond affection" -- meaning that the merciful Lord showers His grace on everyone without exception; but if souls give up the net of worldly attachment and walk on, then they attain bliss, happiness, and well-being. Eight kinds of karma have been enumerated: 1. Mansa karma (karma of the mind), 2. Netra karma (karma of the eyes), 3. Vacha karma (karma of speech), 4. Hasta-praharan karma (karma of striking with the hands), 5. Dehadik karma (karma of the body), 6. Shravan-dhyan karma (karma of hearing and meditation), 7. Krit karma (karma already performed), 8. Svastha karma (karma of health and well-being).

Of these, mansa karma alone cannot be removed. Karmas arise in many different ways, and there are also three defects: 1. Kayik -- karmas that arise from the body, 2. Vachik -- karmas that arise from speech, from what is spoken, 3. Mansik -- karmas that arise from the mind, from its resolves, 4. Sansargik netra karma -- karmas arising from contact, touch, and the like.

Of the kayik faults there are three: 1. theft, 2. adultery, 3. violence to living beings.
Of the vachik faults there are three: 1. slander, 2. false speech, that is, telling lies, 3. harshness, that is, speaking bitter words to one who is present.
Of the mansik faults there are three: 1. trishna, craving -- entertaining trivial sensual desires, 2. dveshbuddhi -- the tendency to see faults in others, 3. anger.

Mansa karma, the story of the princess.

In all, there are thus nine defects, of mind, speech, and body. If one renounces these, then satsang (holy company) becomes truly fruitful. As an illustration of how mansa karma cannot be removed, there is the story of a certain king's daughter. This daughter lived in an upper mansion built on pillars. Once a courtesan came and lodged there, and to the courtesan's lodging a paramour would come. The king's daughter began watching him, and because of this a bondage formed in her mind. Due to this bond of karma, when she lay sleeping, her maidservant one day saw, in her mouth, marks of play, and on her body flecks of blue dye scattered about. The maidservant reported this to the king and queen, who were astonished on seeing it. They summoned a pandit and asked him about it; the pandit said that this was a case of mansa karma having arisen. As for when that karma might be released, he explained that in that city an oilman's son had died, and mourning for him was to be observed; when the townspeople spoke against it, all the other faults of the daughter were then cleared away, but one mark of play and one fleck of indigo dye still appeared to her in her sleep, though they could not be seen once she woke. The pandit was then called again and asked about this remaining trace; he said, "In your city there lives a Vaishnav couple, husband and wife, both devoted, in loyal chastity, to God alone. You have not yet given credence to their standing, and that is why this remaining taint persists; summon them and have their darshan performed, and it will be cured." On hearing this, the king summoned that Vaishnav husband and wife, and through their darshan the karma was indeed removed. For this reason the Vaishnav Jivandasji said: "Brother! Among all forms of karma, mansa karma is the greatest, and it cannot be removed." -- A sakhi (couplet) follows:

_Kabir koti karam palmaa kare, e manko vishaya svaad, sadguru shabda maane nahi, to janam gamaayo baad. ||1||_ (Sadguru Kabirji says: this mind, in the very act of relishing sense-pleasures, commits millions of karmas in an instant. If you do not heed the sadguru's teaching to stay away from these sensual desires, then you squander your human birth in vain.)

Sadguru Kabirji says that this mind commits crores of karmas in a moment while enjoying the taste of sensory pleasures. If you do not heed the teaching the sadguru has given, to stay away from these sensual desires, then you squander your human birth uselessly.

_Kabir kaaya deval man dhvaja, vikhe lehar phaharaaye, man chalante tan chale, taako sarvas jaay. ||2||_ (Das Kabirji says: the body is a temple, and the mind is a flag atop it, fluttering in the breeze of sense-desire; but though the mind may run after sense-objects, if the body too follows suit, then everything one has is destroyed.)

Das Kabirji says that upon the temple that is the body, the flag that is the mind flutters in the wind of sensory desire. But even if the mind runs toward sense-objects, if the body too acts accordingly, then a man's entire wealth is destroyed.

_Kabir manke mate naa chaaliye, chhaandiye jeevki baani, traaku keraa taar jyu, dalti apootha aani. ||3||_ (Das Kabirji says: do not walk according to the mind's own wishes; give up the soul's habitual restlessness -- just as the thread a spinner spins on the wheel is, in the end, wound back onto the spindle, so too should the mind be turned inward and joined to the soul.)

Das Kabirji says that one should not walk according to the mind's own inclination. One should give up the restless nature -- as the spinner of thread, having spun the thread on the spinning wheel, winds it back onto the spindle, so too should the mind be turned inward and joined to the soul.

Shri Vaishnav Jivandasji said: if one has kept the soul under control, then this is the means by which mansa karma can be released -- the mind must be brought under one's control.

In the Samagam, the chapter on the departure to the eternal abode is the last chapter, but this chapter on the removal of women's taint is Jivanji Maharaj's final great work of revolutionary accomplishment. Hence this chapter on the removal of women's taint offers a vision of the pinnacle of revolutionary change that remained to be completed at the very end. But because the inquiring devotees' devotion keeps finding occasion to display Jivanji's teachings, the devout devotees who transcribed copies of the Samagam have, by referring to what Jivanji Maharaj showed us of the words of Padmanabh and Adhyaruji, made an addition to the transcribed copy of the Samagam.

That Samagam is the one of Dhanora-Puniyad -- that is, up to this point, whatever has been added to the transcribed copy of the Samagam was composed by Jivandasji Maharaj during his stay at Dhanero and Puniyad.

In that Samagam of Dhanora and Puniyad, the Vaishnav Jivandasji posed a question. What has been written down is the record of Shri Padmanabhji and of Adhyaruji.

In the year Samvat 1458, on the fifth of the bright half of Magh, on the day of Vasant Panchami, Shri Padmanabhji

sections.title_en: The Account of the Departure to the Divine Abode
sections.translation:
[He] arrived in Patan. This happened in the same connection that on the day King Bali was tricked by [Vishnu in] the Vamana (dwarf) form — on that day the three worlds were measured out: one step was placed in the netherworld (Patal), the second step was placed on earth, in the Patan garden, and the third step was placed in Vaikunth. Because of this, my Lord's divine play (leela) extends beyond Vaikunth itself. Now every living being should know in what connection Shri Padmanabhji came, and in what connection Dhanraj Pandya came. Shri Padmanabhji is an incarnation of Shri Krishna, and Shri Krishna, the flute-holder, is complete with all sixteen divine perfections (kalas) — this account is found in the Padma Purana. And Adhyaruji is an incarnation of Sheshnag, who came having become a servant to his own Lord. He composed twenty-eight hymns (kirtans) carrying the essence of that sacred speech, in order to deliver souls. He said: preserve this collection of sacred words; read it — by reading it you shall attain God. This teaching was spoken by Shri Jivandasji himself. This practice has been handed down from the great devotee Devdasji, of the Somvanshi lineage; the guru of devotee Devdasji is Shri Jivandasji.

THE ACCOUNT OF THE DEPARTURE TO THE DIVINE ABODE

The Dream That Occurred in Bhilapur (Original Samagam, page 308)

That account belongs to Dhanora and Puniyad. After that, in the year Samvat 1738, on the second day of the bright half of Magsar, at the temple of the devotees Bhagwandas and Bai Dhanbai in Bhilapur, a dream came — and this is what it was: devotee Jivandasji had lain down to rest. When just four ghadis of the first watch of the night had passed, all the old devotees who had already departed came there together and began to say, "Your saints are waiting a great deal for you there." Then Bhagwandas asked, "What are you thinking about?" Devotee Jivandasji said, "The whole company of devotees is going toward the western land, so I too must go along with them. The old devotees are waiting; that is why I must go westward. The period I fixed for the devotees was six months; this dream-encounter will be fulfilled in Puniyad."

THE ACCOUNT OF THE DEPARTURE TO THE DIVINE ABODE

That dream-encounter, to be fulfilled in Puniyad — here is what happened. What we call the "Samagam" is a text written in six sections, running from page 3 to page 313. In it:

Section 1 — pages 3 to 64: couplets (sakhis) of Kabir. Section 2 — pages 64 to 70: dohas of Jivanji; pages 70 to 102: couplets of Jivanji. Section 3 — pages 103 to 110: couplets of Jivanji; pages 111 to 147: hymns (kirtans) of Adhyaruji; pages 148 to 214: couplets of Kabir. Section 4 — pages 215 to 231: the Bhaktamal of Nabha Swami. Section 5 — pages 232 to 276: the account (Samagam) of Jivanji. Section 6 — pages 277 to 313: the account (Samagam) of Jivanji.

In this original Samagam, page 309 is torn, and pages 310 through 312 are missing altogether. The second side of page 312, and the reverse side of page 313, are where the writing begins again — but because the pages are torn, the text remains incomplete. For this reason, what stands in the latter part of the Samagam cannot be read. So devotee Nana Parekh combined the account of Jivanji Maharaj's departure to the divine abode with the text of the Samagam, and in this way presents, in heartfelt words, a vivid, lifelike picture of the Sadguru's final departure. Let us now offer an explanatory account of this record of the departure to the divine abode that he has written.

|| Sakhi ||
_Kabir guru videhi roop hai, jara maran nahi kaal,_
_jine guru jaana vansataa, taaka kaun haval ||_
(Das Kabirji says: the guru's form is one that has become free of the body, so for him there is no bondage to the limit of old age or death. But those who think of the guru as something that perishes — what a wretched state will befall them!)

_Gaai gavaavo jivanaa, kaahi sunaavo aap,_
_chidi chun jyoon det hai, aise sadguru baap ||_
(Nana Gopaldasji says: just as birds place morsels of grain into their chicks' beaks, so too is Sadguru Jivandasji a supreme father — he himself sings devotional hymns and performs bhakti, and also has his disciples sing devotional hymns, teaching them and making them hear the glory of devotion to God.)

Kundali:
_Gaai gavraave jivanaa, kahi samjhaave aap,_
_chidi chun jyoon det hai, aiso sadguru baap,_
_aiso sadguru baap, sevakni raksha karataa,_
_bataavi parmaarath panth, doreene aagal dharataa,_
_Trikam sadguru gun amaap, te samje koi harijan,_
_kahi samjhaave aap, gaai gavraave jivanaa._
(Nana Gopaldas says: the Sadguru himself sings devotional hymns and has us sing them, and explains to us the glory of devotional worship. Just as birds feed grain to their young, so he too feeds us the grain that is devotional worship. Such a Sadguru is a supreme father. Such a father-like Sadguru cares for his disciples; he shows them the true path and, taking hold of the rein, leads us forward on the path of devotion to God. Trikam says the Sadguru is filled with virtues beyond measure, which only some devotees come to understand — that the Sadguru instructs and explains, and sings and has others sing, devotional hymns.)

|| Ram Is Truth ||
The holy abode of Puniyad is the dwelling place of all the saints; there devotee Jivandasji resides. The chanting of Hari's kirtan, most auspicious, takes place there; the devotees have gathered together, and wherever this happens, supreme happiness arises. Love grows greater day by day; faith and dispassion (vairagya) come. [The devotees said:] "You are the Lord of grace; you have come to draw out (liberate) our souls."

|| Sakhi ||
_Kabir ke pade pragate, jagmaan Jivandas,_
_dhajaa baandhi dharma dadhaaviyo, jam kinkar paame traas ||1||_
(After Sadguru Kabir, Jivandasji appeared in this world. He proclaimed and spread the kirtan of the Namdev faith, sounded the drum of victory, and made it so firm that it could never be shaken — so that the messengers of Death became terrified.)

|| Doha of Devotee Jivandasji ||
_Kaanto haath Kabirke, tahaan sakal dharma toliyo,_
_jap tap tirath daan, taa moole meetho choliyo ||2||_
(Devotee Jivandasji Maharaj says: the scale of dharma, which shows no partiality of any kind, is held in the impartial hands of Kabirji. When, on that scale, every kind of spiritual practice was weighed, it was found that this path is supreme above all other practices, such as japa, austerity, pilgrimage, and charity.)

This (teaching of Namdev-Kabir means that) every other religion is mere husk and chaff — worthless rubbish. (Great Dharma Panchratnamala, first edition, page 316.) This statement does not appear in the second, third, and fourth editions. But the purpose of saying that other religions are mere husk and chaff is this: sanatan dharma — the Vedic religion, following the Vedic tradition that has continued since ancient times, with its practices of japa, tapa, yajna, vows, and pilgrimage — is negligible in comparison with the loving devotion of Namdev and Kabir. Thus this religion of loving devotion belonging to Namdev and Kabir is a religion that existed even before the Vedic religion, before all others; it stands at the highest, supreme level.

Trikamdas Gordhandas has written in a notebook called Chomika:
_Trilok brahmaand ekvisamaan, bhakt sam dharma na koy,_
_sant sajjan sahu kahe, samjethi sukh hoy ||16||_
(Trikamdas says: in the three worlds and the twenty-one universes — that is, in the entire cosmos — there is no religion that can equal or compare with the religion of the great devotees Namdev and Kabir. All the saints and good people say this. So if we understand and follow the way of these great devotees, our welfare will result.)

"This religion is the original, eternal (sanatan) one; having examined the three worlds and the twenty-one universes, no religion comes close to equalling this religion."

As to how sanatan dharma can be called mere husk and chaff — in a handwritten manuscript, on page 228, there was a thinker named Trikam who, criticizing sanatan dharma, said:

_Trikam taagaa bhramkaa, galme daaryaa sootaa,_
_nem prem pan nahi, kaljugke bhootaa ||58||_
(Trikamlal says: Brahmins wear the sacred thread of illusion around their necks, but they hold no discipline of any kind of devotion within them — so in this age of Kaliyug they are as troublesome as wretched, wandering ghosts.)

_Trikam do chelaa kiyaa, bhali kari bakshish,_
_sab janjaal chhodaayke, diyaa tokraa sees ||59||_
(Trikamlal says: such Brahmins made two or four followers, saddled them with a false burden of worship-obligations, and, having made them give up every other entanglement, loaded the basket of ritualism upon the disciple's head.)

_Sees tokraa dekar, sakal bhitaayaa bhram,_
_patharkaa choonaa karo, ehi sanaatan dharma ||60||_
(Trikamlal says: by loading the burden of ritualism onto the one who commissions the rites, they wiped away the misapprehension that harm would come from not following the path of ritual works. Thus, just as stones are fired in a kiln to make lime, so this sanatan dharma — the path of Vedic ritualism — burns living souls, like stones, in the three kinds of torment, and turns them to lime, so to speak: that is, it condemns souls to the wretched grind of repeated birth and death.)

The newspaper Gujarat Samachar, dated 6 March 2003, page 5, writes in its "Dharmalok" column: rebellion and struggle for reforming the sanatan dharma system can be seen. Abroad, there was Martin Luther; in this country, saints such as Kabir, Kutch's Dada Mekan, and other wise, gifted figures of their time indeed expressed the most intense outrage against the prevailing system, did they not?

|| The Dream-Vision of Bhilapur ||
In the year Samvat 1737, on the second day of the bright half of Magsar, at the temple of devotees Bhagwandas and Dhanbai in Bhila[pur], devotee Jivandasji had lain down to rest. When four ghadis of the night had passed, a dream came, and this is what appeared in it: the old devotees who had already departed, the whole company, had gone there and were waiting for him. All the saints were gathered together, and there a discourse and kirtan were taking place. When one watch of the latter part of the night remained, two devotees came there; they appeared before devotee Jivandasji in vision — no one else could see them. He heard them conversing. They were a great abundance of radiant beauty; they held a red staff in hand; their bodies were fair; they were in the fullness of youth; they had no beard or moustache.

Two devotees came bearing a red staff. Why was the staff red? Red is usually taken as a colour signifying danger. But red is also the colour of love. And the colour of peace and happiness is white — that is why, on auspicious occasions, red roses and white abir (fragrant powder) are scattered. Redness signifies the joy and delight of deep love; thus Das Kabir has spoken of "redness" in this way. Those who came to meet Jivanji Maharaj were lovers of this kind.

_Laali mere laalki, jitaa dekhoon titaa laal,_
_us laali dekhan main gayi, tab main bhai (bhi ho gayi) laal gulaab ||17||_
(Das Kabirji says: the loving devotee became so absorbed in love of God that when he went to experience the joy of that divine love, he found that wherever he looked, he experienced nothing but that very love. And as he went to witness that experience, he himself became so absorbed in divine love that he himself turned into the very embodiment of that loving experience.)

Those devotees spoke to Jivandasji: "I have come to summon you — there Kabirji is present, Rankaji is present, Namdevji is present, Senaji is present, Dhanaji is present, Pipaji is present, Rohidasji is present; Bhagoji too is there."

Devotee Jivandasji asked in particular, "Is Kabirji there?" Then that devotee said, "Ramdevji too is there. Countless devotees are waiting for you — how can things proceed there without you? That is why the devotees have been waiting a very long time." — "Yes, Kabirji is there," [came the answer], and devotee Jivandasji felt great joy.

One can see how great the love Jivanji Maharaj held for Das Kabir must have been, that even where countless devotees already were, he still made sure to confirm whether Kabir was there. He asked: even if all the devotees are there, is Kabir there as well? And on learning that Kabirji indeed was there, he became very happy.

Jivandasji said to those devotees, "Here the devotee(s) and Gopal have great hope; I shall come in the sixth month."

Jivanji's devotees held such deep affection for Jivanji Maharaj that they wished he would stay with them a long time and grant them the benefit of loving devotion. So one can see how much feeling Jivanji Maharaj himself must have held for his devotees, that even to the messengers of God he made the promise that he would come after six months. Thus, even though Jivanji was entirely free of worldly desire, one can see how much affection he held for his devotees.

The devotee(s) said to devotee Jivandasji, "Without you nothing proceeds; we have been waiting a very long time."

Just as Jivanji expressed such love for Kabirji, it becomes clear that Kabirji and the other devotees held just as much love for Jivanji — that they too suffered the pain of separation without him. Jnaniji Maharaj has written a hymn describing what such separation feels like among those who love in this way.

|| Raag Maru ||
_Sant sandesho laayo, sun virahani man laay sundari,_
_Hari preetam tum maahi vase, sakal kahe samjhaay sundari ||tek||_
_Jahaan too jue tahaan sundari, bhitar bharam nivaar sundari,_
_man hi mahi man mohanaa, dekho samje vichaar sundari ||1||_
_Saansaa sakal nivaarke, antargat mein Hari jue sundari,_
_nishche hoy ke nirakhle, poogah mile he soe sundari ||2||_
_Hilmil aanand upajaa, poori mankee aash sajni,_
_dukh koi vyaape nahi re, avichal sadaa vilaas sundari ||3||_
_Tab virahini sukh paaiye, saambhaal piuka sandesh sujni,_
_gyani aatmaa aanagiyo, paayo updesh sundari ||4||_
(Gyaniji Maharaj says: a messenger has brought a message from the saints — listen, O grieving bride, bring it to your heart, O beautiful one. Your Beloved dwells within you — all say so, to make you understand, O beautiful one. Wherever you look, O beautiful one, banish the illusion within you. Within your very mind is your Enchanter — see this, and think it over well, O beautiful one. Having cleared away all doubts, see Hari within your inner self, O beautiful one; once you gain certainty and behold Him directly, you will find yourself united with Him, O beautiful one. Mingling together, joy is born, and the heart's longing is fulfilled, O companion; no sorrow shall trouble you again — there is everlasting, unchanging bliss, O beautiful one. Then does the separated bride find happiness, heeding her Beloved's message, O companion. Gyani says the soul was made joyful, having received this teaching, O beautiful one.)

Devotee Jivandasji said, "My Bal Gopal has a wish for Janmashtami; I shall come after performing the Janmashtami festival. Bow down to those devotees and give them my Ram-Kabir greeting. Also tell them that I have the Janmashtami festival first." Then Bhagwandas asked, "What are you thinking about?" Jivandasji said, "The whole company has departed, going toward the western land; the old devotees are waiting, so I am going westward. That dream-encounter will take place in Puniyad. Also tell them I have the Janmashtami festival [to keep] first." Then those devotees withdrew. Here the devotees asked, "Maharaj, with whom did you hold this conversation? We saw no one."

Devotee Jivandasji said, "The devotees who came, from wherever that place is, came to summon me; they pressed the invitation very affectionately, and I made a promise of six months." That dream-encounter that was to be fulfilled in Puniyad — here is what happened: in Puniyad, at Shyamdasji's temple pavilion, where he had lain down to rest, devotee Jivandasji too had lain down to rest. In the year Samvat 1738, on the second day of the bright half of Jeth, a devotee came like this: with tilak and tulsi, wearing bright clothing; his body was fair; there was no trace of beard or moustache at all; he was in the fullness of youth; there was an abundance of radiance about him; he held a red staff in hand. He spoke, saying they were summoning him.

On the second day of the bright half of Jeth, Samvat 1737, the day the six-month promise came due, the devotee(s) came to summon him. Then Jivandasji said, "I have a wish for the festival; I shall come after performing the Janmashtami festival. Tell those devotees my Ram-Kabir greeting. Also tell them that the Janmashtami festival is two months and twenty-one days away. My Bal Gopal has a great longing for it; the Lord of grace will fulfil his wish. That is why they called me, having set the time-limit of the festival." Then, since Shyamdas and Narandas were near him, he related the whole encounter to them in full.

The devotees asked, "What conversation took place?" Then Jivandasji said, "Devotees had come to summon me; there the devotees are waiting a great deal, so now I must go. I have made the promise regarding Janmashtami first." So he sent for Kahandasji, and when twenty days remained of the appointed period, he had all the devotees summoned; everyone came and sat together. The kirtan of Hari continued day and night from the full-moon day of the bright half of Shravan, without a break.

Jivandasji said, "Prepare the provisions and ingredients [for the feast]; prepare the leaf-plates; hasten the festival preparations; prepare the food — khaja, jalebi, and curry, these three dishes." All the devotees set about their duties. [He said,] "Summon all my Bal Gopals — without me, who will fulfil their wishes?" Then the day of the eighth (Janmashtami) arrived, and everyone came and sat together.

Devotee Jivandasji spoke:
|| Sakhi ||
_Sadguru sandesaa moklaa, kachambchaan sab aav,_
_naam chintaamani jivanaa, je bhaave so paav ||3||_
(Nana Gopaldasji says: the Sadguru has sent an invitation for everyone — young and old, great and small among the people — to come into the disposition of performing loving devotion, to join in bhakti to God. And by joining in it, in whatever way suits you, receive the precious jewel that is the divine Name, which fulfils your heart's desire; become absorbed in that divine Name and take joy and delight in it.)

Kundali:
_Sadguru sandeso mokle, kachaanbchaan sab aav,_
_santaa vachan vichaarine, akho parampad paav,_
_akho param pad paav, kahe chhe Jivandaadaa,_
_samjhaavi chhe vaat, saabad shikhaaman saadaa,_
_Trikam kahevaa bhaav, samje nahi jan achhalkaa,_
_kachaanbchaan sa aav, sadguru sandesaa moklaa._
(The Sadguru has sent such a message: come, everyone, together with your children, and join the fellowship of devotees, to join in devotion to God. Understanding the words spoken by the saint in this way, may you attain refuge in the imperishable divine Name; may you attain that exalted abode — so says the honoured elder Jivandada. Trikamdas feels the wish to explain the secret of his words, but thoughtless people, unaware of what is imperishable, do not understand that the Sadguru has extended this invitation for everyone, together with their children, to join in devotional singing and worship.)

_Baal boodhku jivanaa, Ram bhajanki aash,_
_shoorveer bhaagi chale, daante pakadi dhaas ||4||_
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: from children to the elderly, all devotees hold the yearning to perform devotion to God; they possess great firmness and steadfast resolve. As for the rest — those who used to display valour on the strength of ritualism, the Vedic path, the scriptures, the Puranas, and the paths of yoga and knowledge — they, having lost their courage, came, helplessly, to take refuge in the divine Name.)

Devotee Jivandasji said, "Brothers, if anyone tries to deceive you, do not be deceived by it. The true God is Morli Manohar, the charming flute-player, alone; were there any other, then Brahma and the Vedas would lead you astray."

Morli Manohar alone is the true God — that is, whatever deities exist apart from him would separate us from Morli Manohar, that is, from the true divine essence. Because the divine essence that is Morli Manohar is God's original, true form. From that very essence, and from the navel of Sheshshayi Bhagwan, a lotus arose; from that lotus Brahma came into being, and through Brahma the threefold-natured creation was brought forth. Therefore Brahma and the Vedas, being derived from the quality-transcending divine essence, separate us from devotion to Hari and load our heads with obligation. Brahma became separated from God, and the Vedas became separated from Brahma; thus Brahma and the Vedas, having become separated from God, establish their own authority and carry on their own grandeur.

For five days the joyful festival continued, and all the devotees flourished. Four devotees remained to render service; their names were: 1. the devotee Laldasji; 2. the devotee Gopaldasji; 3. the devotee, third, of Nadiad (Goriyada), Haridasji; 4. the fourth devotee, Rupa Bhagat.

The day of Jivandasji's appointed time arrived. The devotees came and sat together. Devotee Jivandasji asked, "Has everyone — all the Bal Gopals — come?" Kahandasji said, "Maharaj, your Bal Gopals — everyone has come and is seated in the pavilion." Devotee Jivandasji said, "Set my seat there in the pavilion; let me have sight of the devotees." Then Jivandasji went and took his seat. All the devotees came and fell at his feet, sensing that this was the final occasion; they made many entreaties: "Maharaj, take care of us."

Devotee Jivandasji said, "Namdev-Kabir will care for you and protect you." Devotee Jivandasji further said, "We entrust the service to Kahandasji; go and circumambulate the devotees — that will bring [their] grace." Kahandasji went round in circumambulation, bowed to Jivandasji, had his own neck-garland placed [on him], applied the tilak, and all the devotees paid their respects.

Then the devotees said, "Show your grace to Shyamdasji; he is of your own household." Devotee Jivandasji had given his garland to Kahandasji and entrusted the service to him, but he had not given it to his own son. Thus this great soul showed no self-interest of his own. And when the assembly of devotees said that Shyamdasji was indeed of his own household, he took hold of Kahandasji's hand and, through Kahandasji's hand, had the garland placed upon Shyamdasji.

Devotee Jivandasji said, "Dharma belongs to naad (sound)." Devotee Jivandasji took Kahandas's hand, had the garland moved with the thumb, applied the tilak with the thumb, and the garland was placed on Shyamdasji; all the devotees paid homage.

There are certain terms that support the threefold-natured maya (illusion), and even though they turn one away from the path of devotion, they present themselves as if depicting devotion to God — and by such allurement they can lead astray those without a true guru. But if one has found a true Sadguru, one will not be taken in by such enticing words. Among such misleading terms are: japa, tapa, pilgrimage, vows, ritual observances, spirituality, self-knowledge, yoga, meditation, yajna, and supernatural powers. Among these, the words "Omkar" and "Naadbrahm" too have such an effect that they throw devotees who are weak, soft, and incomplete in understanding into confusion. Such confusion has arisen in devotee Nana Parekh and others, who, in this account of the departure to the divine abode, tried to present the statement "dharma belongs to naad." So let us briefly consider the confusion that exists regarding naad and bindu (the drop, or point).

The reason we write here that dharma belongs to naad is this: for devotion to God, one must follow only whatever command the guru has given. Only through such guru-oriented followers can the tradition of loving devotion continue. Here, though the garland was given to Kahandasji, it was given on to Shyamdasji through Kahandasji, at the devotees' request — meaning that the path of loving devotion is the same for every lover of God. This is the intent behind the words "dharma belongs to naad." As for the term "Naadbrahm," that word denotes "Omkar," and therefore, for those of us who follow the loving devotion of the threefold nature marked by the double-r sound, dharma — that is, bhakti — cannot rightly be called a matter of naad in that sense. Jivanji held an open, selfless attitude toward all devotees equally; he did not, therefore, show favouritism toward Shyamdasji out of attachment. The magazine Kalyan, year 35, issue 7, page 1043, writes that the soul becomes conscious through the voice of the inner self; any sound other than that is maya.

"This very naad is that ignorance or illusion which, by its own influence, produces in the soul the illusory reaction of individuated existence. In truth, naad and the individual soul — or maya and the individual soul — are one and the same."

The devotees of Surat district have published a book titled Ramkabir Bhakt Bhajan Sangrah. Its second edition has been given the title "Naad Brahm." A devotee from there told me, "I am the one who had this name given." I did not object to it, but the name "Naad Brahm" seems attractive, and so one is tempted by it; but they probably do not know that the meaning of "Naadbrahm" is "Omkar," and our devotees do not know that there is a difference between Omkar and the double-r sound of this tradition. Neither Omkar nor Naadbrahm can express the true sentiment of the word "bhajan."

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj would never use the word "Naadbrahm." Omkar has been called a "respectable-looking thief," and it is by being deceived by this respectable thief that some of our devotees, mistaking dharma for a matter of naad, have gone astray. Trikamdas Gordhandas, who fought in the trust case, referring to the phrase "dharma belongs to naad," wrote a poem (kavit):

_Naad gharam sadguru kahyo, swaamipane santaap,_
_sadguru vachan uthaaptaan, guru drohnoon paap,_
_guru drohnoon paap, kadaapi tale na kothi,_
_sant shastra sahu gaay, juo uthlaavi pothi,_
_Trikam taalne shaap, vans vaaras sheed saahi rahyo,_
_swaamipane santaap, naad gharam sadguru kahyo._
(Trikamdas says: the Sadguru has said that dharma belongs to naad; and holding pride in lordship [over the seat] leads to suffering the bondage of worldly existence and karma. By transgressing this teaching the Sadguru gave, one incurs the sin of wronging the guru. The sin of offence against the guru cannot be averted by anyone — so the saints and scriptures say; search through the books and read for yourself. Trikamdas says: [Jagdishbhai,] stop bringing upon yourself the curse of the sin of wronging the guru. Why are you clinging to the claim of hereditary succession to Jivanji's seat? You will suffer from the pride of lordship, for the Sadguru has said that dharma belongs to naad.)

This poem was written in connection with the trust case; when it says to give up lordship, it was written to urge that the whole temple be handed over to the trust. It was not Jivanji who said that dharma belongs to naad — the devotees said this out of misunderstanding. As heir to Jivanji, it is not the seat, but the property and the temple, that he was asked to hand over to the trust.

Kahandasji asked, "What do you say, Maharaj?" Devotee Jivandasji spoke:
|| Sakhi ||
_Kahnaa thaa so kah liyaa, ab kahaa kahu samjhaay,_
_sant sevaa karo jivanaa, je Raghupati hoy sahaay ||5||_
(Jivandasji Maharaj said: whatever essential, ultimate truth there was, I have already told you. What more should I now explain? But serve the saints, so that Ram will become your helper — Ram's grace will come upon you.)

Trikamdas Gordhandas has written, in his diary of [Samvat] 2025, on page 43, Kundali no. 3:
_Kahenaa thaa so kah diyaa, ab kahaa karu samjhaay,_
_sant sevaa karo jivanaa, Raghupati hoy sahaay,_
_Raghupati hoy sahaay, sant dhar sadaa rakhchaa,_
_Dropadi soni kaaj, dharyo chhe roop rasaalu,_
_Garud taji gaj kaaj, sukh shayyaane taj diyaa,_
_ab kahaa karu samjhaay, kahenaa thaa so kah diyaa._
(Jivandasji Maharaj said: whatever ultimate, supreme truth there was, I have already told you by now. What more, beyond that, should I explain? But you must serve the saints, and then God will help you; God will give you assistance, for he always watches over and protects the abodes of the saints. He took on a beautiful form to protect the honour of Draupadi and of Seni Bhagat; and for the sake of the elephant, he abandoned Garuda, and even left his serpent-bed, and ran at once to help. Now what more is there to say, to explain further? Whatever was worth telling, I have told it all.)

In the Chomika notebook, page 174, Kundali no. 161 is written [the verse text here is too damaged in the source to be read — unclear]. Jivandasji Maharaj says: I have already told you the essential, ultimate truth; so what more should I explain now? But serve the saints, so that Ram will become your helper. By taking refuge in the saints, Ram will show you grace; moreover your threefold sufferings will also be removed, and even your seventy-one generations will be made pure. Trikamdas says: those who understood according to the Sadguru's teaching felt great joy; so now what more should I say — whatever supreme truth was worth telling, I have already told it.

[The next passage in the source is badly damaged and largely unreadable — unclear.] Jivandasji Maharaj says: I dwell abiding in Gokul, and by my attention I carry on the working of creation; but of my own wish I do not go anywhere, leaving Braj.

When Bhagwan Shrinathji departed from Govardhan, he took two vows. [The verse text here is damaged and unclear.] Bhagwan says: I shall not go anywhere else, leaving Braj — this is my pledge; to relieve the earth of the burden of unrighteousness, I shall take on many forms.

[The verse text here is damaged and unclear.] Bhagwan says: those who dwell in Braj are always dear to me as my own life; I shall not forget them even for a moment, and if I do, I swear it by Nand Baba. — Bhagwan's seven [daily] darshans take place at Nathdwara, and the eighth, the resting (shayan), takes place in Braj; that same resting-place is at Jatipura. The extent of Govardhan is six miles, and its circumambulation is fourteen miles.

[A verse follows in the source that is too damaged to be read — unclear.] Das Kabirji says: Look, look indeed — in this Shri Vrindavan there is always joy alone to be found, in that place where there is not even earth, sky, or moon. There, only the one Name of Radha and Krishna exists; their form, too, is one and the same, and their place too is one and the same. My attention has reached that personal abode of God. I found a Sadguru, and so this work of mine was accomplished. What form Bhagwan holds, or whether he is without form, cannot be told; that Bhagwan, with form or without it, is there with the gopis in the circle of the raas dance. I have shown the four beneficent gifts — tilak, tulsi, the company of saints, and the Name of Hari — as blessings; raising their hands high, they brought divine grace in abundance [the source is unclear at this point]. Even though yogis strive by way of the eight petal-landings of the eightfold lotus — the stations from the muladhara to the brahmarandhra in hatha-yoga — by which one is meant to cross over worldly existence, they do not find the way across. Bhagwan is the one alone who is beyond the three qualities, wholly pure in every attribute; that Bhagwan has come to the inner landing-place of my own heart-lotus. Such is that Bhagwan: from beginning to end, on the bank of the river Jamuna, there flows the sweet stream that is the loving devotion of Shri Vrindavan.

(On this "sweet stream": the revered Yadunathji writes, in Litiyu no. 26, page [unclear]: "The shingi fish lives in the salty ocean, yet it drinks sweet water. A fish that wishes to drink sweet water should not give up the company of the shingi fish — only then can it drink sweet water, only then can a fish come to drink sweet water.") Das Kabirji says: hold fast, with full faith, to this teaching that the Sadguru has given.

[A lengthy verse passage follows in the source that is too damaged to be read — unclear.] Narsinh Mehta says: in the whole of Vrindavan, all the beauties of Braj, together with the Lord of the whole universe who holds the raas dance, sport at will, out of love, in the unbroken play of the raas, in the bowers of delight. That whole Mathura is unlike anything in the three worlds. There, swans and cranes sport, and monkeys too are there; there, bees, koels, and parrots are forever calling. A cool, gentle, fragrant breeze blows there with its coolness; the lovely waters of the Jamuna flow on continually. All the gopis, cowherds, cows, and calves are there; the sweet sound of the flute continually resounds. There, everyone continually repeats only the name "Radhika, Radhika." Each one takes up their own mantra, name, or code of conduct in devotion to that Radhika. When the yearning is drawn toward that Bhagwan who reclines upon the comfortable couch of Shesha, he then bears the name Aadinarayan. That Bhagwan, who forever dwells in Vaikunth and gives aid to Vaikunth, never departs from the raas even for a moment. Even Brahma, Shankar, Parvati, and ascetics such as Sanak and his brothers cannot enter into it even in dream, nor can the wind. The Vedas and the scriptures of dharma, and Sheshnag himself, forever repeat and remember His name; and in that very raas, Narsinh Mehta abides forever.

Then Vaishnav Jivandasji said, "This gathering-place belongs to Namdev and Kabir. If there is any feeling of ownership here, the soul will not attain the Supreme Lord -- this place is only for coming together to sing Govind's glories."

_Sabke sadguru Kabirji, mamat karo jin koi. Aur duniyaku Jivana, sadguru dharki joi. ||8||_ (Kabirji is the true guru of all -- let none hold obstinate pride or rivalry over this. As for the rest of the world, O Jivan, it is the wife of the household who serves as their guru.)

[Najar Samagam p.165; Manuscript 98, p.37; Manuscript 79, p.37] Maharaj Jivandasji says: Kabirji is the world-guru (jagadguru) of the entire universe, so regarding this hold no stubborn insistence, no urge to win, and enter into no dispute. But for all people besides those who practise loving devotion (prem-bhakti), the worldly, illusion-bound wife of their household is their guru.

Trikamdas Gordhandas wrote Kundli-3 on page 1 of his diary of Samvat 2032:

_Sabke sadguru Kabirji, mamat karo jin koi. Aur duniyaku Jivana, sadguru dharki joi. Sadguru dharki joy, maya chhe mahaduhkh deti. Nugra na raheso koy, samaj vin nishphal kheti. Trikam anubhav soy, kahe chhe Shri Guru Jivanji. Mamat karo jin koy, sabke sadguru Kabiraji._ (Kabirji is the true guru of all -- let none hold rivalry over this. For the rest of the world, O Jivan, the household wife is their guru, and as household-guru she gives them great sorrow through maya. Never remain without a guru, for effort made without understanding turns out fruitless. This is Trikam's own realized experience, so says the revered Guru Jivanji: hold no rivalry over this -- Kabirji is the true guru of all.)

Kabirji is the true guru of the entire world, so hold no stubbornness or dispute on this matter. But for everyone except those who practise loving devotion, it is their own household wife who is their guru -- and as household guru, this worldly illusion causes them great suffering. So never remain without any guru at all, because any effort made without understanding turns out fruitless. Trikam says that Sadguru Jivanji has spoken this from his own experience, so hold no obstinate doubt or suspicion about the fact that Kabirji is the guru of all.

_Swamise Hari sath kos, kirtaniya se bis. Harijanke hirde basai, sevakjanke sees. ||9||_ (From a mere renunciant, Hari stays sixty kos away; from a mere kirtan-singer, twenty kos away. He dwells in the heart of the true devotee, and upon the head of the true servant.)

In the section on hypocrisy (Kapat-ka-Ang), Das Kabirji says: from a mere shaven-headed renunciant, God stays sixty kos away; from one who does only kirtan-singing, He stays twenty kos away. He dwells in the heart of the true devotee (one who yearns for Him in separation), and He resides in the head -- the very life-breath -- of the servant-devotee.

_Grihike hirdai basau, vairagike sees._ (He dwells in the heart of the householder, and upon the head of the renunciant.)

[Nani, Notebook No. 2, p.75] He dwells in the hearts of householders and upon the heads of renunciants.

(The Proclamation of Baba Kabirji)

_Kabir swami ko nahi, swami sarajanhar. Swami hokar baith hi, te dhano sahego mar. ||10||_ (Says Kabir: there is no other master in this world; the Creator alone is the Master. Whoever sits enthroned claiming mastership will have to bear much suffering.)

This is the proclamation of Baba Das Kabir. Das Kabirji says: in this world there is no owner or master at all besides God, the Creator of the universe. But whoever lays claim to mastership will have to endure great suffering.

Trikamdas Gordhandas writes a Kundli on page 141 of his diary of Samvat 2030:

_Kabir swami ko nahi, swami sarajanhar, swami hokar baith hi, te dhano sahego mar, bahot sahego mar, sadguru kahai pokari, mudhan samje lagar, akkal gai jeni mari, kahe Trikam thoki nagar, sathno sang chhodi sahi, swami sarajan har, Kabir swami ko nahi._ (Says Kabir: there is no master in this world, the Creator alone is the Master. Whoever sits enthroned as master will have to bear great suffering -- very great suffering, so the sadguru cries out and proclaims. Fools do not understand this in the least, for their wits have deserted them. Beating the drum, Trikam says: truly give up the company of the wicked -- the Creator alone is the Master; says Kabir, there is no other master.)

Das Kabirji says: no one in this world can truly hold the position of master; only God, the Creator of the universe, is the Master of the world. But if anyone claims the right of mastership, he will have to bear great suffering from the bonds of karma. Sadguru Kabir cries out emphatically that such people will have to suffer greatly. Yet fools do not understand even this much, for their good sense has completely deserted them. Beating the drum, Trikam says it is best to give up the company of the wicked, because the only Master is God, the Creator of the universe -- there is no other master besides Him.

(The Couplet Describing the Realm of the Vaishnavs)

_Kabir swami sevak jahan nahi, jahan nahi jap aur jaap. Gun avgunki gam nahi, jahan nahi punya aur paap. ||11||_ (Says Kabir: there, there is no master and no servant, no chanting and no japa; there is no concern for virtue or vice, no sin and no merit.)

This describes the abode in which the Vaishnavs -- the devotees -- dwell. Das Kabirji says that there, no one is anyone's master and no one is anyone's servant, and no one need chant or repeat anyone's name. There, good and bad qualities have no effect at all, and there is no such thing as sin or merit either.

The Master there has no sense of being a master, and among the servants there is no sense of being a servant -- this itself is the mark of a true Vaishnav.

_Rup rekh kachhu vapu nahi, aise Raghupatiray. Aise harijan Jivana, naam nirmal jas gaay. ||12||_ (Raghupati -- Ram -- has no form, shape, or bodily mark at all, such is He; and such, O Jivan, is the true devotee too, who sings the pure, spotless glory of His Name.)

Maharaj Jivandasji says: just as Raja Ram has no form, shape, or bodily figure of any kind, in the very same way God's devotees, too, are without form or feature -- they who worship the pure, holy Name of God.

Revered Yadunath writes in Litiyu (notebook) No. 46, page 18: "formless" means without any shape at all, for whatever has shape also carries the three gunas (qualities of nature). This is a matter worth studying through the Gita; in this Samagam, Jivanji has drawn upon the Gita.

Vaishnav Jivandasji said, "The festivals of Gokul Ashtami and Ram Navami belong to the Merciful Lord (Kripanath). Do not wait for a large group to gather -- whatever each of you can manage to bring, bring that. Keep this instruction of mine: come together and sing the glories of Govind."

(The Sakhi Spoken by His Own Holy Mouth)

_Aap aapni taapani, taapat hai sab koi. Milkar taape Jivana, je sadguruka hoi. ||13||_ (Everyone warms himself at his own fire alone; but, O Jivan, those who truly belong to the sadguru warm themselves together, side by side.)

Maharaj Jivandasji says that everyone, following their own private inclination, undertakes bhajan and devotion on their own terms, wilfully undergoing hardship through japa, austerity, and similar practices by themselves. But those who practise devotion under the sadguru's instruction join together with one another and perform bhajan-kirtan and the like in a way that gives everyone warmth and support.

Maharaj Adhyaruji has said in the Ghodli kirtan:

_Ghodli ja ghat rup anant, guru vachne sahu ek hoe. ||Gho.15||_ (O Ghodli, in every body dwells the Infinite; through the guru's word, all become one.)

O devotee mounted upon the steed of divine love! Just as many different opinions appear among all embodied beings, yet when all of them come under the guru's instruction, they become of one mind. Such a devotee, mounted on the steed of divine love, attains the Lord's refuge.

Vaishnav Jivandasji said, "Have my seat made beneath the lemon tree." He had all the women called. He said to the women, "Bring water for bathing, so that I may wash away my mastership [my worldly identity as 'Swami']." (That is, he told the women to bring the water heated.)

Revered Yadunath writes in Litiyu No. 21, page 37, regarding the title "Swami": Vadhji (of Gordhan Sargai) had once asked Madhavlal, the Swami of the Hansapura seat, "We are the swami [husband] of your wife -- so master of what are you?" -- and was told that the title "Swami" is used with reference to Padmanabh Swami. He was told to ask Trikam about the surname "Swami" in the court case (in the Trust case).

Revered Yadunath told me (Jagdish) that we are followers of Padmanabh Swami, and that is why our surname is "Swami." He also told me that while other people are swami (master) of a wife, we, however, are swami of Indi.

He said to all the women, "Place tulsi leaves upon my head." The women placed tulsi leaves upon him. Then Jivandasji said, "That is enough." He called out to Somdasji and said, "Take my body to the garden at Shahpura and perform the cremation there. There, make a Ram-shila (a tulsi platform). Carry me to that garden." Having said this, Somdasji replied, "Your word shall be obeyed."

_Taham Ajodhya jaham Raghupati, kahannad tam Gokul gaam. Satapuri taham Jivana, jaham sant sangat Hari naam. ||14||_ (Wherever Raghupati is, there is Ayodhya; wherever Krishna is, there is the village of Gokul. But, O Jivan, wherever there is the company of saints and the Name of Hari, there all the seven sacred cities dwell together.)

Maharaj Jivandasji says: wherever Ram is present, only Ayodhyapuri alone is there; and wherever Krishna is present, only Mathurapuri alone is there. But wherever there is the company of saints together with the Name of Hari, there all seven of the sacred cities are present at once.

And he said, "Keep the garden at Puniyad reserved." He then also said, "You will not be able to manage carrying me all the way from Puniyad to Shahpura for the cremation while singing kirtan, nor will you be able to perform any other rite or exertion on my behalf after I am gone. But do dress me in clean, white garments. As much as you are able, sing kirtan and recite katha, and then return home." And he said, "Women, bring the thali, so that we may offer it to the Merciful Lord." Everyone went to fetch the thali. They brought the plate of offerings and placed it at his feet. Vaishnav Jivandasji then offered it to the Merciful Lord, and said, "Let this prasad reach every village where there is tilak and tulsi, wherever my beloved ones are." The prasad was given to all the Vaishnavs, and all those present received the great prasad.

This meant that they would not be able to carry him all the way from Puniyad to Shahpura for the cremation while singing kirtan, nor would they be able to perform any rite or undergo any hardship on his behalf after his passing -- but they were to dress him in clean garments.

At this word, they experienced great joy. Then he said, "The garden at Shahpura belongs to Mota Gopalji. Before the present gathering of Vaishnavs came into being, I had come to Mota Gopal's temple."

In Rest (Vishram) 1, verses 5 and 7, of Maharaj Jivanji's Parcharji (hagiography), there is mention that Mota Gopaldasji gave shelter at Shahpura to Jivandasji when he was wandering at the age of eleven.

_Gaanv Shahapuro taham kahave, sant mandali Harigun gaave. -5_ (There a village called Shahapuro was known; there a company of saints sang the glories of Hari.)

_Sant ek milyo taham aavi, hamare grihmein rahenge bhai. -7_ (One saint came there and met him, saying, "Brother, come and stay in my house.")

There was a village named Shahpura where a company of saints used to sing the praises of Hari. There, a saint -- Mota Gopaldas -- came and met him. He said to him (to Jivanji), "Come and stay in my house."

Then the Merciful Lord's (Jivanji's) order came to be that the cremation should take place at Mota Gopal's garden. Out of quiet regard for Gopaldasji, who had given him shelter in Samvat 1660, he had at first remained silent about this, and so asked for the cremation to be at Shahpura instead of Puniyad. But when Shyamdasji recited Jivanji's fourteenth sakhi, he then said that the cremation should be given at the garden of Puniyad.

He confirmed the tulsi garden of Puniyad as the chosen garden, saying, "Make a Ram-shila there." At that time, invitations for the festival were sent out. Then, as everyone gathered there, all the Vaishnavs together prepared the provisions and cooked dishes. Then, having taken his seat beneath the lemon tree, he asked Samdasji for water to bathe. Samdasji brought water and placed it before Vaishnavji. Then Jetibai, Malibai, Panabai, and other women brought the thali of prasad.

The kirtan continued unceasingly. At midnight, Lachhbai came from Thonhavi, and together with her, Ramabai and Tulsidas also came. Meeting these Vaishnavs amid the gathered Vaishnavs, Vaishnavji felt very great joy.

On the second day, the Vaishnavs of Bhilupur arrived. When it was the last watch of the night, the Vaishnav Mohandas brought a plate of kamod-rice from Hansapura. He had that plate of kamod-rice prasad brought forward. Jivandasji partook of that prasad, and all those present in the gathering received that great prasad.

Then Kahandas asked, "Vaishnavji, what do you have to say?" Vaishnavji then spoke: "In the Vraja clan, the Vedas summoned Brahma; the Vedas sang of that being of light. In the Vraja clan, the Vedas summoned Brahma to that being of light -- He, the charming flute-player, is the true Supreme Lord." This episode concerning Brahma he thus related.

After that, Harmabai showed great heartfelt concern and care for him, and she received Vaishnavji's grace. Vaishnavji then said further, "However much one instructs and admonishes the soul (jiva) in many ways, the soul does not give up its own ignorance (avidya). That ignorance is given up only if one becomes a true guru-oriented soul (gurumukhi) -- then the ignorance is given up. But the soul is not guru-oriented -- so what happens then? For this very reason it is said: the tilak and tulsi are the sign of Kabirji, the sign of the Great One. Whoever bears the tilak and tulsi is called a gurumukh (one turned toward the guru). Otherwise, no one truly becomes a gurumukh."

(The Sakhi about this)

_Dasatan sab manmate, gurumate ko naahi. Gurumate te Jivana, je Haricharan kamalki chhanhi. ||15||_ (All service as practised is done by one's own mind's inclination; hardly any is done by the guru's instruction. But, O Jivan, that which follows the guru's instruction alone reaches the shade of Hari's lotus feet.)

Maharaj Jivandasji says: whoever, having become a surrendered devotee of God's guru, nevertheless practises devotion according to his own private will and does not accept the guru's instruction, cannot be called a gurumukh. But if he practises devotion by following the guru's instruction, he attains refuge in God's own abode.

Trikamdas Gordhandas wrote Kundli 22 on page 116 of his diary of Samvat 2025:

_Dasatan sab man mato, gurumato koi nahi, gurumato te Jivana, je Haricharan kamalki chhanhi, Haricharan kamalki chhanhi, phari nahi garbhma aave, gurugam vin jag manhi, kadi nahi shanti paave, manmate na malse Sai, duhkhi thai jaso din jate, gurumato koi nahi, dasatan sab man mato._ (All service is done by one's own mind's inclination; hardly any is done by the guru's instruction. That which is done by the guru's instruction, O Jivan, reaches the shade of Hari's lotus feet -- and once in that shade, one never enters the womb again. Without the guru's guidance, one never finds peace anywhere in this world. Following one's own mind, one will not find the Lord, and as the days pass one will only grow more sorrowful. Hardly any devotion is done by the guru's instruction -- all service is done by one's own mind's inclination.)

Those who have set themselves up as devotees of God according to their own private will do not follow the guru's instruction. But if one practises devotion following the guru's instruction instead, one reaches the lotus feet of God. Once having reached God's lotus feet, one does not enter the womb again. Without obtaining the secret of devotion from the guru, one can never attain peace and will, in the end, become sorrowful -- because such a person does not practise devotion according to the guru's instruction, but everyone instead practises devotion according to their own will.

Whoever, by the guru's instruction, has taken up the tilak and tulsi -- such a great soul's faults, Vasudevji (God) does not hold in His heart. So who, then, could ever call such a person guru-less? He is called "great" precisely because Vasudevji does not hold that person's faults against him in His heart.

Having spoken on this matter, Vaishnavji said to Harmaba, "Stay here until my festival [death-anniversary celebration]. After the festival is complete, come again on the fifth." A time was fixed; Harmabai made this request to Vaishnavji. Then, when there remained one ghadi (about twenty-four minutes) of the day left, Kahandas asked him -- on that fifth day he asked, "Vaishnavji, what do you have to say?" He then replied, "Brother, in Vrindavan...

...the Vedas summoned Brahma there, and that being of light is truly Shri Krishna. Whoever the Vedas and Brahma speak of, that being of light of which the Vedas spoke -- as proof of that, Shri Krishna revealed Himself to Brahma. That being of light was Shri Krishna, who in the Vraja clan comes as the Merciful Lord grazing cattle. At that very time Brahma performed the arati of Shri Krishna -- that is when it happened. All the Vaishnavs who have come here are singing the glory of Govindji."

Kahandasji asked, "What do you have to say?" Just then Haribhai arrived from Aridha, along with all the other Vaishnavs. Haribhai bowed to Vaishnavji. Accepting Haribhai's bow, Vaishnavji looked upon all the Vaishnavs and addressed the entire assembly as "Ram-Kabir." He said, "Sing the song of Vighna-haran [remover of obstacles]." The Vaishnavs sang five verses -- and as they sang, Vaishnav Jivandasji departed for his own divine abode (swadham), while the kirtan to Hari surged on in waves.

Revered Yadunath writes in Litiyu No. 6, page 62: "If a train is scheduled to leave the station at ten o'clock, then it leaves at ten -- no one asks why it left at ten and not a quarter past ten." In the same way, Maharaj Jivanji's time to depart came exactly as the fifth verse was being sung. As soon as the five verses were sung, Maharaj departed.

There Kahandasji spoke this couplet:

_Baiyan biji vaar, nahi aave aiso davdo. Maya malse kaimvaar, pan nahi hoy sant melawdo. ||16||_ (O sisters, such an occasion will never come a second time. Worldly wealth may be found again and again, but a gathering of saints such as this will never occur again.)

Maharaj Jivandasji says: O devotees of the gopi-bhava (the feminine devotional mood toward the Lord), who have set aside effort through japa, austerity, pilgrimage, vows, mantra, and spiritual practice in favour of that mood of devotion -- the opportunity of this human birth, and of this company of saints that you now have, will not come again and again. Worldly wealth (maya) may indeed be gained many times over, but the good fortune of being together with the saints will not be found again. So gather together with the saints now and complete your devotion to God. This moment will not come again and again.

_Samvat sattarsen saatatris, sud panchami Bhadur maas. Ta din Jivandasji, liyo swadham nivaas. ||17||_ (In the year Samvat 1737, on the fifth of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapad, on that day Jivandasji took up residence in his own divine abode.)

On the fifth day of the bright half of Bhadrapad in Samvat 1737, Jivandasji departed for his own divine abode. Note: this account was completed, as received in a dream at Bhilpur, on the second day of the bright half of Magsar. At that time, there remained two months and twenty-one days until Janmashtami, so the date was postponed to coincide with Janmashtami -- hence it was said that Sadguru Jivandasji departed for his divine abode on the day of Janmashtami. However, Harmaba had actually departed for her own divine abode on the fifth of the bright half of Bhadrapad. Nevertheless, we continue to observe the fifth of the bright half of Bhadrapad as the day of Maharaj Jivandasji's departure for his divine abode.

(Here the Samagam is complete.)

_Rasik jan Jivan bhaye, kini bhakti prakash. Nahana nikat bolayke, rakhya charan nivas. ||1||_ (Jivan became a rasik devotee, one absorbed in loving devotion, and revealed the light of devotion. Calling Nahana [Nana Parekh] close to him, he kept him dwelling at his feet.)

Jivandasji became a devotee absorbed in the delight of loving devotion, and he revealed loving devotion to the world. He called Nana Parekh close to him and kept him under his refuge. (Nana Parekh lived in the time of Dwarkadas.)

_Gaam hamara Darapara, sai hamara Ram. Sadguru Jivandasji, Parakh dhariya naam. ||2||_ (My village is Darapara; my Lord is Ram; my sadguru is Jivandasji. I have taken the name Parakh for myself.)

Says Nana Parekh: my home village is Darapara, and my beloved deity is Ram; my sadguru is Jivandasji. I myself have taken up the name "Parakh."

(Thus ends the complete account of his departure for the divine abode.)

On Saturday, the fourth of the bright half of Bhadrapad, Samvat 2063, corresponding to 15 September 2007, at five o'clock in the early morning, Swami Jagdish Yadunath completed writing this commentary on the Samagam. He has written it according to whatever inspiration Jivanji granted him, to the best of his ability.

The portion of the manuscript concerning this account of his departure for the divine abode had been burnt. Therefore I have written this based on whatever writing survived in the burnt portion. For this account of his departure, Nana Parekh and others wrote in their own language. I have relied on Manuscript No. 79, pages 1 to 5, as well as Manuscript No. 98, pages 32 to 40, and the original Samagam text.
